Overviews

Overview of Books I and II

The Islamic world is not a monolith. Islam as a religion cannot be equated with the Arab world as a political entity. There is an Iranian Islam, just as there is a Turkish, Indian, Indonesian, Malay, and other forms of Islam.

Unfortunately, readers who want to learn about Iran’s archaeology and art, both before and since Islam, can choose from a wealth of books. Far fewer books answer the question that confronts anyone seeking to understand the motives and inner life of Iranian consciousness—the forces that gave these outward forms their shape.

From the beginning, the Iranian world has formed a distinct whole within the Islamic community. Its particular character and calling become intelligible only when we consider Iran’s spiritual world as a continuous whole, before Islam and after its arrival. Islamic Iran has been, above all, the homeland of some of Islam’s greatest philosophers and mystics. For them, speculative thought can never be separated from the fruit it bears or from its practical consequences. These consequences reach far beyond what we now call the social environment: they concern the whole concrete reality that human beings nourish out of their own substance, beyond the limits of this life—the reality that constitutes their spiritual world.

This conviction has guided the author in constructing the work presented here in seven books. It is the fruit of more than twenty years of research in Iran itself, conducted in libraries and among close Iranian friends, together with years of teaching in Paris and Tehran. The method is essentially phenomenological, though it belongs to no particular school of phenomenology. Its aim is to encounter religious experience by allowing what is experienced in religion to show itself as it shows itself to those who experience it.

Hence the essential subtitle of this work: Spiritual and Philosophical Aspects. To speak of an “aspect” is to imply someone who sees it.

Yet here the observer—the phenomenologist—must become a spiritual guest of those to whom the religious reality appears, sharing with them the responsibility of bearing witness to it. Historical interpretation must therefore remain within the horizons of that reality rather than impose upon it some external framework, dialectical or otherwise. Only on this condition can the connections that the author repeatedly draws across different periods be understood as simultaneous expressions of the same underlying reality.

The first two volumes contain Books I and II of the work.

Book I brings to light several essential features of Twelver Shiism, or Imamism, which had deep roots in Iran from the beginning and became the official religion in the sixteenth century. These features are explored through what the author has elsewhere called the “phenomenon of the Revealed Book,” as it appears to those whom the Quran calls Ahl al-Kitâb, the “People of the Book”: the community embracing Judaism, Christianity, and Islam. In every branch of the Abrahamic tradition, interpreters of the Bible and the Quran have faced the same problems and tasks.

Each has sought to discover the Book’s true meaning. On both sides, the search for that truth—the spiritual meaning concealed beneath the literal wording—has led to similar methods for revealing the esoteric, or inner, meaning of divine revelation. The “phenomenon of the Book” lies at the origin of hermeneutics, the art of understanding and interpreting meaning. It seems likely that philosophers so preoccupied today with hermeneutics still have much to learn from the esoteric interpreters of the Bible and the Quran.

The technical term for the inner interpretation of the Quran is ta’wîl: literally, to “lead something back” to its origin, its archetype. Shiite metaphysics is governed by two inseparable ideas. The first is that God, in the divine Essence, is unknowable, inaccessible, and beyond every name.

The second is that God becomes manifest in a pleroma—a complete spiritual order—of Fourteen beings of light, who appeared on earth as the “Fourteen Immaculate Ones”: the Prophet, his daughter Fâtima, and the Twelve Imams. The inner meaning that Shiite ta’wîl draws from the literal statements of the Quran concerns above all these Fourteen. It therefore reveals a distinctive Shiite understanding of prophecy—one that refuses to place the future entirely in the past.

Unlike majority Sunni Islam, in which humanity, after the mission of the final Prophet, has nothing further to await, Shiism keeps the future open. Even after the coming of the “Seal of the Prophets,” something remains to be awaited: the unveiling of the spiritual meaning of the revelations brought by the great prophets. That work of interpretation was entrusted to the holy Imams, whose teachings fill many volumes.

But the full understanding of that spiritual meaning will come only at the end of our aeon, or age, with the return and manifestation of the Twelfth Imam—the Imam now hidden from sight, the mystical center of this world.

This way of interpreting revelation also implies a particular experience of time, expressed in a division of sacred history into periods: the age of the prophets’ missions is followed by the age of spiritual initiation. Here Shiite thought about prophecy meets the aspirations of the Joachimite movement in the West, with its expectation of the reign of the Spirit. Strictly speaking, however, this division already belongs to metahistory: because it concerns the ultimate destiny of humanity, it breaks beyond the boundaries of ordinary history.

The doctrine of the Imams, no less than the interpretation of revelation, confronted Shiite thinkers with problems resembling those that Christian thinkers encountered in Christology. Yet Shiite thinkers generally sought solutions in a direction rejected by official Christian Christology. Perhaps this is how Shiite spiritual knowledge preserved itself from being secularized into a program of social messianism.

Shiite metaphysics and Shiite spirituality are inseparable: each forms the substance of the other. Too long a reliance on accounts of majority Sunni Islam led scholars to identify Sufism with spiritual Islam as such. In reality, Shiite spirituality extends beyond Sufism. There are certainly Shiite Sufi orders, and most Sufi orders trace their spiritual lineages back to one of the Imams.

But the Shiite seeker of inner knowledge is already, by that very fact, on the spiritual Path (tarîqat), without having to join a Sufi order. At the summit of a mystical Sinai, knowing the Imam as one’s personal guide leads to knowledge of oneself.

Book II is devoted entirely to another equally fundamental and distinctive feature of Iranian Islamic philosophy and spirituality, one that was closely joined from the outset to the Shiism of many Iranian thinkers. Its defining word is ishrâq: sunrise, the rising of the light, the dawn (aurora consurgens) and its “Orient.” The philosophy of Ishrâq, understood as a wisdom of Light, is therefore an “Oriental” wisdom, and its philosophers—the ishrâqîyûn—are “Oriental” philosophers in a spiritual and metaphysical sense of the word Orient. They are also frequently called the “Platonists,” in contrast to Islam’s Aristotelian, or Peripatetic, philosophers.

At the beginning of this tradition of the “Platonists of Persia” stands the extraordinary resolve of a brilliant young thinker from northwestern Iran: Shihâboddîn Yahyâ Sohrawardî, who died at thirty-six in Aleppo, Syria, a martyr to his cause, in 1191. His writings plainly state his purpose: to bring the wisdom of ancient Persia back to life, the philosophy of Light and Darkness; in a sense, to bring the Hellenized Magi home to Islamic Persia, using the very resources of spiritual interpretation (ta’wîl) that Islam had placed at his disposal.

Some three centuries before the great Byzantine philosopher Gemistos Plethon, this Iranian thinker brought together the names of Plato and Zarathustra, or Zoroaster, as heralds of a single “Oriental” tradition reaching back to Hermes, the father of the sages. Platonic Ideas were interpreted through Zoroastrian teachings about angels. This interpretation of being acknowledged a third world whose reality philosophies confined to abstract concepts had been unable to establish.

Between the intelligible world and the world of the senses lies the mundus imaginalis, the imaginal world: an entirely real world, not the merely “imaginary” realm to which outward-looking philosophies reduce it. It needs a word of its own: imaginal. Sohrawardî knew that by establishing the reality of this “third world,” he was also establishing the objective reality of prophetic revelations, mystical visions, and the events of Revelation. This theme would remain alive throughout the centuries of Iranian thought.

It is characteristic of this metaphysics of Light that it identifies the primal Source of light with what Zoroastrian sacred wisdom calls Xvarnah, the “Light of Glory.” From that Source proceed the hierarchies of archangels, structured as a synthesis of Zoroastrian angelology and the heavenly hierarchies of the Neoplatonist Proclus. The symbol of Xvarnah opens up inexhaustible connections and echoes. In earlier studies, the author traced correspondences between its forms of manifestation and those of the Holy Grail in Western traditions.

Indeed, the Grail—the mystical cup that mirrors the world—already appears in the heroic epic of ancient Iran. It also appears in Sohrawardî’s work, where it represents the passage from heroic epic to mystical epic, a decisive development in Iran’s cultural history. That transition takes shape in a series of short initiatory tales, almost all written in Persian. Their wealth of symbols allows Sohrawardî to guide the reader toward the goal of the reader’s longing even more effectively than his great systematic treatises. The author gives special attention to two of these spiritual tales, one rooted in Iran’s mystical epic tradition, the other in the wider traditions of spiritual knowledge called gnosis.

Sohrawardî’s “Oriental” tradition has remained active in Iran down to the present day. It also exerted a strong influence in India during the religious reforms of Emperor Akbar.

Together, these first two books present two essential dimensions of Islamic spiritual knowledge, or gnosis, as shaped by the mind and spirit of Iranian Islam. At a time when recent discoveries have given new impetus to the study of ancient Gnosticism and Jewish mystical knowledge alike, these investigations are especially timely.

Overview of Book III

Book III is devoted entirely to Iranian Sufism, as revealed through the work of one of its greatest masters, Rûzbehân Baqlî Shîrâzî (1128–1209). He was a contemporary of Sohrawardî, the Shaykh al-Ishrâq, or Master of Illumination. Yet while Sohrawardî came from northern Iran, Rûzbehân belonged to the south, to Fârs—Persis, or Persia in the strict sense.

His writings and teachings are particularly revealing of the spirituality of Iranian Sufism, especially where it differs from traditional Christian asceticism. The phenomenon of the “unhappy consciousness,” a name familiar to us since Hegel, belongs specifically to the history of Christian consciousness—even if today that consciousness increasingly insists on being “present in the world,” ashamed of its unhappiness or hoping thereby to lessen it. Sufism, too, confronts an opposition that it must overcome, but not the same opposition that made, or has made, the Christian unhappy.

The Christian has been torn between sin and the grace that justifies, between belief and knowledge; more crudely, between “mysticism” and “sensuality”; more abstractly, between factual historical truth and inner truth, between the object of faith embodied in history and spiritual reality unconstrained by time, between the literal wording of revelation and its spiritual meaning. With the secularization of a post-Christian world, the old affliction has merely acquired new names. Sociology assumes the authority formerly held by theology, assisted by psychoanalysis. Instead of sin, people speak of guilt complexes and frustration.

The Sufi, on the other hand, is neither a sinner seeking justification, nor someone sick, nor someone frustrated. He feels no need to be “justified.” He is a stranger, an exile. What he longs for, like seekers of spiritual knowledge in every age and place, is to find himself at home again, and therefore to meet the guide who will show him the way home. For him, this is the meaning of prophecy: the religious Law (sharî’at) revealed by the Prophet opens an inner Path (tarîqat) leading to spiritual Truth (haqîqat).

When that truth is lived and realized personally, it makes the Sufi a free human being. Mystical experience does not oppose prophetic revelation; it fulfills it, because it brings its hidden truth to realization. Without that inner truth, only an abstract monotheism (tawhîd, the affirmation of divine oneness) remains. What overcomes that abstraction is the idea—or rather the lived experience—of theophany, the manifestation of the divine. The divine Essence cannot be known, but divine acts reveal its attributes through countless manifestations.

A theophany is not God becoming incarnate. To perceive a theophany is to recognize iltibâs, the double meaning of every manifested being: it both conceals and reveals the invisible. Without the awareness that makes such a vision possible, one remains in a world of duality and oppositions. The devout believer and the dogmatic theologian alike are then, at bottom, polytheists without knowing it.

This awareness cannot arise by turning away from what is visible and perceptible to the senses. The visible must first be recognized as a veil, then transformed into a mirror. Among all human experiences, one is especially capable of bringing about this transformation: human love for a beautiful being, in which the soul is shaken and carried beyond itself by a manifestation of the divine. Rûzbehân gave Sufism a decisive new orientation by distinguishing two paths.

There are devout ascetics for whom human love has played no part in the beginning of the spiritual journey. And there are those for whom human love is the beginning of divine love. For them, the two loves are written in one and the same book, the book of one and the same love; the task is to learn how to read it. Only these latter seekers, whom Rûzbehân represents so completely, truly deserve the name Faithful of Love, because of their kinship with Dante’s Fedeli d’amore.

On this very path, Rûzbehân was not afraid to appear as a malâmatî: one of those who, in order to conceal the purity of their inner countenance, sometimes deliberately behave in ways that invite public blame. In this respect he may be regarded as a forerunner of another famous man of Shiraz, the great poet Hâfez, whose collected poems Iranian Sufis have always known how to read as a reminder of the mystical life.

At a friend’s request, Rûzbehân wrote a “spiritual diary” that is an invaluable document in the mystical literature of any age; it calls to mind certain passages of Swedenborg’s Memorabilia. It records his visions and dreams from the age of fifteen onward. Here we discover that from childhood he possessed an exceptional emotional intensity and gift for visionary experience. At fifteen he left his home. A vision revealed to him his hidden rank in the mystical hierarchy. Then came an extraordinary succession of visions: angels and beings of beauty, flowering landscapes, glowing red dawns. All Rûzbehân’s books are written in an intensely personal language, vibrating with an almost uninterrupted ecstatic lyricism that can make them difficult to read.

Yet this autobiographical diary gives us the evidence of lived experience through which we can trace the stages and trials by which the unfolding of love leads, along the path of divine manifestations, toward the inner realization of divine oneness, or esoteric tawhîd.

The first trial is the trial of the Veil. Rûzbehân certainly stands within the great tradition of Sufism, but here he contributes a remarkable insight of his own, one that reaches a summit of both lived and speculative mysticism. The “Hidden Treasure” brought the world into being in order to be known, and to know itself in its creatures. Spirit is the primordial act through which the holy spirits—the eternal spiritual individualities of beings—subsist. Every atom of existence is, no doubt, an eye wholly absorbed in contemplating the Light from which it arose.

But the Divine Being then experiences jealousy toward itself. By making itself an object to itself, by revealing itself, it is no longer simply its own witness: it now has a witness outside itself, someone other than itself. This is the first Veil. The Divine Being therefore seeks to draw itself back into itself; it turns this Spirit away from contemplation of God and directs the creature toward contemplation of itself. This vision of oneself by oneself is the second Veil.

The trial of the Veil is the very meaning of Creation: the descent of the holy spirits into earthly existence has no other purpose than to bring them through that trial to victory. To pass through it, the mystic must discover that self-knowledge is the very gaze with which God contemplates himself, and that the mystic is the witness through whom God bears witness to himself. Then the veil becomes a mirror.

Yet to seek what lies beyond the Veil is, Rûzbehân says, to fall into the “madness of the inaccessible.” Since Creation, God has never looked upon any world other than himself; he regards such a world with horror. Those who attain the awareness of being witnesses are the eyes through which God still looks at the world and, by looking, still takes an interest in it. They may remain unknown to everyone, yet it is thanks to them that the world endures. These mystics do more than perform a social role: they fulfill a task of salvation on a cosmic scale.

Here Rûzbehân’s insight comes very close to that of Meister Eckhart. The gaze with which I know God is none other than the gaze with which God knows me. This is the secret of the divine visions through which Rûzbehân advances toward esoteric tawhîd.

That advance is made possible by the unfolding of love, for love alone discovers the identity of witness and witnessed, of the one who contemplates and the one contemplated. It fills an entire book in Persian, perhaps Rûzbehân’s masterpiece: The Jasmine of the Faithful of Love. “With the eyes of the heart I contemplated uncreated Beauty; with the eyes of the intellect I sought to understand the secret of the human Form.” Love reveals the secret of theophanies because a theophany is, in its essence, the appearance of the divine in beauty.

Our age, intent on “demythologizing” everything, has worked so hard to strip beauty of its sacred character that awe in the presence of beauty may now seem strange, even alien. For the Iranian Faithful of Love, by contrast, it is a fundamental experience. The same is true of Ibn ’Arabî, whose influence on Islamic spirituality lasted eight centuries and who stands among the greatest witnesses to this mystical religion of beauty as the supreme divine attribute.

Rûzbehân adopts the Neoplatonic teaching: “Even before the worlds existed, the Divine Being was itself love, the lover, and the beloved.” He immediately confronts the great question debated in Sufi circles from the beginning: is it right to speak of love in relation to God? Whom does the mystic love when speaking of loving God? The whole of The Jasmine answers these questions.

In a sequence of chapters, it explores the prophetic meaning of beauty, contemplating the Prophet of Islam as the prophet of a religion of beauty. Drawing on the full resources of Platonic inspiration, it also uncovers love’s source before the beginning of time, weaving together the great themes of the Eternal Witness and the Eternal Bride. Sohrawardî had already set us on this path of the transfiguration of Eros.

Here, too, love is not transferred from one object to another, from a human object to a divine one. The transformation takes place in the lover. This is why its supreme image is the pair Majnûn and Layla—the Tristan and Isolde of the Persian and Arabic mystical epics. At the height of his love, Majnûn becomes the “mirror of God.” It is God himself who, in the lover’s gaze upon the beloved, contemplates his own eternal face.

This is what it means to reach the vision of vision, the esoteric realization of unity in which there is no longer either I + I or I = I, but I × I = I. In the intoxication of a consciousness carried beyond itself, the mystic may then utter the famous, seemingly excessive declaration of al-Hallâj: Anâ’l-Haqq (“I am God”). The case of al-Hallâj preoccupied Rûzbehân all his life. Again and again he explained and defended this celebrated utterance, in which the divine seems to speak through the human being.

Indeed, it is to Rûzbehân that we owe the preservation of a work by al-Hallâj in his immense Commentary on the Paradoxes of the Sufis. The author previously edited its Persian text. It is a true compendium of the Sufism of Rûzbehân’s time.

Overview of Book IV

Book IV returns to a question first raised in Book I: the relationship between Shiism and Sufism. Its four chapters examine the works of four important writers of the fourteenth and fifteenth centuries, though the second, unfortunately, remains anonymous.

I. The first chapter concerns Sayyed Haydar Âmolî (born 720/1320; died after 787/1385–86). His extensive writings, often cited by later authors, had until now remained unpublished. The author has recently edited two of his treatises, which together form a genuine compendium of Shiite philosophy; for many of the others, sadly, no manuscripts have yet been found. Haydar Âmolî was a man of the north. He spent the first half of his life in his native Tabarestan, a province now included in Mazandaran, on the southern shore of the Caspian Sea. The works available to us so far provide the material for a moving spiritual autobiography, one especially characteristic of an Iranian seeker.

Born into a distinguished Shiite family of Tabarestan, Sayyed Haydar studied, among other places, in Isfahan. Until the age of thirty he enjoyed a brilliant and privileged life. He even served as a minister to his ruler and was briefly caught up in the political turmoil of the period. Then he underwent a profound spiritual crisis. Abandoning every worldly ambition, he took to the roads as a “pilgrim of God,” wearing a Sufi’s threadbare cloak. He traveled to the holy Shiite sites in Iraq, where he spent the second half of his life producing a body of work of enormous scope.

That work marks a major moment in the development of Shiite philosophy and spirituality. By itself, it is enough to show that Shiite thought as such was not, as some modernists would have it, a political invention of the Safavid period. Above all, it helps answer the difficult question of the original relationship between Shiism and Sufism. On a matter so central to understanding Islamic spirituality, a scholar of religion prefers to let those concerned speak for themselves and to take their answers seriously. That is why the discussion in Book I already drew so extensively on Haydar Âmolî’s writings.

Haydar approaches this question directly, for it seems to have been particularly urgent for him and those around him. He answers as a thinker devoted to inner meaning: in his view, Shiism is essentially the esoteric dimension of Islam. A Shiite who confines religion to its outward forms therefore cuts away part of the holy Imams’ own teaching. Conversely, Sufis, by affirming the inner meaning of divine revelation, show themselves to be the “true Shiites.” Unfortunately, they have forgotten their origin and have themselves diminished their inner teaching by excluding the doctrine of the Imams.

Sayyed Haydar wants to end this situation once and for all. He rejects both the Shiites who denounce Sufism and the Sufis who denounce Shiism. He must therefore confront several groups at once: the legalist Sunnis, the Shiites who have forgotten the inner meaning of their faith, and the Sufis who have forgotten their origins and what they owe, at the deepest level, to Shiism. Mollâ Sadrâ Shîrâzî would confront a similar situation some two centuries later. It is a tragic predicament that spiritual seekers in all three branches of the Abrahamic tradition have had to face in their different ways.

In pursuing this confrontation, Sayyed Haydar speaks as a disciple of Ibn ’Arabî, whom he cites repeatedly. Much of his effort goes into describing the passage from the theological understanding of divine unity, or tawhîd, to which the prophets called humanity, to the understanding of unity at the level of being itself, taught by the “Friends of God” in the footsteps of the holy Imams. These pages show how readily Shiite Iranian thought could absorb Ibn ’Arabî’s sacred philosophy, because it recognized in it something already its own. Ibn ’Arabî’s Fosûs was even understood as participating in the phenomenon of the Holy Book, since its author was believed to have received heavenly inspiration for it from the Prophet.

Yet despite his devotion to Ibn ’Arabî’s thought and work, Haydar Âmolî disagrees with him on one point that cannot be compromised. For a Shiite, the very meaning of the doctrine of prophecy is at stake. With all Twelver Shiites, Haydar holds that the Seal of walâyat—the spiritual authority and inner meaning of prophecy—cannot itself be a prophet, namely Jesus, as Ibn ’Arabî maintained. That Seal is, and can only be, the Muhammadan Imamate: in the person of the First Imam as the Seal of universal walâyat, and in the person of the Twelfth Imam as the Seal of Muhammadan walâyat. The whole destiny of the Shiite understanding of sacred history hangs on this distinction, whose full significance Book VII will bring to light. Haydar Âmolî could make no concession here.

Like many of his fellow spiritual writers, Sayyed Haydar had a particular gift for visions in the mundus imaginalis, the imaginal world. His visionary gift went hand in hand with a taste for diagrams. A diagram of a vision he contemplated in the night sky over Baghdad offers a striking image of the structure of the pleroma of the “Fourteen Immaculate Ones.”

II. The second chapter examines a treatise from the same period. Unfortunately anonymous, it gives an extensive commentary on a famous hadith attributed to the Prophet: “The Quran has an outward meaning and an inward meaning; that inward meaning in turn has an inward meaning, and so on through seven depths of inner meaning.” In stating this golden rule of spiritual interpretation—the movement inward toward the meaning of Quranic revelation—the hadith takes us back to the “phenomenon of the Holy Book.” Book I explored that phenomenon at length as the foundation on which the very meaning and vocation of Shiism depend.

Seen from this perspective, the anonymous treatise stands between the great work of interpretation by Semnânî, discussed below, and that of Haydar Âmolî, who devoted six substantial volumes to the Shiite spiritual interpretation of the Quran. The treatise formulates its central problem in terms familiar to interpreters throughout the Abrahamic tradition: what relationship does a revealed text, spoken in a particular language at a particular moment, bear to the eternal truth it proclaims? How does the divine Word come to be expressed in human words?

An objection naturally arises. If the divine Word is eternal, and therefore the events it reveals are eternal, in what sense can they still be called events? Our anonymous author answers by proposing precisely the idea of an eternal event, for which “before” and “after” cannot be measured by the one-way, quantitative time of chronological history. If the phenomenon of the Book marks the divine Word’s entrance into time, its spiritual interpretation (ta’wîl) leads it back to a kind of time that does not belong to history. Here we see the interpretation of the Book at work: it compelled these thinkers to face, and to find a way beyond, the problem of historical time.

As for the seven depths of inner meaning, each is associated with a different name for the Book, drawn from the Quran itself. Every name marks a level of meaning, and each level corresponds to those whose capacity for understanding reaches that depth. Interpretation is thus inseparable from a philosophical understanding of the human being.

We shall encounter this essential connection twice more below. It is a defining feature of a spiritual tradition grounded in the Holy Book’s different levels of meaning and understanding.

III. The third chapter studies a work of spiritual interpretation by Sâ’inoddîn Ispahânî (830/1427), a writer who belonged to an entire family dynasty of Shiite thinkers and spiritual masters. The work interprets an especially enigmatic verse of the Quran: “The Hour drew near, and the Moon was split” (54:1). The author offers something like a practical exercise in interpretation, beautifully illustrating the connection just described between our understanding of the human being and our interpretation of revelation: between ways of being and ways of understanding, between levels of understanding and the individuals capable of them.

By interpreting this verse at different levels of meaning, he sketches a religious typology embracing all the forms of consciousness then represented in Islam. As the penetration of inner meaning deepens, we encounter in succession the jurists and traditionalists (specialists in hadith), the theologian-philosophers of Islam (here, the scholastics of kalâm), the Aristotelian philosophers, the ishrâqîyûn or Platonists who continued Sohrawardî’s teaching, the Sufis, the Horoufîs, and the Shiites.

The author himself once again confronts us with an important question: can a genuine understanding of prophecy, or a genuine Sufism, exist without the Shiite doctrine of the Imams? The philosophical ideas are presented in a way that suggests an understanding of the Imams that dares not—or dares no longer—to speak its own name. This is one of the dramatic features of the history of Shiite thought.

IV. The fourth and final chapter concerns the writings and teaching of one of the greatest masters of Iranian spirituality, ’Alaoddawleh Semnânî (736/1336). By a paradox that is sadly far from unique, all his writings, in Persian and Arabic, still remain in manuscript. He belonged to the generation before Haydar Âmolî. Like Haydar, he underwent a profound spiritual crisis. Once a young page at the court of the Mongol ruler Arghun, he became a Sufi. His teaching follows the line of Najmoddîn Kobrâ (1221), the great master of Central Asian Sufism who was the first to pay close attention to the colored lights whose radiance appears to the mystic’s spiritual awareness.

Semnânî’s teaching is distinguished by an interpretation of the Quran that carries the inward transformation of its meanings to the furthest possible point. The relationship described above between interpretation and the understanding of the human being—between levels of meaning and levels of comprehension—takes on a remarkably original form here, combined with the theory of colored lights perceived in the mundus imaginalis.

At the same time, the succession of prophets, which in Islam recalls the early Judeo-Christian teaching of the Verus Propheta, or True Prophet, is also brought radically inward. This inward movement takes place through a physiology of the subtle organism concealed beneath the human physical body. There are seven centers or organs of this subtle physiology, each called a latîfa. They are not, to borrow Schiller’s expression, the “stars of your destiny,” but the “prophets of your being.” Each corresponds to a prophet, from the “Adam of your being,” through the “Abraham of your being,” to the “Muhammad of your being.”

Each latîfa has its own aura or colored light. Perceiving that radiance reveals to the mystic how far the subtle body has developed—that is, how far the body of resurrection has grown. Every Quranic teaching about a particular prophet must then be understood as referring to the corresponding subtle organ or center. In Sâ’inoddîn Ispahânî’s scheme, different levels of understanding were distributed among different groups of people. Here they have been brought wholly within the individual: the levels correspond to the subtle centers or organs of each spiritual seeker.

Above the seven latîfa, the “prophets of your being,” Semnânî repeatedly and mysteriously alludes to another, named after the Angel of knowledge and revelation: latîfa jabra’êlîya, the “angel Gabriel of your being.” At this summit of mystical understanding of the human person, we glimpse, once again, the secret of a doctrine of the Imams that dares not, or does not wish to, speak its own name.

Semnânî analyzes and describes in detail the cosmic forces and influences that constitute the seven latîfa. His is a magnificent vision, rich in inherited tradition yet unmistakably his own. Semnânî the mystic proves also to be a profound metaphysician, whose system invites many comparisons. His work therefore marks a major moment not only in Iran’s spiritual culture, but in the wider study of metaphysics and mysticism.

Overview of Book V

Book V celebrates the great flowering of thought that marked the Safavid Renaissance in Iran during the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries. This remarkable growth of philosophy, unmatched elsewhere in Islam, did not spring from nothing. Book IV traced some of what preceded it, while the Prologue explained how difficult this Renaissance makes our habitual divisions of the history of philosophy. Isfahan was then Iran’s great center of culture and the arts—though, unfortunately, that did not mean that its philosophers were spared difficulties. More than twenty thinkers and spiritual masters deserve mention as representatives of what the author has proposed calling the School of Isfahan. Only three, each outstanding in his own way, could be included here.

Indeed, the philosophers brought together under the name of this celebrated city differed greatly from one another. Iranian biographical and bibliographical dictionaries generally settle for too simple a division between “Peripatetics” (Mashshâ’ûn) and “Platonists” (Ishrâqîyûn). But the philosophers they call “Peripatetics” are not quite what we are accustomed to understand by that name.

MÎR DÂMÂD (1631) is a striking example. He was the intellectual master of several generations of Iranian philosophers. Much of his extensive work remains unpublished, later overshadowed by the writings of his most brilliant pupil, Mollâ Sadrâ Shîrâzî. If Mîr Dâmâd is to be called a Peripatetic, we must remember that this “Peripatetic” left us not only substantial systematic treatises, several unfinished, but also ecstatic confessions, translated here. They are remarkable for two reasons.

First, they reveal the archetypal Images whose appearance in vision is always close to Shiite consciousness. Second, they show the Avicennian account of the universe bursting into an intensely dramatic vision. The narrative often recalls the account of ecstasy recorded by Plotinus in his Enneads, known to these Iranian philosophers through the work called the Theology of Aristotle.

Mollâ SADRÂ SHÎRÂZÎ (1640), Mîr Dâmâd’s most celebrated pupil, is by contrast a supreme representative of the “Platonists of Persia.” His immense body of work includes, among many other treatises, two great compendia. One is entitled The Four Spiritual Journeys. The other is a commentary on Kolaynî, widely used in Book I of the present work. Though unfortunately unfinished, it remains a monument of Shiite prophetic philosophy.

What first demands a philosopher’s attention in Mollâ Sadrâ is his metaphysics of being. It overturns the venerable metaphysics that gives priority to essence and replaces it with a metaphysics in which the very act of existing comes first. We may fairly speak of the continuing relevance of Mollâ Sadrâ’s concerns. This fundamental choice determines the distinctive positions of a thinker whose influence on Iranian philosophy has lasted to the present day.

Mollâ Sadrâ is the philosopher of metamorphoses and transubstantiations. His vision begins with the Soul’s descent to the depths of the abyss, followed by its ascent: reaching human form, it finally emerges at the threshold of the spiritual world, the Malakût. This is not an evolutionary theory, as some have too hastily suggested. It is a vision of a world rising through a divine action ceaselessly at work.

While affirming the transcendent unity of being, Mollâ Sadrâ’s metaphysics holds that being can be attributed to different things only by analogy, according to the varying degrees of intensity or diminution in the act of being that determines their essences. From this follows his principle of movement within substance itself, or “transsubstantial movement,” whose effects continue even into the human being’s existence after death. Mollâ Sadrâ understands matter in a way close to that of his contemporaries, the “Cambridge Platonists.”

In his thought, the boundaries between spirit and matter dissolve through the mediating reality of the mundus imaginalis, the imaginal world. Here he completes the metaphysics begun by Sohrawardî. He does so through his doctrine of Creative Imagination. This imagination is neither the work of memory nor a recombination of earlier sensory perceptions. It is an imagining Image: the original form in which the world first takes imaginative shape within us, and through which every soul creates its own paradise or hell.

By thus establishing the reality of imaginative experience independent of external perception, Mollâ Sadrâ anticipates modern inquiries, beginning with the work of Gaston Bachelard, that seek at last to establish a metaphysics of Imagination. For Mollâ Sadrâ, this Imagination is like the soul’s imperishable subtle body—the okhêma of Proclus. It shapes his philosophy of Resurrection and his vision of the human being’s threefold growth. For the philosopher, these processes of rebirth begin in this world, insofar as he becomes aware of the mystical implications of the act of Knowing.

Mollâ Sadrâ gives his own distinctive answer to the longstanding question of an essential union, without confusion of individual persons, between the soul and the Active Intelligence, which is the Holy Spirit. Understood in this way, the act of Knowing is fundamentally gnosis: saving knowledge that brings about a new birth. The name of Mollâ Sadrâ Shîrâzî should no longer be absent from our general histories of philosophy.

QÂZÎ SA’ÎD QOMMÎ (1691) also belongs to the School of Isfahan, but represents a very different direction within it. He studied under Rajab ’Alî Tabrîzî and thus came to profess a metaphysics of being unlike Mollâ Sadrâ’s.

Yet he also studied under Mohsen Fayz, Mollâ Sadrâ’s son-in-law and most brilliant pupil. The result was that Qâzî Sa’îd’s sacred philosophy eventually met Mollâ Sadrâ’s in the region of the mundus imaginalis. In his account of being, however, Qâzî Sa’îd insists on a radical distinction: the word “being” has wholly different meanings when applied to the Principle of being and to beings themselves.

The Principle remains, in its very essence, beyond the being of which it is the source; created beings, by contrast, belong essentially to the order of creation. According to the teaching of the Shiite Imams themselves, only the via negationis—negative, or apophatic, theology, which approaches God by saying what cannot be said of God—allows us even to approach the Principle from afar.

All the more necessary, then, is the primordial theophany, the original manifestation of the divine: the metaphysical pleroma of the “Fourteen beings of light.” They are the bearers of the divine Names and Attributes with which affirmative theology is concerned. On all these points, Qâzî Sa’îd Qommî stands close to the teaching of the Absconditum, the utterly hidden divine reality, found in both Ismaili gnosis and the Shaykhi School (see Book VI below).

His commentary on a text deeply studied by the philosophers of Imamite Shiism, the Story of the White Cloud, reads it as a narrative of spiritual initiation. It also allows him to return to his own theory of space and time, for that theory makes it possible to understand events that, while not historical in the ordinary sense, are by no means merely mythical. Here again, the philosophers of the School of Isfahan have something to contribute to debates of our own time.

Overview of Book VI

Book VI is devoted to the Shaykhi School, or “Shaykhism.” The school, whose center at the time of writing was in Kerman in southeastern Iran, did not choose this name for itself. Others gave it to the disciples of Shaykh AHMAD AHSÂ’Î (1826), who was simply known as the Shaykh, so powerful was the impression of his personality on followers and opponents alike.

Several reasons justify giving this school such a prominent place here. Its spiritual teachers were figures of exceptional stature. They produced an immense body of writings, many still in manuscript, marked throughout by a determination to preserve and deepen, in complete fidelity, the whole teaching of the Shiite Imams on divine wisdom and mystical knowledge. Inevitably, their renewal of themes that many Shiites had forgotten appeared to the ill-informed or ill-disposed as a dangerous innovation.

Hence the painful history of the Shaykhi School, one of the episodes in which Imamite Shiism struggled against itself. For Iranian thought, and for the history of spiritual knowledge more generally, this was an especially dramatic moment.

In seeking to preserve and deepen the full inner teaching of the holy Imams—the whole of Imamite gnosis—the Shaykhi masters were led to develop points of doctrine that could be understood only by minds with a particular gift for metaphysics and sacred philosophy. They therefore had to contend with hostile critics who read them without understanding them, or who had neither read nor understood them. Equally troublesome were certain overzealous disciples and admirers who understood no better. This book gives the biographies of Shaykh Ahmad Ahsâ’î and his successors, with enough bibliographical information to suggest the extraordinary scale of their work.

Some have conceded that Shaykh Ahmad Ahsâ’î was a “man of God” of outstanding devotion, while claiming that he never really understood metaphysical questions or the language of philosophers. The pages devoted here to his cosmology and his account of the origin of the human being are enough to refute such superficial and unfounded judgments. Particular attention is paid to the doctrine known as the “fourth pillar.” It has provoked some of the worst misunderstandings and controversies, precisely because it is among the hardest teachings to grasp.

Yet it expresses a fundamental and traditional aspect of Shiite esotericism: by keeping those who bear this spiritual responsibility unknown, it protects the perspective of the final things, and with it the meaning and future mission of the tradition.

Overview of Book VII

Book VII brings together the essential features of this vision of the final things, centered on the person of the Twelfth Imam, the “Imam hidden from the senses but present in the hearts of his faithful.” He is a compelling figure, endowed with all the power of a primordial Image. This Image governs the hidden possibilities within Shiite consciousness, so that what lies concealed there, yet is always on the verge of appearing, can at last become visible. For more than ten centuries, the sacred biography of the Twelfth Imam and the accounts of his manifestations have formed the very history of Shiite consciousness.

More precisely, they form a sacred history: their events take place on the level of visionary experience. As we have repeatedly emphasized, such events are not history in the ordinary sense, but they are even less to be dismissed as myth. This sacred biography begins with the Twelfth Imam’s birth. The account of the mystical betrothal of his mother, the Byzantine princess Narkès, to the Eleventh Imam reveals an attention to Christianity expressed nowhere else in Islam in quite this way. It suggests the possibility of an “esoteric ecumenism,” a spiritual kinship reaching across religious boundaries.

With the Twelfth Imam the “pleroma of the Twelve Imams” is complete. If the Prophet is included in the count, the Twelfth Imam is the thirteenth of the Fourteen Immaculate Ones. Present to both past and future, he is the Seal of the cycle of spiritual initiation that follows the cycle of prophecy. He is therefore also the Seal of prophetic philosophy and of the Shiite understanding of sacred history.

The present age of his “occultation” (ghaybat), his concealment from outward sight, is a time “between times.” It will last until his final appearing—the parousia—brings our aeon to completion. This very concealment protects spiritual realities from being reduced to social institutions or material things. The person and role of the Twelfth Imam correspond strikingly to the Zoroastrian Persian idea of the final Savior or transfigurer, the Saoshyant. Zoroastrian ethics, it has been said, takes the form of something like an order of chivalry. In a similar way, an ideal of spiritual chivalry grew up around the Twelfth Imam.

On one side it connects the moral and spiritual character of ancient Zoroastrian Iran with that of Shiite Iran. On the other, it establishes a link between the spiritual chivalry of Islamic Iran and that of the West, an idea already proclaimed in the West during the twelfth century. Certain Shiite thinkers—for example, a pupil of Mîr Dâmâd—explicitly identify the Twelfth Imam with the Zoroastrian Resurrector. A Shiite tradition likewise identifies him with the Paraclete promised in the Gospel of John. These correspondences govern the whole of Book VII, in which the author seeks to bring their hidden implications to light.

Several texts translated here for the first time show what Shiite consciousness understands by this spiritual chivalry—javânmardî in Persian, fotowwat in Arabic. It cannot be separated from the idea of the cycle of prophecy or from the “Friends of God”: those who participate in walâyat, the inward spiritual reality of prophecy. That is why the authors studied here trace the distant origins of this chivalry to Seth, the son and “Imam” of Adam, in whom it is identified with the very idea of Sufism (tasawwof). Abraham, the father of the knights of faith, is said to have separated fotowwat from tasawwof at the request of his followers. In this way, fotowwat spread through the ideal of fellowship, until every craft and occupation could become an act of chivalrous service.

Some shared names and patterns might at first seem unimportant. Yet the working of primordial Images reveals them to be full of meaning, quite apart from any demonstrable chain of historical influence.

Consider the Green Island, the pleroma of the Twelve, and the concealment of the “thirteenth.” Their images and structures reappear among fourteenth-century “Friends of God”—the Johannite knights of the Green Island at Strasbourg—as well as among the twelve (or thirteen) knights in a famous unfinished poem by Goethe. The very recurrence of the name “Friends of God” is striking. It is given to people whose ideal and way of life belong neither to the clergy nor to the laity, but precisely to the spiritual knight. This was also the ideal proposed in the twelfth century by Wolfram von Eschenbach, who forcefully proclaimed the idea of a chivalry shared by West and East, Christianity and Islam.

Book II already explored the convergences between Parsifal’s Quest for the Grail and the Iranian epic, between prophetic philosophy and the mystical epic. Once again, then, we must ask: where does the philosopher stand? These thinkers affirmed that philosopher and prophet share a common calling, and they understood the prophets’ mission as one of spiritual chivalry. For them, therefore, the philosopher’s service is also a divine service—an idea that certain Jewish Kabbalists have expressed with particular excellence. Something like a spiritual chivalry thus arises wherever we encounter the “phenomenon of the Holy Book.” It is an Abrahamic chivalry, because Abraham is its father and because it bears walâyat: the inner spiritual dimension of all three branches of the Abrahamic tradition.

Just as the Twelfth Imam is the Seal of the “Friends of God” and the Seal of spiritual chivalry, so a Shiite tradition identifies him with the Paraclete of John’s Gospel. Here the philosophers of Imamite Shiism divide sacred history into periods in a way that corresponds to the scheme developed in the twelfth century by Joachim of Fiore, whose influence on Western philosophy continued for centuries. On both sides, this division rests less on chronological time than on an intuition of time as it is spiritually lived; in objective historical time, these periods actually coexist.

And on both sides, everyone called to the life of a spiritual knight belongs already to the reign of the Spirit, the Paraclete, the walâyat of the Twelfth Imam. Neither tradition awaits the revelation of a new Book. What they await is the spiritual understanding (intelligentia spiritualis, ta’wîl) of everything that has come before. Its living instruments are the “Friends of God,” or Viri spirituales, the spiritual men; it frees human beings from every form of bondage and every hell.

We return, finally, to a fundamental problem already raised in Book I: the widespread secularization of the West. The reign of the Paraclete originally meant the Church of John replacing the Church of Peter. Later, the idea of the Paraclete’s reign was secularized into a program of social messianism. We have already noted how difficult it is to translate words such as “laicization” and “secularization” accurately into Persian or Arabic. Those words presuppose the existence of the Church as an institution, a phenomenon that has no equivalent in Islam.

Our social and political ideologies are, in fact, secularized theologies. What they have produced is certainly not the Church of John. Rather, they have produced something like a post-Church of Peter: a form succeeding the Church while retaining its principal features in secularized form. What happens, then, when such ideologies enter traditional societies that lack the theological history these ideologies presuppose? This question concerns metaphysicians no less than sociologists.

Book V

The School of Isfahan

Chapter I The Ecstatic Confessions of Mîr Dâmâd

(1041/1631)

1. Mîr Dâmâd and the School of Isfahan

More than one “passionate pilgrim” has fallen under Isfahan’s spell, losing himself in dreams among its gardens, beneath the shade of its green domes. Art historians and archaeologists have preserved the legacy of the Safavids and kept alive, in the present, the significance of this great city of art in Islamic Iran. André Godard has movingly described the magnificent sight that greets the thoughtful traveler on an autumn evening, as the gentle light begins to fade.

Having climbed the lower slopes of the mountain to the south, the traveler turns to look across an immense valley bordered by deserts. From one side to the other stretches a lake of greenery, out of which rise glazed domes and towers. Isfahan, Godard writes, “isolated amid deserts, secret, wonderfully adorned, and laden with history, is an image of exaltation in solitude more truly even than Toledo or Aranjuez. Perhaps it is impossible to understand fully the art, and the soul, of Iran without knowing the poignant beauty of this city1.”

Indeed. Yet it is into spiritual Isfahan that we wish to enter, to discover something of the hidden lives of those souls whose meditations infused the city and its surrounding landscape, transforming both into a spiritual city and a spiritual landscape bearing the distinctive imprint of Iran. This is not an easy task. Walking beside a colleague who is an archaeologist or art historian, the philosopher, the student of the “divine sciences,” might well feel a certain frustration. He knows that thinkers whose names and some of whose works are familiar to him once lived, meditated, and taught in these gardens, in the exquisite shade of these old colleges.

Yet finding definite traces of their presence is not always easy2. At least the traces of Mîr Dâmâd have not vanished. The Sadr madrasa, where he taught, still stands in the heart of the Great Bazaar. Its four sides still enclose a broad, delightful garden planted with trees, along whose paths philosophers and theologians of every age still walk in solemn reflection, as Sadrâ Shîrâzî, Mohsen Fayz, and so many others must once have done. We would need to call to mind, too, the masters who lived and taught in the other colleges, and the generations of attentive students who followed them.

Together they sustained a philosophy and a theology bearing their unmistakable stamp. They carried within themselves the challenge and the hope embodied in Shiism, and drew upon the rich possibilities for philosophical reflection contained in the figure of the Imam. Their lives of study—sometimes secluded, sometimes stirred by fierce debates in which their deepest convictions were at stake—continued until the days of the pensive, weak Shah Soltân Hosayn (1694–1722). Withdrawn into his excessively exquisite little prayer chamber and oblivious to the Afghan threat, he allowed a sudden catastrophe to unfold: the sack of Isfahan, the end of the Safavid dynasty, and the scattering of its libraries.

For more than two centuries, however, a spiritual family of philosophers, theologians, and theosophers had flourished there. Some years ago, we proposed gathering their shared concerns—without overlooking the differences to which we shall return—under the name “School of Isfahan.” This name seems, indeed, to have entered the vocabulary of our Iranian colleagues. To this day, the names and principal works of these thinkers are familiar to every Iranian theologian and every philosopher of the traditional schools. Their influence has remained fruitful from century to century. It was transmitted throughout the Qajar period, and today their works, particularly those of Mollâ Sadrâ Shîrâzî, are helping to inspire a revival of traditional philosophy, precisely because the problems they explored have never ceased to matter.

In the West, by contrast, recognition of this school’s importance has come only in our own time. It is strange that so many European travelers and residents who wrote about Persia in the very period when these thinkers lived had no real contact with the philosophers of Isfahan.

Perhaps one consolation amid the moral disarray of our iron age is that certain spiritual and philosophical conditions now exist—or might be brought into being—that make at least some communication between souls possible. That is why the names and works of the School of Isfahan, whose thinkers lived at the same time as Giordano Bruno and Jacob Boehme, Descartes and Leibniz, now confront us as urgent invitations to encounter them. The “Platonists of Persia” (Ishrâqiyân-e Iran) were contemporaries of the “Cambridge Platonists.”

We must put an end to the sorry state of affairs in which a comparative history of philosophy leaves its column for the Middle East desperately empty between the great mystic Jâmî (1495) and the Bâb (1850)3.

We must also overcome the situation Edward Browne lamented more than thirty years ago, when he complained that the most interesting subject in Shiite theology had “scarcely yet received from European Orientalists the attention it deserves4.” The deeper reason for this neglect is no doubt that the task exceeds the technical training of an Orientalist as such. It requires another kind of preparation, and above all an inborn calling: that of the philosopher, the theologian, or, more broadly, the seeker in the ilâhiyât, the “divine sciences”—sciences that the agnosticism of our age no longer knows very well how to distinguish from the “human sciences.”

Yet philosophers and theologians have rarely abandoned their customary programs to venture into Oriental studies. Even without this deeper obstacle, the neglect would have had its excuses. The sources are not always easy to reach. Many works survive only in manuscript, and manuscripts in private collections can be particularly difficult to locate.

Considerable progress has been made in recent years, with catalogs published for major public collections, but the work is far from complete5. Other essential works were published long ago in densely printed lithographic editions, now extremely rare and furnished with neither contents pages nor indexes. The unfortunate researcher enters an enchanted forest where finding his way requires training and an unfailing memory.

Our immediate task, then, is the rediscovery of the sources. It calls for a united effort by philosophers trained in Oriental studies and a new generation of Iranian philosophers, whose responsibility it is to make this spiritual universe present in our time—a universe whose meaning and message have lasting value. For all the complexity of the undertaking, I do not think it unduly optimistic to say that it has begun6.

Many pages of the present work have already evoked the School of Isfahan and suggested its defining features. The spiritual types outlined by Sâ'inoddîn Ispahânî (Book IV, Chapter III) gave us an opportunity to recall the difference between the fate of Avicennian philosophy in Iran and its fate in the medieval Latin West. The more closely we study the thinkers of Isfahan, the more striking that contrast becomes. Comparative philosophy thus has an especially fruitful task before it: to bring forward a contrasting witness to the path eventually taken by the West. I say contrasting witness deliberately. This comparison must attempt something much more serious than identifying formal patterns.

Because Avicenna’s works were translated from Arabic into Latin, we can speak of a shared Avicennian moment in East and West during the twelfth and thirteenth centuries. That common element gives us, in itself, a point of reference from which to identify the divergence that then widened from century to century. The decisive comparison will not be based on the different historical and social circumstances of the two worlds, but on the horizon proper to the “divine sciences.” Seen from that horizon, the survival of Avicennian philosophy in Iran and its failure in the West must have a significance that has scarcely yet been examined7.

Since the research initiated by Étienne Gilson, we have known that medieval scholasticism and Cartesian philosophy are not wholly unrelated worlds. The dramas that marked the history of medieval scholastic philosophy continued to reverberate—sometimes even to repeat themselves exactly, beneath a different vocabulary—in the most “modern” philosophy. Among these dramas we must count the failure of Latin Avicennianism and its submersion by Averroism.

As we have already suggested, the opposition between Avicenna and Averroes becomes a symbol of the different destinies of two cultures. For a long time, historians supposed that Islamic philosophy disappeared into the sands after Averroes, while Averroism passed into the Latin West and endured there. Latin Averroism continued to be represented in a number of Western universities until the eighteenth century. New commentaries extended Averroes’ thought in the West, while in Iran it was Avicenna’s work that continued, down to our own time, to stimulate successive generations of commentators.

The contrast is striking: the name of Averroes (Ibn Roshd) remained almost unknown in the East. The crises that Averroism was to provoke in Western consciousness had no real counterpart there. While new Western commentaries developed the work of Averroes, Avicenna’s thought grew in Iran, century after century, through new commentaries of its own. Meanwhile, two other names, long unfamiliar in the West, came to exercise an ever greater influence on the philosophy of eastern Islam: Sohrawardî and Mohyiddîn Ibn 'Arabî.

We have already attempted to trace the achievement of Sohrawardî, the young master who, in the twelfth century, “revived the theosophical wisdom of ancient Persia” (Book II). From then on, ancient Iran was no longer merely a store of epic memories and legends for Islamic Persia. Through the interpretive genius of the Shaykh al-Ishrâq, it became a spiritual tradition integrated into Islamic spirituality. As for the vast body of work left by Ibn 'Arabî—perhaps the greatest visionary theosopher of all time—Haydar Âmolî has already shown us how easily Shiite theosophy took it into itself, recognizing in it something of its own inheritance.

There was only one point of disagreement: the question of the Seal of walâyat, the spiritual authority or guardianship that continues the inner meaning of prophecy. Once that issue was settled, nothing stood in the way of Shiite theosophy’s assimilation of Ibn 'Arabî’s work. The Shiite commentaries on the Fosûs, including those of Haydar Âmolî and Sâ'inoddîn Ispahânî, and the great fifteenth-century work of Ibn Abî Jomhûr, bear witness to this. Mollâ Sadrâ’s thought, too, would be deeply shaped by his meditation on Ibn 'Arabî.

At the same time, the traditions (hadith) transmitted from the Shiite Imams—above all the great collections of Kolaynî and Sadûq Ibn Bâbûyeh—became the subject of systematic theosophical commentaries. Those of Mollâ Sadrâ and Qâzî Sa'îd Qommî are monumental works, revealing how powerfully the Imams’ teachings stimulated philosophical meditation. Our thinkers were perfectly aware of this. Unfortunately, the body of traditions attributed to the Imams remained little known, if not entirely unknown, in the West for a very long time.

Thus, when one emphasizes what was, and remains, self-evident to these thinkers, one may be met with discreet, perhaps ironic irritation—as though one had invented the whole thing!

In short, all these elements taken together—Sohrawardî’s theosophy of Light, Ibn 'Arabî’s mystical gnosis, and the prophetic philosophy and spirituality of walâyat taught by the Imams—give us some sense of the intellectual and spiritual atmosphere in which Iranian Avicennian philosophy lived and flourished, right down to our own day. Avicenna’s own works, of course, continued to be read and commented upon; I have already mentioned the highly individual commentaries of Mollâ Sadrâ and Ahmad 'Alawî, among others.

But these Avicennian thinkers did not remain confined to questions settled once and for all. Their Avicennianism expanded with each new generation.

It is for this reason that we described Iranian Avicennianism as a contrasting witness—a witness able to shed light on the Latin Avicennianism that was so soon defeated in the West, and to disclose the reasons and circumstances of that defeat, together with its consequences. It need only show what its own centuries-long existence in the Iranian world made possible. The conditions and development of what we may call “Illuminationist Avicennianism” and “Shiite Avicennianism” were wholly different from those of the episode in medieval Latin scholasticism known as “Avicennizing Augustinianism.”

Avicenna’s theory of knowledge, whose central idea and further implications we have had occasion to discuss, could provide the framework for a comparative study that remains to be undertaken. Such a study should ask what analogies or affinities exist between the doctrine of the Active Intelligence among the Latin Averroists and Hegel’s conception of Spirit in his phenomenology. At the very time when a form of philosophical consciousness was being prepared and developed in the West—a form that would culminate in Hegel’s philosophy of historical Spirit, whose interpretations or ruins still weigh upon the recognized problems of Western thought with the burden of their mythology—the philosophers of Isfahan were pursuing Avicenna’s theory of knowledge in an altogether different direction.

Earlier, we emphasized the identification of the Active Intelligence ('Aql fa''âl), the “Angel of Knowledge,” with the Holy Spirit. In the Islamic understanding, this Holy Spirit is identified—returning in this respect to certain Christian conceptions from before the Council of Nicaea—with Gabriel, the “Angel of the Annunciation” sent to Mary (Maryam) and the “Angel of Revelation” who communicates divine revelation to the prophets. This identification immediately places philosophical inquiry within the aims and ultimate purpose of a “prophetic philosophy.” As we noted before, its angelology of knowledge culminates in an Imamology of Knowledge: an understanding of knowledge centered on the spiritual role of the Imams.

Here a philosophy of the Holy Spirit stands opposed to the dialectical philosophy of historical Spirit, of Spirit descending into historical time. It is a prophetic theosophy that leads every history back to metahistory, the order of spiritual meaning beyond ordinary historical events. It finds expression in the idea of the cycle of prophecy and the cycle of walâyat, directed toward the advent of the Twelfth Imam, the “Hidden Imam,” whom some of our authors—Haydar Âmolî, for example—explicitly identify with the Paraclete named in the Gospel tradition, which they also knew. This ordering gives each spiritual individuality a place and a meaning confirmed by Avicenna’s theory of knowledge.

By contrast, a totalitarian dialectic of historical Spirit, whether Averroist or Hegelian in inspiration, destroys that individuality. It also destroys the imaginal world, the realm of real spiritual images and events. Without that world, spiritual events and the facts of sacred history face a false dilemma: if they cannot be fitted into the record of empirical history, they must be dismissed as myth.

Yet in the traditions of the Imams themselves we encountered a principle of interpretation that already outwitted the traps of historicism. Spiritual events do not simply fall “into history.” Their meaning and content transcend the limits and visible circumstances of the historical world to which they are related. But on the level of their own world, they have a time and a “history” of their own.

Hence the fundamental difference between Shiite ta'wîl—the spiritual interpretation practiced by Haydar Âmolî, Mollâ Sadrâ, or Semnânî—and the Averroist ta'wîl that escapes into “allegory.” In the last analysis, the choice is this: either preserve the proper subject matter and meaning of the ilâhiyât, the “divine sciences,” or absorb them into the “human sciences” and nothing more. This is undoubtedly too brief an account to provide all the arguments it requires. Still, it had to be included here as a preliminary outline. For one thing, it helps us locate the School of Isfahan, and with it Iranian philosophy as a whole, in relation to Western philosophy, by suggesting the landmarks of a comparison.

For another, it challenges the distorted conception that had mutilated the very idea of Islamic philosophy by, paradoxically, overlooking its most important province. We have read brilliant syntheses explaining that when the “Arabs” look back beyond Islam into their own past, they find nothing but the desert. Such a claim deserves closer examination in light of what is now known about the antiquities of pre-Islamic Arabia. In any case, when we speak of Iranian philosophy and the School of Isfahan, it is not the “Arabs” who are in question.

We must remember that every Iranian adolescent, studying Ferdawsî’s Shâh-Nâmeh, finds himself not in a desert but in the company of the heroes of the Iranian epic. So, too, does the Iranian philosopher familiar with Sohrawardî’s work. Perhaps it is only because some writers never even suspected the repeated rebirths of philosophy in Iran that they could speak of the hardening and decline of Islamic thought, and blame it on an exclusive, rigid Aristotelianism. It is difficult to speak of intellectual stagnation in the case of Haydar Âmolî, Mîr Dâmâd, Mollâ Sadrâ, Qâzî Sa'îd Qommî, or their pupils. It would be no easier to speak of rigid Aristotelianism among the Ishrâqîyûn, the “Platonists of Persia.” And anyone who has spent time with Avicennian philosophy knows, as Averroes himself knew, how hard it is to find in it Aristotelianism pure and simple, whether rigid or otherwise.

In fact, the judgments just mentioned arise more from sociological surveys of philosophy than from genuinely philosophical investigation. Such swift overviews may give the mind an immediate satisfaction, but they hold many disappointments in store for demanding scholars, who eventually discover that the very tasks capable of opening new vistas were neglected. Those tasks take time. They require us to examine the details and to work patiently into the depths of the thoughts and visions preserved in substantial works that, as we have said, are not always easily accessible.

Above all, the metaphysician must remain within the horizon of the “divine sciences” (ilâhiyât), resisting interpretations that may flatter contemporary tastes but whose first effect is to distort what those sciences are actually concerned with. That is all we wished to suggest in our preliminary approach to the spiritual city of Isfahan.

We could have no better guide into that city than Mîr Dâmâd. He was, in a sense, the leading figure of the School of Isfahan, the intellectual master of several generations of philosophers, even though the works of his brilliant pupils seem in practice to have displaced his own. His name is familiar to anyone in Iran with even a modest education in philosophy and theology. Certain forms of popular devotion revere him almost as a saint.

Yet his reputation seems scarcely to have crossed the borders of the Iranian world in the broad sense: the regions where Persian predominated as a language of learning and culture. Thus manuscripts of Mîr Dâmâd’s works are still numerous in Pakistani libraries but exceedingly rare elsewhere.

The honorific title given to him is revealing in itself. He is called Mo'allim-e thâlîth, the “Third Teacher.” The First Teacher, Magister primus, is understood to be Aristotle—an Aristotle also credited with the celebrated Theology—while the Second Teacher, Magister secundus, was and remains al-Fârâbî, the philosopher who set Avicenna “on the way.” As we may suspect, this title implies a division of the history of philosophy into periods quite unlike the one ordinarily accepted in the West today.

Yet it must fit the theosophy of history, the “prophetic philosophy,” whose outline we recalled above for this very reason. If Iranian consciousness allows some six or seven centuries to pass after al-Fârâbî before recognizing a philosophical event deserving the name “appearance of the Third Teacher,” it is because it perceives in the work that dominates Iranian Shiite Avicennianism something of decisive and exceptional importance. We have just tried to suggest what that something is by tracing the characteristic features of the School of Isfahan.

We can gather those features into a single picture by bringing together the men whose honorific names have made them symbols: Shaykh Sadûq (Ibn Bâbûyeh), the “trustworthy” transmitter of thousands of traditions from the Imams and a pillar of Imamite Shiism; Shaykh al-Ra'îs, Avicenna, the “chief philosopher”; Shaykh al-Ishrâq, Sohrawardî, master of the Light of the East, of cognitio matutina, the knowledge of dawn; Shaykh al-Akbar, Ibn 'Arabî, Doctor maximus, the Greatest Master; and Mo'allim-e thâlîth, Mîr Dâmâd, Magister tertius, the Third Teacher.

There are others, of course, and we have already named several of them. Brilliant as the Safavid Renaissance was, and favorable as the circumstances open to philosophers could be—despite the restrictions Mollâ Sadrâ would experience so painfully—the School of Isfahan did not spring into being from nowhere. Mîr Dâmâd’s own teachers, and the spiritual figures mentioned in the preceding book, remind us of all that made it possible. Nor should the school be treated as a single, undivided body of doctrine. Important differences of detail separate Mîr Dâmâd’s philosophical positions from those of his most famous pupil, Mollâ Sadrâ Shîrâzî, and both from those of Mollâ Rajab 'Alî Tabrîzî and his disciple Qâzî Sa'îd Qommî. These differences are themselves the surest sign of philosophical vitality.

Yet all these thinkers share one defining feature of their spiritual character, one we have already found in Sohrawardî and shall find again in Mîr Dâmâd and his successors. They are philosophers, but also profoundly spiritual men. Their philosophy does not remain merely theoretical—not because they seek what we today call practical results and useful applications, for a philosophy that looked to those things for its justification would already have betrayed its vocation.

For these thinkers, putting philosophy into practice means transforming the philosopher’s entire inner life. It means fostering in themselves, in their students, and in everyone touched by their teaching the perfection of a human type devoted to “divine wisdom”—a type whose necessity and meaning today’s homo oeconomicus, the human being conceived solely in economic terms, may no longer even suspect.

So although Mîr Dâmâd has a reputation as a particularly obscure philosopher, the two ecstatic confessions translated later in this chapter show that he was much more besides. They reveal the secret of his ultimate experience, at the summit of his soul. We remain faithful to his own teaching when we say that he was a complete philosopher because his philosophy led him to ecstatic experience, and a consummate mystic because that experience helped him to articulate a metaphysics of ecstasy. In every respect, this is both the teaching and the practice of Sohrawardî.

Above all, then, we should remember that this philosopher, famous for his difficulty, was also a soul alive with mystical experience. Such a union refutes, by the evidence of lived experience, the crude classifications encouraged by an overly dogmatic psychology of character—classifications that would treat as mutually exclusive the spiritual gifts that an ishrâqî sage is called precisely to unite in himself.

In Sohrawardî’s case, it means opening the Book of Oriental Theosophy with a reform of logic and ending it with a reminder of ecstasy. In Mîr Dâmâd’s, it means being a speculative theologian—but in a sense that recalls the Latin speculum, “mirror”: the soul itself becomes the mirror of its visions, and when it discovers this, self-knowledge culminates in mystical experience. For his own pen name (takhallos), Mîr Dâmâd chose the word that most perfectly expresses Sohrawardî’s philosophy: ishrâq, illumination.

His reputation for obscurity is illustrated by one of those anecdotes in which Iranian humor gives itself free rein. The story concerns the outward form of the first event awaiting every human being after death: the questioning by the two angels Nâkir and Monkir. They ask the deceased what faith he held and in what God he believed.

So it was with Dâmâd, who naturally could not answer like everyone else. His God? Ostoqos al-ostoqsât: the Element of Elements . . . The two angels are dumbfounded. Nothing like this reply has ever been heard before. What are they to do? They take the matter to the Lord God, who answers them kindly: “Yes, I know. All his life he said things of that sort, which even I could never understand.

“But he is an upright, harmless man. He deserves to enter paradise.”

What, then, really accounts for the obscure covering in which this thought is wrapped? We must certainly not regard it as a weakness in a mind unable to master its own ideas or find their proper expression. Rather, we should see it as a form of protection—protection from the difficulties and harassment that none of our philosophers, or their students, entirely escaped. This is beautifully illustrated by another anecdote, this time a dream, which contains a wise lesson. After his master’s death, Mollâ Sadrâ sees him in a dream and asks: “Why do people condemn me as an unbeliever (takfîr) when they did not condemn you, even though my doctrines do not differ from yours?”

Mîr Dâmâd replies: “Because I presented philosophical questions in such a way that the jurists and official theologians could make nothing of them. No one but the sages versed in divine wisdom (ahl-e hikmat) could understand them. You, however, do the opposite. You explain philosophical questions so clearly that any ordinary schoolmaster who happens upon your books can grasp what is at stake. That is why they pronounce you an unbeliever, whereas they could do nothing against me8.”

Should we see a triumph of this “discipline of secrecy,” so rigorously observed by Mîr Dâmâd, in the attitude toward him of the great theologian Majlisî—an attitude that appears paradoxical at first sight? Let me say at once that I am not sure.

But the case is so instructive from another point of view that it is worth recalling. Our evocation of spiritual Isfahan would be incomplete without at least a passing reminder of the paradoxical position of Shiite spiritual thinkers that we examined at the beginning of this work (Book I, Chapter III).

Mohammad Bâqir Majlisî (d. 1111/1699–1700) is the great theologian of what we may call, though the term is not entirely appropriate, the outward or exoteric Shiite “orthodoxy.” He was an opponent of the Sufis. His aversion to them was so great that he felt compelled to defend the posthumous reputation of his own father, himself an eminent theologian, Mohammad Taqî Majlisî (d. 1070/1659–1660), by emphatically denying that he had ever felt the attraction to Sufism that, in fact, he seems very much to have felt.

Whatever position we take, we cannot withhold our admiration or gratitude for Majlisî’s prodigious labor in organizing Shiite theology. Besides the many books he published in Persian, some kind of research office—an organization whose details are unknown to us—enabled him to produce an immense work: the twenty-six folio volumes of his theological encyclopedia, the Ocean of Lights (Bihâr al-Anwâr).

But there is more. It was with a certain delighted astonishment that I discovered, amid the dense pages of this encyclopedia, a long account of Mîr Dâmâd written by Majlisî himself. Nothing could be more respectful than its lavish words of praise. Not only does Majlisî quote a beautiful letter from Mîr Dâmâd to his friend Shaykh Bahâ'oddîn 'Âmilî; he even reproduces in full the Risâlat al-Khal'îya, the ecstatic confession translated later in this chapter (§ 3). He introduces it with these simple words: “Among the extraordinary treatises of Mîr Dâmâd, this epistle is evidence of the godlikeness (ta'alloh) of his inmost consciousness. It shows how holy his life was, and what form that life took9.”

Thus the same theologian who was a resolute opponent of the Sufis pays tribute to Mîr Dâmâd the ecstatic mystic.
