“When I saw the hostility that anyone wishing to reform the ignorant and uneducated arouses in our day, when I saw the infernal fire of stupidity and error blazing at full strength [...], and when I came up against the incomprehension of people blind to the lights and secrets of wisdom [...], people whose sight has never passed beyond the boundaries of material appearances, whose thought has never risen above the dwellings of darkness and their dust—people who, because of their hostility to knowledge and gnosis, and because they utterly reject the path of philosophy (hikmat) and certainty gained through personal experience (îqân), have no access to the higher knowledge of divine wisdom ('olûm moqaddasa ilâhîya) or the loftier secrets of gnosis, the knowledge which the prophets and Friends of God expressed in symbols and which the philosophers and gnostics ('orafâ) also pointed toward [...]—then this suffocation of intelligence, this freezing of human nature brought about by the hostility of our age, forced me to withdraw to a remote region, to hide myself in obscurity and distress, cut off from my hopes and brokenhearted [...].

“Following the teaching of the one who is my master and support, the First Imam, forefather of the holy Imams who are witnesses and Friends of God, I began to practice taqîyeh, the discipline of keeping spiritual mysteries concealed.82 ...”

What Mollâ Sadrâ experienced in Ispahan was not peculiar to his age, as perhaps he believed. His vocation and determination were to live and teach Shiism in its fullness, including the mystical knowledge drawn from the Imams' own teaching. In this way the philosopher became caught up in the spiritual tragedy underlying the glorious Safavid period: Sufism had become suspect precisely because it had triumphed with the dynasty, while Shiism had to win back its own identity if it was to preserve its gnostic tradition.

The conversation Sadrâ held in a dream with his master Mîr Dâmâd (see p. 20 above) shows that he continued to feel the effects of this tragedy even in the last period of his life. The harassment of the narrow-minded drove the young philosopher away from Ispahan's vigorous intellectual life and into a remote refuge. He chose the small town of Kahak, some thirty kilometers southeast of Qomm.

Leaving Qomm along the road to Ispahan, one turns off after about a league and a half onto a track running eastward across some fifteen kilometers of desert toward a mountain range. There a high valley opens, displaying the contrast so characteristic of the Iranian landscape: the desert's bare stone gradually gives way, as one climbs the valley, to the enchantment of luxuriant greenery.

Kahak is a place of gardens, enchanting in itself. It also has a small mosque, built in the eleventh Islamic century, with an unusual plan, where Mollâ Sadrâ may once have prayed. Two more recent monuments complete the scene: an Imâm-zâdeh, a shrine associated with a descendant of an Imam, of exquisite design (the Imâm-zâdeh Ma'sûmeh), and a romantic-looking fortress built of fragile material.

I retain a vivid picture of all this, for I needed to know the landscape in which Mollâ Sadrâ spent nine or eleven years83 meditating and writing, himself living in “the exaltation of solitude.” So a few years ago, in November 1962, I went there on pilgrimage with two dear Iranian companions.

But to grasp the full mystical geography of this landscape, one must, on the return journey toward Qomm, leave the main road once again and follow another track eastward to Jam-Karân, to the sanctuary of the one who, for more than ten centuries, has himself been the secret history of Shiite consciousness: the Twelfth Imam, the Hidden Imam.

There we could be sure of finding, invisibly present, all the pilgrims who had gone before us—not only Mîr Dâmâd, Mollâ Sadrâ, Mohsen Fayz, and Qâzî Sa'îd Qommî, but all those who, generation after generation, shaped Shiite thought and gave it its unique place in the religious history of humanity. (We shall return to this sanctuary later; see Book VII, Chapter II below.)

Yet Mollâ Sadrâ, in his turn, had to leave this landscape of mystical landmarks, whose center is the radiant dome of the sanctuary at Qomm.

Thus began the third period of his life. During his nine or eleven years at Kahak, he had reached the personal spiritual realization for which philosophy is the indispensable starting point, but without which philosophy, for him and for those who shared his outlook, would be a barren illusion.

However hard a personality of Mollâ Sadrâ's stature may try to keep his retreat secret, he can never quite succeed. He could not prevent students and disciples from seeking him out, and his reputation spread accordingly.

It is therefore not especially surprising to learn that Allâhwêrdî Khân—an Arabic-Persian name equivalent to our “God-given,” Adeodatus—who governed Fârs from 1003/1594–1595 until his death in 1021/1612, had a large madrasa, or college, built for our philosopher-shaykh in Shîrâz. He invited him to return to his native city and take charge of teaching at the new institution. This magnificent college still stands in Shîrâz (the Madrasa Khân), where one can visit the recently restored hall in which Mollâ Sadrâ gave his lectures.

I see no decisive reason to reject the explicit testimony of the historians who attribute this initiative to Governor Allâhwêrdî Khân. Nor is there reason to rule out the possibility that it was during the governor's lifetime, and therefore still under Shah 'Abbâs I (1587–1629), that Mollâ Sadrâ accepted the invitation to teach in Shîrâz and entered the third period of his life.84 When Allâhwêrdî Khân died, Mollâ Sadrâ was forty-one and in the fullness of his powers.

His teaching during these years in Shîrâz allows us to speak of a “School of Shîrâz” just as we have spoken of the “School of Ispahan.” Since Mollâ Sadrâ had been Mîr Dâmâd's disciple, this School of Shîrâz was also, in a sense, an offshoot of the School of Ispahan. Thomas Herbert, a seventeenth-century English traveler, recorded that “Shîrâz has a college where philosophy, astronomy, physics, chemistry and mathematics are taught, and it is the most famous college in Persia.”85

We can readily picture Mollâ Sadrâ's life there. He lived wholly absorbed in teaching, writing his books—some of which, alas, remained unfinished—and looking after his students. Nothing defines him better than the high moral teaching he gave them and practiced throughout his own life. It can be summed up in four demands made of anyone who wishes to advance along the spiritual path: give up the possession of riches; give up worldly ambition and the pursuit of advancement; give up sectarian or unthinking conformity (taqlîd); and give up every form of the spirit of denial (ma'siyat).86

These are the principles of an ethic entirely consistent with the strict distinction Mollâ Sadrâ drew between the “scholars of this world,” driven by worldly ambitions, and the “seekers of the other world”—those, as we might say today, whose inspiration remains directed toward the ultimate destiny of human life.87 Despite his enormous workload, Mollâ Sadrâ made the pilgrimage to Mecca seven times. He died at Basra on the return journey from his seventh pilgrimage and was buried there in 1050/1640.

The work through which this profound thinker, a spiritual man in the fullest sense—an intellectual who never betrayed his calling—continues to make his presence felt among us is immense. Almost all of it was published in Iran in lithographed editions during the last century; it comprises a little over forty titles.88

Some books run to a hundred pages or so, while others are monumental works of several hundred folio pages. Together they address the whole range of Islamic philosophy. Some follow a plan shaped by Mollâ Sadrâ's own research; others are commentaries, but so expansive and original that they too must be considered works in their own right.

We have already noted that Mollâ Sadrâ wrote a commentary on the metaphysical portion of Avicenna's great Shifâ' (The Healing),89 as well as on Sohrawardî's major work, the Book of Oriental Theosophy (Hikmat al-Ishrâq). Later we shall offer extracts from this fundamental commentary, which brings into view two great moments in the Iranian tradition of Illumination (ishrâq).

In commenting on Kolaynî's Book of the Sources (al-Osûl mina'l-Kâfî), one of Shiism's foundational works preserving the teaching of the holy Imams,90 Mollâ Sadrâ was building a monumental Summa of Shiite philosophy, which he unfortunately did not live to complete.91 He also composed a Tafsîr, a commentary on extensive portions of the Qur'an.92 Its principal concern is to uncover the Qur'anic text's hidden, spiritual, or gnostic meaning.

Alongside the works of his predecessors and successors, it shows us how the spiritual interpretation of the Qur'an has been an essential source of philosophical meditation in Islam (see Books II and III above). This was especially bound to be true of Shiite Islam, for reasons we have already explained and will return to shortly.

The Summa in which Sadrâ Shîrâzî gathered the fruits of all his labors, investigations, and meditations is the celebrated work he called The Four Spiritual Journeys (Kitâb al-Asfâr al-arba'a al-'aqlîya).93 It is a monument of scholarship and thought, filling no fewer than a thousand folio pages in the old lithographed edition.

More than any other work, it stirred the devotion of disciples and commentators. Together they form an impressive succession, beginning with two of his most famous immediate disciples, both also his sons-in-law: Mohsen Fayz and 'Abdorrazzâq Lâhîjî. It continues from generation to generation down to our own time, taking in, during the last century, 'Abdollah Zonûzî and his son Mollâ 'Alî Zonûzî, Mollâ Hâdî Sabzavârî, and so many others.

Here, in outline, is more than three centuries of Iranian philosophy.94 The questions raised by Shaykh Ahmad Ahsâ'î and the Shaykhî school cannot be properly understood without a sound knowledge of Mollâ Sadrâ's work. That is why they have been so poorly understood by theologians unfamiliar with mystical gnosis ('irfân), though all the more eager to stamp about on ground that is slipping away beneath their feet.

In short, I maintain that no serious study of the philosophical situation of Shiism is possible without familiarity with Sadrâ Shîrâzî's thought and writings. That, ultimately, is what matters.

What deep intention animated him throughout his life? To answer, we must first resist the illusion that we have “explained” a philosopher or a philosophy merely by identifying and cataloguing its “sources” and “precursors.”95 Such an inventory only prepares the way for the essential task: to establish the breadth of the thinker's horizon, the angle from which he sees, and the underlying lines of thought that connect, for example, the metaphysics of being, the doctrine of the Imams, and the philosophy of Resurrection.

In the end, Mollâ Sadrâ can be explained only through Mollâ Sadrâ himself. We may collect all the sources, quotations, and allusions we please; none of them will ever produce a Mollâ Sadrâ unless there is already a Mollâ Sadrâ to bring them together into an order and a structure that only he could give them.

Earlier I spoke of “Shiism in its fullness,” because the mystical and theosophical implications of that fullness reveal the motive behind the philosopher's twofold spiritual struggle: first against himself, then against the dark forces of a hostile outer world.

Mollâ Sadrâ fought the first of these spiritual battles during his years of solitude at Kahak. Nothing less was at stake than his most personal destiny, the meaning of the course his life had taken, and the passage from the philosopher's theoretical speculation to the certainty that the gnostic—the 'ârif, the one who knows through direct experience—has lived and verified for himself. Unless these two forms of knowing are united, there is no complete philosopher, no philosopher in the truest sense. This has been the whole purpose of ishrâqî spirituality since Sohrawardî.

But for Sadrâ Shîrâzî, as for his predecessors and successors, the union finds its essential fulfillment within Shiite spirituality.

Let us examine the matter more closely.

The word ishrâq has enjoyed an extraordinary place in Iranian philosophy since Sohrawardî used it in the twelfth century to characterize the wisdom of ancient Persia that he sought to revive. There is little of substance to add here to our earlier discussion (Book II), but a reminder is never wasted when it helps us understand what follows.

Let us therefore bring together, in a few lines, the essentials we need to keep in mind in reading Mollâ Sadrâ. Ishrâq signifies the splendor of the rising dawn and the morning illumination that bathes all who are present to that dawn. It also signifies the source and origin of this light: the Orient, the place and hour of the rising sun.

Every part of this imagery must be carried over into the world beyond the senses. The “Orient” here means the world of Light and of beings of light; the dawning illumination rises from the Orient of the hierarchical Intelligences and falls upon human souls exiled in the western realm of darkness.

Let us recall as well that the wisdom arising from this Orient of the soul, and therefore called “Oriental” in keeping with this mystical geography, is neither philosophy nor theology in the ordinary modern sense of two separate disciplines whose relationship has to be worked out. This “Oriental” wisdom (hikmat mashriqîya or ishrâqîya) is divine wisdom, hikmat ilâhîya—the exact equivalent of the Greek theosophia.

It guides the seeker beyond the philosopher's abstract knowledge, which knows things through an intervening form or concept—a knowledge by representation ('ilm sûrî)—toward direct vision, toward the illumination of a presence that rises in the soul's own Orient. This other form of knowing is no longer called representational but knowledge by presence ('ilm hozûrî). It is “Oriental” knowledge because it illuminates, and it illuminates because it comes from the “Orient.”

As we have shown, this is the mystical meaning of “Orient” and “Oriental” in the phrase Oriental Theosophy (Hikmat al-Ishrâq), the divine wisdom which, for Sohrawardî, belonged to Zoroaster and the sages of ancient Persia. We have also seen that, in ordinary philosophical usage, the Ishrâqîyûn, the philosophers of Illumination, are contrasted with the Mashshâ'ûn, the Peripatetics; in this sense the term corresponds to Platonists or Neoplatonists. These Neoplatonists of Islamic Persia have a long history, and they belong to the same spiritual family as Neoplatonists in every age and place.

“Oriental” knowledge, ishrâq, is the moment when the light of the soul's Orient—its origin before earthly existence—rises upon it. This was the very experience Mollâ Sadrâ lived through in the exalted solitude of Kahak.

He confides the experience to his reader in the prologue to his great work: “When I had persevered in that state of withdrawal, anonymity, and separation from the world for a long time,” he writes, “at last my inward striving set my soul ablaze; through repeated spiritual exercises my heart was kindled into towering flames.

“Then the lights of the Malakût, the angelic world, poured out upon my soul, while the secrets of the Jabarût, the world of pure cherubic Intelligences, were unfolded to it, and the mysteries of the divine Unity permeated it. I came to know divine secrets that I had never understood before; symbols and hidden meanings (romûz) were unveiled to me as no rational argument had ever been able to unveil them.

“Or rather: every metaphysical secret that I had previously known through rational demonstration I now perceived intuitively, in direct vision.” (Notice that the language describing this spiritual experience places it in complete harmony with those of Sohrawardî and Mîr Dâmâd. Unshakable certainty springs not from logical argument, but from immediate presence, experienced intuitively and sometimes in visions.) “Then,” Mollâ Sadrâ continues, “God inspired me to offer a sip of the drink I had tasted, to quench the thirst of those who seek [...].

“And so I have composed a book for pilgrims in search of spiritual perfection. In it I disclose a wisdom bestowed by God (hikmat rabbânîya) that can lead seekers toward the Majesty enveloped in Beauty and Rigor.”96

That book is the great Summa Mollâ Sadrâ entitled The Four Spiritual Journeys. What did he mean by this title? He explains it himself at the end of the prologue. It draws on the traditional vocabulary of Islamic mystical gnosis. The first journey begins in the world of created beings and leads to God (mina'l-khalq ilâ'l-Haqq). Along the way it examines the composition of beings, the whole field of physics, matter and form, substance and accident. By its end, the pilgrim has risen to the suprasensible plane of divine realities.

The second journey then begins from God, in God, and through God (fî'l-Haqq bî'l-Haqq). Here the pilgrim remains on the metaphysical plane and is initiated into the Ilâhîyât, the Divinalia, the divine realities: questions concerning the divine Essence, Names, and Attributes.

The third journey follows a course of thought opposite to the first. It “descends” again from God to the world of created beings, but now “with God,” or “through God” (mina'l-Haqq ilâ'l-khalq bi'l-Haqq).

It follows the procession of beings from the Light of Lights and opens the way to knowledge of the hierarchical Intelligences and the multitude of suprasensible universes, whose levels rise above the physical world perceived by the senses. Here we encounter the whole of cosmogony and angelology.

Finally, the fourth journey takes place “with God,” or “through God,” within the created world itself (bi'l-Haqq fî'l-khalq). Above all, it initiates the pilgrim into knowledge of the soul, which means knowledge of oneself—the knowledge of the “Orient.” It also opens the way to esoteric tawhîd, the recognition that God alone truly is, and to the meaning of the saying: “Whoever knows his soul”—that is, whoever knows himself—“knows his Lord.”

Finally, it opens the perspectives of eschatology, of the great Return (Ma'âd): the boundless worlds awaiting the human being who has crossed the threshold of death.97

These few lines can give only the faintest idea of the great Summa in which Sadrâ Shîrâzî erected a monument of Iranian Islamic thought. If we wished to characterize our shaykh in broad historical terms, we would have to list the distinguishing features of Shiite philosophy already encountered in the School of Ispahan.

In one sense, he is an Avicennian: Mollâ Sadrâ knew Avicenna's works extraordinarily well and wrote commentaries on them. At the same time, he is an ishrâqî Avicennian. That is to say, he has traveled the whole distance between Avicenna and Sohrawardî—a distance symbolized by the symbolic distance between the ending of Avicenna's story of Hayy ibn Yaqzân and the opening of Sohrawardî's Tale of the Western Exile.

Moreover, Sadrâ offers a highly personal interpretation of Sohrawardî's metaphysics of illumination. He is deeply steeped in the teachings of the great mystical theosopher Mohyiddîn Ibn 'Arabî (d. 1240), and, like Haydar Âmolî before him (see Book IV, Chapter I above), he invites us to investigate more deeply what might be called Ibn 'Arabî's implicit, or “crypto-,” Shiism.98

Above all, however, Mollâ Sadrâ is a Shiite thinker, profoundly formed by the teachings of the holy Imams and committed to Islam as those teachings disclose it. These are only points of orientation. Neither the man nor his work can be “explained” as the sum or product of the influences we have just distinguished.

Prior to all of them stands what Ibn 'Arabî's vocabulary, which Sadrâ shares, calls his “eternal haecceity” ('ayn thâbita): his own individual archetype. This is what originally called the “materials” of his work together and fused them into the unique whole they became. It is therefore the first and final “explanation” of the structure of his entire work. The axis of that structure is the doctrine of the Shiite Imams, as we can see in his great commentary on Kolaynî's Book of the Sources—sources that are, in the fullest sense, the sources of “divine knowledge.”

Here Mollâ Sadrâ engages in his other spiritual struggle, this time against devout forms of agnosticism: blind literalism, an exclusively legal understanding of religion, and, in short, every attitude that for one reason or another rejects the Imams' teaching about the inner meaning of revelation, thereby rejecting the very essence of mystical gnosis, or 'irfân. Mollâ Sadrâ's stated intentions help us understand the philosophical situation of Shiism. They also reveal the enduring significance of his work and its continuing living power within Shiite thought.

2. The Shiite Thinker and “Prophetic Philosophy”

How does the Shiite vision present itself to the 'orafâ—those who not only profess what is called 'irfân-e shî'î, Shiite gnosis, but regard Shiism itself, the doctrine of the Imams, as the very essence of Islam's inner spiritual knowledge, its esotericism: as Islam in its fullness and therefore as the true spiritual Islam? The answer emerges from the discussions already developed in this book (see Books I and IV above), in which Mollâ Sadrâ's commentary on Kolaynî's corpus, together with the writings of Haydar Âmolî, has served as our principal guide into the Imams' thought.

Yet, once again, because a recapitulation can be valuable, I think it useful to bring together the main steps that lead Mollâ Sadrâ to a thesis of decisive importance: that, within Islam, Shiism alone has been able to bring divine Revelation and philosophical intelligence into harmony, like the voices of a symphony.

For the 'orafâ, Shiite doctrine is founded on two inseparable poles: the sharî'at, the literal form of divine Revelation, and the haqîqat, that Revelation's spiritual, gnostic truth. These correspond to the outward, literal, visible aspect (zâhir) of divine Revelations and their inward, secret, esoteric reality (bâtin). Consequently, they correspond also to prophecy and the Imamate. Having stated the matter this way, we can trace the path that leads to it. For clarity, let us distinguish five stages.

  1. Everyone agrees on why prophets are necessary. A prophet here is not someone who “predicts the future,” but an inspired, more-than-ordinary human being who delivers a divine message that humanity could never attain by its own powers. Prophets are therefore extraordinary human beings whom divine inspiration appoints as mediators between the unknowable Godhead and human ignorance or helplessness. There have been six great prophets entrusted with revealing a divine Law, a sharî'at, to humanity. Their names—Adam, Noah, Abraham, Moses, Jesus, and Mohammad—mark the successive periods that together form the “cycle of prophecy” (dâ'irat al-nobowwat). The Prophet of Islam was the Seal of the Prophets (Khâtim al-anbiyâ'). After him, no further prophet will come to reveal a new divine Law.
  2. The Shiite idea can be traced historically not only to the Prophet's immediate circle but also to what the Prophet himself said about the person closest to him, Imam 'Alî ibn Abî Tâlib. This idea reveals the tragedy implicit in the closing of the prophetic message. Shiism asks a fundamental question: if humanity has always needed prophets in order to live through its destiny, what becomes of it now that the last prophet has come and there will never again be a prophet-messenger (rasûl)? A second, equally serious question follows. The Book revealed from heaven to a prophet is no ordinary book. Its meaning is not confined to its outward, literal wording, nor can it be exhausted through philology and dialectical reasoning. It is a Book with hidden depths. The secret meaning of a divine text, of a divine Word, cannot be reconstructed by syllogisms. It can only be handed down by “those who know” to those in whom this spiritual truth, in turn, becomes an immediate certainty, bringing about in them a new birth—their spiritual birth. Since the full reality of Qur'anic Revelation embraces both what is apparent and what is hidden, zâhir and bâtin, outward and inward meaning, there must remain after the Prophet a “Keeper of the Book” (Qayyim bi'l-Kitâb) who can initiate others into its complete meaning. This is the teaching of the Imams themselves; Mollâ Sadrâ is simply its interpreter.
  3. This is why Shiite theology holds that the “cycle of prophecy” has been succeeded by the “cycle of walâyat,” the cycle of spiritual initiation and guidance. More precisely, what has ended is lawgiving prophecy (nobowwat al-tashrî'), the mission of a prophet who reveals a sharî'at. But under a new name, walâyat, another kind of prophecy continues: not the giving of a new Law, but a permanent prophecy concerned with inward and hidden realities, an esoteric prophetic message, or nobowwat bâtinîya. In Mollâ Sadrâ's vocabulary, the term follows from the very definition of walâyat as the “inward dimension of prophecy” (bâtin al-nobowwat). This permanent prophecy began at the dawn of earthly humanity and will continue until the appearance of the Imam who announces the Resurrection (Qâ'im al-Qiyâmat).
  4. The metaphysical foundation of this doctrine lies in the “Mohammadan Reality,” also called the “eternal Prophetic Reality” (Haqîqat mohammadîya). This reality has two “dimensions,” two “aspects,” and therefore requires two forms of manifestation. Its outward dimension appears in the lawgiving prophet; its inward dimension appears in the Imam. Together the “Fourteen Immaculate Ones” (tchahârdeh Ma'sûm)—the Prophet, his daughter Hazrat-e Fâtima, and the Twelve Imams—form the pleroma of light, the complete spiritual assembly of eternal prophecy. The twelve Imams share one and the same essence; their “persons of light” shone forth in pre-eternity. During their brief appearances on earth they were the “Keepers of the Book,” initiating disciples into its complete, inward meaning. (Their teachings, as we have said, fill several folio volumes.)
  5. Just as the fullness of lawgiving prophecy had to be manifested on earth in the one who was the “Seal of the Prophets,” so the fullness of walâyat, the inward dimension of prophecy (bâtin al-nobowwat), had to be manifested in the “Seal of walâyat.” This Seal is the Mohammadan Imamate: in the First Imam, as the Seal of universal walâyat, common to every period of prophecy; and in the Twelfth Imam, as the Seal of Mohammadan walâyat. (This is the Shiite position that Haydar Âmolî defended so forcefully against Ibn 'Arabî; see Book II, Chapter I above.) Yet the Twelfth Imam, present both to the past and to the future, whose Manifestation—his return or parousia—will reveal the hidden meaning of every divine Revelation since the dawn of human life on earth, is at present invisible. We live in the time of his occultation (ghaybat), which will endure until human beings have made themselves capable of seeing him. In the figure of the Hidden Imam, Shiism has discerned the deepest mystery of human history, a mystery also foreshadowed in Zoroastrianism by the Saoshyant, in Buddhism by the Buddha to come, Maitreya, and in the Christianity of the spiritual reformers, from the thirteenth-century followers of Joachim of Fiore onward, by the expectation of the reign of the Holy Spirit.

Brief as this summary is, it is enough to remind us that Islamic philosophy and spirituality cannot be reduced to the three groups to which our histories have traditionally allotted their chapters on Islamic philosophy: the so-called Hellenizing philosophers (falâsifa), the Motakallimûn—the practitioners of Sunni Kalâm, or dialectical theology, representing the scholastic tradition of Islam—and, finally, the Sufis.

We already know that there is something more. It is precisely this further dimension that has helped us understand why philosophy, generally considered to have exhausted itself elsewhere in Islam after Averroes at the end of the twelfth century, underwent such a magnificent rebirth in the Shiite world of Iran, with the School of Ispahan.

When a researcher succeeds in entering the heart of Shiite thought, an entirely new horizon opens. Outside that horizon, the question of philosophy's place in Islam, and of its relation to Islamic dogma, has been posed on a false footing.

We have already seen why. Wherever it is held necessary to pass from what is apparent to what is hidden, from the outward to the inward meaning, facts themselves are transformed into symbols, and thought is called upon, again and again, to go beyond itself into the night of symbols.

A symbol is silence: it speaks, and it does not speak. It is not an allegory and can never be deciphered once and for all, as a celebrated saying of the Fifth Imam so aptly affirms. The first question, then, is whether one recognizes that divine Revelation has hidden meanings and, consequently, that there is an esoteric Islam into which the Imams initiated their followers—or whether one rejects all this outright in the name of a religion confined to the letter and the Law.

In the first case, philosophy will be at home, and it will take the form of a “prophetic philosophy.” In the second, there is no longer even any place to speak of philosophy. The tragedy endured by Mollâ Sadrâ, and by many others before and after him—including Haydar Âmolî, as we have seen, some three centuries earlier—was that their accusers called themselves Shiites too.

Yet the paradox is only apparent. In the eyes of the 'orafâ, the gnostics, some people may claim the name of Shiism while, by rejecting gnosis ('irfân), destroying what constitutes its very essence: the indissoluble union of zâhir and bâtin, outward and inward meaning.

An anguished echo of this tragedy runs through all Mollâ Sadrâ's writings. It was the tragedy that drove him into voluntary exile at Kahak, away from the persecution of zealots devoted to the letter and the Law. In the prologue to The Four Spiritual Journeys,99 for example, he denounces those willfully ignorant people whose minds cannot rise beyond the forms of material things, beyond the “dwellings of darkness and their dust.”

Hostile to a gnosis and philosophy they have never understood, they seek to banish all philosophy from the traditional religious sciences, even though this leaves them unable to understand the divine secrets expressed by the prophets in enigmas and symbols (romûz). These people declare that the gnostic philosophers have fallen victim to a divine ruse and have been led astray.

In his book The Three Sources, Mulla Sadra turns on one of these ignorant critics with magnificent force: “Have you not considered,” he asks, “that the person who has been led astray might be someone like you? If all knowledge is as you understand it, if it must be received word for word from tradition and from the shaykhs, why does God, in several verses of the Quran, condemn those who base their beliefs on just such conformity and put their trust in it? When the Commander of the Faithful, the First Imam, declares, ‘If I wished, I could produce a commentary on the opening surah of the Quran alone that would weigh as much as seventy camel-loads,’ did he acquire such knowledge from a human teacher, through ordinary instruction?”100

Mulla Sadra then appeals to the very texts Haydar Amoli had invoked three centuries before him. To begin with, those who seek inner knowledge have the decisive authority of the Fourth Imam, Zayn al-Abidin (d. 95/714), who declares in one of his poems: “I hide the jewels of my Knowledge, for fear that an ignorant man, seeing the truth, might crush us. ... Lord, if I disclosed a single pearl of my gnosis, they would say to me: ‘So you are an idolater!’ And some Muslims would consider it lawful to shed my blood!

“What is most beautiful in what is offered to them, they find abhorrent.” What, Mulla Sadra asks, is this knowledge of which the Imam speaks so movingly—this sublime knowledge, beyond ordinary understanding, which makes someone appear impious, even idolatrous, in the eyes of the Muslim majority? His answer is straightforward. He finds it in a declaration by Abdallah ibn Abbas, one of the Prophet’s best-known Companions, who once exclaimed before a gathering near Mecca: “If I revealed to you how I heard the Prophet himself interpret the verse concerning the creation of the seven heavens and the seven earths (65:12), you would stone me.”101

Thus anyone admitted, by divine grace, to the ultimate secret of the prophetic message risks being stoned by an enraged crowd of the ignorant. Must we look any further for the reasons behind the tragedy? Is there any other explanation for why the Imams of Shiism were surrounded by no more than a handful of knights of the faith?

Mulla Sadra can therefore readily show that the knowledge which so frightens ordinary people and the doctors of religious law is neither dialectics nor philology, medicine nor astronomy, geometry nor physics. None of what the interpreters concerned only with the Quran’s outward meaning—Zamakhshari and others like him, for example—offer is the Quran’s true knowledge, the true inner understanding of divine Revelation.

All of it belongs to philology, grammar, and dialectics; it never penetrates beyond the husk, the outer covering. The Quran’s true knowledge is something altogether different.102 And it is precisely this genuine understanding of the Quran, grounded in the Imams’ esoteric teaching, that assigns the philosopher the task of prophetic philosophy.

To make clear the “straight path” (sirat mustaqim)—or, to use a traditional expression going back to Philo, the “royal road”—which steers equally clear of the literalism of a religion reduced to law and of a rationalism that simply denies, Sadra explains the role of philosophical reflection in the prologue to his commentary on Book III of Kolayni’s great work, the Kitab al-Hujja, a treatise on the Imam and the Imamate.

Quranic Revelation is the light that makes sight possible; but it can do so only when the teaching of the Imams lifts the veil of literal appearances that covers it. Philosophical reflection is the eye that sees and contemplates that light. For vision to occur there must be light, but there must also be eyes that look. Remove the light and the eyes will see nothing.

Yet stubbornly close the eyes—as the literalists and doctors of the Law do—and nothing will be seen either. In both cases darkness triumphs; nor is the condition of someone who opens only one eye, and so sees with the vision of a one-eyed man, any better. Bring philosophical understanding and divine Revelation together, however, and there is “light upon light,” as the Verse of Light says (Quran 24:35).

Indeed, as we know, the successive parts of that Quranic verse refer, in their esoteric meaning, to the Fourteen Immaculate Ones. This is why Mulla Sadra solemnly proclaims his thesis: in Islam, the Shiite school alone has achieved this harmony, this symphony of divine Revelation and philosophical understanding. It has done so because the Shiites draw their knowledge and wisdom from the “Niche of Lights” of prophecy and walayat—the spiritual authority and guidance of the Imams.103 In other words, the philosophy of Shiism is, in its very essence, “prophetic philosophy.”

We should not be too quick to assimilate this situation to others familiar to us. What had to be overcome here was not a conflict between contingent historical truths and necessary truths of reason, nor the question of how truth can be historical and how history can be truth. That has been the whole problem of faith and knowledge confronted by Christian philosophy, from Origen through Leibniz to Hegel.

Nor was it a conflict between dogmatic truths defined by the authority of a Church’s teaching office and philosophical truths discovered through personal effort. No: the light of the holy Book, unveiled by the Imam as a personal guide, shines directly, without intermediary, upon the believer’s inner vision. Philosophy and theology do not confront one another as two already established authorities, one belonging to the individual and the other to an institutional teaching office. Their separation is a phenomenon peculiar to the West, with roots in medieval scholasticism.

By contrast, we must always bear in mind that, for our “Eastern” thinkers, the being of the Pleroma, the fullness of the heavenly world—the Angel whom philosophers call the Active Intellect ('aql fa''al, the Greek nous poietikos), is identified with the Holy Spirit who communicates divine Revelation to the prophets. This heavenly Intellect is also the source of our knowledge.

We have insisted on this point before: identifying the Angel of Knowledge with the Angel of Revelation does not mean reducing Spirit to reason. It means that the calling of the prophet and that of the philosopher bear a common imprint. This is precisely what allows philosophy, at its highest point, to become “prophetic philosophy.”104

We are therefore very far from the doctrine of “double truth” that emerged in Western Averroism. Here, in “Eastern” philosophy, two lights come together and interpenetrate, giving rise to hikmat ilahiya: divine wisdom, or theosophy, which the Imams themselves were the first to call ma'rifat qalbiya, the knowledge of the heart. For Mulla Sadra, this is Shiism—Shiism in its fullness.

We can now see even more clearly why a thinker for whom the inner, gnostic faith of Shiism is fundamental should also be, quite naturally, an Ishraqi, a philosopher of illumination. What, after all, did Suhrawardi teach? That mystical experience without prior philosophical formation runs a serious risk of going astray. Conversely, as we recalled above, a philosophy that neither seeks nor leads to personal spiritual realization is sheer vanity. The whole design of The Book of Eastern Theosophy answers to this demand.

In a densely argued passage of his commentary on Kolayni, Mulla Sadra in turn places the spirituality of the Ishraqiyun, the philosophers of illumination, in an intermediate position—a barzakh, a place of meeting between two ways. It joins the method of the Sufis, whose chief aim is inner purification, with the method of the philosophers, who seek pure knowledge. We have already referred twice to this passage, so decisive does it seem to us for understanding the spirituality of Iranian Islam.105

After commenting on the Imams’ theory of knowledge and distinguishing the various degrees of inspiration (ilham), Mulla Sadra pauses in this passage to discuss the Sufis’ spiritual method at some length. He observes: “As for reflective thinkers, and those who know how to take the measure of things (dhawu'l-i'tibar), they certainly do not deny the existence of this method or the possibility that it may reach its goal in exceptional cases. Such, indeed, was the case with most of the spiritual states (ahwal) experienced by the prophets and the awliya, the friends of God.

“Outside such cases, however, they consider the method hazardous; they judge its fruits slow to ripen and doubt that all the conditions it requires will ever be met. ...” His final conclusion is this: “The best course is for the pilgrim journeying toward God (al-salik ila'llah) to bring the two methods together.

“Let his inner discipline and purification (tasfiya) never be without philosophical reflection (tafakkur); and, conversely, let his philosophical reflection never be without an effort toward spiritual purification. Better still, let his spiritual method itself be a barzakh, an intermediate way joining the two paths (bayna'l-tariqayn). Such is the path followed by the Hukama' Ishraqiyun, the Eastern theosophers.” This is exactly the doctrine Suhrawardi professes in the prologue to his great book.106

This position also explains why Mulla Sadra could sometimes speak harshly of certain Sufis:107 those who make a show of despising intellectual effort and whose contempt for philosophy leaves them just as blind as their opposites, the little-minded defenders of a religion reduced to law.

In fact, Sadra Shirazi belongs, along with many others, to a type of Shiite spiritual seeker who speaks the technical language of Sufism without belonging to any organized tariqa, or Sufi order. For Shiite 'irfan—the inner knowledge of Shiism—is already itself the tariqa, the spiritual path; and the bond of personal devotion to the holy Imams is already the beginning of initiation.

From here we can begin to see how Mulla Sadra’s major doctrines form a coherent whole, though we shall confine ourselves to two fundamental aspects.

First, his metaphysics of being culminates in a metaphysics of Presence; as this rises into a metaphysics of “witnessing,” it reaches the summit of prophetic philosophy.

Second, from that very summit we can trace a continuous line toward a metaphysics of active Imagination and the imaginal world, culminating in a metaphysics of Resurrection. Mulla Sadra himself will lay out this continuous line when he summarizes his whole doctrine in eight theses (below, § 4). Here we shall briefly recall how his metaphysics of being becomes a metaphysics of Presence.

We shall then draw out the principal features of his metaphysics of Resurrection from the final portion of his extensive commentary on Suhrawardi’s Book of Eastern Theosophy. Since we have just heard him explicitly identify himself with the spiritual method of the Ishraqiyun, we will thus have brought together these two moments of “Eastern theosophy” as defining moments in Iranian philosophy and spirituality.

Mulla Sadra’s metaphysics of being is “revolutionary” in that it overturns the venerable metaphysics of essences taught by Farabi, Avicenna, Suhrawardi, and many other “essentialists.” In their account of reality, an essence or quiddity (mahiyya)—what a thing is—remains immutably what it is. The word is, in saying so, does not imply actual existence. Existence was held to be merely a way of considering an essence, adding nothing to it because it did not constitute what that essence was.

Mulla Sadra reverses this perspective. In his commentary on Suhrawardi, this reversal will allow him to give the metaphysics of Ishraq, or illumination, an “existential” interpretation. Readers will find far more technical detail than we can offer here in our translation of and commentary on the Book of Metaphysical Penetrations (Kitab al-Masha'ir).

In particular, we showed there how illuminating it is to compare the vocabulary of being in Latin and Greek with its vocabulary in Arabic and Persian.108 Such comparisons will provide a foundation for the comparative study of being that still awaits us. For the first ways in which different traditions understand being reveal affinities or deep differences between philosophical systems and, through them, between cultures—even between different regions of a single culture.

In Mulla Sadra’s metaphysics of being, no essence precedes its own act of existing. An essence is by being what it is; the intensity of its act of being what it is determines the degree to which it exists. This act of being can take place at every level of the scale of existence, from mental existence (wujud dhihni) through all the levels of existence beyond the mind: sensible, imaginal, and intelligible.

Since it is the act of being that determines an essence, the same essence, far from being immutable, can undergo degrees of intensification or weakening according to its acts of being, along a scale that is practically without limit. Motion is thereby introduced into the very category of substance. This gives rise to Mulla Sadra’s distinctive doctrine of “intrasubstantial motion” (harakat jawhariyya).

No longer do we have, as we did with his philosophical predecessors, a realm of unchanging essences. In his thought we can speak of a mobility, a restless striving within being, extending from one end of the scale of beings to the other. An essence is thus capable of passing through a cycle of metamorphoses, each stage corresponding to another level of the universe.

Consider, for example, the idea of a body. To understand its essence, we must not confine its act of being to the physical world as perceived by the senses.

We must follow it from the simple Element—the word denoting, in traditional physics, essentially a qualitative state—through successive metamorphoses: from mineral to plant, from plant to animal, and then to the state of a living, speaking body capable of understanding spiritual realities. There is a material body, but there is also a psychic body and a spiritual body (caro spiritualis).

We shall see later that each of these last two is the “temple,” the dwelling place, of a future rebirth and resurrection. During our present earthly life, we determine whether we shall be capable of such a resurrection or whether, defeated, we shall fall below what we could have become.109

There is, then, something like a tremendous upward surge of being, rising from the depths of inorganic existence to the emergence of earthly human form, and going still further beyond it. For the human being, as he exists in this world, is still a being in between.

We must not misunderstand this: Mulla Sadra’s vision reaches far beyond, and moves in quite another direction from, the evolutionism that has become a dogma in the West. In that doctrine everything unfolds along a horizontal line, on one and the same level of being. People speak endlessly and carelessly of the “meaning of history,” forgetting that to speak of such a meaning one must at least possess an eschatology—a vision of ultimate destiny.

The movement of Mulla Sadra’s universe, like that of all the thinkers we are considering, is not the movement of a world evolving but of a world ascending. Its orientation is vertical, Gothic in style, we might say. It corresponds to the Mabda' and the Ma'ad, the Origin and the Return, through which metahistory—the dimension of reality beyond ordinary historical time—breaks into our world.

This irruption of metahistory, together with our example of the body and the metamorphoses through which it takes part in being’s upward movement, gives us what we need to suggest how profoundly Mulla Sadra’s “existential” metaphysics differs from contemporary “existentialism.” Elsewhere we have examined at greater length the texts in which Sadra’s concept of existence becomes clear as a concept of Presence, so that the degree of the act of being, or existing (wujud), is defined in terms of Presence (huzur).110

As our shaykh explains, the astronomical heavens, for instance, are not present to the Earth considered as a physical mass. Nothing belonging to the world of phenomena—matter, extension, bodily volume, spatial distance—can be present to anything else in this sense. A being is present to itself, is present to another, and can have another present to it—indeed, there can be any such presence at all—only to the extent that the being becomes “separated” (tajrid) from the conditions of this world, which is subject to extension, volume, distance, and chronological time.

The more completely it frees itself from those conditions, the further it moves from what makes absence, concealment, and death possible. It is therefore also increasingly freed from the conditions of a being destined to end, a “being-toward-death.” For Mulla Sadra and all the Ishraqiyun, the more intense the degree of Presence, the more intense the act of existing. And the more fully this existence is an act of being that extends beyond death, the more fully the being makes up its “lag” (ta'akkhor) behind total Presence. Our shaykh’s entire philosophy of Resurrection develops this fundamental insight.

Because his metaphysics of being is an “existential” metaphysics that gives existence priority over essence, it culminates in Presence, which is itself the act of being of a spiritual being. (A thing is not “present” to another thing.) Because this metaphysics has no agnostic reflex that would rule out knowledge of spiritual realities, and because it conceives of being as an ordered hierarchy of many levels and worlds, its idea of Presence cannot possibly privilege “presence in this world.”

Quite the opposite: it liberates the human being from this world, since this world is incompatible with the act of true Presence. Presence, as Mulla Sadra understands it, is certainly a presence that is “committed,” to use a fashionable word.

But it is committed, here and now, beyond death and on the far side of death, to a destiny after earthly life—the destiny we shall discuss later, and one it is much less fashionable to speak about today. Such Presence cannot be ensnared by the apparent history of this world, because commitment in the fullest and truest sense can only be to what belongs to metahistory.

A being can undertake that commitment only when its “polar dimension” is revealed to it; and that revelation already makes its act of existing an act of presence to the worlds beyond death. Nor does our existence in this world emerge from some preceding nothingness. Sadra expressly invokes the passage in which Ibn Babuyeh affirms the general Shiite belief in preexistence—the preexistence of Spirits before bodies.

The scale of being, and the reach of the many forms of Presence embraced by “knowledge through presence” ('ilm huzuri), cannot be measured by the same standards in this traditional metaphysics as in a philosophy paralyzed by agnosticism. To Mulla Sadra, the assumptions of the latter philosophy could only deepen a being’s “lag,” compelling it to remain behind itself. We are clearly far from what is called “existentialism” today.

Are there philosophical arguments we might exchange in order to convince one another about such matters? We hardly think so. These are things given in immediate experience: either one perceives them or one does not. No dialectical argument can change that, and phenomenological analysis must be all the more attentive to them.

The idea of Presence, as we have said, implies that of a witness, a shahid. An eyewitness is someone who is “present to” something, who sees directly. Suhrawardi had already maintained that if we trust the testimony of observations made by Hipparchus and Ptolemy in astronomy, we should also trust the testimony of those who have entered the Malakut, the spiritual world.

In Mulla Sadra, the metaphysics of Presence develops into a metaphysics of witnessing, culminating in the doctrine of the Imams at the summit of prophetic philosophy. The spiritual understanding of the Imams is, above all, a theosophy founded on testimony and witnessing. We have already glimpsed this summit (Book I, chapter VII, § 4). Here it will be enough to recall the ways in which Mulla Sadra leads us toward it.111

One of the most important titles the hadith give the Twelve Imams is “Witnesses of God.” In that capacity, each of the Twelve has a twofold role: toward God, to whom he is present and who is present through him to human beings; and toward human beings, to whom God is present through him and who, through him, are present to God.112

Existence understood as Presence, and Presence understood as a union of a special kind between the knower and what is known—this is the insight that allows Mulla Sadra to penetrate the meaning of the Imam’s simultaneous presence in both directions. It allows him to place Shiite teaching about the Imams, and the persons of the Twelve Imams themselves, not merely on the level of their earthly appearance and historical lives but on the level of their metaphysical reality as God’s eternal Witnesses.

The metaphysics of Presence unfolds into a metaphysics of the witness borne by God’s Witnesses: those who are present to God and through whom God is present to humanity and humanity is present to God. The very idea of walayat traces out and completes this circle. This is what gives full meaning to the saying: “Whoever dies without knowing his Imam dies the death of those who remain unaware.”

It is in the same capacity that the Imams are also called both the Treasurers and the Treasures of divine knowledge: they are at once the medium and the object of God’s own knowing. For everything the Divine Being knows is known through its knowledge of itself—in an act of self-knowledge. What the Divine Being knows in this way are the forms of beings. Just as it knows the beings of the cosmic creation through their Angels, so it knows, through the Imams and the awliya, the beings who are accomplishing their Return toward it. This parallel is essential.113

The gnostic’s ('arif’s) knowledge of the Imam is not simply knowledge of his outward person as he appears in physical form; anyone can know him in that way. Truly to know the Imam is to be present to the Imam’s Presence as Witness of God. The Presence of this Witness to God means God’s Presence to itself in that eternal Adam, in the hidden, inner reality of the “Muhammadan Reality” that is the primordial theophany, the first divine self-disclosure. This self-presence is, by that very fact, the emergence of manifested being on the spiritual plane.

To be present to the Imam is therefore to be present, through him, to the God to whom the Imam himself is present as Witness; and through this same Witness, God is present to everyone who is present to the Witness and to whom the Witness is present.

If we fail to understand that it is through and within this Witness that Deus absconditus, the hidden God, becomes Deus revelatus, the revealed God—if, in other words, we do not understand that this Witness, the Imam, provides both the form and the content of all human knowledge of God—then monotheism, reduced to an abstraction, falls into the trap of metaphysical idolatry. It confuses the Witness with the One on whose behalf the Witness testifies and to whom he answers: the One who can be reached only through the testimony he gives to himself within this Witness.

We can now understand how, through this reciprocity of Presences, the Imam becomes, in Mulla Sadra’s spirituality, the inner Witness and Guide (Hujjat batina). This is why we have already seen the famous saying, “Whoever knows himself knows his Lord,” overlaid, as though in a transparent image, by another: “Whoever knows his Imam knows his Lord.”

The mysticism of Najm Kobra, for its part, introduced us to the inner master, the invisible Guide (shaykh al-ghayb, ostad ghaybi). And Semnani’s way of reading sacred texts, together with his vocabulary, had already led us to speak of “the Imam of your being.” In doing so, we were anticipating what the doctrine of the Imams now shows us: how that very doctrine contains the foundation and the secret of its own inward realization.

The profound link between Mulla Sadra’s prophetic philosophy and Shiite spirituality thus comes into view. The Ishraqi metaphysics of Presence culminates in a metaphysics of the Imamate as divine Presence to the human being, who is himself present to his inner Witness and Guide. The Imams, as Witnesses, are that Presence.

We shall see later how Qazi Sa'id Qommi arrives at a closely similar analysis by taking up another theme furnished by the hadith.

A few pages ago we said that from the doctrine of the Imams, at the summit of prophetic philosophy, we could glimpse a continuous path leading to a metaphysics of Resurrection. We have now learned that the Imam is the Witness whom God beholds and through whom he beholds: God knows the believer through that believer’s “inner Imam.” Through the Imams he knows and looks upon the beings who are making their Return toward him.

But this Return is precisely the upward surge of being, the restlessness that sets beings in motion at every level of its hierarchy. Mulla Sadra seeks to account for this movement through his “existential” metaphysics, in which the act of being of each creature opens into a cycle of metamorphoses. The present “cycle of walayat,” whose place in the prophetic philosophy of Shiism we have just recalled, marks the phase of this Return corresponding to humanity’s present condition.

Since the Imam is the Perfect Human Being (al-Insan al-kamil), Adam in the true sense, the metaphysical Adam (Adam al-haqiqi), we can discern a connection between the doctrine of the Imams and the understanding of humanity of which that doctrine is the supreme expression. The philosophy of Resurrection discloses precisely the secret, the inner meaning, of that connection. Its nature and significance will have to be developed in future research.

Here we wish only to sketch the metaphysics of Resurrection as it emerges from the masterly glosses Mulla Sadra wrote in the margins of Suhrawardi’s Eastern Theosophy. Alongside the fundamental principles of his metaphysics of being, this metaphysics of Resurrection brings into play two further defining doctrines of Sadra Shirazi: one concerning active Imagination, the other the imaginal world.

3. Toward a Metaphysics of Resurrection

Mulla Sadra’s collected glosses on Suhrawardi’s Book of Eastern Theosophy form a substantial work: in a typeset edition they would fill a hefty volume of some six hundred pages. The modest title should not mislead us. Under the name of glosses, scholia, or marginal annotations (hashiyat, ta'liqat), Sadra Shirazi has in fact produced a monumental and deeply personal work.

Some of these glosses occupy only a few lines; others have the scope and weight of complete lectures, in which the commentator examines Suhrawardi’s text in depth, almost always striving to establish his own position. His response ranges through every shade, from admiring agreement to reservation and criticism. Perhaps what we possess here are the texts of lectures Mulla Sadra delivered either during his years in Shiraz or even earlier.

These glosses begin with the first book of the first part of the work by the Shaykh al-Ishraq, the Master of Illumination, and continue to the end of the fifth and final book of its second part. Elsewhere we have expressed the hope that a critical edition will soon appear, and described the form in which the glosses are preserved in the only lithographed edition so far published.114

I shall recall only that, when working particularly closely on the glosses to the second part—the characteristic portion of Suhrawardi’s book—I found it necessary, for ease of reference, to count them and give them consecutive numbers from beginning to end. I arrived at a total of six hundred and forty-six glosses across both parts, allowing for a possible margin of error, though it should not amount to more than a few.

Whenever a gloss is numbered in the pages that follow, that number refers to my sequence. We also give the corresponding page in the old lithographed edition and, where appropriate, the page of Suhrawardi’s own text in our edition, identified by the initials H.I. All the glosses we discuss here concern Book V of the second part of Eastern Theosophy, the book devoted above all to the last things and to resurrection.

We shall follow these glosses as one follows a rhapsody, for a rhapsody rather than a systematic construction is what they are.

Yet the teachings of the master of Shiraz grow and deepen, taking on the themes closest to his heart as Suhrawardi’s text calls them forth. At the beginning of Book V, that text first confronts him with the question of transmigration (tanasukh): the passage of a soul from one body to another. Mulla Sadra will explain in what sense he finds transmigration inconceivable, and how we might interpret the ancient sages, including Pythagoras and Plato, who upheld it.

But a more pressing problem takes hold of him. The Muslim thinkers who preceded him seem to have left Mulla Sadra with a choice. Either resurrection is understood as ma'ad jismani, a bodily resurrection, taken by literalist theologians to mean the material restoration of the elemental, physical body; or it is understood with the philosophers of the Avicennian school as ma'ad ruhani, a resurrection that is purely spiritual.

We shall see Mulla Sadra reject this dilemma and dismiss the theologians and philosophers alike—Ghazali no less than Avicenna—while explaining why both have failed to develop a genuine “philosophy of Resurrection.” What they lacked was an account of the reality of the interworld, the realm between the sensible and the intelligible that Suhrawardi was the first to give a place within a philosophical scheme. They lacked, in fact, the faculty through which that interworld can be grasped and understood: active Imagination, whose irreplaceable power of knowledge Ibn Arabi demonstrates again and again.

Consequently, neither side could conceive what the “body of resurrection” truly is: the acquired body (jism muktasab), shaped by the human being’s spiritual powers in their own image, the caro spiritualis, or spiritual flesh. Ibn Arabi’s writings therefore assume a particularly important place in Mulla Sadra’s treatment of the question.

Throughout the movements of his thought, however, Mulla Sadra remains faithful to a golden rule, which, as we have seen, he explains admirably in the prologue to his great commentary on Book III of Kolayni’s collection, the Kitab al-Hujja. The hadith in that book deal especially with the understanding of prophecy and the Imams in Shiism. It is above all when they address a subject such as resurrection that Mulla Sadra and his fellow thinkers show how foreign to them is the disastrous separation of philosophy from theology that goes back, in the West, to the age of medieval scholasticism.

For Quranic Revelation and philosophical knowledge are inseparable from a standpoint that rises above the level at which we are accustomed to separate theology from philosophy. That higher standpoint joins them together and is called 'irfan, or mystical theosophy—the wisdom of spiritual knowledge. We have already heard Mulla Sadra state in strikingly concise terms the metaphysical law that makes the two inseparable at this higher level: divine Revelation is the light that makes seeing possible; the philosopher’s meditation is the light that sees.

To dispense with the former, as certain extreme Mu'tazilites do, is to wander in the night. To dispense with the latter, in the devout agnosticism of the literalists, is to remain blind. 'Irfan, mystical theosophy, is “Light upon Light.” That is why not even the shadow of the Latin Averroist idea of “double truth” can arise here.

Whoever perceives the different levels of being can perceive, at the level proper to it, a spiritual truth that is, on that very level, the literal truth of eschatology: the truth of the Quran and of the hadith of the Prophet and the holy Imams alike. And Mulla Sadra says explicitly that this was the distinctive spiritual gift of Shiite theosophy within Islam. There is still much in this teaching for us to explore.115

A dozen or so glosses at the opening of Book V already reveal the direction of Mulla Sadra’s thought and lead toward a common goal. Above all, they represent his effort to establish the reality of the interworld and to show how it stands in symbolic correspondence with both the sensible and the intelligible universes. Everything depends on this account of reality if the passages of divine Revelation concerning the last things are to be understood in their spiritual truth (haqiqat).

Yet that spiritual truth, when perceived by the faculty suited to the level of being to which the divine indications refer, is at the same time both symbolic and literal truth. The function of a symbol must never be confused with that of an allegory, as so often happens. We have had occasion to insist on this many times. Allegory remains on the same plane of being and evidence as ordinary perception.

Allegorical interpretation drains visionary events of their life and distorts them because it cannot, in fact, comprehend the reality of any events other than those perceived by the senses. Such interpretation is characteristic of rationalist thinkers, including extreme Mu'tazilites. Literalist theologians, for their part, reveal the same inability to rise to a higher level of perception. If allegorism is a flight from reality, literalism is a fall into absurdity.

Yet it sometimes happens that, through mere habit, people call an interpretation “allegorical” when it possesses all the qualities and merits of genuine symbolic interpretation.

Gloss no. 567 in our continuous numbering provides an extensive “introductory lesson” to Book V of the second part of Suhrawardi’s Book of Eastern Theosophy.116 It prepares the ground for a teaching on the imaginative faculty in relation to resurrection. Its necessary counterpart is the existence of the mundus imaginalis, the imaginal world, as a real interworld governed by laws of its own: a world whose reality is perceived specifically by the imaginative faculty.

The initial problem can be summed up in a question: How are we to understand all the Quran’s teachings about the world to come—paradise and hell, and, in short, the very idea of ma'ad jismani, bodily resurrection—without falling either into the literalism of theologians who are not philosophers or into the allegorism of rationalist philosophers? Mulla Sadra’s chief effort will be to distinguish tanasukh, transmigration, from ma'ad, literally the “Return,” as these two ideas are ordinarily understood, and then to show how the Return must be understood if even the idea of transmigration is to acquire a new and true meaning.

Our shaykh rejects tanasukh when it means the “pouring” of a spiritual entity out of one body and into another. He finds that idea as childish as the literalist theologians’ conception of the Return. One way of understanding the soul’s journey is to see human form as the “first threshold” through which the Soul passes as it descends into the world of Matter.117 On that account, should the Soul fail to fulfill the meaning of its earthly existence, it falls still further into the circles of lower creation.

Mulla Sadra takes the opposite view. For him, human form is the highest earthly limit of the Soul’s ascent from the deepest abyss. Human form is thus the threshold of the Malakut, the spiritual world. Here, the meaning of the last things and the very idea of resurrection clearly depend on a gnostic account of the Soul’s history—a spiritual drama whose details remain to be studied across the whole of Mulla Sadra’s work.

In the gloss under discussion, the argument begins by drawing, for the moment only, on the Peripatetic theory that things are composed of matter and form—hylomorphism. In that theory, each kind of matter actually exists by virtue of the Form that makes it actual. Conversely, each Form exists through and for the matter that it brings into actuality. Under Peripatetic assumptions, it is unthinkable that either should continue to exist independently of the other.

We must remember, however, that the Platonism already present in Avicenna’s doctrine prevented him from fully accepting the Peripatetic definition of the Soul as the form, or entelechy (perfection), of an organic body possessing life only potentially. For the Soul is, first of all, a spiritual being sufficient unto itself. Mulla Sadra therefore holds that a Form can possess, not merely as the form of an organic body but in itself, a perfection and a way of being fully actual by which it exists independently of all matter. More precisely, it becomes the very matter of the forms and images it itself brings into actuality.118

But precisely in this case, because the Soul—the Espahbad Light119—was temporarily united with the material body it had to govern, a certain way of being a soul has been actualized within it. Certain perfections of its being as a soul, affecting its deepest being, its very substance (istikmalat jawhariyya), have become actual through its use of an earthly human body as an instrument.

To take the idea of tanasukh literally, then, we would have to imagine that a soul which has already become an actual human soul could return to a state of mere potentiality in relation to an earthly human body—and thus become once again a human soul only in potential.

It would follow that a Form, once it had become actual, could return to being merely potential; that a soul which had become actual could become a soul in potential again. This is unacceptable.

The idea of maʿād—resurrection, or the return to life beyond death—does not present this difficulty, provided we do not imagine it as the soul's “return” to a physical organism reconstructed independently of it. That would simply bring us back to a variation on tanāsukh, the transmigration of souls.120

No: the resurrection body (the body of the world beyond, jism ukhrāwī) is a body that the soul has formed for itself. It is the body the soul has acquired (jism muktasab) through its activity, its love, its conduct, and its habits, whether good or bad. “This acquired body stands in the same relation to the soul as a shadow to that which casts it.” (We should compare this with Semnānī's doctrine, discussed above in Book IV, Chapter IV, §5.)

To understand maʿād in its true sense, and therefore to see how it differs from tanāsukh, we must set aside every image of a physical transfer from one place to another—as though the soul left one material body only to enter another waiting to receive it.

We must think instead of a passage from one mode of being to another: for example, the passage from the intellectus materialis, or potential intellect, to intellect and intelligible reality in actuality.

We thus arrive at the notion of a “transfer in substance” (intiqāl jawharī), which is also a metamorphosis: the “acquired body” represents the new mode of being into which the soul has passed.

We must conceive of an unbroken process of renewal (ittiṣāl tajaddudī), an uninterrupted succession of transformations of being (akwān ittiṣālīya). We might say that the true idea of maʿād replaces transmigration with transubstantiation, and the passage of a soul from body to body (tanāsukh) with metamorphosis. The picture of a soul being poured from one vessel into another—of a “transfer in place”—leads to insurmountable difficulties.

But a progression from imperfection toward perfection, from lesser to greater intensity, from this world to another world, is not only possible: it expresses a truth that can be realized and verified through experience (mutaḥaqqaq). This ascent of the human being, degree by degree and world by world, will reappear later (Glosses 610, 620, and 629) as a foundation of Mullā Ṣadrā's thought. It also reveals his kinship with the Neoplatonic theosophers of the West since the Renaissance.

Mullā Ṣadrā's understanding of the human being also has a profound affinity with Ismaili gnosis.121 Through its conduct, habits, and actions, every soul brings into actuality a mode of being—an independent act of existence (wujūd istiqlālī)—that survives the dissolution and disappearance of the material body. This mode of being, the body the soul has acquired, gives it a hidden kinship of nature (munāsabat fī'l-bāṭin) with one of four kinds of beings: angel, demon, animal, or wild beast.

The soul becomes a being of one of these kinds, existing as a pure Form, independently of any matter that would receive it passively. Or rather, as we recalled earlier, the soul itself is now the “matter” of the Forms brought into actuality within it.122

Our shaykh even suggests that this may be the key to understanding what Plato and his predecessors meant when they spoke of souls passing into the bodies of animals whose nature resembled their own. Their words are to be understood as symbols of a “second birth” or “second growth” (nashʾat thāniya), taking place in the world beyond, not in this world (see below, Gloss 629, on the three stages of human growth). The same applies to Qur'anic verses sometimes interpreted as teaching tanāsukh (41:20; 24:24; 6:38; 5:65; 17:99, among others), and to all the other symbolic figures found in the hadith.123

If, then, we understand this passage as taking place in the world beyond rather than here below, and as a transformation in the mode of being—a “transfer in substance” (intiqāl jawharī) that becomes the acquired body (jism muktasab), not a movement from one physical place to another—we begin to see how transmigration, understood now as transubstantiation, converges with resurrection (maʿād). Both are being understood in their true sense. That is why, Mullā Ṣadrā observes, it has been said that there is no religious doctrine in which the idea of tanāsukh is not rooted.

But for that to be possible, our picture of the world must include a plane of being on which this event is literally true—not, of course, in the sense in which a physical event is literally true. Here the philosophers reveal their limitations.

“What astonishes me,” declares Mullā Ṣadrā, “is that Avicenna, with all the power of his genius, came to recognize that the hidden meaning of the transmigration (tanāsukh) spoken of by the Pillars of Wisdom—Plato, the Pythagoreans, the disciples of Buzurgmihr—lies in symbols (rumūz) and parables (tamthīlāt) of the prophetic teaching; and yet he was unable to resolve the problem of tanāsukh by an analysis that disclosed its true meaning (ʿalā'l-taḥqīq).

“He could not do so because he had not grasped the authentic meaning of bodily resurrection (maʿād jismānī) in a way that satisfied both philosophy (ḥikmat) and religious law and theology (sharīʿat).” Mullā Ṣadrā immediately explains why Avicenna failed to reach this understanding and therefore had to stop at the idea of a purely spiritual (maʿnawī) resurrection.

What strikes us most in a passage from Avicenna's treatise on resurrection, the Risālat al-Aḍḥawīya,124 is the repeated expression as if. His entire account of the human being's destiny after death is cast as a philosophy of as if. Speaking of the vicious qualities that remain in souls after the death of the body, and that themselves constitute their punishment, Avicenna says it is as if these souls (kaʾannahā) were still in material bodies after death.

The soul's presence in the body does not mean that it is mixed with the body, or simply placed alongside it; rather, the soul receives certain effects produced by the bodily faculties, while being able to act only upon its own body. This creates a double obstacle to the soul's attaining its proper perfection, or even becoming aware of the desire and delight that belong to its own nature. If it has not overcome this condition, the condition remains within it after death.

We can then say it is as if the soul were still in a body; as if the effects surrounding it took the form of animal bodies or savage beasts; as if a soul corrupted by vice had been placed, after death, in a body corresponding to those vices.

Unfortunately, piling up these instances of “as if” is not enough—indeed, does not even lead toward—the recognition of a body that is wholly real without being a material body of the physical, elemental world. Mullā Ṣadrā concludes: “This is the furthest a philosopher can go if he does not acknowledge the existence of another bodily world, distinct from our material and physical world.”

To understand bodily resurrection in its true sense, then, we must establish the existence of what Mullā Ṣadrā elsewhere calls “subtle spiritual matter” (mādda rūḥānīya laṭīfa). The expression corresponds to spissitudo spiritualis—spiritual density or substantiality—used by the seventeenth-century Cambridge Platonist Henry More.125 It also recalls Geistleiblichkeit, “spiritual embodiment,” a favorite theme of the well-known Swabian theosopher F. C. Oetinger, a follower of Boehme and Swedenborg in the eighteenth century. Alongside this, we need a cosmology with room for the realm of subtle bodies: the intermediate world (al-ʿālam al-awsaṭ), the celestial Earth in which lie the mystical cities of Jābalqā, Jābarsā, and Hūrqalyā.

Suhrawardī was the first to define, in philosophical terms, the function of this intermediate world, an indispensable part of the cosmology and eschatology of the “Oriental Theosophy.” It is not the world of Platonic Ideas (muthul Iflāṭūnīya), but a world of substantial, self-subsisting Forms and Images, described as “suspended” (muʿallaqa).

This technical term means that they have no material substrate (lā fī maḥall) in which they inhere, as an accidental quality inheres in a material body—for instance, blackness in a black object. They subsist like images in a mirror: the substance of the mirror is not the material substrate of the image. This world partakes of both the intelligible and the sensible. Its own organ of perception is the imaginative faculty. It is the mundus imaginalis, the imaginal world (ʿālam al-Mithāl).126

In Gloss 567, which we have just examined and discussed, Mullā Ṣadrā opens his commentary on Book V of the Oriental Theosophy with something like a master class. All the great themes are already present. And already his attitude toward the Shaykh al-Ishrāq, the Master of Illumination, begins to show its complexity. He ends this lesson by expressing a further surprise: Suhrawardī, who so convincingly established the existence and necessity of the intermediate world—the subtle world of Image and Imaginal reality—does not seem to understand the hidden meaning of the ancient sages' tanāsukh in quite the way Mullā Ṣadrā does.

Yet we have the impression that Ṣadrā finds in Suhrawardī an interpretation very close to his own.

To decide the matter, we would have to follow Suhrawardī's text and Mullā Ṣadrā's explanations closely, step by step. We cannot do that here.

But this opening lesson will help us understand the later Glosses on which we particularly wish to dwell. Above all, there is Gloss 616, where Mullā Ṣadrā perceptively reveals the organic connection between his philosophy of resurrection and the whole of his theosophy.

We will encounter Avicenna's position again, already clearly placed in perspective here.

We will also see the way prepared for another major Gloss, Gloss 629, in which Mullā Ṣadrā describes the human being's destiny after death through the threefold structure of human nature: physical human, psychic human, and spiritual human (jism, nafs, rūḥ—body, soul, spirit). This same triad is fundamental to Christian Gnosis (sōma or sarx, psychē, pneuma), though it was abandoned by official Christian anthropology at the Second Council of Constantinople, in 869 CE.

One thesis will gradually become clearer and more emphatic, a thesis on which, for Mullā Ṣadrā, everything else depends: the active Imagination, the power that forms images, is not an organic faculty bound to the material body and perishing with it, as so many philosophers have taught. It is a spiritual faculty that the soul “takes with it”; this image-forming power is the soul's subtle or imaginal body.

Hence Mullā Ṣadrā's particular eagerness to draw on Ibn ʿArabī at this point.

Let us note a few striking statements from the Glosses that prepare us for this conclusion.
