It preserves accounts of extraordinary debates attended by representatives of all the religions then in existence. 3) Kitâb al-I'tiqâdât, a book setting out the Shiite profession of faith; it contains thoroughly Platonic teachings on the soul's pre-existence and descent.

4) Finally, the great Kitâb al-Tawhîd, a collection of the Imams' traditions dealing with everything involved in affirming the divine Oneness (tawhîd). It shows how the teaching concerning the Imams is the only possible “affirmative” or cataphatic theology compatible with the apophatic theology—the via negationis, or tanzîh—required by the affirmation of divine unity. This is the book on which Qâzî Sa'îd Qommî wrote his masterly commentary, comparable to Mollâ Sadrâ's commentary on Kolaynî's Kâfî. These are two monuments of Shiite spiritual philosophy.

Thus we find ourselves in Qomm once again, some seven centuries later, with our philosopher.

Qâzî Sa'îd was born there, then, in 1049/1639. His father, Mohammad Mofîd Qommî, was himself a hakîm, a sage or philosopher. Young Sa'îd naturally began his studies in Qomm, then came to Isfahan around 1068/1658, where his principal teachers, as we noted above, were Mollâ Rajab 'Alî Tabrîzî and Mollâ Mohsen Fayz Kâshânî, the most famous pupil of Mollâ Sadrâ Shîrâzî 160.

In his youth he had also studied medicine. He had an elder brother, Mohammad Hosayn, just as gifted as himself, who had also studied under Rajab 'Alî Tabrîzî and who, besides writing a major Persian commentary on the Qur'an, was an expert in medicine. To distinguish Sa'id from his brother, people nicknamed him Hakîm kutchak—something like the younger philosopher.

The Safavid ruler Shah 'Abbâs II (who reigned from 1052/1642 to 1077/1677) likewise treated him with great respect, as did the members of his court, and appointed him to judicial office.

Hence the title under which he is generally cited: Qâzî (Qâdî) Sa'îd Qommî, Judge Sa'îd of Qomm. He spent most of his life in Qomm, teaching and receiving visits from thinkers and other notable figures who came to consult him.

Nevertheless, we find evidence of frequent journeys between Qomm and Isfahan, a distance of only about 250 kilometres. Between 1084/1673 and 1088/1677 he was certainly in Qomm, where several of his writings are dated.

But he was in Isfahan in 1093/1682, for the manuscript of the first volume of his great commentary on Sadûq's Tawhîd was copied there on his instructions, reviewed in full by him, and annotated in his own hand, with the date Rajab 1093/July 1682. He was also in Isfahan between 1099/1688 and 1102/1691, when he wrote the Arba'înîyât and his commentary on the Tradition of the White Cloud, while continuing work on the Tawhîd commentary. Apart from this we have many scattered autobiographical remarks in his writings, but they chiefly concern his inner spiritual life. He died in Qomm in 1103/1691–1692.

As we can see, we know rather little about the outward circumstances of our philosopher's life. As with all his fellow thinkers, his real life is in his work; it is there that we must look for clues to the path he followed. The works are not lacking in references to dreams and waking visions or to particular events, but these belong above all to his spiritual autobiography.

What is certain is that the teachings of his two masters, Mohsen Fayz Kâshânî and Rajab 'Alî Tabrîzî, shaped his thought together. The first awakened his deep inclination towards what we might call a Shiite ishrâqî philosophy of illumination, grounded almost entirely in the traditions of the holy Imams. Mohsen Fayz, himself a mystical philosopher and a prolific author of some two hundred books and treatises in Arabic and Persian, was an akhbârî 161. Qâzî Sa'îd, too, was an akhbârî philosopher.

We shall return later (Book VI) to the centuries-old opposition between the akhbârîs and the osûlîs. For now, leaving other considerations aside, let us say only that the former, as represented by such figures as Mohsen Fayz and his pupils, appear as Shiite spiritual philosophers who insist on taking the traditions in their entirety. They accept all the reports transmitted from the Imams instead of submitting them to the often rationalistic criticism practised by others. Through ta'wîl 'irfânî, spiritual and mystical interpretation, they can discern the hidden meaning of traditions that rationalistic theology dismisses as incomprehensible or absurd.

From his other teacher, Rajab 'Alî Tabrîzî, Qâzî Sa'îd inherited a firm and original position on the metaphysics of being, one he shared with the other pupils of that teacher: his own brother Mohammad Hosayn, 'Abbâs Mawlawî, and others. This position denies that there can be any analogy of being—or of any attribute whatever—between the Necessary Being and a being that has a beginning. It is neither nominalism nor agnosticism.

Rather, it expresses the conviction that the uncompromising demand of Tawhîd, divine Oneness, can be met only by negative or apophatic theology, which denies every Name and qualification of the transcendent divine Essence. At the same time, this negative theology establishes both the necessity and the meaning of divine manifestations, or theophanies.

The works themselves have this distinctive feature: although conceived on an ambitious scale, they remained unfinished, as did many writings of Mîr Dâmâd. Even so, their extent is considerable. We shall chiefly mention the following.

1) Kalîd-e behesht (The Key to Paradise) is a short work written in Persian 162, in which Qâzî Sa'îd outlines the fundamental theses of his metaphysics, the ideas underlying all his writings. In agreement with his teacher Rajab 'Alî Tabrîzî, he argues that the word “being” cannot have a common meaning (ishtirâk ma'nawî) when applied, on the one hand, to the Being that is Necessary in itself (Wâjib al-wojûd) and, on the other, to a being that is not necessary in itself (momkin al-wojûd) 163. The two uses of the word share only a verbal form (ishtirâk lafzî): they are, in fact, homonyms. For the Necessary transcends being and every category of being.

Indeed, this supreme philosophical reality lies beyond even metaphysics ('ilm ilâhî), the discipline that studies being (wojûd) as found in what exists (mawjûd).

We shall return to this point, for this fundamental thesis governs how negative or apophatic theology is connected with the idea of divine manifestations and, consequently, with the whole spiritual understanding of the Imams.

2) The Kitâb al-Arba'în, a “Commentary on Forty Hadiths,” written by Qâzî Sa'îd when he was thirty years old. Unfortunately it remained unfinished: the commentary reaches only the twenty-eighth tradition, with a gap after the eighteenth. Collections of “forty hadiths” form a whole literature of their own. Their inspiration is a saying of the Prophet promising special glory on the Day of Resurrection to anyone who preserves for the community forty traditions suited to its religious needs 164.

Within Shiism this became a pious way for an individual to bring together the teachings that answered his own theological or devotional concerns, while presenting them as an anthology of authoritative texts received from the Imams. Several traditions in Qâzî Sa'îd's unfinished collection reappear in his great commentary on the Tawhîd. It seems that, increasingly absorbed by this second and overwhelming task, he could no longer pursue the first. He refers to his earlier commentary on many occasions, and scholars need to read the two together: both are dense and richly documented.

3) The Kitâb al-Arba'înîyat, or Book of Forty Treatises. The words completing its title explain its purpose: “for the unveiling of the Lights of the hieratic world.” Once again we meet the number forty, with its evident mystical significance. This work must not be confused with the previous one. Here too, however, Qâzî Sa'îd was unable to complete his plan. He wrote ten treatises between 1089/1670 and 1102/1690–91.

The first sets out a spiritual interpretation (ta'wîl) of the canonical Prayer (Salât), its inward meaning, and belongs alongside another treatise on the same subject that we shall mention below 165. The tenth is entitled al-Talâ'i' (“The Vanguard” or “The Scouts”) or al-Bawâriq al-malakûtîya (“Flashes of Lightning in the Malakût”). In it the author addresses several philosophical problems by the methods of spiritual knowledge ('irfân). He recalls a spiritual vision he experienced in Qomm and refers to his teachers and contemporaries. Begun in Isfahan in 1095/1684, the treatise was incorporated into the Arba'înîyât collection in Safar 1102/November 1690.

We have some reason, however, to think that another work by Qâzî Sa'îd, the Commentary on the Narrative of the White Cloud (Sharh hadîth al-ghamâma), forms an eleventh work in this collection, which in any case remained incomplete. In principle it could also have belonged to the preceding collection, despite its length. There therefore seems no need to list it separately in his bibliography.

We shall later summarise this very important commentary, which reveals the narrative of the White Cloud as a genuine account of initiation.

4) Qâzî Sa'îd also wrote a series of glosses on the so-called Theology of Aristotle, perhaps for use in his teaching. We hope to examine them elsewhere, since they reveal even more clearly the spiritual character of a Shiite philosopher of illumination. It is also worth noticing that this text of Plotinian origin, so influential in the medieval and Renaissance West and annotated by Avicenna himself, was still receiving extensive commentary from one of Persia's Platonists in the seventeenth century 166.

5) Finally, there is Qâzî Sa'îd's magnum opus: his vast commentary on Ibn Bâbûyeh Sadûq's Kitâb al-Tawhîd, whose author and subject matter we have outlined above. Sadûq's book, for which no critical edition yet exists, runs to sixty-five chapters and gathers a great body of traditions from the Imams. These are fundamental both to the Shiite understanding of apophatic theology and to the entire theology of the Imams that develops from it. Just as Mollâ Sadrâ Shîrâzî produced a true compendium of Shiite spiritual philosophy by commenting on Kolaynî's Kâfî, Qâzî Sa'îd produced his own great compendium by commenting on Shaykh Sadûq's Tawhîd. There is a further resemblance: despite the labours of their authors, both works were left unfinished.

Yet what their authors completed is already monumental. Qâzî Sa'îd intended his commentary to have at least four parts, in four books or volumes. Manuscripts of Books I and II can be found in several Iranian libraries; those of Book III are far rarer. One sometimes hears of a Book IV, but no manuscript has yet been found, and everything suggests that such reports arise from confusion with the commentary by Ni'matollâh Jaza'erî 167.

Book I ends with the commentary on an exceptionally long hadîth recounting a meeting between the Tenth Imam, 'Alî-Naqî (d. 254/868), and a disciple who sought him out at Samarra, in the military camp where the Abbasid government held him captive. The disciple wants to be sure that the Imam approves every article of the faith he professes. The tradition thus forms, on its own, a complete Shiite profession of faith.

Because this profession and the Imam's explanations end with a review of the five fundamental religious practices—prayer, fasting, pilgrimage, almsgiving, and struggle for the faith—Qâzî Sa'îd was led to write what amounts to a separate treatise in his commentary, entitled “The Inner Meanings of Divine Worship” (asrâr al-'ibâdat). Bibliographers often treat it as an independent work 168. Elsewhere we have devoted a long study to the third section of the tradition's concluding passage, which deals with the “inner meaning of the pilgrimage” (asrâr al-Hajj) 169.

We shall return to it briefly below, for it is one of the texts that show most clearly what the understanding of the Imams means for both cosmology—the structure of the universe as perceived by Shiite consciousness—and the performance of obligatory religious acts, whose meaning is transformed by their inner or esoteric interpretation.

We noted earlier (Book I, chapter IV, section 5) that Qâzî Sa'îd's understanding of time and temporality is essential to spiritual interpretation, which by definition operates on the plane of metahistory, beyond the limits of outward historical sequence. We should therefore return to it here. His commentary on the Narrative of the White Cloud gives us the opportunity. This narrative becomes an account of initiation because it describes an exploration of regions of the world beyond the senses, from which the travellers return spiritually transformed.

Qâzî Sa'îd's commentary is valuable as an introduction to the interpretation of all narratives of this kind. Needless to say, there is no possible confusion between what we today call “astronautics” and what these mystics and others like them experience as entry into the Malakût: the realm of spiritual counterparts or, if we prefer, the enduring archetypal Images of the things and events in our visible world (molk). The “heavens” of the Malakût are not the space or “heavens” of astronomy. Astronomical space, however dizzying its distances, always belongs to the molk.

In relation to the Malakût it occupies the same position as “Earth” in relation to “Heaven.” Along with a short account of apophatic theology and the doctrine of the Imams, these are the only aspects of Qâzî Sa'îd Qommî's thought that we can consider here. His name, like those of many other masters of Iranian thought, has remained unknown in the West for far too long.

Let us hope that future critical editions will make it easier to study his writings, produced largely in “the holy city of Qomm, the Well-Protected,” writings at once traditional and original, which we ourselves have had to consult entirely in manuscript.

2. Apophatic Theology and the Structure of the Imamate

A hadîth that leads Qâzî Sa'îd, in developing the Imam's teaching, to set out the demands of apophatic theology (tanzîh) takes us back to the episode mentioned earlier in connection with the origins of the pilgrimage to Qomm. The opening of the tradition refers explicitly to that event. The caliph al-Ma'mûn, moved by a scruple of conscience whose motives remain unknown to us, had decided to name the Eighth Imam, 'Alî Rezâ (153/770–203/818), as his successor, his future caliph 170.

We can imagine the dismay of the Imam's followers in Medina, and the hesitation of the Imam himself, described to us as gentle and thoughtful. This political outcome had nothing in common with the meaning he and his predecessors gave to the Imamate.

Yet how could he evade the caliph's summons? When al-Ma'mûn announced his decision to his court and to all the Hashimites gathered around him, an outcry followed. The objections were unanimous. An inexperienced man—perhaps even an ignorant simpleton—was to succeed the Abbasid caliph! What everyone actually feared was that the Imam's accession to the caliphate would overturn the established order. For their part, the Shiites knew all too well that the conditions for establishing the Imamate, in their understanding of the term, were not present.

In the end the appointment came to nothing: the holy Imam died, mysteriously poisoned, in the year following his designation as the caliph's heir. Al-Ma'mûn, called back to Baghdad by political complications, showed extreme grief. Around the Imam's tomb, not far from Tûs, the birthplace of Ferdawsî, a famous shrine grew up, with a hospital, library, and theological school. For centuries the pilgrimage to Mashhad in Khorassan has remained one of the great sacred destinations of the Shiite world.

Imam Rezâ can scarcely have stayed more than a year at Merv. This was long enough for al-Ma'mûn's vizier Fazl ibn Sahl—the Zoroastrian convert whose sympathies for Persian and Shiite matters we have already recalled—to organise religious conferences attended by Zoroastrians, Manichaeans, Buddhists, Christians, and Jews. Imam Rezâ emerges from these gatherings as a commanding personality. The records of these memorable encounters have survived in the great work of Shaykh Sadûq mentioned above (p. 127) 171.

The Imam had set off on the long journey from Medina in Arabia to Central Asia, a journey that took several months. When the tradition we are discussing opens, everything is in place for his ordeal. This is no courteous exchange of views of the kind Fazl ibn Sahl would later arrange. The atmosphere is tense. Al-Ma'mûn has formally informed his entourage of his decision, only to be challenged: summon the Imam, they say, and they will give such proof of his ignorance that the caliph will be convinced. When the Imam appears, the Hashimites surround him: “Abû'l-Hasan, ascend the pulpit! Show us a profession of faith around which we may unite in worshipping God.”

“Then the Imam ascended the pulpit. For a long time he sat motionless and silent. At last he stood. He gave glory to God and invoked blessings on the Prophet and the members of his House. Then he began his sermon.”

We can quote only its beginning here. Needless to say, it utterly defeated the secret hopes of those who had dared issue the challenge. In this sermon, upon which Qâzî Sa'îd comments so admirably from beginning to end 172, the Imam sets out the demands of tanzîh, the via negationis traditionally called “apophatic” or “negative” theology in Eastern Christianity. He begins by recalling the rule of tawhîd, the affirmation of the One: the act of recognising the singular, utterly transcendent oneness of God. This requires us to deny, or “set aside,” every qualification and attribute of God. For every qualification and everything that bears a qualification is, by that very fact, something created, whether the attribute is understood as identical with an essence or as something added to it.

We must therefore understand how the idea of a “creating subject” (khâliq) is neither a qualification nor an attribute, nor the underlying subject of a qualification. Consequently, whoever imagines that God can be known through the qualities human beings ascribe to him does not know God. Throughout the sermon, the Imam pursues every last refuge of an “affirmative theology” that forgets the foundations and paradoxes of apophatic thought.

“The first service rendered to God,” the Imam declares, “is spiritual knowledge (ma'rifat) of him; the first act of worship, the first true devotion, is knowledge, gnosis. The source of knowledge of God is the affirmation of his oneness (tawhîd). The fundamental rule of this affirmation is to exclude from him every qualification.

“For our intellects attest that every attribute (sifat), and every thing that is described by an attribute (mawsûf), is something created (makhlûq). Everything created points to a creating subject (khâliq) that is neither an attribute nor the thing described by one. Every attribute and every thing described by it points to a relationship with something else. Every such relationship shows that it has had a beginning. Everything that has had a beginning shows that it cannot have existed from before all eternity.

“Therefore whoever claims to know God's Essence by likening it (tashbîh) to something else does not know God. Whoever claims to have reached the very ground of the One does not understand his oneness. Whoever imagines correspondences for him does not encounter his true Reality [...]. Everything known in itself is something made (masnû'). Everything that subsists in something other than itself is something caused (ma'lul). Through God's works we may infer God. The intellects profess spiritual knowledge of him, but the foundation of that affirmation is the innate disposition (fitrat)...”

From Qâzî Sa'îd's commentary on the beginning of the Imam's sermon, let us draw out the following point. To know a thing is to grasp or encompass it (ihâta, comprehendere). As long as the soul does not encompass it, knowledge of that thing has not become actual for the soul. This is so whether we are speaking of knowledge through the presence of a mental form or species ('ilm hosûlî, representational knowledge), knowledge by immediate presence ('ilm hozûrî), or knowledge through a unitive merging (ittihâd) of the knower and the known.

The Imams often repeat a fundamental teaching: whatever qualification we give to something measures the scope of our understanding (jihat al-ihâta, modus intelligendi). Every judgement that attributes a quality reflects the subject's own manner of understanding. The soul understands only by returning to itself. It grasps or encompasses only what it can contain within itself, and it can explain only what it contains. The soul therefore cannot understand anything that is not embraced within its own essence.

Whoever understands a thing—that is, encompasses it, goes all the way around it (mollit)—thereby stands above it. The very act of intellectual understanding involves a kind of mastery over its object (fawqîya 'aqlîya): it is the cause of that object as understood, for it makes the thing into an object of thought.

In the last sentence of the passage just quoted, where the Imam declares, “The intellects profess spiritual knowledge of him ...,” Qâzî Sa'îd asks us to weigh every word. This is ma'rifat, a mystical knowledge professed or affirmed (i'tiqâd) by the intellect, not produced by it as one of its effects, as other objects of thought would be. The intellect is neither the source nor the guarantor of this profession. Qâzî Sa'îd warns against philosophers who maintain that the divine Reality (al-Haqq) cannot be perceived by the senses or the imagination, but can be apprehended by intellectual intuition ('aql). In the strict technical sense of 'aql, he says, that is absolutely impossible.

Yet the root of the Arabic word 'aql carries the idea of making a bond or fastening a tie; this guides us towards the meaning of ma'rifat in the Imams' own technical vocabulary, as attested in their reports (akhbâr). Knowledge called ma'rifat involves a bond of the heart, a commitment of the heart ('aqd qalbî). It is knowing as recognition, assent, and spiritual awareness, awakened by the contrast between what is created (momkin) and the One of whom it is said, “There is nothing like unto him.”

No positive attribute can be assigned to that One. Even a negation is valid only when immediately balanced by the negation of that negation, for God cannot be described even by the contrary of an attribute. This is the double negation in which Ismaili reasoning about tawhîd excelled, a double negation whose circle encompasses only the emptiness of what cannot be described. To overstep this boundary of apophatic theology is to commit an act of violence, a violation.

Nor is assent itself produced by the intellectual faculty ('aql). It arises as an innate awareness from humanity's original, fundamental nature (fitrat), as first established by the creative Act: this fitrat is the very divine Light from which human beings were created. Here too lie the beginnings of knowledge through the heart (ma'rifat qalbîya) and inward vision through the heart (basîrat qalbîya), themes of equally fundamental importance to other Shiite spiritual philosophers, including Mollâ Sadrâ.

What matters here is that these propositions, drawn from Qâzî Sa'îd's commentary on the Eighth Imam's sermon, agree with the systematic account of his metaphysics of being that he gives elsewhere, precisely where he follows his teacher Rajab 'Alî Tabrîzî in taking a position different from Mollâ Sadrâ's. In the Persian treatise Kalîd-e behesht (The Key to Paradise), Qâzî Sa'îd sets out an understanding of being that he considers faithful to the Imams' teaching, but that distinguishes him from the 'olamâ, the religious scholars, and from the “moderns” (mota'akhkhirîn). He identifies the concept of a being as such with the concept of what is not necessary in itself (momkin al-wojûd).

The idea of a being includes the meaning of something that is not being in and of itself but has or possesses being (sâhib-e wojûd), just as the concept of something white includes the meaning of a thing that possesses whiteness. Once we distinguish being from having being, it follows that wherever we say something possesses being, the act by which it exists must be other than the essence to which that act is attributed. Otherwise the attribution would make no sense: a thing cannot be its own predicate.

Predication requires two distinct terms. It is precisely into the interval opened by this difference that the need for a cause enters—a cause that cannot be the essence itself, since nothing is the cause of itself, but must be other than that essence. This need for another is the very definition of momkin al-wojûd, the being that is not necessary in itself. And this is the only kind of being we can understand. Our category of being is, by that very fact, the category of created being.

The Necessary Being (Wâjib al-wojûd) cannot, under any circumstances or in any respect, fall under the concept of being available to the human understanding. It is neither substance nor accident, neither something countable nor anything else by which we ordinarily describe beings. It is radically impossible, and unintelligible, to describe the Necessary by applying to it, in any manner whatever, the familiar attributes of being. It is not even one in the ordinary sense of the word.

For ordinarily, to call something one is to say that it possesses numerical unity, a unity distinct from its essence; the unity of the Necessary is not numerical unity. Its unity is its very Essence. It is Unity itself, not an essence described by Unity, but that very Essence which, in being Unity, gives Unity its essence—monadam monadari, as Leibniz put it.

It follows that the Necessary Being cannot be an object of any science, not even of metaphysics, the theological science ('ilm ilâhî), for this science studies the concept of being as being. Therefore, when we speak of a being in the sense employed by our metaphysics and when we speak of the Necessary Being (Wâjib al-wojûd), the word “being” has no common content or meaning (ma'nâ) in its two uses: there is no ishtirâk ma'nawî, no shared meaning. There is only a shared word, pure homonymy (ishtirâk lafzî).

The Necessary is sheer Essence (dhât). It is impossible and unintelligible to ascribe qualities to it, whichever position one adopts among those held by the exoteric theologians—whether one takes such a quality to be identical with the Essence or instead something other than the Essence 173.

This position is uncompromising. No analogia entis, no analogy of being, is possible between the First Principle and the beings brought into existence by its creative act, in the mystery of an absolute beginning. The Principle is hyperousion, beyond being. “There is nothing like unto him.”

Yet at the very limit where apophatic theology can fulfil tawhîd only in silence, at the horizon of a transcendence that remains forever inviolate, a Figure arises. It is this Figure that makes intelligible God's own divine speech about God addressed to humanity, for the Figure bears the Names and Attributes through which God makes himself known to human beings. Something in Qâzî Sa'îd's position is especially characteristic of the way Neoplatonism bore fruit in Islam. Certainly all the thinkers we have encountered read the so-called Theology of Aristotle, which is in fact a paraphrase of Plotinus.

But Qâzî Sa'îd, who himself annotated that Theology and was inspired as well by the teachings of the Imams and by the meaning of the Imamate, maintained a position corresponding to that of Proclus.

Consider the passages in Proclus' Platonic Theology where he argues that his interpretation is the one truly faithful to Plato's thought. Other Platonists went no higher than Nous, Intelligence, treating it at once as the cause of being and as the first being. Proclus, by contrast, affirms the absolute transcendence of the Principle of being: the One beyond substance, beyond being itself, beyond even Intelligence. Intelligence is the One within being, the first being, and the point from which multiplicity unfolds 174. Proclus' position among the interpreters of Plato thus parallels the position of Shiite philosophers such as Qâzî Sa'îd in relation to other schools. Of course all these thinkers agree that the First Principle (al-Mabda' al-awwal) lies beyond 'Aql, beyond Nous.

But Proclus and our thinkers face the same decisive question. Is the First Principle itself already within being and therefore a being? As absolute being (wojûd motlaq), is it the First Being? Or, as the source of being, must it stand beyond being (hyperousion), like Proclus' absolute One? If it does, the “first being” is not the Principle but the First Emanation from it. The first option, which places the Principle as the First Being, is generally that of the Ishrâqîyûn, the philosophers of illumination, as well as Haydar Âmolî, a disciple of Ibn 'Arabî.

The second leads to a metaphysics of being represented above all by Ismaili gnosis, particularly the treatises of Abû Ya'qûb Sejestânî 175, and, within Twelver Shiism, by Rajab Borsî (eighth/fourteenth century), Rajab 'Alî Tabrîzî, his pupil Qâzî Sa'îd Qommî, Shaykh Ahmad Ahsâ'î, and the school that followed him (see Book VI). In other words, everything turns on whether a thinker holds that “being” has one and the same meaning in every case—or at least an analogous meaning—when we say that the Principle is and that the beings deriving from it are; or whether, like Qâzî Sa'îd, the thinker insists that these uses of the word are radically different.

The second choice means that our concepts of being and of a being (wojûd and mawjûd, esse and ens) reach no further than created being.

We shall see with Shaykh Ahmad Ahsâ'î that even the expression “absolute being” (wojûd motlaq) contains an implication: the passive past participle motlaq (absolutum, “set free” or “made absolute”) presupposes a motliq, an active agent who “absolves” or releases this absolute, who issues the command that makes it absolute, and who alone is therefore its sufficient reason.

But the being “found there”—which is the meaning of the Arabic mawjûd—is always already constituted being, being-that-has-been-made. What makes being must therefore be beyond being: a “non-being above being.”

If Qâzî Sa'îd's position, like Ismaili ontology, exemplifies a particular aspect of Neoplatonism in Islam, and especially in Shiite Islam, it is because it corresponds to the Neoplatonic interpretation of Plato inaugurated by Plotinus 176. It is no longer a matter of making God one being among others, even the most perfect being (Ens supremum). That view belongs to the Platonic tradition against which Proclus himself protested.

As Pierre Hadot observes, that tradition could include an apophatic theology, yet “never went so far as to deny that God was a being, or Being par excellence. With Plotinus, God or the Good ceases to be one of the beings” 177. The most difficult problem is then to locate God in relation to beings and non-beings.

We must explain in what sense God himself may be described as non-being; we must distinguish “non-being above being” from “absolute non-being,” and thereby define God as “non-being above being”—ultimately as “beyond both beings and non-beings.”

Let us return to Qâzî Sa'îd's analysis of why we make judgements that attribute qualities. Here we seem to find the same idea as in Porphyry, Plotinus' disciple: “the soul itself is the principle that distinguishes the levels of reality.” If “absolute non-being is only a mirage of the soul” when it turns away from what can be understood by the intellect, then, similarly, if God appears to the soul as “non-being above being,” that is because the soul, faced with his utter otherness, experiences itself as nothing in comparison with him 178.

Hence this “non-being above being” also receives the name al-wojûd al-haqq, the true being or true Existent. But no qualification can be given to this true Existent, since all the qualifications available to our ontology apply only to created beings.

How, then, can we avoid the trap of ta'tîl while escaping, through tanzîh, apophatic theology, the trap of tashbîh? The latter consists in likening the true Existent to created beings by giving it qualifications that can apply only to created beings, even when raised to the highest degree. The former consists in emptying God of all significance, relegating him to a beyond that no longer concerns us.

As we already know (see Book I), this is the great problem at the heart of Shiite spiritual philosophy: through the dark cloud of divine unknowability breaks the dawn of the divine manifestations. The darker the cloud, the more radiant the dawn. This is what gives Qâzî Sa'îd's understanding of the Imams its distinctive character. At the highest horizon there must appear a Figure in which God is manifested (mazhar), capable of bearing the Names and Attributes that cannot reach the depths of the divine Essence. These Names and Attributes reveal the divine acts without unveiling the mystery of the Essence. The Figure can be given different names.

In Neoplatonic language it is Intelligence (Nous, 'Aql). In the language of Muhammadan prophetic philosophy, it is the eternal Muhammadan Reality (Haqîqat mohammadîya), which in turn can receive many symbolic names: First Determination, Universal Mercy, Muhammadan Light, the Logos or Word (Kalima) before which the Great Abyss withdraws, Reality of Realities, Pre-eternal Matter, absolute walâyat, essential love, and others.

Whatever its name, the relationship through which the divine manifests itself between the manifesting form (mazhar) and the hidden Reality appearing in that form—the inner reality (bâtin) of its outward appearance (zâhir)—cannot be settled by dialectical argument. Qâzî Sa'îd has warned us that it calls for an organ of perception other than the reasoning intellect ('aql fikrî). It presupposes what the Imams themselves called ma'rifat qalbîya, knowledge through the heart. Apophatic theology and knowledge through the heart, inner vision or the vision of the heart (tanzîh and ma'rifat or basîrat qalbîya), are inseparable.

For the only possible “affirmative” or cataphatic theology is one directed towards the Muhammadan Reality, and this Reality is unveiled only to the inward vision of the heart as the organ of spiritual knowledge. In Qâzî Sa'îd's thought, in keeping both with the Imams' teaching and with the Neoplatonic tradition, the First Principle remains beyond substance and beyond being. It is not the Principle, therefore, that can be called “first being,” “Light of Lights,” and so on. These names belong precisely to the Muhammadan Reality, the dawning of the being of beings: the One that is, the point at which the Many burst forth.

The Muhammadan Reality (Haqîqat mohammadîya) is one of the most difficult themes in Shiite thought. It corresponds to the theologies and spiritual philosophies of the Logos in Christianity and Neoplatonism, but is more complex because this Muhammadan Reality is a pleroma, a complete spiritual fullness: the pleroma of the “Fourteen Immaculate Ones” (Tchahârdeh Ma'sûm), in the metaphysical reality of their “persons of light” (ashkhâs nûrânîya). It is therefore not simply a single hypostasis or divine emanation, but a metaphysical structure.

The fourteen beings of light are one and the same Light, one and the same Essence. Qâzî Sa'îd devoted himself to understanding this structure. Starting from a conception of being that underpins apophatic theology, his thinking leads to a doctrine of the Imams that we may call structural. The two examples that follow will illustrate this description, and at the same time the originality of Qâzî Sa'îd's visionary perception.

Naturally, Qâzî Sa'îd agrees with the other Shiite spiritual philosophers in recognising two “dimensions” within the Muhammadan Reality. One is turned towards created beings; the other is turned towards the divine Presence. The first is its outward or exoteric dimension (zâhir): nobowwat, prophecy and the prophetic mission.

The second is its inner or esoteric dimension (bâtin): the Imamate or walâyat, “divine nearness” or “divine friendship.” This nearness belongs to the Awliyâ' Allah, the Friends, those near to God, those beloved of God—a name that, in its strict sense, designates the Twelve Imams.

Hence the definition tirelessly repeated by our authors, and throughout this book: walâyat is the esoteric, inward reality of prophecy (bâtin al-nobowwat). The two cannot be separated. For one thing, walâyat underlies the spiritual gift of prophecy, so that every nabî, every prophet, is also a walî, a friend of God.

But there is a deeper reason: prophecy and walâyat share a single fundamental law and are one and the same Light, regarded sometimes in its outward, sometimes in its inward aspect, both in spiritual worlds and in worlds visible to the senses. This is the meaning of the saying attributed to the Prophet and repeated in different contexts: “'Alî and I are one and the same Light.” That Light appears in two persons, the Prophet and the Imam. And when we say “the Imam,” we mean all Twelve Imams, for each of them, and all of them together, manifest the one Imamate, single in its Essence.

In every pair of terms—prophet and Imam, outward and inward, tanzīl (the revelation that brings spiritual meaning down into the written words of the Book) and ta'wīl (the interpretation that leads this meaning back to its spiritual source)—each term becomes fully real only through the other. The relationship between the Imamate, manifested in each of the twelve Imams, and the person of the Messenger, who is both the beginning and the Seal of all messengers, is affirmed in numerous hadiths. There is, for example, this tradition from the Fifth Imam, Muhammad Bāqir: “The Messenger of God said: The first thing God created was a Light. He brought it forth from His own Light, drawing it from the majesty of His Sublimity. Then He separated from it [literally, ‘unstitched,’ fataqa] the light of ʿAlī [the Imam].”

The hadith goes on to allude to the mysteries of preexistence and to a mysterious procession around the Throne. It concludes with a declaration echoed in the most celebrated traditions of the Imams. Speaking on behalf of the Twelve, the Fifth Imam says: “We are the First and we are the Last. We are the Word of God. We are the beloved of God. We are the Face of God. We are the custodians of divine Revelation. We are the guardians of the Temple of the divine Mystery. We are the source from which Revelation is drawn. Within us lies the meaning of ta'wīl.”179

It is this relationship between nubuwwat (the prophetic mission) and the Imamate that Qāzī Saʿīd contemplates and explores throughout his great commentary on Ibn Bābūya's Tawhīd. His reflections lead him in a characteristic direction. He concentrates on the properties of the number twelve—the twelvefold unity that constitutes the structure of the Imamate—and seeks to give that structure a concrete spiritual image. His aim is to bring forth one of those imagines agentes, active images, whose metaphysical foundations and role in knowledge we discussed earlier (Book II, Chapter VII). Such an image allows us to verify, through the actual points of reference provided by the geography of imaginal space, the order in which spiritual realities appear, assert their presence, and take recognizable form.

Sometimes the imaginal form of this twelvefold structure is supplied directly by a hadith. This is the case with the mysterious tradition of the “Twelve Veils of Light.” At other times it is Qāzī Saʿīd's own meditation that uncovers the spiritual structure of the Imamate within a particular geometrical figure. He does precisely this when contemplating the cubic form of the Kaaba. Transfigured into the spiritual Temple of the Imamate, the Kaaba becomes the secret of all spiritual life, the qibla—the direction toward which one turns—of a pilgrimage that coincides with the entire course of a human life. We can consider only these two examples here.

The hadith of the “Twelve Veils of Light” brings the doctrine of the Imams into relationship with the creation of the cosmos, and also with the divine wisdom of history and metahistory. It describes, in symbolic form, the journey of the Muhammadan Light through the Pleroma, the fullness of the divine world, before its successive “descents” (tanazzulāt) from world to world, through seventy thousand veils, until it reaches our own world.

The hadith appears in an unusual collection by Shaykh Ṣadūq Ibn Bābūya devoted to the “properties and virtues” of numerical series. Appropriately enough, the tradition of the Twelve Veils appears in the chapter on groups of twelve. Its chain of transmission (isnād) leads back through the Sixth Imam to the First Imam.180 Qāzī Saʿīd commented on this tradition more than once. We shall encounter it again later in his commentary on the “Tale of the White Cloud.”181

Here is an attempt to translate it:

“God created the Muhammadan Light (Nūr muḥammadī) before creating the Heavens and the Earth, the Throne (ʿarsh) and the Firmament (Kursī), the Tablet (Lawḥ) and the Pen, and before creating the hundred and twenty-four thousand prophets. And together with this Light [or, according to another version, from this very Light] He created twelve veils (ḥijāb): the veil of Power, the veil of Sublimity, the veil of Grace, the veil of Mercy, the veil of Felicity, the veil of Generosity, the veil of Dwelling, the veil of Guiding Direction, the veil of Prophecy, the veil of Exaltation, the veil of Reverential Awe, and the veil of Intercession.182

“Then He caused the Muhammadan Light to dwell for twelve millennia within the veil of Power; eleven millennia within the veil of Sublimity; ten millennia within the veil of Grace; nine millennia within the veil of Mercy; eight millennia within the veil of Felicity; seven millennia within the veil of Generosity; six millennia within the veil of Dwelling; five millennia within the veil of Guiding Direction; four millennia within the veil of Prophecy; three millennia within the veil of Exaltation; two millennia within the veil of Reverential Awe; and one millennium within the veil of Intercession.”183

What we have here, our philosopher explains, is the account of the Muhammadan Light's progression before its manifestation on earth in the cycle of prophecy, from Adam to the Seal of the Prophets. The twelve Veils of Light are the twelve Imams and the twelve spiritual universes belonging to them respectively. These universes are expressed symbolically as twelve millennia.

Here the word “millennium” does not indicate a measurable duration of time; it is equivalent to the Gnostic term Aiōn (Aeon), or saeculum. These twelve universes express, in numerical symbolism, the structure of metahistory. Its cycle, unfolding in “subtle time,” is the archetype of the cycle that will take place on earth as the cycle of walāyat, the spiritual guardianship of the Imams. That earthly cycle will be its inverted image: the image, in the direction of return and ascent, of what the hadith describes in the direction of descent.

The Muhammadan Light progresses from Imam to Imam without ever leaving behind the preceding veil of light. Instead, it incorporates into itself the inward, hidden reality represented by that veil. This is why the Light dwells for twelve millennia—the entire cycle—in the first veil, eleven millennia in the second, ten in the third, and so on, until it reaches the Qāʾim, the twelfth and final Imam. It is impossible to grasp the depths of Shiite thought concerning the Imams unless we take traditions of this kind seriously. The vision they express is metaphysical and transcendental: it comes before, and determines the conditions of, every empirical perception and every shape we give to history.

Elsewhere,184 Qāzī Saʿīd places these twelve veils at the summit of an infinity of other veils. These represent the spiritual universes that guard the approach to the Majesty of the “non-being that transcends being.” They are the seventy thousand veils mentioned in a sermon by the First Imam—the number seventy thousand here being neither an arithmetical nor a statistical figure. Several interpretations have been offered by thinkers such as Ghazālī, Rūzbihān Baqlī, and Najm Dāya Rāzī. Some understand these veils as the coverings successively assumed by spirits as they descend to “the lowest of the depths,” a theme familiar throughout Gnostic thought.

There is also an astrological interpretation. Others see the veils as the forms in which the divine Names manifest themselves. Qāzī Saʿīd then offers his own interpretation, inspired by Quran 41:53. These are the veils of the “world of the horizons” and the “world of souls,” of the macrocosm and the microcosm: a symbolic explanation of the seven Heavens and the seven Earths. “Whenever the pilgrim journeying toward God lifts one of these veils, it is as though he tears open that Heaven, rises to it, and enters it. As Christ said: No one enters the Kingdom (malakūt) of the Heavens unless he has been born twice.”

But above these veils stand the “seventy thousand Tabernacles of Majesty,” and higher still, beyond the Tabernacles, stand the twelve Veils of Light: the Twelve Imams, the twelve universes or millennia (Aeons) in which the Muhammadan Light dwells before its earthly manifestation.

In yet another passage,185 Qāzī Saʿīd bases his commentary on a conversation between the Fifth Imam, Muhammad Bāqir, and his disciple Jābir ibn ʿAbdallāh. During this exchange, the Imam does more than explain a Quranic verse: he brings about in his disciple a visionary experience that reveals its meaning. The verse is: “We showed Abraham the malakūt of the Heavens and the Earth” (6:75).

But what is this malakūt of the Earth? The Imam explains: “It consists of twelve universes, having the configuration (hay'a, the Gestalt) that you see. Whenever one of us, the Twelve Imams, has completed his time in this world, he takes up his dwelling in one of those twelve universes, until the last of us, the Qāʾim [the Imam of the Resurrection], comes to be in the universe which we inhabit together with him.”

Qāzī Saʿīd comments that these twelve universes are the twelve Veils of Light described in the preceding hadith, where they already marked the stages of the Muhammadan Light's descent from the Pleroma into this world. They are the respective universes of the Imams, each made manifest in our world through the Imam who corresponds to it. The first universe, where the Source of Life is said to be located—the source from which Khiḍr drank—is the universe of the First Imam, ʿAlī. This Source of Life is walāyat, because it is through the knowledge and recognition (maʿrifat) of walāyat that eternal life becomes a reality, from Imam to Imam, in every “true Shiite” (shīʿī ḥaqīqī).

The second universe belongs to Imam Ḥasan ibn ʿAlī; the third to Imam Ḥusayn; and so on. When the period during which one of these universes is manifested in this world comes to an end, its Imam withdraws into the malakūt of his own universe. Thus, from Imam to Imam, until the Twelfth, the Perfect Human Being grows toward completion as the totality of these universes. This growth takes the form of an ascent: the Light rises back toward the Malakūt from which it descended. We shall give a complete translation of the visionary setting of this hadith later (pp. 184 ff.).

Qāzī Saʿīd also discovers this same twelvefold structure in the architecture of the Temple of the Kaaba. Since we have discussed the subject at length elsewhere,186 we shall confine ourselves to a few reminders. In Qāzī Saʿīd, as in all his fellow thinkers, the understanding of the imaginal world's reality gives rise to an exceptionally vivid awareness of spiritual form—form in its full, almost sculptural sense. As he meditates upon it, the form of the Temple made of physical stone becomes intelligible and is transfigured into a spiritual form. He first discovers within it a structure and a set of relationships that correspond to those of the doctrine of the Imams: the structure of the cubic Temple “shows” why the Imamate is limited to twelve Imams, and no more.

Then, once the form of the Temple is freed from its material character and revealed as a spiritual form, it discloses itself as the very secret of the spiritual human being, the inner human being. In doing so, it also reveals the secret (sirr), the inward meaning (bāṭin), of the pilgrimage and its ritual acts. Qāzī Saʿīd is a metaphysician. If we are tempted to describe him as a “structuralist” or Gestalt philosopher, it is only to suggest that one can be both of these things while remaining a traditional metaphysician.

His commentary shows how the twelve Imams, in their twelve persons of light, symbolize the twelve functional relationships essential to the structure of the cubic form of the “Throne established upon the Primordial Water”—the Intelligence understood as light, as a “center that surrounds” the realities it knows. This is the theme developed throughout the chapter devoted to the inner meanings of the pilgrimage (asrār al-ḥajj). That chapter forms part of the treatise on the inner meanings of divine worship (asrār al-ʿibādāt), whose place within Qāzī Saʿīd's great commentary on Ibn Bābūya's Tawhīd we noted earlier.

The Kaaba, with its cubic structure, has its corresponding forms, or archetypes, in the spiritual universes that precede and transcend our material, sensible universe: in the Jabarūt, in the Malakūt, and in the ʿālam al-mithāl, the mundus imaginalis, or imaginal world. In each universe, of course, these forms exist according to the mode of being proper to that universe.

Some exceptionally beautiful traditions of the Imams—the image of the Celestial Tent and that of the White Cloud—suggest how the design of the earthly Kaaba imitates, or “recounts” (ḥikāyat), the heavenly Temples. They also suggest how the secret concealed in the Black Stone, now set into a corner of the Kaaba, is connected with Adam's inner drama. This is the motif of the White Pearl set within the heart of the spiritual Temple, a motif that resonates with the “Hymn of the Pearl” in the Acts of Thomas. From this perspective, the entire ritual of the pilgrimage unfolds as a mystical initiation. Act by act, in the course of the liturgy, the pilgrim repeats what Adam first accomplished at the direction of the Angel Gabriel, and brings about within himself a potential restoration of the paradisal state.

If we bring together the two imagines agentes, the image of the twelve Veils of Light and the image of the Temple, we can identify a structural analogy between two relationships. On the one hand stands the relationship of the Muhammadan Light to the twelve Veils of Light—that is, to the twelve Imams and their respective universes. On the other stands the relationship of the Temple's configuration, its Gestalt, to the twelve edges of its cubic form.

The number twelve is the symbolic key to the Imamate, or walāyat. Because walāyat is the “inner reality of prophecy,” this twelvefold structure is also the hidden and necessary structure of the Muhammadan Reality itself, the first manifestation of the Inaccessible, the “non-being beyond being.” The twelve Veils reveal this structure in the successive order of the metahistorical world's “subtle time”; the twelve edges of the Temple's cubic form reveal it in the simultaneous order of pure imaginal space.

The space of the Temple, the Kaaba's archetype, holds together in simultaneous coexistence the twelve universes of the Imams. Their successive manifestations in this world gradually build the spiritual Temple as the image and form of the Perfect Human Being, the Homo maximus (Ādam al-kabīr). Humanity's sacred history is the gradual building of a Temple that encompasses the malakūt—the suprasensible reality—of all twelve universes of the twelve Imams. Just as the hierarchy of their degrees within the Pleroma marks the successive stages of the Muhammadan Light's descent, so their manifestations on earth lead that Light back to its origin, drawing earthly humanity along with it in a continuous ascent toward its own malakūt.187

In its inward meaning, the pilgrimage to the Temple of the Kaaba is the pilgrimage of a human life whose guiding axis is the Malakūt. And it sometimes happens that, under the guidance of the Imam, a few chosen individuals are granted the privilege of entering the world of the Malakūt for a time, with the eyes of inner vision fully open. Such an experience is attested by one of the most extraordinary visionary traditions of Shiite Islam, a true account of initiation: the “Hadith of the White Cloud” (ḥadīth al-ghamāma). Our Qāzī Saʿīd devoted to it a commentary worthy of both a profound philosopher and a great spiritual master. It is this work of his that we now wish to examine.

3. The “Tale of the White Cloud” as an Account of Initiation

The “Tale of the White Cloud” introduces us to a world that is simply another region of the world into which Swedenborg's Memorabilia lead us. For this reason, rather than beginning with any other philosophical premise, I would like to quote a few lines from Kant's lectures on psychology. These passages offer an exceptionally clear account of what it means to have a visionary experience of the other world. They also reveal what Kant ultimately thought of Swedenborg himself and his work: “The other world is not another place, but another kind of intuition.

“As far as objects are concerned, the other world remains this same world. As far as substances are concerned, it is not different; it is simply perceived through spiritual intuition.” And again: “Intuitive knowledge of the other world can be attained only by giving up something of the understanding that we need for the present world.” Finally, after explaining the meaning of blessedness and damnation in the spiritual world, Kant states quite literally: “Swedenborg's thought on this point is altogether sublime.”188

And indeed, throughout the “Tale of the White Cloud,” we find that the images and events encountered in the Malakūt are the malakūtī, “celestial” or “imaginal,” aspect of realities belonging to the sensible world. As such, these images are the hidden face and hidden meaning of sensible things. But when those things reveal themselves to inner vision, the relationship is reversed: sensible reality itself becomes their hidden meaning.

Here we must be particularly careful. Reference to a sensible object serves only to help us understand the corresponding appearances within the mundus imaginalis. Its purpose is certainly not to explain those appearances away, for that would mean falling back to the level of the world of sensible appearances. To pass into the imaginal world is for the face that was visible to become hidden, and for the face that was invisible to become manifest.

We cannot explain that newly revealed invisible reality by concealing it all over again. To do so would reduce the experience to allegory and confuse the imaginary with the imaginal. The “Tale of the White Cloud” is not an allegory. It recounts a concrete visionary experience, which presupposes what we may call a realism of the imaginal.

As it appears in the text commented upon by Qāzī Saʿīd Qummī, this hadith is a genuine account of initiation. Under the Imam's guidance, the initiates undertake a journey that is a real entry into the world of the Malakūt. This is the world we call the mundus imaginalis, and we can best understand its place by returning to our commentator's account of the universe's three fundamental planes or levels (ḥaḍarāt, literally “presences” or “dignities”). The first is the “world of mystery” (ʿālam al-ghayb), the suprasensible realm of the Cherubic Intelligences. The second is the world of sensible perception, the world of visible phenomena (ʿālam al-shahādat).

The third arises through the union of these two worlds. It is the world of imaginative perception (ʿālam al-khayāl), also called the ʿālam al-mithāl, literally the mundus imaginalis. In this world, intelligible and intellectual realities appear in forms that resemble sensible appearances but are perceived through the imaginative faculty. Knowledge, for example, may appear as milk or water; Islam as a pillar; faith as a handle; and the Angel Gabriel as a young man of perfect beauty.

The tale belongs to the same family as Suhrawardī's accounts of initiation, especially the “Tale of the Crimson Archangel” and the “Tale of the Western Exile,” and, more broadly, to the immense literature of “journeys into the Beyond.” Among these we may include the account of the journey to the Green Island, “in the land of the Hidden Imam” (see below, Book VII, Chapter II, section 2).

Everything in these accounts follows an exceptionally rigorous pattern. As in Swedenborg's Memorabilia, the correspondence is never forgotten between the images seen in the Malakūt—the real imaginal forms, the imaginalia or apparentiae reales—and what is taking place, even in this very world, within the hidden depths of human consciousness. We may say that the “Tale of the White Cloud” is an account of initiation whose purpose, episodes, and consequences are comparable to those of the anagōgē, the spiritual ascent that took on the meaning of a “sacrament of immortality” for the mystical community whose sacred book was probably the Chaldaean Oracles. These Oracles were studied and interpreted with particular devotion by the later Neoplatonists, including Proclus and Syrianus (see above, Book II, Chapter II). For whoever has entered the Malakūt and there reached the Source of Life has been reborn, and is henceforth beyond the reach of death and nothingness.

Qāzī Saʿīd wrote a commentary on this tale so extensive that it constitutes a book in itself; here we can give only its substance. The commentary forms the eleventh and final treatise of his unfinished Summa (see above, p. 131), which was intended to comprise forty treatises (Kitāb al-Arbaʿīniyyāt).189 The hadith itself does not appear to be recorded in Majlisī's great encyclopedia. Qāzī Saʿīd, however, cites as his authoritative source a collection by Shaykh Ṣadūq Ibn Bābūya, along with two other collections.190

We should make clear at once that this account must not be confused with another lengthy narrative, which does appear in Majlisī's encyclopedia and is known as the “Tale of the Carpet” (ḥadīth al-bisāṭ).191 That narrative describes the journey of the Imam and his companions to visit the Seven Sleepers (see Quran, Sura XVIII), whereas our tale describes a visionary exploration of Mount Qāf, the cosmic and psycho-cosmic mountain.

The “Tale of the White Cloud” is narrated by Salmān Pārsī, also known as Salmān Pāk—Salmān the Persian, or Salmān the Pure. He is a Persian knight of Zoroastrian origin who set out in search of the True Prophet and mysteriously became something like the Prophet of Islam's companion in initiation.

Six individuals are gathered around the First Imam in his house in Medina. Among them are his two young sons, al-Ḥasan and al-Ḥusayn, who will later become the Second and Third Imams. The young al-Ḥasan introduces the central theme when he addresses his father with these words: “Solomon, the son of David, asked God for a power such as no one after him would possess [an allusion to Quran 38:35]. Do you possess something of Solomon's power?”

Toward the end of the tale, we shall learn that the Imam, in his metaphysical reality, is the inward essence of every prophetic gift. From the beginning and for all eternity, he is the one who holds the power of the Seal that he himself bestowed upon Solomon. The Imam's affirmative answer to his son's question therefore leads the young al-Ḥasan to express this wish: “We would like to contemplate something of that Malakūt over which God has granted you sovereignty, so that people's faith may grow as our own faith grows” (§§1–3).192

The Imam grants this devout wish immediately, and a mysterious journey without movement begins. It will lead our pilgrims first into the Malakūt of the vegetable kingdom, and then into the Malakūt of the realm of organic life. From there they penetrate the Malakūt of human reality, passing through a series of levels: first, the Malakūt of vegetable life within the human being (anima vegetabilis); next, that of organic life within the human being (anima vitalis); and finally, that of the thinking soul (anima rationalis).

This entry into the human Malakūt will be experienced as an ascent to the summit of Mount Qāf, the psycho-cosmic mountain. Since the laws of chronological time have now been suspended, our pilgrims will find themselves living alongside people and events belonging to the “past.” They will then glimpse the secrets of mysterious and distant universes. The entire journey will unfold in five stages.

When the companions return to awareness of this world, they will have become men of the Malakūt. At the end of his commentary, Qāzī Saʿīd will therefore be able to tell his reader: “We have explained all this to you so that you too may take your place with the Imam's companions upon the malakūtī cloud [the White Cloud], and rise with them to the Malakūt.”

The first of these explanations, however—the one prompted by the Imam's gesture that causes the Cloud to appear, and on which our understanding of everything that follows depends—concerns the folding inward of chronological time and the space of the sensible world.

4. The Folding Inward of Chronological Time and Sensible Space

Indeed, the guiding thread of Qāzī Saʿīd's commentary, from one episode to the next, is the initiates' entry, under the Imam's guidance, first into the Malakūt of space and then into the Malakūt of time. This entry, by its very nature, causes the space and time of the sensible world to fold inward.

Admittedly, from this point of view, space occupies a privileged position in relation to time. At the level of physics, Qāzī Saʿīd explains, we must approach the question of space through the surfaces of physical objects. At the metaphysical level, however, what concerns us is the Space of spaces, understood as the Throne (ʿarsh) of everything that has spatial existence. Even the word “distance,” when used at this level, can be understood only by analogy with our own world. Everything in this world is like an outer husk enclosing the kernel that is the other world; physical surface is itself no more than the husk surrounding the distance with which metaphysics is concerned.

Yet at whatever level we consider it, space belongs to the order of what is simultaneous and stable, whereas time, at the physical level, belongs essentially to the order of what is successive and unstable. When this time folds back into a higher order of time, its instability comes to an end: the temporal order is stabilized into a spatial order. Here we may recall Gurnemanz's words to Parsifal: “Here, my son, time becomes space.”

The drama unfolded by the account of initiation thus appears as a redemption of time, a reclaiming of what has been surrendered to time, precisely insofar as the initiate is admitted into the space of the Malakūt. This is one of the most important perspectives from which we must contemplate the hadith of the White Cloud and its commentary.

We must therefore keep in mind the philosophy of time that preoccupied our author throughout so many pages of his works, and that ultimately provides the key to his commentary on the “Tale of the White Cloud.” He deals with it explicitly in the prologue and returns to it once more during the final episode.

Indeed, as soon as we confront the questions raised by hermeneutics—by the spiritual understanding of the Quran's true meaning—we cannot avoid appealing to an interpretation of time itself, to the philosophy of the “forms of temporality” developed by Qāzī Saʿīd Qummī (see above, Book I, Chapter III, section 5).

We are well aware that a full account of this theme, as treated by our philosophers, would require an entire book. Nevertheless, we cannot proceed without drawing from Qāzī Saʿīd's commentary on the “Tale of the White Cloud” a few fundamental observations that complement the more extended analyses he has offered elsewhere.193

First, Qāzī Saʿīd firmly rejects the notion of time as a line stretching from pre-eternity (azal) to post-eternity (abad). If he must give time a geometrical form, he prefers that of a sphere or circle representing the “time of times,” or “absolute time.” The capacity of this sphere or circle corresponds exactly to that of the sphere or circle representing the “Space of spaces,” or absolute space. The two spheres are coextensive: they coincide in their entirety and already coexist as complete wholes.

Unfortunately, this is not how time appears “among us”—what our author calls dense, compact time, the time of the sensible world. Because the perceiving subject is confined within the narrow limits of sense organs belonging to a material body of an inferior order, the different parts of time, space, and movement do not coexist for that subject. Their coexistence cannot be perceived.

As Qāzī Saʿīd writes: “The one who is chained within the Sijjīn [the abyss, hell] of sensible perceptions is incapable of perceiving all the parts of time and movement simultaneously. But the inability to perceive something does not mean that what is not perceived does not exist. Nothing prevents these parts from coexisting within the vessel of everlasting duration (fī ẓarf al-dahr, the Aeon), and from being present there simultaneously.”

Everything changes, of course, when the perishable body of material flesh is replaced by a subtle body whose very substance is pure light (mādda nūriyya). Such are the bodies of the Imams. They were created from the purest portion of the substance from which the spirits of creatures were formed: the subtle body of light belonging to the Throne (jism laṭīf nūrī ʿarshī). The original body of their followers, too, was created from the radiance of the Imams' light.

Qāzī Saʿīd writes:

“Movement, with all its pasts and futures, and time, with all its pre-eternities and post-eternities, as they appear to anyone observing sensible things, are two magnitudes that rise upon the carpet of stability and permanence. Both are oriented toward the Kaaba of the All-Powerful King. They carry the actions of human beings from the abode of transience to the abode of enduring existence.

“Thus the days and nights are like a line of camels bringing the caravan of creatures toward the abode of stability, while the months and years that have passed move to meet the ‘Promised Day,’ accompanied by the clouds of evening and the clouds of morning.

“But consider the mountains. Although they appear fixed to our senses and our ordinary powers of judgment, they are perpetually moving—as the Quranic verse says: ‘You see the mountains and think them motionless, yet they move as the clouds move’ (27:90). In the same way, but in the opposite direction, times and moments, despite their passing and coming to an end, are stable essences, permanent realities, when seen by the Intelligence and the Soul of the World.

“The modes of existence that prevail among sensible things are therefore reversed. The knower must understand that apparent [outward] fixity does not exclude hidden [inward] movement, and that restlessness [movement] at the sensible level does not exclude repose, stability, and permanence at the level of the Intelligence [Nous]…

“Space and time, to the gaze that penetrates to the depths of things, are two corresponding planes or levels, two sublime Thrones for the beings above and the beings below. In their union and stability, pre-eternity and post-eternity embrace one another within a single moment; manifestation and concealment embrace one another within a single place. When they separate and appear gradually, the first becomes distinct from the last, and the hidden [the inward] becomes distinct from the manifest [the outward].”

To understand this, Qāzī Saʿīd explains, we must imagine that everything which concretely exists—whether in a material state, that is, compact and dense, or in a spiritual state, that is, subtle—forms a unity, a single individuality. Just as each individual being has its own quantity (miqdār) of matter and its own measure of space, so each has its own measure of time: a unique, personal time, possessing dimensions of length and breadth. Every individuality thus has a time different from every other individuality's time, just as it occupies a place different from the place occupied by another. Contemporaneity in the true sense therefore presupposes at least some correspondence between these different times.

Now, something can happen to any given measure of time that resembles what happens to a piece of wax when we compress it or stretch it out. Its shape and extension change, but the quantity of its substance neither increases nor decreases. And so it is with the body and its time: the subtler the body, the subtler its measure of time becomes, and the greater the capacity and extent that time can attain.

There is, then, the compact, dense, opaque time (zamān kathīf) of the sensible world. There is the subtle time (zamān laṭīf) of the “imaginal” world of the Malakūt, which must not be confused with “imaginary time” (zamān mawhūm). Finally, there is the absolutely subtle time (zamān alṭaf) of the intelligible and intellectual world of the Jabarūt.

When speaking of subtle time, we can describe either a folding inward or an expansion of time. It depends on whether we regard the moments dispersed throughout succession as gathered together and made present to the subject, or regard the subject as becoming present to all those moments at once. These are merely two perspectives on one and the same event.

Without any change in its own measure, the time allotted to a spiritual individuality can thus encompass an immense expanse of being. Conversely, that individuality can have before it a multitude—or even the totality—of the moments of existence, all present in perfect synchrony. Succession becomes simultaneity. Time becomes space as it is raised, through successive degrees of refinement, to an ever subtler state of being.

Qāzī Saʿīd writes:

“So long as you have not emerged from the narrow confines of your senses and entered the kingdom of your own Malakūt [that is, the suprasensible realm of your subtle body, as you exist in the celestial world of the Malakūt], you must know—or rather, you must remember—that movement, time, and space correspond to one another at their respective levels [the levels of the Mulk, the Malakūt, and the Jabarūt]. Likewise, the different universes have boundaries and points of reference that correspond to one another.

“The subtler space becomes, as we pass through these universes arranged in ascending degrees of subtlety, all the way to absolute subtlety, the subtler movement and time become as well.

“The malakūtī body [the subtle body of light belonging to the Malakūt] possesses perfect subtlety and luminosity. No curtain or barrier can hide anything from it; neither earth nor heaven can obstruct its passage. Such is the condition of the Angels who descend from the supreme station (min al-maqām al-aʿlā) to communicate revelation to the prophets. Such, too, is the condition of the prophets when they rise to the station described in the Quranic verse as ‘the distance of two bows, or nearer still’ (53:9).

“The celestial individualities of the Malakūt (ashkhāṣ malakūtiyya) are not subject to the necessity of being in one particular place rather than another within sensible space. Every place stands in an equal relationship to them. The totality of places, in relation to these beings, is comparable to the relationship of the Earth to Heaven.

“And what is true of space is true also of malakūtī time and malakūtī movement. Their subtlety is such that all the times and movements belonging to our world are gathered and folded into the time and movement of the Malakūt. Indeed, a single portion of malakūtī time or movement, when unfolded, is equivalent to months and years of our own time.

“If this is true of the Malakūt, imagine what must be true of the worlds that stand even higher than it.”

Qāzī Saʿīd recalls this entire theory of subtle time and space at the beginning of his commentary because the whole interpretation of the “Tale of the White Cloud” depends upon it. There are two reasons for this.

First, the tale as a whole describes an experience of absolute time, of the simultaneity of different times as they exist permanently within the Malakūt. Second, the experience takes place through the subtle body. Consequently, the measure of time allotted to each participant in the events of the tale undergoes a transformation analogous to what happens to the piece of wax in our philosopher's earlier comparison.

What we find here, then, is a conception of the gradual refinement of “subtle matter” that can be compared—just as Mullā Ṣadrā Shīrāzī has already led us to do elsewhere—with the spissitudo spiritualis, the spiritual density, of the Cambridge Platonists, particularly Henry More. This conception has the power to overcome the dualism of thought and extension that has caused so much difficulty for philosophers in the West.

We can begin to sense all this from the very opening of the tale. The six companions—sons or disciples of the First Imam, ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib—are gathered in his house, engaged in a spiritual conversation with him. His young son al-Ḥasan addresses to his father the request we read earlier.

In response, the Imam rises, performs a prayer of two rakʿāt—two cycles of ritual prayer—and walks into the courtyard of his house. The disciples keep their eyes fixed upon him.

“Then the Imam stretched out his noble hand toward the west, and held it there until a cloud became visible to us, emerging from the palm of his hand. He spread out this cloud until he caused it to remain suspended above the house. Behind this cloud there was another cloud” (§5).

From the very beginning of this scene, baṣīra, inner vision, is already at work. It is the faculty through which entry into the Malakūt becomes possible. Without realizing it, the participants have been withdrawn from the world of empirical perception. What they are now perceiving is no longer the sensible world.

Every detail marks a stage in this transition. This is why Qāzī Saʿīd attaches such importance to the meaning of each one. Unfortunately, we can retain only what is essential to his interpretation.

Our commentator begins by observing that the secret (sirr) of the scene, from this very moment, is that everything is taking place within the Malakūt. The Imam acts and reveals himself to his companions through his subtle, malakūtī body. But the companions do not yet know this. They will understand only after the scene of “transfiguration” that occurs a little later, when they have all taken their places together upon the White Cloud.

First comes the gesture of the Imam's hand. This hand is in fact a member of the Imam's subtle body, his malakūtī hand (al-yad al-malakūtī). For this hand, there is neither nearness nor distance. Our Earth, compared with the Earth of the Malakūt, which is its inner, hidden reality, is no more than “a walnut in relation to you when you hold it in the hollow of your hand.”

And why does the Imam extend the hand of his subtle, malakūtī body toward the west?

“Because the dimension of walāyat, which is the inward reality and secret of prophecy, is situated on the western side of the higher world, just as the sun of prophecy is situated in the east of that higher world. This is because the Friends of God (Awliyāʾ Allāh) are illuminated by the light of the prophets and are brought to their perfection through the guidance of the prophets.”

The placing of walāyat in the west corresponds to a theme found in other authors, including Shams al-Dīn Lāhījī. In their writings, the cycle of walāyat appears as the night of inward meaning, while the spiritual journey is portrayed as a passage through that night, advancing by way of symbols.

Since the power and sovereignty of the Imams belong to the western side of the higher world—the “place” of walāyat—we can now understand the full meaning of the Imam's gesture at the beginning of the tale, when he stretches the hand of his subtle body toward the west.

As for the two clouds brought into appearance by that gesture, Qāzī Saʿīd suggests their meaning by referring to a hadith of the Sixth Imam, Jaʿfar al-Ṣādiq.194 This tradition states:

“The Imam ʿAlī is sovereign over what is upon the Earth and over what is beneath the Earth. It happened that two clouds appeared before him: a heavy cloud and a light cloud. The Imam chose the heavy cloud. Now, the heavy cloud contained dominion over what is beneath the Earth, while the light cloud contained dominion over what is upon the Earth. But the Imam gave his preference to the heavy cloud.”

Our commentator explains that “what is upon the Earth” means what is apparent, external, and outward—the exoteric. “What is beneath the Earth” means what is hidden, internal, and inward—the esoteric. It does not mean the underworld or hell (infernum) at all, but the Malakūt.

In the hadith we are examining, the light cloud follows the heavy cloud. This is because the Imam commands both. Although he has expressed a preference for the heavy cloud, he remains sovereign over everything upon the Earth and everything beneath it, as the tradition explicitly declares.

Having established this general principle, Qāzī Saʿīd sets out to explain the metaphysical reality (ḥaqīqat) represented by the two clouds. He begins with two premises, from which the truth of what is symbolized will emerge—that is, the truth of the reality perceived imaginally in the form of a “cloud.”

A) The premises. The first is this: the heavy cloud—the first cloud that the Imam's hand “spreads out” in our tale—represents dominion over what lies beneath the Earth, in other words, over inward reality. As such, it gathers time into itself, causing it to fold inward. For the journey through metaphysical realities (ḥaqāʾiq), those belonging to the inward level of existence, takes place outside the laws of chronological time, the dark and dense time called kathīf.

The light cloud, on the other hand—the second cloud in our tale—represents dominion over what is upon the Earth, in other words, over outward reality. It gathers into itself the visible aspect of the Earth: place, and the spatial character of place.

It follows naturally that within the hierarchy of being, this second cloud, representing outward reality, appears only in second position. For the folding inward of time brings about the folding inward of space, and not the other way around.

The second premise is this. The philosophers of divine wisdom hold that every species in the visible world has a corresponding being in the Malakūt. With God's permission, this being governs and protects the species, preserving its unity and holding its multiplicity together.
