Then the Imam withdrew from them and returned to us. He touched our bodies and our hearts with his hand, saying: ‘Remain steadfast in faith.’ Then he went toward them again and once more called them to faith.

“We watched them. Again they refused. Then a single great cry rang out. I swear by the One in whose hand my soul rests! At that moment I thought the earth had turned upside down and the mountains had been flattened. And I saw the people of 'Âd lying on the ground like hollow trunks of palm trees (Quran 69:6–7). Then the Imam said to us: ‘May God never allow your faith to weaken!’” (§ 28).

Reflecting on the paradox of this shared presence within the Malakût, Qâzî Sa'îd writes:

“Understand that there is no contradiction between what happens in our story, which describes how the people of 'Âd perished by the Imam’s sword, and the Quranic account describing how they perished in the violence of an unceasing hurricane. Nor is there any contradiction between the Quranic account of their wrongdoing in centuries past and the battle that the Imam wages against them before the eyes of the companions. For the hurricane, like every host among the divine hosts, obeys the Imam by God’s permission.

“And the Imam himself is the ordeal that strikes his enemies, because he is the Supreme Sign (al-âya al-kubrâ) which they reject. It was through him and by his command that the destruction of earlier generations took place, just as the salvation of the believers among those generations came about through his grace and mercy. For the Imam is present with every prophet, secretly and in a suprasensible way (malakûtan wa sirran: literally, ‘as Malakût’). And it is precisely this companionship within the Malakût that the Imam now allows Salmân the Pure and the other companions to see.”

Thus the teaching of the visionary account reaches its conclusion in what amounts to a direct demonstration, within the Malakût, of a celebrated hadith encountered many times in the course of this work. In it the Prophet declares that “the Imam was sent secretly with every prophet before me, whereas with me he was sent openly.” Because the spiritual reality of the Imam is the inner meaning of the prophetic message, it carries within itself the secret of sacred history—hierohistory—the spiritual, hidden, invisible history of humanity.

Only through the Malakût is authentic contemporaneity established. Those whose individual measures of time have reached the same degree are present together in the same region of the Malakût. And only in the Malakût does the whole become visible, in a way that cannot be compared with the fragmentary vision afforded by the “opaque time” of our historical existence.

VII. The Hour of Noon

Beyond comparison indeed! After one final flight, about which we are told nothing except that the earth now appeared to the companions no longer even the size of a shield, but as small as a little coin—a dirham—the story of the White Cloud ends with a swift return to earth. The companions find themselves once again in the Imam’s house, which they had never physically left, in less than the blink of an eye. The muezzin was chanting the call to the noon prayer.

“And yet,” Salmân the Pure explains, “we had set out at sunrise. Thus we had been to Mount Qâf, traveled around it, and returned within a period of five hours” (§§ 29–30).

These five hours correspond to the five “stations” (maqâmât) that the Imam showed his companions in the Malakût, each station marking one hour. But these five hours are obviously an estimate made according to the outward measurements of our earthly, “opaque and dense” time. There is otherwise no common measure between earthly time and the time of the Malakût, where one can be contemporary with both past and future, and where time becomes space: the space of the soul’s inner distances, which the soul crosses at a speed proportionate to the strength of its longing.

The word “hour” in the Malakût must be understood in the sense it bears in the Quran, where “the Hour” signifies the Day of Resurrection. This is why the reference to “the hour of noon” appears so full of meaning to Qâzî Sa'îd. Noon is the hour when beings cast no shadow; according to certain Iranian traditions, it is always noon in Yima’s Var, his mysterious enclosure. What this hour of noon ultimately announces is the meaning of the story of the White Cloud as an account of initiation.

The companions’ ascent into the Malakût has made them people of the Malakût. That is why, at the beginning, we recalled another mystical ascent: the anagôgê, which for the community that revered the Chaldean Oracles as its sacred book possessed the meaning of a “sacrament of immortality.” Here the companions who have undergone this initiation have passed by the Spring of Life. They have attained the perfectly balanced stature of the spiritual human being. This is what it means to reach the hour of noon, the hour when the muezzin sounds the call to midday prayer.

“That they have reached the hour of noon,” Qâzî Sa'îd writes, “indicates that during this journey they have reached the equator of human reality and the equinoctial line of the Imam’s walâyat, for he is the Seal of absolute walâyat.”212

And this is why it would be beside the point to subject this visionary hadith, or any similar hadith, to a purely “historical criticism.” What purpose would be served by asking whether this episode occurred in one particular year or another during the Imam’s earthly lifetime? Or whether Salmân was truly the “transmitter” of the account, or whether the text was composed at a later date? Nothing that takes place in it occurs within ordinary chronological history. Its very purpose is to draw us out of that history.

If we treated the text in this way, what would remain in our hands but the torn fragments of a chrysalis? For at what date, in what realm of verifiable historical events, could we place the moment when the Imam truly appeared in this way to a devoted Shiite believer, together with the events that truly followed in the Malakût? We encounter an accomplished reality only where it is actually accomplished. And here its accomplishment does not take place on the stage of visible history. The reality of the hour of noon in the Malakût corresponds to the liturgical time of the muezzin’s call to prayer. Liturgical time is not historical time.

All the elements that make up the spiritual philosophy of the Imams have been contemplated in this way. As in Suhrawardî’s visionary narratives, there comes a privileged instant when a doctrine becomes an event personally experienced in a vision. That is how we come to possess this hadith. Whatever year the person who wrote it down may have taken up his pen, it was indeed Salmân the Pure who told what he had seen—what, to use Semnânî’s language, the “Salmân within his own being” had been capable of seeing.

And if Qâzî Sa'îd Qommî wrote the commentary whose essential meaning we have tried to bring out, it was with an intention he made clear from the very beginning: to lead his reader to take a place upon the White Cloud as well, and rise into the Malakût. Even if the reader cannot fully realize that intention, Qâzî Sa'îd remains one of those Iranian philosophers and spiritual thinkers from whom there is much to learn for anyone who wishes not to “belong to his time” or “keep up with his time,” according to the commonplace slogans of our age, but to be his own time, and to be it completely.

Qâzî Sa'îd’s metaphysics of time is the surest antidote to the illusion of an anonymous, impersonal time supposedly shared by everyone. The fact that several beings coexist within chronological time is not enough to make them contemporaries. The idea that every being possesses its own particular measure, or quantum, of time—which, like its own quantum of substance, passes through different states of density and subtlety—allows us to determine much more surely who our contemporaries are and who they are not.

Contemporaneity, or synchronism, exists when the measure of time belonging to different beings has reached the same state or degree. It means that together they aim toward the same height on the horizon of the Malakût. They can be there together, for example, at the “hour of noon,” and so become contemporaries of the same events, because the measure of time that is truly their own has broken through the irreversible time of History. Entry into the Malakût, and into the time of the Malakût, can only be a mysterium liturgicum, a liturgical mystery. That is what the muezzin’s call to the noon prayer announces to the companions.

Epilogue

At the end of this brief study of Qâzî Sa'îd Qommî, a question inevitably arises for the philosophical researcher who has become familiar with a text such as the “Story of the White Cloud” and with the interpretation given to it by a traditional theosopher. The question is this: what impression can this story and its interpretation make on a reader today, when everything in our civilization and culture tends to keep us on this side of Mount Qâf? We can indeed say everything.

For what we call the “human sciences”—sociology and social history, psychology and psychoanalysis—as well as those sciences once called the “divine sciences,” which no longer dare speak their name since a certain theology lost sight of its object along the way: all these disciplines, through the interpretations they impose upon the facts over which they have made themselves judges, tend to close every passage that might allow us to enter Mount Qâf and pass beyond it.

I have sometimes asked myself this question while reflecting on the similarities between the visions described in the “Story of the White Cloud” and certain visions recorded in Swedenborg’s Memorabilia. During one such reflection, I happened to read an article about Strindberg. We know that, at the end of experiences of extraordinary suffering, Strindberg was able to write that Swedenborg had been his guide, the Virgil who enabled him to pass through hell. In that article I found these words quoted:

“From atheism to Swedenborg is only a single step.”213

The deeper truth suggested by this brief saying then appeared to me as follows. It is easier to cross Mount Qâf after a devastation that has shattered the Image of himself that Man possessed by virtue of his origin—an origin he knew to be heavenly—than it ever has been, or ever will be, for a comfortable rationalist orthodoxy to make that crossing. Nor does it become any easier when such an orthodoxy is replaced by a theological conformism that throws itself into a frantic pursuit of history, vainly hoping to find salvation in history itself. That race is lost before it begins, even at the cost of the “betrayal of the intellectuals.”

Yet perhaps the metaphysical devastation brought about by our “human sciences” and by a theology in disarray may, on the contrary, make it easier for a few people to rediscover the path to Mount Qâf. What our “human sciences,” no less than a theology concerned solely with outward meanings, have forgotten is that the masters and schools who knew and transmitted the esoteric—that is, the spiritual—meaning of the Bible and the Quran always understood that this spiritual meaning belonged to a transcendent and enduring world. That world remains hidden behind the outward appearance of events that occurred in the “opaque and dense” time of historical chronicles.

Spiritual meaning is not established by reference to a date in chronology, nor as an expression of a social condition. It is the expression of a state of the Malakût. Consequently, whenever scientific facts or discoveries, or new interpretations elevated to the status of established facts, have caused alarm, and people have responded either with apologetic arguments or, as so often today, by trying to outdo the discoveries themselves, the reason has always been the same. They have forgotten that all these facts and discoveries, however immense the expanses of space and time they reveal, remain on this side of Mount Qâf. I believe this symbolic language is particularly appropriate here.

But when there are no longer any “divine sciences,” what can a theology accomplish if it too remains on this side of Mount Qâf? Long before modern scientific discoveries, the vastness of time and space, and the multitude of worlds, had already been revealed to traditional theosophy, as the “Story of the White Cloud” shows us.

But all this presupposed the folding of our time and space back upon themselves. It was revealed as something lying beyond Mount Qâf. That makes all the difference. It would therefore be absurd to confuse traveling from one planet to another by physical means with entering Mount Qâf.

But if a traditional mystical theosophy still exists, it is precisely its task to make use of these discoveries, just as it makes use of any other phenomenon, and turn them into new possible points of entry into the Malakût. I believe Qâzî Sa'îd Qommî and his fellow thinkers would have proceeded in just this way. His metaphysics of being as light seems to call us in precisely this direction. With its own particular variations, this metaphysics belongs to the metaphysics of Light widely professed by the traditional theosophical schools of Christianity and Islam, and by Jewish Kabbalists.

Qâzî Sa'îd Qommî’s doctrine of individual measures, or quanta, of time and space is simply a consequence of an analysis applied to the entire metaphysics of being. Through this analysis, the gulf between what is called Spirit and what is called Matter disappears. There is one and the same Light, differentiated into countless degrees of condensation and subtlety. There is “spiritual matter,” and there is matter in its “material state.” The body, in the world of the Malakût, becomes a subtle spiritual body. Generally speaking, we may say that this traditional metaphysics of Light anticipated many of the results of our modern physics of light, insofar as modern physics has made any rigid boundary between the “material” and the “immaterial” increasingly difficult to maintain.

If I mentioned Strindberg a few lines earlier, it was precisely because Swedenborg’s doctrines revealed to him a metaphysics of Spirit in which spirit is no longer the opposite of body. In this understanding, the idea of body is not limited to the perishable physical body, which is merely its outermost limit. It also embraces a spiritual embodiment, a spiritual corporeality that constitutes the substantial reality of Spirit itself. This idea of spiritual corporeality is essential both to the Platonists of Persia and to all those influenced by the Cambridge Platonists.

And it is here that the work of our Shiite theosopher may be seen to stand in a significant correspondence with another body of thought—one which it might, moreover, help us to clarify. I am thinking of Milton’s doctrines. His Paradise Lost and theological writings show that he had devoted considerable attention to the study of Kabbalah and the Neoplatonists. This example illustrates particularly well the kind of contemporaneity we have been considering. Milton, who died in 1674, and Qâzî Sa'îd Qommî, who died in 1691, were contemporaries in chronological time.

Yet each remained entirely unaware of the other. The dates of the seventeenth century that we can place beside their names are not enough, by themselves, to make them contemporaries in the precise sense in which we are using that word. What makes them contemporaries is the teaching they profess. We might represent their doctrines as two parallel lines, one of which—Milton’s—comes to an end before reaching its full development. Milton professes a doctrine of the Absconditum, the unknowable God of the theology that approaches the divine through negation, similar to that of Shiite theology.

Because he does not accept the Trinitarian theology of the Council of Nicaea, Milton regards the Logos, the “Son,” not as a principle coeternal with the “Father,” but as the Deus revelatus: the God who is brought into being and manifested, at once the creator of the world and the substance of his creation. He sees in Christ a second creation, who is both creator and substance of the Elect. His doctrine of the Holy Spirit recalls the uncertainties of pre-Nicene Christology concerning the two figures of the Son and the Spirit, and it has certain affinities with the ways in which the Holy Spirit is understood in Islamic theosophy. To the extent that Shiite Imamology and Quranic Christology correspond to the form of Christology associated with Arius, we could draw a parallel here with the theosophical doctrine of the Muhammadan Light, or Muhammadan Logos, and the Imam’s role in salvation.

Although philosophical anthropology would have much to learn from it, no comparative synthesis of this kind has ever been attempted. It seems that such an undertaking could bear fruit only if it developed within a horizon that was no longer “Christian” in the historical sense of the word, but Christic: centered on the spiritual reality of Christ. That, however, is not the aspect on which I intend to concentrate as I draw this study to a close. The point I want to bring into focus is Milton’s conception of matter. This conception is fairly well known. It has sometimes been called a Christian materialism.

But it would be just as accurate to call it an absolute spiritualism. For Milton’s idea of matter, which he shares with the Kabbalists and Neoplatonists he had read, is also the idea we find in a Shiite theosopher such as Qâzî Sa'îd Qommî. It is the idea of a universal first matter, a materia prima universalis, common to everything we call spirit and everything we call body: a universal matter passing through every degree of subtlety and density.

Thus there is no longer an essential difference between spirit and body. There is a difference of degree. But a continuous range of degrees requires an intermediate realm. And that is precisely what the Illuminationist (ishrâqî) and Shiite traditions designate as the mundus imaginalis of the Malakût:

“the world in which bodies become spiritual and spirits take on bodily form.”

Perhaps, then, what Milton lacked, to a greater or lesser extent, was a rigorous account of the reality and structure of this Malakût—an understanding that Islamic theosophy had possessed since Suhrawardî. For the completion of the whole Image of the human being after death cannot take place without the light of the Malakût. Given his starting principles, Milton cannot conceive of the human being simply as a combination of what scholastic philosophy called soul and body.

Still less can he understand death as the separation of soul and body, leaving a formless, shapeless soul to exist on its own while waiting to be reunited with its resurrected body. Such fragile conceptions are capable of bringing an entire system down in their eventual collapse. For Milton, the immortality of the soul without the immortality of the body makes no sense. Certainly, since all things have come forth from God (fuisse omnia ex Deo), nothing can perish, and in that sense death does not exist.

But paradise has been lost, and its loss brings about the phenomenon of death. This is why Milton so firmly maintains the idea of the complete resurrection of the whole human being, following the complete death of that human being. He holds, of course, that time—as the measure of movement, marked by the revolutions of the stars—does not exist for the dead. Consequently, those who are resurrected will awaken as though they had only just died. It is here, it seems to me, that Qâzî Sa'îd’s doctrine of the time of the Malakût can help bring this Image of the whole human being into clearer focus. For Qâzî Sa'îd would agree with the anthropology professed by Milton.

The complete human being consists of a triad: spirit, soul, and body. This triad already exists here and now, each of its elements possessing its own allotted measure, in conformity with the conditions required by our sensible material world, the molk. Resurrection is the passage of this entire triad from its present condition in the sensible material world into the state of the Malakût. It is, by that very fact, the definitive passage from the “opaque and dense” time of our world into the subtle time of the Malakût. And death is nothing other than this passage.

The reader of Qâzî Sa'îd may therefore wonder whether Milton stops too soon. Why should resurrection still be regarded as something to be awaited after death? Why should we suppose that there is an interval separating us from it, an interval measurable in the units of our “opaque and dense” time, with the simple qualification “as though” attempting to abolish that interval? Such a conception would be understandable if resurrection took place on this side of Mount Qâf. But resurrection takes place beyond Mount Qâf. On the graves of those who lived before our post-Christian age, one can often read an inscription such as:

“Here lies So-and-so, awaiting the resurrection.”

The reader of Qâzî Sa'îd Qommî will have the impression that the roles have been reversed. Those who are waiting are the ones who still inhabit “opaque and dense” time, those whose time has not yet folded back into the time of the Malakût.

But for those who have departed, the event has already taken place. They are within the time of the Malakût, which is no longer a time of waiting. We have seen that Solomon has already been resurrected in the Malakût. The end of “opaque and dense” time does not come about through an accumulation of centuries upon centuries. Such time would remain exactly what it was even if we moved to another planet. Its end lies in the “involution of time”—in the passage into the Malakût and into the time of the Malakût. This is the meaning of the Prophet’s saying: Man mâta faqad qâmat qiyâmatuh. Whoever has died has already entered upon his resurrection. The correspondence I have just tried to sketch is only one example. Almost everything along this path remains to be done.

But perhaps this example will be enough to suggest that, when certain theologians of our day—usually hostile to anything reminiscent of Platonism—systematically oppose the immortality of the soul to the resurrection of the dead, the materials on which they base their conclusions are far from complete.

By contrast, the magnificent hymn to Light at the beginning of Book III of Paradise Lost vibrates with an esoteric presentiment of the Malakût, written by a poet whose eyes could no longer see the light of this world:

So much the rather thou Celestial Light Shine inward, and the mind through all her powers Irradiate, there plant eyes, all mist from thence Purge and disperse, that I may see and tell Of things invisible to mortal sight.214

Book VI

The Shaykhi School

Chapter I Shaykh Ahmad Ahsâ'î (1241/1826)

1. The Shaykhi School

If the preceding pages have brought certain essential features of Shiite thought and spirituality into focus, it should not be difficult to see where the Shaykhi school belongs within them, why it matters, and why this book could not leave it out. We should not pretend, however, that the work is nearly finished. Much research remains to be done before we can understand the school in detail and trace its roots in the spiritual knowledge—the gnosis—taught by the holy Imams.215

The terms Shaykhism and Shaykhi school follow common usage in Iran, Iraq, and India. The school came to be known by these names because of Shaykh Ahmad Ahsâ'î, regarded as the shaykh above all others and therefore as its founder.

Yet he never set out to “found” a new and separate school. His sole purpose was to remain completely faithful to the spiritual and philosophical teaching of the holy Imams of Twelver Shiism, and to bring that teaching back to life in its fullness. It might therefore be more accurate to speak of integralism, provided we understand the word in its original sense—preserving something whole—and do not burden it with the emotional and political associations it has acquired in the modern West. Shaykhi integralism was not concerned with upholding doctrines laid down by a Church, rescuing a threatened liturgy, or defending a crumbling religious hierarchy.

What it opposed, above all, was a pious agnosticism content with the outward forms and rules of religion, and a theological rationalism that had closed itself off from the deeper sources of inner life. Its defining commitment was an unconditional respect for the entire spiritual tradition inherited from the Imams, together with the form of spiritual life inseparable from that tradition. Taken together, these make possible an Imami Shiism preserved in its full and undiminished form: the “perfect Shiism” whose technical meaning merely confirms the original sense of shi'a, the “followers of the holy Imams.”

The contrast becomes clearer when we consider the transformation Twelver Shiism underwent under the Safavids. Having always been a minority religion, it became the state religion of Iran in the opening years of the sixteenth century. We have already touched on this transformation elsewhere in this work.

Some form of official “clergy” was bound to emerge, even though there was no Church in the Christian sense. And with an official clergy came an “orthodoxy” of the kind that, wherever it arises, tends to distrust gnosis, theosophy, and the mysticism of individual salvation. When people look only at this outward aspect of the change, they too often content themselves with a sociological or political explanation.

But that is to see religion only from the outside. It misses what religious consciousness itself is directed toward and, with it, what makes Shiite religious life distinctive. Such explanations do at least bring something important into view: the very outward structure against which Shiism, understood as a religious idea, is inevitably engaged in struggle.

The preceding discussion should have guarded us against some widespread misunderstandings of what lies at the heart of Shiism. The issue is not a political dispute within the history of our world. It is not simply the “legitimacy” of the descendants of Ali, nor merely how much reverence is due to the Ahl al-Bayt, the members of the Prophet's household. Something quite different is at stake.

We can begin to sense it when we recognize that the governing theme of the entire teaching is Imamology—the understanding of the Imams and their spiritual significance—and that this theme sounds through every “octave” of the universe. Since the prophetic message of the final Prophet, twelve Imams have fulfilled the initiatory role of spiritual guides.

The last is the Imam of our time, the Hidden Imam, who dwells in the mystical world of Hûrqâlyâ. Together with the Prophet himself and Fâtima the Radiant (al-Zahrâ)—his daughter and the source of the Imams' line, called the “meeting place of the two Lights,” the light of prophecy and the light of spiritual initiation (majma' al-nûrayn)—they form the fullness, or pleroma, of the “Fourteen Immaculate Ones.”

Yet we do not understand this sacred company primarily by considering the brief earthly lives of its members.

We must contemplate what these persons are as eternal beings, existing before the cosmos. Their level of being is the Lâhût, the divine sphere, which stands above the Jabarût, the realm of the pure angelic Intelligences. Beneath that lies the Malakût, the world of the Soul and of imaginative perception; beneath it, the Molk, the sensible world brought forth through the activity of the Soul.

At the level of the Lâhût, the Fourteen Immaculate Ones are the primordial manifestation of God—the first theophany—in the Haqîqat mohammadîya, the eternal Muhammadan Reality. They are the divine Names and Attributes, the only aspects of the divine that our knowledge and devotion can reach. As the instruments through which the divine becomes manifest, they are also the only conceivable means by which the divine can enter into relation with human beings in this earthly world. Through their activity, the cosmos itself comes into being.

When contemplated in this way, in their eternal essence and personhood, the Fourteen Immaculate Ones occupy a level of existence comparable, in a certain sense, to the Aeons of Valentinian Gnosticism. If Imamology has a role in Shiite theology corresponding to that of Christology in Christian theology, the closer comparison is with a Gnostic form of Christology—or, better still, with a wisdom centered on the figure of Christ, a Christosophy. All these universes are related to one another through symbols. Each has its own heavens and earth, arranged in an order that reproduces the succession of the primordial divine manifestations.

The pattern governing the supreme pleroma of the Lâhût is thus repeated as we descend from world to world, until at last it unfolds in the dimension of earthly time. (See, in the preceding book, pp. 185 ff., the “Twelve Veils of Light”: the twelve Imamic universes through which the Muhammadan Light passes before appearing in this world.) The essential task of esoteric interpretation, or ta'wîl, is to discover within historical time a pattern of succession that corresponds to the structure of the pleroma. It is to uncover the true, hidden meaning: the enduring spiritual history, the parable that shines through the account of outward, material events. This is something altogether different from tracing “historical currents” or “influences” along a single chain of cause and effect confined to the sensible, material world.

We are dealing instead with a history that has several dimensions, including the dimension beyond ordinary history—metahistory. To move between these dimensions, we must perceive an underlying structure that remains constant, an isomorphism. Think of a melody played at different pitches: the individual notes change, but their relationships remain the same. It is still the same melody, the same musical figure, the same form.

Yet if we are to understand Imamology on this scale, extending through every universe, we must accept the whole body of traditions handed down under the names of the holy Imams, as the Shaykhi school does. Once criticism of these traditions gives way to unacknowledged rationalist assumptions, this entire theosophical vision of the Imams disappears. With it disappears the understanding of the spiritual or esoteric meaning (bâtin) of the Quranic revelation and of the earlier prophetic revelations—and therefore the practice of ta'wîl, their spiritual interpretation.

Shiite thinkers had, of course, accomplished an immense amount in the roughly three centuries between Nasîroddîn Tûsî and the Safavid restoration. We should recall here 'Allâmeh Hillî, Rajab Borsî, Haydar Âmolî, Sâ'inoddîn Ispahânî, Ibn Abî Jomhûr, and many others. Their work bore fruit in the philosophical schools that subsequently flourished, above all in the thought of Mîr Dâmâd and the School of Isfahan, which we have already discussed. This philosophical renaissance remains a distinctive feature of Iranian Islam, without parallel elsewhere in the Islamic world.

But the Safavid restoration brought two developments at once. It created favorable conditions for Shiite philosophy, or philosophical Shiism, while also confronting it—at the very moment when it was emerging, so to speak, from concealment—with the organization of the Safavid state's official Shiism. Inevitably, Mullâ Sadrâ Shîrâzî, his students, and their successors encountered considerable difficulties with the official “clergy.”

To some extent they too had to practice taqîyeh: the discipline of concealing inward beliefs and teachings. For official Shiism had then undergone a development all too familiar elsewhere in Islam: the growing dominance of fiqh, religious law and jurisprudence, until these threatened to become synonymous with theology itself. Understanding does not come easily between the foqahâ, scholars concerned exclusively with religious law, and the 'orafâ, mystics devoted to spiritual knowledge and theosophy.

Yet from generation to generation, right down to our own day, the effort of the 'orafâ and the followers of hikmat ilâhîya has never ceased. As we have had occasion to emphasize, hikmat ilâhîya is not quite what we mean by either philosophy or theology. It is a search for divine wisdom that embraces and transcends both—literally, a theosophia, for which the Arabic expression is an exact equivalent of the Greek.

Unfortunately, because the official religious establishment was absorbed in legal learning and the formal distinctions of case-based jurisprudence, anyone who pursued this wisdom risked being suspected of undermining religious belief by introducing philosophy. Mullâ Sadrâ had already denounced this confusion in impassioned passages echoing what Haydar Âmolî had written some three centuries earlier. To abandon everything that belonged to 'irfân, inner spiritual knowledge, would have been to mutilate the most precious part of the Imams' inheritance.

How could those who knew so many sayings of the Imams—the very sources of “Imamic theosophy”—possibly consent to that? In a sense, Shiism was compelled to conceal part of itself even from itself, and to preserve its character as an esoteric religion. Its followers found themselves in the position that seekers of gnosis have faced everywhere and in every age.

This brief sketch of the situation—a familiar subject of conversation in Iran—also helps us locate the Shaykhi school. Above all, its determination to restore Imamism in its entirety makes it a metaphysical and spiritual re-formation, something of a very different order from the modern “reformist” movements found elsewhere in Islam, many of which emerged under Western influence.

The Shaykhis sought a spiritual philosophy drawn exclusively from the words of the Imams and rejected the predominance of legal questions and considerations. Most mojtaheds, the jurists empowered to exercise independent legal judgment, could hardly be expected to understand that intention at once. More precisely, the Shaykhis were raising questions the jurists' habits of mind left them unable to accommodate—questions all the more alarming because they called the jurists' own role into question.

This does not mean, however, that Shaykhism simply joined the camp of the philosophers and spiritual thinkers associated with Mullâ Sadrâ's school, whether Avicennian or ishrâqî (followers of the philosophy of Illumination). There are certainly points of intersection, but for the Shaykhis the sources remain the texts of the holy Imams alone; their method of thought is far more interpretive—hermeneutical, in the Stoic manner—than dialectical. An equal distance separates Shaykhism from Sufism.

The place given to a shaykh within Sufi tarîqat, or spiritual orders, seems to the Shaykhis to usurp the authority of the Hidden Imam: it makes the Sufi master a substitute for the Imam, which is incompatible with the meaning of his ghaybat, his occultation or concealment. Rather, the devout Shiite and the Shiite seeker can have only one shaykh: the Imam himself, their personal guide, the “invisible master who is present in the heart.”

The result is a distinctive kind of doctrine and spiritual life. It shares certain features with the philosophers—notably the ishrâqîyûn, the Illuminationists—and with the Sufis, yet it takes the form of neither, because it is shaped entirely by the teaching of the Imams. We have already noted that Sufism (tasawwof) does not encompass every form of mystical life in Islam.

And here the difficulties of research begin. The teaching of the Imams forms an enormous body of writings. It includes not only the texts preserved in Majlisî's great encyclopedia, but also those scattered through other collections, especially traditional reports (hadith, or akhbâr) in which the “Gnostic” tendencies are particularly evident.216 These latter texts call for extensive investigation, beginning with the ways Ismaili writers made use of them. This body of writings is more than the foundation for interpreting the Quran's hidden meaning in accordance with the teaching of the Imams; it amounts to an entire encyclopedia of knowledge. It is to this body of texts that Shaykhi scholars refer whenever they declare their fidelity to the Imams' teaching in its entirety.

We shall have occasion later to explain why and how the Shaykhi position toward these writings overcomes the opposition between the akhbârî and osûlî schools.

The first question a historian of religions is likely to ask concerns how this body of writings was formed.

But even if we could reconstruct perfectly every stage through which these traditional reports were transmitted and compiled, we would still have approached them only from the outside. To understand what role they play in the religious consciousness of Shiism, we would need instead to uncover the overall structure of the collection: how its different themes are grouped, how they recur, what concerns give them their shape, and so on. Shiite authors themselves offer some clues.

Khwânsârî, for example, provides several,217 while showing a respect and admiration for the person and writings of Shaykh Ahmad Ahsâ'î that stand in marked contrast to the hostility through which others have misled unwary researchers. His indications show that, although the Shaykhi school aims at restoration and renewal, it does not represent a doctrinal innovation within Imamism. It rightly claims the whole tradition of Shiite theosophy, reaching back to its earliest witnesses.

So many eminent names appear even in the incomplete list Khwânsârî gives from memory that it would be rash to condemn Shaykhism as gholow, or “extremism.” As we have already said, what is at issue is not “extremism” but “integralism,” in the word's original sense. The term describes both a fact and the intention behind it: the desire to preserve an entire tradition. That desire gives no grounds for passing a disparaging judgment on a school that remains an integral part of Shiism.218

Unfortunately, judgments of this kind seem to have led astray the few Orientalists who have so far paid any attention to Shaykhism, preventing them from sensing the profound spiritual worth that deserves their sympathy. For our part, we confess that we have never really understood the passions this school has aroused.

Considerations appear to have entered the debate that have little to do with the life of the spirit—the only concern proper to a philosopher and a scholar of religion. We have also had to acknowledge that the kinds of attacks directed at Shaykhi doctrines give us no reason to believe their authors had read the books closely, or truly understood what they were attacking. Some judgments are so strange that one wonders whether they were made under the necessity of ketmân, or taqîyeh: the discipline of esoteric concealment prescribed by the Imams and made especially necessary by the circumstances described above.

We hear, for instance, that Shaykh Ahmad Ahsâ'î was certainly a very holy man, but no metaphysical philosopher. Even the short extract from one of his books that we shall present below would be enough to disprove that. We hear that he understood neither the problems nor the technical language of the philosophers—of Mullâ Sadrâ, for example, on two of whose works he wrote substantial critical commentaries.

Yet Shaykh Ahmad himself discussed those questions and that vocabulary with complete command, and showed a clear understanding of how his own terminology and way of posing the problems differed from theirs.219 We even hear that, although the shaykh was undoubtedly wholly faithful to the teaching of the Imams, he did not really understand their texts either. We still await even the beginnings of evidence for that charge.

In any case, the Imams' words can be interpreted on several levels of understanding. It is arbitrary to treat fidelity to a tradition and originality of thought as incompatible. To reproach a thinker for his originality is to reproach him for following his vocation—and, in the end, to mistake a living tradition for a funeral procession.

There is no need to linger over these distressing controversies. We have mentioned them because they have made it harder for researchers to gain access to the Shaykhi school's authentic thought. The texts themselves are difficult, and its books are hardly to be found on ordinary bookshop shelves. Its questions and its whole technical vocabulary must be learned before they can be understood. So it is not altogether surprising that serious study has scarcely begun. Bábism and the Bahá'í faith, on the other hand, have received attention, notably from E. G. Browne. Often, by repeating or intensifying hasty and passionate judgments, writers have held Shaykhism “responsible” for them.220

We shall have occasion to explain again why, however interesting these religious movements may be in their own right, they cannot possibly be regarded as “offspring” of the Shaykhi school. If this claim is the principal reason for the accusations against Shaykhism, critics should at least begin by taking seriously the books in which the Shaykhis have set out to show—and to prove—that these alleged offspring are not theirs. Scholarly fairness demands as much.

The shaykhs who led this school left behind a vast body of work: some thousand writings, of which only about a third have been published, the rest surviving in manuscript. The first three shaykhs were naturally of foremost importance: Shaykh Ahmad Ahsâ'î (1753–1826), his first successor Sayyed Kâzem Reshtî (1798–1843), and then Shaykh Mohammad Karîm-Khân Kermânî (1809–1870), who belonged by birth to the Qajar imperial family. They and their successors were as remarkable for nobility and strength of character as for their astonishing literary productivity.

The autobiographical material we possess from the first three shaykhs helps us understand the deep reaches of consciousness beyond ordinary awareness from which Shiite devotion to the holy Imams arises. That devotion already finds expression in the visionary pattern of their adolescent dreams; it cannot be separated from the lofty spiritual philosophy we have just recalled in outline.

Part of the account that follows grew out of the publication, some fifteen years ago, of a substantial Persian work by the then leader of the Shaykhi community, Shaykh Sarkâr Âghâ, who died recently, in December 1969.221 He undertook it in response to a request from those responsible for the library of the shrine of Imam Rezâ in Mashhad, who were then preparing its catalogues. The work offers both an excellent account of the present state of scholarship and an indispensable introduction to Shaykhism—and therefore to the study of Shiism over the last two centuries.

For the first time, it brings together, in sequence, biographies of the great mashâyekh, the leading shaykhs who have ensured the school's continuity down to our own day, alongside a systematic and comprehensive bibliography of their works in Persian and Arabic, whether published or still unpublished. We would therefore like to outline these biographies, enriched by previously unpublished documents, and give some indication of the monumental writings each shaykh left behind.

At the end we shall be able to dwell on only a few points of doctrine; these will serve as the sketch of a program for future research. Naturally, we cannot attempt here a systematic comparison with the more or less reliable accounts of historians who do not belong to the Shaykhi school. Our purpose is to present the school's own perspective, the understanding of itself expressed in Shaykh Sarkâr Âghâ's work.

2. The Life and Work of Shaykh Ahmad Ahsâ'î

(1166/1753–1241/1826)

The biographical section of this great work follows a plan that reveals a distinctive sense of history and of time, worthy of a phenomenological study in its own right. It begins in the present and works backward, shaykh by shaykh, to the founder—the reverse of the approach familiar to historians who normally begin with origins. Here we think it better to set aside that movement backward through time and follow a chronological order more in keeping with our usual habits.

Although most biographical collections include an entry on Shaykh Ahmad, they must be used with care and discrimination. As Sarkâr Âghâ observes (pp. 164 ff.), their authors most often know nothing of the terms and problems of hikmat, spiritual philosophy, and even less, if possible, of Shaykh Ahmad's own distinctive language. The misunderstandings are compounded by inadequate information and superficial observation.

Certain propositions, for example, originated in Sunni thought but gradually came to be taken for granted without Shiites even realizing their source. Shaykh Ahmad's departure from such propositions therefore need not have the significance that an ill-informed writer might assign to it. Fortunately, we have first-hand information of unquestionable authenticity. There is Shaykh Ahmad's autobiography, recovered by Sarkâr Âghâ, which gives a detailed account of the mystical experiences of his youth and already traces the entire course his life would take.

In addition, three contemporary treatises provide a body of information corroborated by testimony passed down through the generations within the Shaykhi community.222 And there is one further indispensable source for his biography: Shaykh Ahmad's own writings. Many of his treatises were composed in response to questions put to him by contemporaries. We should study these exchanges closely, both to see how he clarified his teaching and to understand the response it drew from those around him.

Shaykh Ahmad Ahsâ'î was born in 1166 AH (1753) in a small settlement near al-Ahsâ', in the territory of Bahrain. He traced his ancestry back ten generations, to the second half of the fifteenth century, and came from an entirely Arab family.223

But this was eastern Arabia, along the Persian Gulf, a region where historians have seldom thought to look for philosophers and thinkers. The name al-Ahsâ', however, is not without symbolic resonance in the history of Islamic gnosis. In the eleventh century, Nâsir-e Khosraw gave a lengthy account in his travel journal of the remarkably ideal conditions he found in the small Qarmatian state he visited and admired.224 Nor should we forget that it was during the roughly fifteen years Shaykh Ahmad spent in Iran that his teaching inspired the response and enthusiasm without which there would probably never have been a movement called “Shaykhism.”

Moreover, since the time of his second successor, the Shaykhi school's center has been in Kerman, in southeastern Iran, where it has a theological school, a college, and a printing press. We should also bear in mind that, at the time of writing, Iran officially maintains special ties with Bahrain, recalling the period when Bahrain formed part of its territory.

More important for understanding Shaykh Ahmad's character, however, are the considerations suggested by his autobiography, rediscovered in his own handwriting. Sarkâr Âghâ originally intended to publish it in Persian translation, but happily decided instead to reproduce the Arabic original (pp. 166–179). Shaykh Ahmad wrote it at the request of one of his sons, Shaykh Mohammad Taqî. It records many traits that, as in the lives of spiritual figures from other cultures, reveal an aptitude for mystical experience from childhood onward.

While playing with boys of his own age, young Ahmad would often suddenly leave them. Some familiar object had appeared to him in a strange new light; that alone was enough to draw him away into solitude and keep him there in prolonged meditation. He especially loved to dream among the traces of abandoned encampments, among the ruins of temporary dwellings built from perishable materials. His imagination would lose itself in melancholy recollections, accompanied by abundant tears.

The fire of a secret passion consumed him. Those around him showed little concern for religious thought or observance. Young and old, however, liked to gather frequently for noisy entertainments filled with singing and instrumental music. Ahmad could not keep himself from joining in, only to find, when alone again, that he was torn between a resolution never to go back and a secret desire to return. Then something apparently trivial happened. One day a man whose name he does not give asked him to help compose a poem.

But Ahmad knew nothing of grammar. Fortunately, a young companion was studying the subject with a local shaykh, one Shaykh Mohammad ibn Shaykh Mohsin. Ahmad borrowed a text from him—the 'Awâmil of Jorjânî—and copied it out in full. His parents later found him asleep with the pages gripped tightly in his hand. So it was decided that he too should go and study with the same shaykh.

He would never have admitted his desire to study, any more than he would have confessed to anyone his secret attraction to the gatherings that afterward filled him with such remorse. Many years had to pass before he could overcome his extreme reserve and bring himself to tell his son, in detail, of the visionary experiences of his adolescence. That account is an invaluable document for the psychology of religious experience.

Although his entire teaching can be described as an integral Imamology, it was not a theory constructed late in life from books. It was a lived experience, born with the awakening of his consciousness and rooted in the mystery of his personal calling. We might say that, from his youth, Shaykh Ahmad embodied the fundamental Imami religious feeling from which the doctrine itself springs. He gives brief accounts of some ten visions.

Together they reveal a consciousness mysteriously and completely possessed by the spiritual archetypes represented by the holy Imams. These visions were preceded by a number of prophetic dreams. The first was of a young man holding a book, who proceeded to give a remarkable ta'wîl, or spiritual interpretation, of two Quranic verses (87:2–3), drawing from them a profound philosophical teaching. After this, young Ahmad felt a thoroughgoing distaste for the study of grammar and philology pursued as ends in themselves.

He began visiting various shaykhs, but not one could teach him anything resembling what he had heard in his dream. As a result, he withdrew further and further from those around him. He was present among his family only “in body.” “At that time I saw so many things that I cannot possibly tell of them all.” Among “these things,” one image recurred: he would climb onto the roof terrace of a house or ascend the summit of a high mountain.

A mysterious object would descend from the sky, something intangible and unreal, and he would have to grasp it. Then one night he entered a mosque “in a vision.” There he found himself before three figures, whom he learned to be the Second Imam, Hasan ibn 'Alî; the Fourth, 'Alî ibn Hosayn Zayn al-'Âbidîn; and the Fifth, Mohammad Bâqir. This vision marked the beginning of a whole series of dreams in which he received personal spiritual initiation.

The first such “meeting” recalls certain features of Mîr Dâmâd's vision in the mosque at Qomm (see above, Book V, Chapter 1, section 2). Ahmad asked Imam Hasan to teach him a prayer in the form of a poem that he could recite whenever he wished the Imam to appear. He was taught the words and has preserved the complete text for us.

Yet however faithfully he recited them, the vision did not return. At last he understood what the Imam had intended: that Ahmad should bring his entire inner being into harmony with the spiritual meaning hidden in the poem.

As he was to explain years later in a letter to a friend, a letter confirming his autobiography point by point,225 it was this inward condition, this fundamental “perfect harmony,” that made the visions that followed possible. He wrote: “It is related that Imam Mohammad Bâqir said: If one of the faithful loves us, grows in love for us, and devotes himself to knowing us, there is no question he can ask without our inspiring its answer in his heart. Then things were opened to me that I do not know how to describe to other people.

“All of it arose because I had brought my inner being into harmony with the spiritual meaning of the poem Imam Hasan had taught me.” A life of intimacy now began with each of the Fourteen Immaculate Ones: the Prophet, Fâtima al-Zahrâ, and all twelve Imams, including the Hidden Imam. “I saw strange and marvelous dreams in the heavens, in the paradises, in the world beyond the senses and in the barzakh—the intermediate realm—figures and colors that dazzled the mind” (p. 175).

These dreams can rightly be called “initiatory.”

Indeed, the teaching Shaykh Ahmad later developed across so many books cannot be separated from the instruction he received in them. He himself wrote: “Whenever a problem held me back in waking life, I would see its explanation in a dream, whenever, having called the holy Imams to mind in my dream, I saw one of them” (p. 181). “Then the question appeared to me together with every proof supporting it, so that, even if the whole world had joined forces against me, no one could have made me doubt it, because I had seen” (p. 177).

The culmination of these visionary experiences came when Shaykh Ahmad dreamed of the Tenth Imam holding a bundle of papers: these were the ijâzât, the authorizations or licenses granted to him by each of the Twelve Imams (p. 178).

We can do no more than register this spiritual fact and ask not so much what explains it as what it implies. Every one of these dreams was an occasion of instruction that would later find its way into his writings. In his autobiography he told his son: “If you wish to understand that what I say is sincere, study carefully the books in which I discuss philosophy.

“In most of these books, and on most questions, my position differs from the solutions given by the philosophers and by the scholastic theologians (motakallimûn). Once you have thoroughly reflected on my teaching, you will see that it agrees with the traditions of our guiding Imams, and you will not find a single point where it contradicts them.

“On the other hand, you will discover that most philosophers and scholastic theologians contradict the teachings and traditions of the Imams. If you want to understand why, have the fairness to acknowledge the truth of what I am telling you, for I never speak without a proof drawn from the Imams.”

Shaykh Ahmad's experience, like that of all the great visionary mystics, has the character of an archetypal phenomenon, as impossible to reduce to something else as the perception of a sound or a color. A phenomenology of religious experience can only attend to descriptions of such experiences and to what they imply. It must not try to derive them from something else, or explain them away through imagined chains of cause and effect. Its task is to discover what form of consciousness makes possible the perception of events and worlds inaccessible to ordinary consciousness today.

Indeed, Shaykhi ontology and cosmology give special attention to the mode of existence of the “intermediate world,” which establishes and guarantees the validity of visionary perceptions. Throughout his life, Shaykh Ahmad maintained absolute confidence in the ijâzât granted to him by the holy Imams in that intermediate world.

In every branch of knowledge and every matter, he invoked the Imams as his support, his authority, and his source (istinâd and i'timâd), calling to mind what they had revealed to him in his visionary states. His entire consciousness rested upon his visions, which, he repeatedly testified, taught him things he had never heard from any shaykh. Visions, revelations, dreams: here they take the archetypal forms proper to Shiite consciousness. These are spiritual facts that cannot be treated lightly. As Sarkâr Âghâ reminds us, numerous traditional reports, or akhbâr, attest that “the visions of the perfected believer (mûmin kâmil) have the value of direct perception” (p. 185).

Yet Shaykh Ahmad was right to close the short spiritual autobiography written for his son with these words: “Such things are not well suited to explanation, especially to the ignorant and the envious” (p. 179).

In any case, apart from the rather obscure shaykh who taught him grammar as a boy, Shaykh Ahmad nowhere names a particular master whose acknowledged disciple he had been or from whom he had received his spiritual authorization. Nor does the Shaykhi community's own tradition identify any shaykh whose name he personally invoked as the source of his authority, his istinâd. This would later be the case for Sayyed Kâzem in relation to Shaykh Ahmad, for Shaykh Mohammad Karîm-Khân Kermânî in relation to Sayyed Kâzem, and for so many other spiritual seekers in relation to their masters.

At most, we find a passing reference that hints at a brief encounter with far-reaching consequences.226 Shaykh Ahmad may therefore be counted among those whom Iranians call the Owaysîs: people whose only true spiritual master has been the shaykh al-ghayb or ostâd-e ghaybî, the guide in the world beyond the senses, the inward and personal master. Shaykh Ahmad himself tells us who that unseen guide was in his case. In doing so, he reveals the deeper meaning of Shiism's method of spiritual guidance, as we recalled above, and the bond between speculative Imamology and inward experience.

This did not prevent him from being in contact with numerous teachers. He exchanged questions and answers with shaykhs and other eminent figures, who expressed their agreement with his views (tasdîqât) and their reverence for him. This was true of his early stays in Iraq as well as his long periods in Iran. Over the years distinguished shaykhs awarded him detailed ijâzât, authorizations whose texts would fill a whole volume if reproduced in full.227

Accordingly, he referred to this entire body of authorizations, but never singled out one named master. That attitude accords perfectly with what Shaykhism would call the “Fourth Pillar” of Shiite doctrine: no individual teacher's authority can ever be “substituted” for the prerogative of the Imam (see Chapter III below). In any event, no one ever doubted his extraordinary learning or spiritual distinction.

His first contacts outside his homeland bear this out. He remained in Bahrain until about the age of twenty, leading a life that, although we lack detailed information about it, we may imagine to have been devoted chiefly to meditation. Did he set out because a compelling command received in a vision made him sense a calling to teach, despite his own preference for solitude? Whatever the reason, in 1186 AH (1772) Shaykh Ahmad departed for the Shiite holy places in Iraq.

Many celebrated scholars were gathered there at the time,228 and he entered into sustained discussions and scholarly meetings with them. Attending the majlis, or learned gathering, of Sayyed Mahdî Tabâtabâ'î, he asked him for an ijâzat and presented one of his own works, a commentary on 'Allâmeh Hillî's Tabsira.229 After reading it, the Sayyed told him: “O Shaykh! It is you who should be granting me an ijâzat” (p. 204).

To his own students he declared: “This shaykh is a Sign (âyat) among the Signs of God. It is extraordinary that he should have been born and raised in a country generally lacking in learning and philosophy, where people know only a few questions concerning ritual prayer.

“The appearance of a person so complete, uniting every kind of excellence, can be explained only as a divine grace.” He added: “I myself cannot understand this shaykh's loftier problems, for I know only fiqh and the osûl,” jurisprudence and its principles (ibid.). If only all jurists and specialists in fiqh had shown the same modesty before passing judgment on the shaykh's teachings!

For what delighted those around him was that God had raised up an Imami scholar who knew the spiritual wisdom handed down from the holy Imams and could debate on equal terms with the philosophers and the motakallimûn, the scholastic theologians. Instead of pronouncing curses and accusations of unbelief (takfîr), like so many mullahs concerned only with law, or even forbidding philosophy itself, he could meet these thinkers on their own ground.

Shaykh Ahmad remained for some twenty years at Najaf and Karbalâ, the Shiite holy places in Iraq. In 1209/1794 a severe epidemic brought that stay to an end. He returned home, but less than four years later, in 1212/1797, came back on a new pilgrimage. He spent the next seven years traveling back and forth around Basra, frequently changing his place of residence to escape the crowds drawn to him by his growing reputation.

In 1221/1806 he made a decision that would have profound consequences for Iranian Imamism: to undertake a pilgrimage to Mashhad, to the shrine of the Eighth Imam, 'Alî Rezâ. It would lead to his first stay in Iran of roughly ten years. As so often happens in Iran, one plans a visit of a few weeks and ends up remaining for years. Setting out from Basra in 1221/1806 with his family and a few friends, he followed a route—hardly the shortest by modern standards—that took him through Yazd, in southeastern Iran, on the road to Kerman.

Many scholars were living in Yazd at that time, and all welcomed Shaykh Ahmad with exceptional warmth and reverence. Not a day passed without lengthy scholarly discussions, in which he was asked to comment on and resolve difficult questions. On Fridays and feast days he was requested to lead the prayers. Before long it became impossible for him to leave Yazd. The most he could obtain was permission to continue his pilgrimage to Mashhad, on the promise that he would return.

There he received the same welcome.230 Once back in Yazd, he remained for about five years, occupied with teaching and with composing a multitude of treatises in answer to the questions put to him. His reputation spread so widely throughout Iran that the sovereign, Fath 'Alî-Shâh Qâdjâr, wrote him a moving letter and, so eager was he to speak with the shaykh, offered to come to Yazd himself.231 In the end Shaykh Ahmad went to Tehran, where the ruler urged him to settle permanently.

But the shaykh preferred to return to Yazd. Soon afterward, apparently following a command received from the First Imam in a dream, he decided to return to Iraq.

This time his journey took him through Isfahan, then the “navel of Iran,” the “dome of Islam,” or what we might now call the country's spiritual and intellectual capital. Once again he received an extraordinary welcome from scholars and the heads of the philosophical schools. His books were eagerly sought, copied, and recopied. After forty days he resumed his journey.

The governor of Kermânshâh, then the royal prince Mohammad 'Alî Mîrzâ Dawlatshâh, came out to meet him, accompanied by all the scholars and dignitaries, as far as four farsakhs—some twenty-five kilometers—from the city. The situation he had encountered in Yazd repeated itself. Shaykh Ahmad remained in Kermânshâh for two years, during which people from every quarter sought his teaching and advice. Then, wishing to make the pilgrimage to Mecca, he set out again, having firmly promised to return (1231/1816).

And indeed, once the pilgrimage was complete, Shaykh Ahmad reappeared in Kermânshâh in 1234/1819. This new period in Iran would last about five years. The prince and the people welcomed him with the same enthusiasm as before. Because the city lay on the pilgrimage route to Mashhad, he could meet many fellow scholars as they passed through.

But now a succession of disasters unfolded.

First the prince-governor died. Then came a devastating drought, followed by floods. A quarter of the city lay in ruins. An epidemic broke out and spread across Iran. Shaykh Ahmad and his companions set out for Mashhad by a route roughly corresponding to the one used today: Qazwîn, Qomm, Tehran, where he visited the shrine of Shâh 'Abdol-'Azîm, then Shâhrûd, Neyshâpûr, and Mashhad.

At every stage the epidemic seemed to grow worse. From Mashhad the little caravan headed south again toward Yazd, passing through the oases of the central desert: Torbat, then Tabas. Beyond Tabas the road was infested with Baluch bandits, so the governor provided an escort of cavalry and infantry. Shaykh Ahmad thus entered Yazd preceded, this time, by an entirely unexpected military procession. He remained there only three months.

At Isfahan the reception was overwhelming, triumphant. It included not just the governor, scholars, and dignitaries, but the whole population: old and young, men and women. The shaykh was asked to lead the prayer in the royal mosque (Masjad-e Shâh). The rows of worshippers spilled out onto the great maydân, the celebrated square of Shâh 'Abbâs. One shaykh, fond of statistics, counted as many as sixteen thousand people there on a single evening (pp. 211–214).

It is against this background of widespread reverence and enthusiasm—evidence that Shiite religious consciousness recognized itself in Shaykh Ahmad Ahsâ'î and his teaching—that we must judge the regrettable incident at Qazwîn. Western writers have sometimes claimed that Shaykh Ahmad “was excommunicated by the mojtaheds.” This language is entirely inappropriate and wholly out of proportion to what actually happened. It translates the event through a particular Western way of seeing things, speaking as though there were a Church in a setting where no central teaching office or binding dogmatic authority exists.

Nor was there ever an assembly of mojtaheds to consider the matter. The takfîr pronounced at Qazwîn—the declaration that someone is an unbeliever—was a personal, private initiative of Mullâ Mohammad Taqî Barghânî. It neither had nor could have had anything like the meaning or force of a decision by a Church council. Shaykh Sarkâr Âghâ's account brings out both the historical and the human dimensions of this affair particularly well (pp. 190–202).

First there were reasons that were human, all too human, and easy enough to understand. The welcome given everywhere to Shaykh Ahmad and his teaching, including at Qazwîn, wounded the pride of certain individuals. Something like a wind of spiritual renewal was blowing through Shiite consciousness. The distress of these injured vanities was joined by fear: an established authority was being shaken, a privileged position put at risk.

Second, Mullâ Barghânî was far from being a leading figure. He was a preacher. He had indeed bestowed on himself the title a'lam, “the foremost scholar” of Qazwîn, but neither his writings nor his sermons had persuaded his colleagues to share that opinion. Of those who happened to attend the majlis he convened, only four or five joined him in his takfîr, and even they were neither mojtaheds nor scholars of particular eminence.

Tonkâbûnî himself, who can hardly be suspected of favoring Shaykh Ahmad, is obliged to acknowledge this. Neither then nor afterward did Mullâ Barghânî's takfîr command anything resembling general agreement. More telling still, his own son, Shaykh Ja'far Yazdî, who had suffered greatly because of his father's conduct, later spent many years in Kerman on terms of close friendship with the Shaykhis.232

The question discussed at the small gathering hastily convened on Molla Barghani’s initiative was that of ma'âd jismânî, the bodily resurrection. I have dealt at length elsewhere with the Shaykhi teaching on this essential religious doctrine, so I shall only touch on it briefly here.233 Through its account of the human being's fourfold bodily nature and its conception of a subtle spiritual body (jism hûrqalyî, caro spiritualis), Shaykhism stands at an equal distance from the philosophers and the literalist theologians. (For Molla Barghani to claim that Shaykh Ahmad's teaching on this point agreed with that of Molla Sadra Shirazi, he must have misunderstood the writings of both.) When the Shaykhis say that "the elemental body does not return," they mean that the "materialism" of theologians who cling to the literal meaning of scripture leads them into absurdities that amount to blasphemy.

To Molla Barghani, however, this understanding of bodily resurrection was tantamount to denying it. He had an excuse: his education had done little to prepare him for metaphysical questions. But in that case, Sarkar Agha observes, those who lack the capacity to understand the wisdom (hikmat) taught by the Prophet and the holy Imams would do better not to discuss it.

At heart, the entire affair was merely a symptom of the deeper unease whose causes we noted at the beginning of this account. The Shaykhis regard the hostility of the religious jurists (foqahâ) toward hikmat ilâhîya—divine wisdom, encompassing philosophy and spiritual theosophy—as a contradiction of the traditions and teachings that Shiism has inherited from the Prophet and the Imams. In a letter written later to a friend, Shaykh 'Abdul-Wahhab Qazvini, Shaykh Ahmad pointed out that his doctrine of the "resurrection body" could appeal to the most explicit statements by authorities such as the Sixth Imam, Ja'far Sadiq, Nasir Tusi, 'Allameh Hilli, and even Majlisi himself (p. 198). Unfortunately, his opponents were unable to rise to the level at which such a discussion properly belonged. Shaykhism, by contrast, breathed new life into the questions of cosmogony and eschatology: the origin of the world and its final destiny, Mabdâ' and Ma'âd.234

What, precisely, did the man who initiated this takfîr—this declaration that another Muslim was an unbeliever—stand to gain? Certainly, today its immediate significance is no longer the same for either side; nor, for that matter, is the significance of such a declaration in general. Even at the time, it failed to win the support of a majority, let alone acquire any binding religious authority.

Yet it was shamefully exploited to stir up unrest and to give free rein to resentments that could not be openly acknowledged. Most serious of all was the decision to thrust into public controversy questions that the public was in no position to understand. Among the poorer and less educated people, this created an opinion about the "Shaykhis" that was wholly uninformed about the issues involved, yet all the more ready to provoke disturbances. We shall see this hostility at work, unfortunately, on several occasions in Kerman.

After this painful incident, Shaykh Ahmad spent another year in Iran, at Kermanshah, before returning to Karbala, where he hoped to spend the rest of his life. Molla Barghani then began writing letter after letter to those jurists in Iraq whom he thought he might win over. The intrigues multiplied scandalously. Forged documents were even produced to alarm the Ottoman governor, Dawud Pasha, who was already deeply hostile to Shiism. These discreditable maneuvers eventually created such a dangerous situation that Shaykh Ahmad decided to withdraw with his family to Mecca. They set out on the journey for the last time.

But when they were three stages from Medina, the shaykh developed a fever and departed this world on 21 Dhu'l-Qa'da 1241 AH (28 June 1826). He was buried in Medina, in the cemetery of Baqî' rafî', near the graves of four of the Shiite Imams and the Bayt al-Ahzân, the House of Sorrows, with which the poignant memory of Fatima remains associated.235

Thus ended the earthly life of Shaykh Ahmad Ahsa'i, a life devoted, as he himself had wished, entirely to the veneration of what he regarded as the purest essence of Shiism. His influence upon its spiritual life was undoubtedly immense, and the possibilities opened by his work are far from exhausted.

There is something curious here. On the one hand, Shaykh Ahmad cannot be traced back to any particular spiritual master among his contemporaries. On the other, although he had children and grandchildren, no members of his family line are now known by name.

We can speak only of his spiritual descendants: those called the Shaykhis, who are numerous in Iran and Iraq and are also found in India. It should also be noted (p. 217) that in Kuwait and several cities of Azerbaijan there are groups which, although they do not call themselves Shaykhis, trace their spiritual ancestry to Shaykh Ahmad and Sayyed Kazem. Conversely, there are others who adopt the Shaykhi name although their teachings bear little resemblance to those of the two masters.

This confusion has more serious dimensions. Among the students (tâleb) who gathered around Shaykh Ahmad and Sayyed Kazem were some who were not, for all that, Shaykhi disciples (tâleb shaykhis). Nevertheless, the improvised ideas put forward by these students have been attributed to the two masters themselves. To create and perpetuate this confusion, people have even appealed to the authority of Khwansari, the great historian of leading figures in the Islamic world, whose deeply respectful and admiring words about Shaykh Ahmad we have already noted.

In fact, his Arabic text has been strikingly misunderstood.236 This misreading gave rise to the opinion, which has influenced some Orientalists, that Babism "came out of" Shaykhism. What we shall say later about the "fourth rokn" will show decisively that, if this proposition is true at all, it is only in the strict sense of "coming out": that is, leaving Shaykhism, placing oneself outside it, breaking away from it.

In the end, Sarkar Agha concludes, "there are we, who are called the Shaykhis and who are disciples of the Shaykh because we find in his teaching the whole tradition of Shiism, with all the possibilities contained within it." He adds, with no small courage: "This name was given to us; we did not choose it.

"But we accept it as a title of honor precious above all others, because in its true meaning and content it is, for us, equivalent to the name Moslimûn—Muslims. And because we are distinguished in this way through our attachment to our eminent Shaykh, we are sometimes described as a minority. That designation, too, is a source of pride to us, for even in the time of the holy Imams their companions and friends were never anything but a minority."

What, indeed, is a Shiite? "The word existed already in the Prophet's lifetime, to designate those who professed love and devotion toward the Imam and separated themselves from those who had separated themselves from him. That was how they were recognized—not by the fact that they observed prayer, fasting, almsgiving, and so forth.

"Yet even then, and ever since, they could always be counted on the fingers of one's hands. Many traditions (akhbâr) praise this minority. Let those who today heap suspicion and slander upon us know that they are treating us just as people treated the companions and friends of the holy Imams in their day. When, in the time of Imam Ja'far Sadiq, these companions came to complain that people called them Râfizis, Ja'faris, and other such names, the Imam reassured them, saying: Do not grieve; be patient. From the beginning of the world, ordinary people have always treated the Friends of God in this way" (pp. 221–222).

These proud words deserve to be quoted here, for they convey a whole spiritual atmosphere more vividly than any commentary could.237

As for the writings of Shaykh Ahmad Ahsa'i, they form a vast body of work whose study is indispensable to anyone wishing to penetrate the deeper mysteries of Shiite thought. Thanks to Sarkar Agha's work, we now possess a systematic and comprehensive catalogue. It lists no fewer than 132 titles, all Shaykh Ahmad's recorded writings being in Arabic. The true number is higher, since many titles refer to collections containing as many as ten or more individual treatises (risâla).

We must also remember that a considerable number of works have been lost: the shaykh did not keep copies of the treatises he wrote at the request of his correspondents and those who consulted him. Moreover, his library was kept in Karbala, in the house of his disciple and successor Sayyed Kazem, and that house was pillaged twice.

The catalogue is systematically arranged into nine sections: theosophy; Shiite doctrine; religious addresses and sermons; law; jurisprudence; Quranic commentaries; practical philosophy; literature; and collections (II, pp. 8–85).238 Approximately seventeen treatises remain unpublished. All the others appeared in lithographed editions, which are unfortunately now quite old. Particularly worth recalling are Shaykh Ahmad's extensive and highly individual commentaries on two works by Molla Sadra Shirazi. These are essential for understanding how Shaykhi theosophy relates to the "Eastern theosophy" (hikmat mashriqîya) of Suhrawardi as interpreted by Molla Sadra.239

The Sharh al-Ziyârat al-jâmi'a is an extensive commentary on a text of "spiritual pilgrimage" honoring the Twelve Imams. With the Shaykhis, we may regard it as Shaykh Ahmad's most precious work: a veritable comprehensive statement of Shiite theosophy.240 The Fawâ'id ("Teachings") and the expanded version prepared by the author himself contain philosophical foundations of great importance.241 A large collection of ninety-nine treatises—actually more, for the reason already given—was published under the title Jawâmi' al-Kalim.242 We must reserve a more detailed discussion of all this for another occasion.

PreviousIII. Qâzî Sa'îd QommîNextII. The Successors of Shaykh Ahmad Ahsa'i

Chapter II The Successors of Shaykh Ahmad Ahsa'i

1. Sayyed Kazem Reshti (1212/1798–1259/1843)

The Shaykhi community enjoyed the good fortune of being led, after Shaykh Ahmad Ahsa'i, by a succession of figures as remarkable for their strength and nobility of character as for their truly extraordinary scholarly productivity.

Until now, anyone wishing to write the biography of the disciple whom Shaykh Ahmad expressly designated as his nâ'ib, his deputy and successor, had only incomplete sources at hand. The first was Sayyed Kazem's own account of his trials, especially his controversies and disputes with people whose names would otherwise have been forgotten.243 Further research has now enabled Sarkar Agha to discover two treatises (risâla) written by students of Sayyed Kazem, containing at last the material needed for a proper biography.244 We shall draw from them a very brief account.

Sayyed Kazem belonged to a noble family of Hosayni sayyeds—that is, descendants of the Third Imam—originally from Medina, which had settled in Iran two generations earlier. His grandfather, Sayyed Ahmad, had fled Medina during an outbreak of plague and taken refuge in Rasht, in the region southwest of the Caspian Sea. He settled there and established a family. His son, Sayyed Qasem, was born there, married there, and became one of Rasht's leading citizens. It was in the same city that Sayyed Kazem was born, in 1212 AH (1798).

His dreamy, contemplative childhood reveals dispositions strikingly similar to those we encountered in Shaykh Ahmad's own early life. A tutor was appointed to teach him the outward, or exoteric, sciences (zâhira). But the young man was consumed by two desires: to travel far from home and to be initiated into the higher forms of knowledge. Unfortunately, his family saw matters differently. Once again, a series of "initiatory dreams" strengthened his resolve and hastened his decision.

One fact deserves particular attention.
