This leads him into a searching analysis of mashî'at, the divine Primal Will. He shows that in the creative Act, mashî'at is at once the subject, the object, and the purpose of that act, as well as its matter, form, and instrument. The Primal Will thus appears as a primordial, metaphysical Adam (Adam al-akbar, the Greater Adam, or Homo maximus). It is the zenith of which Adam “our father,” who came into being without father or mother, is the nadir in the world of our earthly history.

The eternal Primal Will is the primordial Adam, “the first of the Adams” (awwal al-âdamîyîn); and Eve, this Adam's equal, is the release of being (jawâz, itlâq), absolute being—that is, being absolved from nonbeing, from the Great Abyss. In this primordial heavenly Adam, Matter and Form each exist in their own right and, at the same time, through one another. In Adam “our father,” by contrast, they exist through the divine Act and then successively through each other. After Adam, being propagates through the “nuptial union” of matter and form.

“The nadir of the divine Primal Will is our father Adam, for he had no father or mother other than himself. He came into existence from himself alone, and from him the human race came into being through nuptial union and successive generations. Likewise the Primal Will has no father or mother other than itself, and from it things come into being through nuptial union and successive generations. When we say of Adam that he had ‘no father or mother other than himself,’ we mean that Adam was born of his own Matter, which is the father, and of his own Form, which is the mother [...]. The Primal Will is the primordial Adam; the Eve of this Adam is the freedom to be (the absolution of being).

“Eve is therefore Adam's equal, neither more nor less than he” (§§159–160, 164). And in his commentary the shaykh explains: “Adam is the nadir of this Primal Will because the Will itself is the First Adam. It is composed of matter and form. Its matter is light, while its form is the temple of tawhîd, divine oneness. Adam's father was his matter, and his mother was his form [...]. When I say that Eve is the equal of this Adam, I mean that there is nothing possible to which the Primal Will is not joined, and conversely nothing in the Primal Will that remains outside the possible.”

Here we can already see a fundamental transformation of Aristotelian hylomorphism, the doctrine of matter and form. The terms “matter” (hylê, mâdda) and “form” (morphê, sûrat) remain, but their roles have been reversed.

In contrast to the association suggested by our Indo-European words materia and mater (“mother”), matter here is the father and form is the mother. This is one of Shaykh Ahmad's central theses, always present in his thought. He is well aware that he is reversing both the vocabulary and the conceptual order of the philosophers. Matter here is light: being itself, the act of existing. Form is quiddity—what a thing is—the dimension of shadow that fixes, determines, and delimits that light. It is form that gives birth to the new being. The shaykh will often speak of being as metaphysical “matter.” Few things have more surprised his critics.

But rather than declare that he failed to understand the philosophers, we would do better to try to understand precisely what he is saying, and the language in which he says it.

Chapter IV examines the creative Act, the divine act of bringing things into being (fi'l), as we have already defined it: the act accessible to us in the way “God reveals Himself to us through ourselves.”

Considered as the self-manifestation of divine Energy, the creative Act can be analyzed into four moments or phases. Together they form a unity called Mercy, Rahma, whose role is reminiscent of Sophia in other theosophical traditions and which here is the metaphysical androgyne, Adam-and-Eve. This “universal divine Mercy” is indeed one of the names, one of the ways of conceiving absolute being: being that the creative Act has released and set free to exist.

When the shaykh writes, in language faintly recalling alchemy, that “God took four parts of the moisture of Mercy by means of that very moisture,” the four parts are simply Mercy itself. Mercy is what takes hold, what is taken hold of, the means by which it is taken hold of, and that from which it is taken. Grammatically speaking, it is as though the roles assigned separately to the nominative, accusative, instrumental, and ablative cases all belonged to one and the same reality.280 This places us as far from creation ex nihilo as from a theory of emanation.

As for the fourfold structure into which the act of divine creation can be analyzed, its first two phases are mashî'at, the divine Primal Will concerned with calling being into existence (kawn), and irâda, the act of willing concerned with determining being ('ayn)—with what a being is in the very act of existing. These first two phases make up what the shaykh calls “first creation” (khalq awwal), or “first quiddity” (mâhîya).

The third and fourth phases are qadar or taqdîr, the act that apportions to each individual being its proper measure, its own share (the handasa îjâdîya, an “existence-giving geometry” that structures being in each individual instance), and qazâ, the “decree” that brings this apportionment into full effect. Together these last two phases constitute “second creation” (khalq thânî), or second quiddity. Between the first and second creations, however, an event takes place that gives this metaphysics of being the character of a metaphysical drama. A question is put to the primordial Adam and repeated at every level of the universe: A-lasto bi-rabbi-kom?—“Am I not your Lord?” (Qur'an 7:171).

In a sense, this pre-existent questioning plays the same role as the prelude to Plato's Gorgias. According to the answer they give—ranging from genuine assent to a refusal disguised as “yes”—the human beings pre-existing within this cosmic Adam choose their own destiny: their quiddity, the measure and capacities of their being. They choose, in other words, whether they will experience their existence in this world as an act of Mercy or an act of Wrath. The seeming contradiction between “predestination” and responsibility is overcome, because a person's responsibility is engaged by an act that the person performed before earthly existence.

We find the same fourfold pattern at every stage and level of Shaykh Ahmad's analysis of the cosmos and of the human being. It appears, for instance, in his explanation of the symbolism of the Throne ('Arsh), with its four pillars, four colors, and four archangels. It also embraces the pattern employed in the philosophical science of the alphabet, or science of letters ('ilm al-horûf). Shaykh Ahmad therefore makes a long digression into this difficult discipline, in which our theosophers share the interests of the Kabbalists. The digression culminates in a return to the doctrine that identifies being (wojûd) with Light (nûr) and quiddity with the shadow that receives the light and brings forth its manifestation. As we have said, this is the doctrine that determines his understanding of “matter” and “form,” overturning the traditional vocabulary of hylomorphism while still retaining its terms.

This is the central theme of Chapter V. Its first part is devoted to the various “series” or “sets” of universes presented in Sadûq's Khisâl.281

What does it mean to speak of two, three, four, five, or six worlds—the six days of Creation—then seven, eight, and so on, up to twelve universes? Here we encounter again certain themes already discussed in connection with Qâzî Sa'îd Qommî. We also see Shaykh Ahmad's concepts become more precise: “spiritual matter” (mâdda ma'nawîya) as “molten Light” (Nûr dhâ'ib), and “elemental matter” (mâdda 'onsorîya) as “frozen” or “solidified Light” (jâmid). This enables him to take a highly original position in relation to Majlisî on tajarrod, separation or immateriality (Greek khôrismos). For the great official theologian of Shiism, complete separation or immateriality can apply only to God.

There can be no “separate” substance other than God, and Majlisî comes close to declaring unbelievers—pronouncing takfîr upon—philosophers who apply tajarrod to other beings. Shaykh Ahmad maintains, however, that only certain Islamic philosophers are open to this charge, and that Majlisî's condemnation does not touch the theosophers who remain faithful to the Imams' teaching. This position is characteristic of a particular current within Shiism. The First Intelligence has its own “matter,” just as a mineral has matter.

But the Light that constitutes being undergoes countless degrees of “condensation,” so the Intelligence differs from a mineral as heaven differs from earth, without there being any need to speak of tajarrod in the strict sense. Our theosophers thus meet certain later Western Neoplatonists whose thought has been described as “Christian materialism.” It would be more accurate to call it “spiritual realism,” a view for which the opposition between materialism and spiritualism no longer has meaning. (We have in mind, once again, Robert Fludd and the Cambridge Platonists.) Already we can discern, in Shaykh Ahmad Ahsâ'î as in Qâzî Sa'îd Qommî, certain enduring lines of thought within traditional Persian philosophy, from the Safavid to the Qajar period.

As the preceding chapter has shown, Shaykh Ahmad often expresses his metaphysics of being through an account of Adam—an Adamology. In this fifth Fâ'ida we learn to distinguish three “Adams” in the spiritual world, which is “pre-Adamic” in relation to “Adam our father.” The first is the Greater Adam (Adam al-akbar, Homo maximus): the divine Primal Will (mashî'at) and the “Heaven of absolute walâyat.” The second Adam is the “Muhammadan Light” (Nûr Mohammadî), with its fourteen beings of light.

The third is the Universal Intelligence, the Intelligence of that Light, whose “children” are the individual intelligences. Their relationships are complex. From this Adamology follows the teaching on matter and form which, as we have seen, overturns classical hylomorphism. Matter becomes the masculine element, the “father,” while Form or quiddity becomes the feminine element, the “mother,” receiving the amount of matter appropriate to its own specification. The consequences are revolutionary, extending from mineralogy to aesthetics, and even more immediately to anthropology and the doctrine of the Imams.

In contrast to the Aristotelian-Thomist tradition, it is Form here, not matter, that provides the principle of individuation. “At the level of sensory perception, matter is individualized by the imaginal Form (sûrat mithâlîya). As for Form, although it belongs to the imaginal world, it appears to sensory perception through its conjunction with elemental matters. But this conjunction holds in the invisible, suprasensible world (ghayb) of the Intelligences as much as in the visible world of material bodies. It applies to the outer world and also to thoughts themselves.

“Thus, in the true sense worth seeking to know, being or existence, wherever something other than God is concerned, is matter (mâdda). This is the correct position, contrary to what the majority of philosophers maintain” (§265). In other words, the claim is not that some previously existing matter is being. It is that being, the act of existing, is matter—and that this matter which is being is itself light. “For if being were something other than matter, its definition would be incomplete without that other thing.

“But being is the most evident of all things: it is its own definition. Being is the matter of things, because it is what is most evident in every thing.

“Yet precisely because its self-evidence is so overwhelming, being remains hidden from most people. They imagine it to be an object of pure thought, a mere concept; or they take it as the copula in a logical judgment; or they identify it with what truly is. All these opinions are mistaken. The truth is that being which has a beginning is, in each thing, the matter proportionate to that thing.

“But what truly is, no one knows except itself. Every doctrine is therefore false that makes it the root of being, or makes being its shadow. There can be no conceptual participation here (analogia entis), because the sacred, transcendent divine Selfhood (Dhât moqadassa) cannot fall under an essence held in common with anything else. There can be no analogia entis, no common proportion between the divine Selfhood and anything whatsoever” (ibid.). This is exactly the doctrine of Qâzî Sa'îd Qommî, as we have already noted.

“As for the technical vocabulary used by the ancients and the philosophers, when they held that Form is the father while matter is the mother, they did so because they believed that a being's growth and acquisition of character (takhalloq) take place within matter, making matter the mother. Nothing could be further from the true relation of things. That matter is the father and Form the mother, on the other hand, follows from the sayings of the Imams. Take, for example, this saying of Imam Ja'far: ‘God created the faithful believers from His Light and dyed them in His Mercy. This is why one believer is the brother of another through his father and mother. His father is Light and his mother is Mercy’” (§267).

When we say that a ring is made of silver, we mean that the silver entering into it is the matter from which it is made. To say that a believer was created from Light is to say that Light is the matter; and it is this Light that the Imam calls the believer's father. “If we adopt the philosophers' definition of the human being as a ‘thinking living being’ (hayawân nâtiq), then the light is the share of living nature (hissa hayawânîya), and mercy the share of thinking nature (hissa nâtiqîya). Living-being is matter; thinking-being is Form. By matter we mean being, existing: the first thing emanating from the divine creative Act, since only one thing emanates from that Act. Form is the configuration that shapes this Emanation into the multiplicity of its specifications and individual beings” (§273).

We have deliberately included these lengthy quotations in order to place Shaykh Ahmad's fundamental criticism of the usual definition of the human being as hayawân nâtiq—the thinking or “speaking” animal, animal rationale—in its proper setting. The supposed unity of an animal genus, evolving through successive forms from protozoan to human being, is merely a logical concept, a construct of the mind. Matter does not receive Form. Rather, Form receives, in each case, the amount of matter suited to it, and Form gives birth to the new being. It is impossible to classify or define the human being as a variation within the animal genus, because of the drama that intervenes between first creation or quiddity and second creation or quiddity (see above).

There is a vital reality (hayawânîya) elaborated in the celestial Spheres (falakîya). This reality belongs to animals as an essential constituent, but for the human being it is only accidental. The human essence is instead the spiritual vital reality of the malakût, the spiritual world (h. qodsîya malakûtîya). More than this, the Imam—that is, each of the “Fourteen Immaculate Ones”—possesses a divine spiritual vital reality (h. q. ilâhîya). The human reality, the spiritual life proper to humanity, stands in relation to this divine reality as animal existence stands in relation to human existence. Just as the “animal” condition is accidental to what makes a human being human, so the human condition is accidental to the Imam's divine spiritual reality.

Hence the idea of a hypostatic union between the Imam's divine spiritual nature (malakûtî lahûtî) and human nature, insofar as the latter shares the biological reality of this world, is inconceivable. What can be considered, in any case, is the human reality as a living being of the malakût, at the level of a caro spiritualis, a spiritual body. Then what takes place is an epiphany of the Imam's lâhût, his divine dimension, within the human malakût. This is the scene described at the beginning of the tradition of the White Cloud. We might say that whereas Christology revolves around the union of two natures, divine and human, the decisions reached by Imamology depend on the idea of a threefold nature, as outlined above.

Comparative theology and theosophy have here a vast, still unexplored field of inquiry, and this alone would justify speaking of a “renewal.” But in using that word in the heading to these pages, we were thinking first of the renewal of the very problems of metaphysics when the doctrine of the Imams becomes its guiding principle. We have seen enough of this without taking the analysis of Shaykh Ahmad Ahsâ'î's Fawâ'id any further. The doctrine of the Imams provides the horizon for the mind's highest speculations.

For that very reason it also determines the distinctive character of the Shaykhi community within Shiism. The teaching of the Imams points to the existence of a hidden spiritual hierarchy, whose highest members can be present in this world only incognito for as long as the Imam remains in occultation (ghaybat). This concerns what the Shaykhi school calls the “fourth pillar” (rokn râbi') of its doctrine. Behind it we can discern, almost as through a transparent veil, the idea of a certain ideal brotherhood familiar from the esoteric traditions of the West.

We must spend a few pages on this teaching, since it was unfortunately among those that provoked the most criticism, precisely because it was misunderstood or not understood at all.

3. The “Fourth Pillar”

At the end of the preceding section we again used the word ghaybat, which properly denotes the occultation, or hiddenness, of the Twelfth Imam—the Imam of our time, the Hidden Imam. Among Shiite spiritual masters, however, the meaning of the word sometimes widens to include the suprasensible, secret dimension of beings and things: their spiritual form. This dimensio mystica, or mystical dimension, then becomes the key to hierognosis, a form of spiritual awareness that perceives realities in their proper forms. Nothing belonging to the worlds beyond ours is frozen or reduced to our habitual ways of imagining things, or brought under the control of religions concerned with worldly power.

Shaykhi theosophy rests on four pillars (rokn): divine unity, the doctrine of prophecy, the doctrine of the Imams, and the Shiite community. There is nothing novel here in comparison with the program of Shiite religious books generally; it accords entirely with the Imams' teaching. At the same time, this fourfold plan indicates how a complete account of Shaykhi Shiite theosophy would have to be organized. The doctrine of the Imams would be the keystone of the whole structure.

For the fullness of the “Fourteen Immaculate Ones” is understood and contemplated first of all in a sphere of existence ontologically prior to the brief appearance of their individual earthly persons. This fullness constitutes the world of lâhût, the divine dimension, at the very first flowering of being. As pre-cosmic entities, the “persons of light” of the Fourteen Immaculate Ones are the acts of primordial divine self-manifestation, or theophany. They are the divine Names and Attributes, the only aspect of divinity that can be known to us; they are the divine instruments of creation, its “operations at work,” the agents of cosmogony.

Ontologically “below” the world of lâhût lie the worlds traditionally called Jabarût, Malakût, and Molk, the last being our world as it appears to the senses. All these universes correspond symbolically to one another. An adequate understanding of the human being must therefore encompass them all. It includes the structure of the human being's fourfold body; the idea of an archetypal subtle body, the jism hurqalyî (the body on the plane of Hûrqalyâ, closely related to Proclus's okhêma, the subtle vehicle of the soul); and, intimately connected with this subtle physiology, the conception of Heaven and Hell as realities within the human being. These are central themes of the doctrine, both in its “physics” of the Resurrection and in its understanding of visionary experiences such as the Prophet's mi'râj, his heavenly ascent.

Since we have discussed these subjects at some length elsewhere, we shall do no more than mention them here.282 Needless to say, Shaykhi thought draws upon a remarkably powerful metaphysical imagination, unquestionably nourished by the transmitted sayings (akhbâr) of the holy Imams. This imaginative reach exceeds the capacities of those interlocutors whose learning is confined to fiqh, the purely legal science. Such a disparity of intellectual and spiritual levels usually has disastrous consequences for constructive discussion.

The “fourth pillar,” which has provoked so much writing and controversy in Iran, provides an example. Yet this article of Shaykhi doctrine does nothing more than give effect to a precept of the Imams expressed through two traditional terms: tawallâ, sympathetic attachment and allegiance to someone; and tabarrâ, aversion, repudiation, and separation. As noted above, the texts decisively settle whether Mohammad Karîm-Khân “invented” this doctrine. He did not. The principle of the fourth pillar was taught by his predecessors, and on this point Shaykhi teaching shows complete continuity.

We can trace the idea at least as far back as Nasîroddîn Tûsî283, and further still. It means that the bond of spiritual allegiance uniting every Shiite, every follower, to the Imam also demands solidarity and loyalty toward all those joined by that same allegiance to the Imam, in a hierarchy of spiritual degrees.

Here a characteristically Twelver Shiite idea comes into view, one that can exist only within Twelver Shiism because it is determined specifically by the ghaybat, the Imam's occultation. The fourth pillar concerns the shape and structure of the Shiite community. Rooted in the esoteric idea underlying the shî'a and tashayyo'—Shiite allegiance and identity—it shows that its adherents fully understand what the Imam's occultation entails. It rules out turning the spiritual into a social institution, or giving spiritual forms and hierarchies an outward, material embodiment that would identify them with the established organizations of visible history.

The only structure compatible with it is a spiritual fellowship, an Ecclesia spiritualis, a spiritual community. The hierarchy of its members can never be known or recognized from outside. The spiritual qualification that determines its degrees has nothing to do with secular claims or temporal functions; it lies beyond the reach of sociology. It remains a personal, secret gift bestowed by the Imam.

This means acknowledging both spiritual beings superior to this world and, among human beings, a hierarchy based solely on spiritual worth—on greater or lesser spiritual closeness to the Imam. Its members can never invoke that rank publicly, since it is not directed toward exercising power in or over this world. The hierarchy itself remains hidden within the esoteric community and cannot be equated with the positions of outward authority that necessarily arise in the organization of a community here below. A thorough study would need to draw on several major Shaykhi works.284 Here we shall simply set out the state of the question, following the indications in Shaykh Sarkâr Âghâ's book, to which we now return (pp. 95–143).

All Shiites agree that three kinds of knowledge are indispensable pillars of religion in its fullness: knowledge of divine unity (tawhîd); knowledge of the prophetic mission in general (nobowwat), and especially of the last Prophet; and knowledge of Hazrat Fâtima and the Twelve Imams.

But the building could not stand without a fourth pillar: to be in friendship and communion with all the friends of these august Persons, to separate oneself from all who separate themselves from them, and to have nothing in common with their enemies. This is the injunction expressed by tawallâ and tabarrâ, explained above. The only difference of opinion is that some Shiite scholars regard this solidarity as one of the practical consequences (forû') of religious faith, while others count it among its principles and foundations (osûl). The Shaykhis take the latter view, and the lineage of this teaching can be traced at least to Shaykh Mofîd (d. 413/1022) (p. 104). Conscious solidarity and fellowship with all the friends of the Imams, the Awliyâ, together with separation from their enemies: that is the fourth pillar, the IVe rokn. Who, then, are these Awliyâ?

Everyone recognizes that some people are more spiritually perfected than others, closer to God than others. Within this elite there must also be degrees of knowledge, spiritual awareness, and devotion. The Qur'an calls them the ashâb al-yamîn, “companions of the right”; the sâbiqûn, “those who go before”; the moqarrabûn, “those brought near”; and so forth. Already in the Imams' own time there were remarkable individuals endowed with profound knowledge and perfected spirituality; such people have continued to appear ever since. Outstanding examples include Salmân Pârsî, Abu Dharr, the two Jâbirs, Mofazzal, and the last two nâ'ib—deputies—of the Twelfth Imam during the “minor occultation” (ghaybat-e soghrâ): Hosayn ibn Rûh Nawbakhtî and 'Alî ibn Mohammad Samarrî. At the latter's death in 329/940, the “major occultation” (ghaybat-e kobrâ) began.

The Imam's gaze rested upon all these men, and each received certain mystical and visionary gifts from him. Shiites recognize them all as guides acting on the Imam's behalf,285 and accept that others like them may still enter the Imam's presence, even during the major occultation—in other words, in our own day.286 The fourth pillar's bond of friendship and solidarity embraces the whole succession of these Awliyâ, invisibly succeeding one another from century to century. That they are guides and intermediaries is the meaning given to Qur'an 34:17 by Shiite interpretation.287 Knowledge of this category of higher beings is as necessary as knowledge of each of the “Fourteen Immaculate Ones” (pp. 107–110).

But we now live in the time of the great ghaybat, the major occultation. After seventy years of minor occultation, the last nâ'ib—the Imam's deputy or representative—received an order from the Imam himself not to invest anyone else with that office (see Book VII below). “The matter now belongs to God”: these were the last words of 'Alî al-Samarrî, the Imam's final deputy, as he was dying.

In inaugurating the major occultation, the Great Absence, those words gave the Shiite spiritual outlook its particular tone, that desperatio fiducialis which is despair sustained by trust, a pessimism alive with hope. At the same time they transferred the whole structure of the Shiite community to the invisible spiritual plane. From that point on, the figure of the Hidden Imam dominates the horizon of Shiite consciousness—or rather, he is the very history of that consciousness. The meaning of this history is therefore utterly different from what our modern dogmatists call the “meaning of history.”

Just as the Imam exists but remains hidden in a world beyond our dialectical constructions and ready-made certainties, so the spiritual hierarchies emanating from his Person, and in a sense shaped by him, have never ceased to exist. They remain hidden with him until his final Epiphany. It is not, therefore, that the Bâb (“threshold” of the Imam) and the nâ'ib have ceased to exist. They exist, but are hidden, rigorously concealed in an inviolable anonymity, just as the Imam exists yet remains the “Hidden Imam” until his final manifestation, or parousia. The underlying principle had already been developed by Suhrawardi in the prologue to his Oriental Theosophy: earthly humanity, indeed our world itself, could not persist in existence for a single instant if the mystical pole (the Hidden Imam) were no longer there, together with all his invisible Companions, the Friends who from generation to generation are the “Perfect Shiites.”

Yet these persons cannot declare themselves or make themselves known by name. Consequently, there can be no possibility—much less any obligation—of knowing who they are individually. The Imam's instruction to refer henceforth to the sages who know and transmit the Imams' sayings and teachings concerns a category of people. It does not designate any individual among them, or publicly invest anyone by name with a superior rank.

During the ghaybat, it is impossible to know which of the Perfect Shiites is the Bâb and nâ'ib. This is the precise force of a hadîth transmitted by Mofazzal: “The Bâb of the Twelfth Imam is concealed by the very fact of the Twelfth Imam's concealment.” Everything written about the necessity of knowing these guides and about their mediating role must therefore be understood as requiring knowledge of their spiritual category, not knowledge of them as individually identifiable persons who have been appointed by name (pp. 110–111). The endless and pointless controversies surrounding the fourth pillar arose from a failure to grasp this essential distinction.

This spiritual category of higher beings ultimately embraces the whole hidden hierarchy familiar from Sufism: the qotb (pole), the awtâd (the stakes supporting the “cosmic tent”), the abdâl (the substitutes or those who succeed one another), the nojabâ and noqabâ (the spiritual Nobles and Princes). This hierarchy rests on certain hadîths288 and is claimed as an integral part of the Shiite idea, which Sufism, on this account, merely adopted. Shaykhi thought is concerned above all with a twofold hierarchy: the Nojabâ and Noqabâ, the spiritual Nobles and Princes. The fourth pillar calls for acknowledging their existence as a whole.

The Shaykhis have never said or claimed that any of their shaykhs was the Imam's particular Naqîb or Bâb. Certainly, insofar as the category of Awliyâ also includes all learned people whose guidance believers follow, there is no reason why Shaykhi scholars should not belong to it. In that case, however, membership is only a general attribute, just as one might say “Zayd is just.” During the occultation, no one can be designated and recognized as “the first person after the Imam”—that is, as the Bâb, exercising an office to which the qualification Nâtiq wâhid would be publicly and visibly attached. We shall explain that expression shortly.

The reason things must be so lies in the very nature of the ghaybat, whose meaning the Shaykhis seem to have explored with exceptional depth. The Imam is the “Hidden Imam” essentially because of a condition of human consciousness: human beings have veiled him from themselves and made themselves incapable of knowing and recognizing him (pp. 115 ff.). His manifestation is inconceivable, we might say, because the necessary conditions for that manifestation to be perceived do not exist. How could he show himself to people who cannot see him? “The time has not yet come.” As Mofazzal's hadîth teaches, his concealment entails the concealment of his Bâb and, consequently, of all the Perfect Ones from ordinary people.

Were they to announce themselves, they would confront humanity with a choice it is not capable of making. They would be arrested or banished; alternatively, the choice would degenerate into wretched rivalries and personal ambitions. For the day when the decisive choice is laid bare is precisely the day of the final manifestation. What the Shaykhis have affirmed, then, is that these higher beings, the “Perfect Shiites” (Kâmilân-e Shî'a), must exist, and that their existence must be known. They have never meant that these beings must manifest themselves, still less that one must recognize a supposed public manifestation of them (ibid.).

We can therefore say that, on this point, Shaykhi thought has carried a fundamental Shiite insight to its limit. What it gives us is a phenomenology of the ghaybat: an account of concealment and invisible form as conditions of spiritual experience. If the Imam, the first and last divine manifestation, is now the Hidden Imam, this is not because of some external event that suddenly took place on a particular day in the past. The death of the last nâ'ib merely marks a point of reference. The transition from minor to major occultation marks a reversal in humanity's lived experience of time: the time of presence becomes the time of absence.

Human beings themselves have veiled the Imam from their sight. They have become incapable of seeing him, having paralyzed or lost the organs that perceive divine manifestations, the organs of the dimensio mystica. This is why neither the Imam nor his companions can appear openly, publicly, and without a veil. Such an appearance would require human beings to possess a faculty of perception through which they could recognize the Imam and his companions when they became visible.

But humanity, in its present condition—whatever explanation we may give for that condition—so completely lacks such a faculty that any public declaration by a person claiming to be the Imam's Bâb, let alone the Imam himself, takes the form of an imposture. It is precisely this deception against which the Imam warned his followers in his final message to his last deputy.

After these explanations, there should be no ambiguity left concerning the fourth pillar, and therefore none concerning the idea in which it culminates: wahdat-e Nâtiq, the oneness of the one who speaks. This gives Shaykh Sarkâr Âghâ an opportunity to make certain observations that deserve our attention. They concern the entire Shaykhi position and reveal his reservations about the future of a spiritual Islam. This final theme had been discussed in detail by Shaykh Mohammad Karîm-Khân Kermânî and was not new: his predecessors had also addressed it.

But it is a difficult technical question, not readily understood by ordinary people. It comes from traditions (akhbâr) that ordinary believers rarely have occasion even to hear about. It should therefore never have been discussed outside the circle of specialists in hikmat ilâhîya, divine wisdom, rather than being exploited by agitators.

There are, besides, many religious questions still unresolved, or whose solutions are far from having become established certainties. They remain matters for inquiry, the work of the ahl-e nazar, those who pursue intellectual investigation. Questions on which there has been settled agreement since the beginnings of Islam are very few, and even those have often taken several generations to settle. If we believed our critics, the shaykh declares, ordinary people, the untrained ('awâmm), would have to be regarded as more learned than scholars, simply because they agree among themselves about their accepted, ready-made convictions while scholars disagree.

We would then have to adopt the opinions of the crowd and forget the prophets and sages, together with all the research invited by teachings that have yet to be explored (pp. 120–122). This solemn protest against conformism merits our attention. Against the paralysis of thought, so often regarded as a fate hanging over Islam, it sets the determination to carry every question beyond its present limits, a continual spiritual reformation whose aims are broader than those of any program of social reform.

As for the final idea, wahdat-e Nâtiq, in which the fourth pillar culminates, its meaning follows from everything we have said. The technical term nâtiq, “the one who speaks,” belongs to the familiar language of Shiite tradition. It is especially well established in Ismaili gnosis, where it carries a particular nuance.289 That there is only one (wâhid) who speaks can be understood only in the light of our preceding discussion of the hierarchy of “Perfect Shiites,” a hierarchy invisible during the Imam's occultation.

The word nâtiq can describe the Imam as one who “speaks” in God's name or in the Prophet's name. In that case the sâmit, the “silent” Imam, is the one who comes after him. Generally speaking, each of the Twelve Imams was nâtiq during his own time as Imam, while his future successor remained the sâmit, or “silent” Imam (p. 124). The term can also be applied to certain Shiites, describing them as “Perfect Ones” (kâmilûn, bozorgvârân). Examples include Salmân Pârsî and those like him: mirrors reflecting the image of the Imam whose Bâb they were, guiding others in his name and toward him. The term nâtiq, in this usage, also has a proper or literal meaning and a figurative meaning.

We shall return to the latter at the end.290 In its proper sense, the nâtiq are the Imams and the prophets; in turn, the most eminent of the Shiites—the most learned and spiritually perfected—have also been nâtiq. Among that elite, the one who, by virtue of his spiritual qualification, was the “first person after the Imam,” the Bâb-e a'zâm, was in the proper sense the nâtiq of the Shiites. In relation to him, the others were sâmit: silent.

What the Shaykhi masters have affirmed is that, by the Imam's arrangement, “there is a Salmân in every age.” In their terminology he is called nâtiq, and there is only one such nâtiq (wâhid), because he is the Perfect Individual (fard-e kâmil), the foremost among the Shiites. He is their center, the earthly pole or nadir of the Imam, who is the heavenly pole.

In relation to the Imam, he is like a burning wick whose fire is nothing but the communication of an invisible Fire. He corresponds to the heart in relation to the human body. These statements, of course, make sense only in the light of a belief accepted throughout Shiism: that there exist higher beings, the Nojabâ and Noqabâ, mentioned above. Their hierarchy among human beings rests entirely upon their inward spiritual worth, their closeness to the Imam. They may never claim it as a title, publicly display it, or use it for any worldly purpose. The shaykhs in the Shaykhi line of transmission (silsila) have therefore affirmed that in every age there exists this Nâtiq wâhid, the “Perfect Shiite” and supreme Bâb of the Imam.

But not one of them has ever claimed to be that person or demanded recognition as such. Quite the contrary. They have affirmed his existence because the human world, earthly humanity, cannot be without him. They have equally affirmed that he cannot be publicly manifested: human beings cannot identify him, single him out, or proclaim his name and person. His name and identity remain the Imam's secret, for the very reasons already given, bound up with the nature of the ghaybat and the time of the ghaybat (pp. 127–131).

Mofazzal's hadîth thus has strict and decisive consequences. Anyone who publicly proclaims himself the Imam's Bâb thereby places himself outside Shiism, because he profanes its fundamental secret, violates the occultation, and breaks with the expectation of the final revelation. No school has argued this point more forcefully than the Shaykhis. This is why Bábism and the Bahá'í faith, whatever interest they may have as religious phenomena in their own right, can appear from this standpoint only as the very negation of Shaykhi thought.

To derive them from Shaykh Ahmad Ahsâ'î is a mistaken perception of spiritual relationships, or an unjustified claim of descent. It requires considerable inattention and a serious lack of philosophical experience to think otherwise. More importantly, this very point helps explain why Shaykhi thought, although its 'irfân (mystical knowledge) so often speaks the same language as Sufism, nevertheless takes a stand against Sufism—or, more precisely, against the Sufi understanding of the role and authority of the shaykh. The issue arises insofar as the shaykh of a tarîqat, a Sufi order, tends to be recognized by that order as the Imam's visible nâ'ib, and to assume that role openly, in his own name and person.

This distinction must not be forgotten when we speak of the relationship between Shiism and Sufism. A remark recounted to me in Tehran some twelve years ago by an excellent friend who knew these matters well casts a particularly clear light on it.291 An eminent shaykh of Qom, Hajj Sayyed Mahdî Qawâm, used to tell his students: “Certainly you must be 'orafâ—people who know mystical theosophy—and practice tasawwof, Sufi spirituality.

“But take great care never to enter a tarîqat, a Sufi order. You must not bind yourself or submit to any shaykh. In binding yourself to him, you inevitably bind yourself also to the limits of his person and his spiritual horizon. The mystical Shiite ('irfânî) must choose the Imam himself—one of the holy Imams—directly as his only Qotb, his only spiritual pole, and follow this personal guide directly, without an intermediary.” All spiritual teaching is thus centered on the search for, and encounter with, an invisible personal master (ostâd-e ghaybî), who is the Imam. We have seen an exemplary instance of this in Shaykh Ahmad Ahsâ'î's life. If we ask what form Shiite spirituality takes, I know of no more illuminating answer. The personal encounter with the Imam may occur in a dream or in a waking vision.

We shall explain later (Book VII) how such an encounter is possible without in any way weakening the strict conditions of the ghaybat. For the conditions of the Manifestation do not yet exist. The time of the parousia, the Imam's final appearance, has not yet come. Or rather, that appearance is the culminating act of an eschatology—a movement toward the final unveiling—that must not simply burst upon the world unexpectedly on some distant day, but must be fulfilled within and through the very time of the occultation. The ripening of the Imam's final revelation through the time of his hiddenness: this is the “meaning of history” when the Imam's history is understood as the history of Shiite consciousness. It is the growth of his inward presence in the hearts of his followers, as their invisible guide and master.

This last point brings us to a final question, one that both complements and sums up the matters considered here, since its answer involves all the fundamental positions we have surveyed. The Shaykhis have been asked how and why they, in particular, felt called to reveal and affirm the fourth pillar. Clearly, they cannot try to justify by any chain of causes what they experience essentially as a divine gift.

But they have understood both its meaning and its imperative in the light of the fundamental Paraclete idea of Shiism: the Imam's final epiphany as the Paraclete will disclose the hidden meaning of every religious Revelation. The Shaykhi conviction is that Shiism contains a multitude of teachings still concealed, and that the reason for their concealment—the obstacle to making them known—lies not with God but with human beings. The historical circumstances of the Shiites certainly made taqîyeh, the prudent concealment of one's beliefs, necessary.

Even when circumstances became outwardly more favorable, especially from the Safavid period onward, official stability encouraged an almost exclusive concern with the outward meaning of the transmitted reports (akhbâr) and with fiqh, legal scholarship, which degenerated into case-by-case casuistry and formalism. The fundamental metaphysical questions—those concerning walâyat, haqîqat (spiritual truth), and ma'rifat (spiritual knowledge)—were so neglected that it remained impossible to examine them without observing a certain esotericism and practicing taqîyeh.

But the time of the ghaybat is precisely a time in which this veil of secrecy is gradually lifted. The unveiling of the fourth pillar is one example.

Esotericism thus becomes here a principle of movement and progress: a progress that constitutes the very meaning of an eschatology already unfolding, from the mission of the “last Prophet” to the final appearance of the last Imam. Consequently—and this is Shaykh Sarkâr Âghâ's conclusion—instead of suspecting the Shaykhi masters of claiming for themselves a status that their entire conduct rejects, we should read their books and consider why they have, on the contrary, condemned anyone who makes the absurd claim to be recognized as one of the Nojabâ or Noqabâ (pp. 132 ff.). Their aim was to bring a theologoumenon, a theological idea, into the light, not to designate some particular person by name, since that would contradict the very conditions of the ghaybat.292

Far from claiming this distinction for themselves, they have exposed the absurdity of every such claim. They have warded off a danger that always remains possible within Shiism, precisely by placing this spiritual qualification on the plane of existence and level of consciousness demanded by the Imam's occultation. In one sense, we might say, nothing could be more esoteric than the Shaykhi position, since the structure and hierarchy of the Shiite community remain “secret,” suprasensible, and invisible.

Yet nothing provides a better antidote to the claims of every counterfeit esotericism. The Nojabâ and Noqabâ belong to “another world.” They may nevertheless live in this one, dressed as craftsmen, farmers, or simply as scholars (p. 137).

But they can give no outward sign of their invisible rank that would lead to their recognition in this world, on worldly terms. And if someone happened to recognize one of them, that person would have no right to betray the secret. Each of them, we might say, is bound by the strict law of the Knights of the Grail: “... and his power remains sacred so long as he remains unknown to all.”

The misfortune is that here, more than anywhere, Shiite esotericism far exceeds ordinary awareness and the assumptions people commonly accept as settled. It has happened that the word nâtiq was taken not in its proper Shaykhi sense but in the merely figurative sense (majâz) mentioned earlier. Because the oneness of the Nâtiq was then understood as applying to scholars in general—scholars of the outward law ('olamâ-ye zâhirî)—critics concluded that the Shaykhi doctrine meant there could be only one such scholar in each age.

We can understand the alarm caused by this mistake, but it would be frankly comic if it were not also a rather serious symptom. Much needless speaking and writing were required to explain that the number of outward religious scholars, the 'olamâ-ye zâhirî, has always been unlimited in every age (p. 140).

Our account of the Shaykhi school has necessarily been brief. Still, we hope it has suggested the complexity and extraordinary richness of its theosophy, and the importance of its place in Shiite thought. We hope, too, that it will help dispel certain hasty judgments about the school—judgments which, alas, abound in the history of philosophy whenever that history is not written from firsthand study.

4. Eschatology and the Correspondence of Time and Space

To conclude, we should insist on one further point. It will allow us to begin comparing two schools of Shiite thought, while extending the eschatological perspective that has just opened before us. In ordinary theological usage, “eschatology” refers to the events of the end (eschaton): the end of this time, of our Aeon. Viewed within chronological time, eschatology is therefore essentially a matter of waiting; hence the Hidden Imam is called the “Expected Imam.”

But every departure from the dimension of chronological time is, in that very sense, also an eschatological event. All hierognosis, all visionary perception, is eschatological, because it brings to an end the conditions of time as measured by the chronology of this world. We saw a striking example in the tradition of the White Cloud, as interpreted by Qâzî Sa'îd Qommî. To be capable of perceiving spiritual forms is already to belong to their world, to have stepped, even if only momentarily, outside the “opaque and dense” time of this world.

When the Shaykhis call the perception of the dimensio mystica—the malakûtî, or spiritual dimension—“seeing things in Hûrqalyâ,” they mean a kind of eschatological vision. An eschatology that is not simply an event destined to occur without warning on some distant day, but is already being fulfilled in the present, implies the capacity to “see things in Hûrqalyâ.” It means perceiving here and now, through their mystical dimension, the whole reality of beings and things—of which chronological succession allows us to perceive only a part at any given moment.

Hûrqalyâ is the highest of the three “emerald cities” beyond Mount Qâf, a name we first encountered in the work of Suhrawardi. Hûrqalyâ is the mundus imaginalis, the imaginal world, the world of imaginal forms and archetypal images. Beings and things “seen in Hûrqalyâ” possess the depth of a mirror. This does not mean that such vision is an inferior form of knowledge, still awaiting a higher, face-to-face encounter. Rather than recalling Saint Paul's words, velut in speculo, “as in a mirror,” should suggest here the true, original meaning of all speculative mysticism: a form of spiritual insight grounded in the mirror.

Without that transparency, not only does the real relation between the suprasensible and the sensible remain unseen; so does the interrelation of all the universes, which serve one another as mirrors, as “places of epiphany” (mazhar). Vision in speculo, “in the mirror,” begins as soon as the perspective of suprasensible Forms opens, beyond the conditions of “opaque and dense” time. This is why we have emphasized the fascination that the laws of optics held for our medieval metaphysicians of light. The degree to which a person can perceive things “in Hûrqalyâ” depends on the degree of esoteric knowledge attained. In other words, the degree of spiritual consciousness depends on how close one has come to the place of Return, which is also the place of Origin.

To Shaykh Mohammad Karîm-Khân Kermânî, Shaykh Ahmad Ahsâ'î's second successor, we owe a striking way of giving form to this idea. We should begin by recalling it. It will then be easier to understand the isomorphism—the correspondence in form—between patterns in time and patterns in space that arises within the eschatological perspective we have just defined, a perspective in which the thought of Shaykhi theosophers and that of Ismaili Shiite theosophers converge.

We spoke earlier of an eschatology—an unfolding of the last things—“already taking place since the mission of the last prophet came to an end.” It would be more accurate, following a passage by Shaykh Mohammad Karîm-Khân Kermânî, to say “since the very beginning of the cycle of prophecy.”293 That takes us back to Adam himself, “the earthly Adam” (not the “Greater Adam,” the Homo maximus discussed earlier).

Adam, “our father,” was the first of the seven great prophets, the prophet of the first of the seven periods making up the “cycle of prophecy.” Two words, mabda' and ma'âd—origin and return—name the two great acts of a drama that can also be called cosmogony and prophetology. The first act is the “descent” of the Intelligence (Ennoia) into the earthly world: the cycle in which the cosmos comes into being.

The second is the Intelligence's “ascent,” taking our world upward with it. That ascent begins with the cycle of prophecy, inaugurated by Adam. The lowest point reached by the descending Intelligence coincided with Adam's appearance. “Then, through him and through all those who call people to God, this summons rang out in the world: Now turn around and return.”

Here we meet a characteristically Gnostic vision once again. Shaykhi spiritual philosophy also describes the history of a world in what might be called a “Gothic style”: its governing axis is vertical, not the horizontal prospect of limitless evolution. This is not a history made up of irreversible outward events. Rather, history's very advance is a turning back toward its origin.

Seen in terms of form, what is repeated on the scale of an entire world seems to correspond to the “miracle of the octave” to which we referred earlier when explaining the law of spiritual interpretation (Book I, Chapter II, section 4). “During the Descent,” our shaykh writes, “God's guarantors were the cosmic utterances through which the cosmos came into being. During the Ascent, they are the inspired utterances of the language of prophecy.

“Through the prophetic speech of the Messengers, the world begins to ascend, to make its gradual return. If the ages of the past should be disclosed to you, you will see them beneath your feet, arranged vertically—not beside you, not ahead or behind you on a horizontal plane.”

This is precisely where our familiar way of thinking about history is liable to lose its footing. “The story of our world,” the shaykh writes, “is the story of a man who must be raised from the bottom of a well.” The image of the well is familiar throughout Gnostic traditions, from Mandaeism to Suhrawardi's “Tale of Exile” and the visionary writings of Najm Kobrâ.294 It prompts Mohammad Karîm-Khân to give a dramatic account of the ascent, from which I can retain only the conclusions here.

“We must reach the spiritual level at which the Friend, the Imam, becomes visible” (notice that the Imam, in Shiite language, is the very figure whom Sufism calls the mystical Beloved). “The Imam cannot come before we ourselves have arrived; we would not even see him. To acquire the capacity to see him is to rise higher, and to rise higher is to reach the place where the Imam becomes visible—the place the theosophers call Hûrqalyâ.”

The last things, then, and the Imam's return or parousia, are not an external event destined to erupt unexpectedly on some future day. They are a Presence progressively realized through acts that anticipate it. That is why the shaykh tells his reader: “You yourself, if you are capable of sensing it, will catch in the pages of this book, and in the words it contains, a fragrance carried from the flowers of the world of Hûrqalyâ.”

Shaykh Sarkâr Âghâ devoted an entire chapter of a substantial book to developing these pages.295 Where is Hûrqalyâ, this mundus imaginalis, this imaginal world? It is not quite the world of Plato's Ideas. It is the world of Image-Ideas, of the Forms and Figures of the sensible universe in a state of “subtle matter”—a world possessing extension, but made of pure light. It is reasonable to call it the “eighth clime,” beyond the “seven climes” that together comprise the earthly universe.

But we must not forget that it also lies within the unseen dimension of our own world: more precisely, within an invisible realm that becomes visible to inward sight once we understand how the eternal Forms belonging to the world of the Soul (Malakût) come into contact with the perishable materials of the sensible universe.

These Forms come into contact with the world in the same way that a human figure “enters” a mirror. The connection is incidental; there is nothing essential about the relationship. The mirror can break at any moment, and the connection can be severed.

In truth, the eternal Forms never “descend” from their own world, any more than a person actually “enters” a mirror, or the physical mass of the sun “descends” upon the Earth. What “comes into this world” from the eternal human soul is its outline, its image, its projected shadow. That image comes to the surface of the sensible mirror, and its appearance there is an act performed by the soul itself.

We have seen how five universes are layered within the scheme of worlds: the world of the Creative Imperative (the Lâhût, the fullness or pleroma of the Fourteen Immaculate Ones in their eternal substance); the world of the Intelligence; the world of Spirit (rûh), which forms an intermediate realm between the world of the Intelligence and the world of the Soul; the world of the Soul, which is the realm of the Forms of beings; and finally this visible, sensible world in which we now live, “the plane at which all the universes reach their final destination.

“The higher eternal Forms, those belonging to the world of the Soul, have reached this place. Here they have been hidden in the earthly dust of this world, although in another sense they have already departed from it. For this world is the tomb of the higher universes. All the beings inhabiting those other universes have been buried here, in this Earth.

“By the command of the Lord of the worlds, they must shake the dust from their heads and rise, delivered from their tomb. Each must find its own Dwelling again, must return home.” To leave the tomb is to leave behind all that decays and perishes, just as an image “leaves” a mirror when the mirror breaks.

We might note in passing that the oldest Ismaili Gnosis had already offered this inward meaning of the tomb. A saying attributed to the Prophet declares: “Between my tomb and the pulpit (minbar) from which I preach lies a garden among the gardens of paradise.”

A tenth-century Ismaili writer, Mohammad Sorkh of Nishapur, explains it as follows. This saying cannot be understood in its outward, literal sense. Ordinary people think only of a gravestone placed there: they look at it, pray before it, and call the place a “garden,” unaware that the saying can be understood only according to Gnostic truth, not its literal appearance.

The Prophet's pulpit represents precisely that literal appearance: the outward form of revealed religion, with its commands and doctrines. The tomb, meanwhile, represents philosophy. For in that tomb, the outward form of religion and its doctrines must undergo the decay and dissolution of death, just as a human material body decomposes in the grave. The garden of paradise between pulpit and tomb is the garden of Gnostic Truth: the field of resurrection from which the initiate's incorruptible Form arises.

Needless to say, this understanding is far removed from certain ideas about philosophy that prevailed in the medieval West, whether the Averroist doctrine of double truth or the theologians' conception of philosophy as ancilla theologiae, the handmaid of theology. Here philosophy marks a stage of initiation. It is indeed the “tomb” of theology, but only because the religion of spiritual wisdom (Dîn-e haqq) rises again from that in-between place—between dogma and tomb—where untransformed doctrinal belief must die and be transfigured. It is a new dawn, preceded by the night of death.296

This corresponds exactly to the “being taken up into the heights” described by our Shaykhi authors. It does not mean, they tell us, abandoning this world, changing the present conditions of the physical body, flying off to some place in the sky, or having to undergo the exitus of physical death to escape this elemental earthly world, which our senses perceive.

Certainly, we must speak of a mystical death—the death evoked by so many traditions—which allows us to reach that other world even while we remain in this one. That is the whole point. We reach it when our eyes open to the other world and we are inwardly transformed into Hûrqalyâvis, people of Hûrqalyâ. Only then are we, in the true sense, companions of the Hidden Imam, equipped with the organs of perception belonging to the world beyond.

Shaykh Sarkâr Âghâ next asks us to grasp an image familiar both to the earliest Shiism and to Ismaili Gnosis: the appearance or parousia of the Resurrecting Imam as the day “when the Sun rises in the West.” We are told that this means the point and moment at which the present world completes its decline.

“We must never forget the true meaning,” the shaykh tells us, “which is the spiritual meaning.

“We must understand that our world has neither east nor west in itself, just as the sun has no rising or setting. What we call its revolution in its orbit is our own revolution, the revolution of human beings. Whenever we turn away from this world and advance spiritually toward the world beyond, the earthly world sinks toward its setting, while the light of the other world rises in the East.

“The east and west in question are east and west in their true sense: the spiritual East and West, independent of the compass points of sensible space—not the figurative east and west of our geography. A sun rising in the West therefore announces the hour of sunset, the final decline of this world. And that Light is the most sacred being of the Imam.”

These lines have far-reaching implications. Perhaps we are too ready to assume that a world arranged along a vertical axis, oriented toward a “celestial pole,” necessarily belongs to a geocentric picture of the universe, an imago mundi with the Earth at its center.

But we can observe what happens in a school such as Shaykhism when the heliocentric picture replaces the geocentric one. The Copernican revolution produces results rather different from those familiar to us. Understood in its spiritual meaning, heliocentrism now reveals what the true East is. The movement formerly understood in geocentric terms as the sun's revolution becomes the revolution of ourselves, the inhabitants of Earth.

Yet this is a revolution of our very being: as we advance toward our West, our decline and end, we move at the same time toward the East, the other world, our daybreak and our origin. Then it is the Earth that we see setting in the West: no longer the sunset, but the setting of the Earth. In a sense, this heliocentric revolution makes possible the ascent first projected and outlined within a geocentric vision.

We can go further. The insistence on spiritual meaning produces precisely the reversal of perspective described by Swedenborg when he relates the three meanings of divine Revelation to three universes: natural, spiritual, and celestial. What was above and at the origin—the celestial—had come to occupy the most deeply hidden center. What had thus been buried in the center now returns to its original place, in excelsis, on high.

Earthly time, the brief tomb in which the eternal Forms are confined, becomes their celestial space, through which they regain their origin. In this way there occurs a distinctive correspondence of forms—or better, a symmorphosis, a convergence into one form—between form in time and form in space. We first encountered a clue to this at the beginning of the present work, in the correspondence between perceiving forms in a mirror and a particular way of hearing the world musically. The same correspondence, in which time becomes space, was already suggested to us by Qâzî Sa'îd Qommî's commentary on the hadîth of the White Cloud.

This return from forms succeeding one another in time to forms that endure in space seems to be an essential movement of thought for anyone capable of “seeing things in Hûrqalyâ”: perceiving the dimensio mystica, the mystical dimension of beings and things, as already fully real. Such perception means grasping together what chronological time presents only in succession. The image of the “sun rising in the west,” whose significance for our Shaykhi authors we have just seen, is equally characteristic of Ismaili Gnosis, where it too is associated with the Imam's manifestation.

One further convergence between Shaykhi and Ismaili spiritual philosophy deserves mention.

However much the different branches of Shiism diverge in doctrine and position, they share a certain way of thinking. To speak of an eschatology already being fulfilled is to say, as we have seen, that every perception of the last things here and now is a perception of the dimensio mystica of beings and things: of a complete whole, even though that whole has not yet appeared within the successive order of chronological time.

To perceive its completeness already is, in one way or another, to perceive it no longer in time but in a space no longer ravaged by the endless coming and going of things. It is to perceive it in the space of Hûrqalyâ, and so to put an end to the conflict between time and space in which death triumphs.

The theme of the hexaemeron, the “six days of creation,” offers a striking example. Both Shaykhi and Ismaili thinkers discover a correspondence between temporal and spatial form. From another angle, this is an exercise of ta'wîl, spiritual interpretation, which here means “leading back” what is successive to what is simultaneous.

Once we have grasped the simultaneity to which the sequence of the “six days” can be returned, the “seventh day” in turn gives spatial form to the time of the Imam of the Resurrection (Qâ'im al-Qiyâmat). The “seventh day” ends the conflict between space and time. That is the aspect under which we must understand the relationship between eschatology and the correspondence of temporal and spatial forms—an aspect that, like many others in this book, I can do no more than briefly indicate.

Shaykh Ahmad Ahsâ'î, in his book of “Teachings” (Fawâ'id), whose first five chapters we examined earlier, offers a decisive interpretation of these “six days.” In two different ways he leads the temporal form of six successive days back to the spatial form of six universes existing simultaneously.

In broad outline, his first interpretation is this: the “six days” in which, according to Scripture, “God created the Heavens and the Earth” are the six worlds that make up the macrocosm. They are: (1) the world of the Intelligences; (2) the world of the Souls; (3) the world of Nature; (4) the world of the substances of the swirling cloud of atoms (al-habâ'), where each atom is the quantum of being invested in a particular existent—that is, the quantity of matter (maddâ) or light (nûr) which serves as the “father” of every being composed of matter and form; (5) the world of the Image (mithâl), the world of imaginal forms, which receive matter in its elemental state in this world and in its subtle state in the Malakût. These forms are the quiddities, the essential “whatnesses” or “mothers” of individual beings; and (6) the world of material bodies.

His second interpretation starts from the unchanging consistency of divine creation, which makes all these correspondences possible: “You will find no disharmony in the creation of the Merciful” (Qur'an 67:3). The shaykh understands the “six days” as belonging to the “second creation” (a technical expression we explained earlier). They are the constitutive elements present in every being. None of these “days,” therefore, can appear before the others.

All are given together, along with the matter that provides a being's quantum of existence (light, its “father”) and the form that provides its quantum of quiddity (Mercy, its “mother”). The shaykh names them using the same terms that logic applies to the predicaments or categories. He expressly insists, however, that he means something quite different by those terms: in the ordinary list of logical categories, they refer only to accidents added to a substance. To keep the terminology precise, I shall use the traditional Latin names here.

We therefore have another series of six—a group of six which, in certain respects, corresponds to the first. The shaykh bases this interpretation on hadîth from the Sixth and Eighth Imams. The six “days” that constitute the structure of every being are as follows:

  1. The first day is the quantum (kamm, quantity): the particular measure of being or substance (qadar jawharî) allotted to each being.
  2. The second day is the quale (kayf): quality or mode, with its various specifications.

  3. The third day is the quando (waqt), or when. Here the shaykh distinguishes three categories. They are founded on a distinction we already encountered in Qâzî Sa'îd Qommî, who differentiates opaque time, subtle time, and absolutely subtle time. But Shaykh Ahmad develops this distinction in a remarkable way. He places those three degrees within each of the three orders of duration: chronological time, sempiternity, and eternity.

    a) First comes chronological time (zamân), which has three degrees: subtle, intermediate, and dense. These correspond to different states of the body, from subtle bodies to material bodies—for example, the Sphere of Spheres, the other celestial Spheres, and the body of the sublunary world.

    b) Next comes dahr (aevum, aiôn), sempiternity, which likewise has three states: subtle, the time of the Jabarût or world of the Intelligences; intermediate, the time of the Malakût or world of the Souls; and opaque or dense, the time of the “substances of the swirling cloud of atoms.”

    c) Lastly comes sarmad, eternity. It too has three degrees, corresponding to the moments of the fourfold Creative Act discussed earlier (p. 269): subtle, the time of mashî'at, the primordial Will; intermediate, the time of the prestructuring of beings (taqdîr, handasa wojûdîya); and dense or opaque, corresponding to the “decree” (qazâ) and the “signature” (imzâ).

  4. The fourth day is the ubi (makân), or where: place, the “vessel containing whatever flows into it.” Its modes correspond in structure to those of the quando. There is an eternal place (sarmadî) for eternal realities (sarmadîyât), a sempiternal place (dahrî) for sempiternal realities (dahrîyât), and a temporal place (zamânî) for temporal realities (zamânîyât).
  5. The fifth day is situs, or jihat: the orientation (tawajjoh) of a being toward its principle, and of that principle toward the being. It is also the sense or direction in which the being extends outward from its origin.
  6. The sixth day is rank (roiba): the position, nearer to or farther from its source, of the influence received by a being.297

It is easy to see that the third and fourth “days,” as Shaykh Ahmad analyzes them, already give thought everything it needs to establish the correspondence between forms in time and forms in space. They thus make it possible to transform time into space—or, in eschatological terms, to pass from the time of this world into the time of another world that brings the first to an end. Unfortunately we cannot pursue the matter here.

We must be content to set out the striking convergence, the shared movement of thought, between Shaykhi and Ismaili spiritual philosophy, particularly as we find it in the great Iranian Ismaili thinker Nâsir-e Khosraw.

Naturally, a thinker such as Nâsir-e Khosraw makes no secret of his impatience with the pious chatter of literalists. Those who practice spiritual interpretation (ahl-e ta'wîl) hold that God's Book is a guide to the spiritual life. And it is hard to see what spiritual benefit anyone could gain from learning merely that the physical heavens and earth did not once exist, that the Creator then needed no fewer than six days to produce them, and that afterward he took his seat on a throne.298

Ismaili thinkers—above all Abû Ya'qûb Sejestânî in the tenth century and Nâsir-e Khosraw in the eleventh—therefore apply an interpretation operating at two higher levels of meaning: the esoteric and the esoteric within the esoteric. At each level “time becomes space,” and what succeeds one thing after another is understood as existing simultaneously.299

In its outward sense, a “day” is the time the sun takes to travel from the eastern horizon to the western horizon. That measure of time corresponds to the extent of the Earth's surface covered by its light.

But this relationship merely measures how Nature (tabî'at, physis) works in the world through its powers. These powers are six in number: movement and rest, matter and form, time and place. Our Ismaili authors therefore make the following distinction. Outwardly, “day” means the sun's illumination of the world as it moves from east to west. Inwardly, the first day is Nature's illumination of the world through movement; the second, through rest; the third, through Matter; the fourth, through Form; the fifth, through time; and the sixth, through space.

The effects and traces of these six “days-as-powers” remain permanently impressed upon every being and every thing in the material world. Each expresses them according to its own inward law.

Thus the outline of every material object has six faces, six directions: below and above, behind and in front, left and right. The six faces of a physical solid are the hexaemeron, the six ever-present “days” of Creation. (Exactly the same argument appears in Shaykh Ahmad Ahsâ'î: the geometrical boundaries of a solid are the six simultaneous “days” of its creation.300) And the seventh day? The seventh day is the whole itself—the solid or physical person that supports and completes those six faces. It is also the whole's dimension beyond the senses, for it is the soul that perceives form as a whole. As the “seventh” face of a solid with six sides and three dimensions, the “seventh day” is, in a sense, its “fourth” dimension.

Considered in relation to the cosmos as a whole, it is the Human Form that completes the cosmic process and carries it beyond itself.

Considered in relation to the sacred cosmos, the spiritual world, it is the Form of the Resurrector, the last Imam. By announcing the Resurrection of Resurrections (qiyâmat al-qiyâmât), he will inaugurate our world's passage from its present cycle of concealment (dawr al-satr) into the cycle of manifestation (dawr al-kashf) destined to follow it.

We have now reached a higher level of Ismaili spiritual interpretation, “the esoteric within the esoteric.” Here the six days of the creation of the sacred cosmos are the six great prophets entrusted with a Revelation, the six periods of the complete cycle of prophecy. A prophet's “day” is the period belonging to that prophet, from the moment he is called until the coming of the Imam who closes his period. There have been the “days” of Adam, Noah, Abraham, Moses, Christ, and Mohammad.

“If people understood this spiritual interpretation,” Nâsir-e Khosraw writes, “they would see the prophetic religions standing in their proper places, where each was brought forth: the Mazdeans on the third day, the Jews on the fourth day,301 the Christians on the fifth day, Islam on the sixth day.”302 The Qur'anic verse speaks of the creation of the Heavens (plural) and the Earth (singular) to signify that the outward forms of religions are many and appear to be in conflict, while their inward meaning—their ta'wîl—is one.

The Throne upon which the Merciful establishes himself on the seventh day is the person of the Resurrector (Qâ'im), the last Imam, through whom and in whom the inward meaning of all Revelations will be unveiled. The last Imam himself is the “seventh day.” His person gathers together and sums up the “six days” of prophecy, just as the complete form of a physical solid gathers together its six faces. At different levels of meaning, both complete and recapitulate the “six days of Creation.”

The whole secret history of humankind—the six millennia symbolizing the cycle of prophecy—moves toward the appearance of this perfect Human Form, the Resurrecting Imam (al-walad al-tâmm, the Perfect Child). His millennium, the seventh in the cycle, is the seventh day of the creation of the sacred cosmos. For no one, not even one of the six great prophets, has yet received the fullness of everything. The seventh day has not yet dawned: “the day when no soul shall have power over another soul, and the command shall belong to God alone” (82:19).303

There is, of course, a difference between the eschatology of Twelver Shiism and Shaykhism on the one hand and that of Ismaili Shiism on the other. I think we can express it most briefly by saying that Twelver teachings about the Imam correspond symbolically to the heaven of the fixed stars, the sphere of the twelve constellations of the zodiac, whereas Ismaili teachings correspond to the seven planetary heavens and their moving stars.

For Twelver Shiites, the last Imam is already here. He has already appeared, but his divine splendor is now hidden in a world beyond the senses until the hour of his manifestation or parousia. For the Ismailis, the last Imam is the secret of the future, the Form of superhuman perfection that humanity will bring forth on the Last Day. That day cannot dawn until the whole cycle of planetary revolutions is complete.

Yet on both sides the “time of the Imam” takes spatial form as an Earth beyond this Earth: among the Shaykhis, the mystical Earth of Hûrqalyâ; among the Ismailis, the Earth mentioned in the Qur'anic verse concerning the creation of the Heavens and the Earth. This cannot mean our present Earth, for Scripture says it is “illumined by the light of its Lord.”

Our Earth, by contrast, remains in Darkness, although the light of physical day shines upon it. No: the verse concerns the mystical hexaemeron, “that other Earth, still concealed in the night ... upon which, it is said, the esoteric community is already established through the steadfastness of faith, not through any material settlement ... and which is the Earth of light.” On that Earth the darkness of religions confined to the literal word and the Law will have been dispersed.304

This, in the broadest outline, is how the texts of Shaykhi Twelver Gnosis and Ismaili Gnosis present the structural correspondence of time and space. I believe we could easily verify here the laws of “hermeneutic perspective,” the perspective opened by spiritual interpretation, which we sketched in Book I of the present work. At the same time, an intellectual undertaking comes into view.

Though it works specifically upon the forms of biblical or Qur'anic Revelation, it differs neither in scope nor in intention—only in method—from contemporary efforts to analyze and bring together the harmonic forms perceived throughout Nature, in every kingdom and at every level of the universe. It is as true to say that living beings grow and live in time but die and disappear in space as it is to say that they grow in space and likewise vanish in time.

The opposition between time and space, their separation and their power to destroy one another, is experienced as something demonic. That is the tragedy of every living creature: having to fulfill its task in time, only to surrender everything it acquired or won in space during that time—and the reverse is equally true.305

Thus the symmorphosis of form in time and form in space, abolishing the law by which each destroys the other, is envisioned in Shiite spiritual philosophy as the “form of Resurrection,” the “perfect form of the Imam,” the “Earth of Light,” and the “seventh day of Creation.”

Seen in this light, Shiite eschatology offers its own resolution of the tragedy faced by every living being: thrown into time, yet feeling within itself an insistent presence that protests against its destruction by time. The Imam's space—the “Earth of Light of Hûrqalyâ,” where time becomes space—appears as salvation from chronological time.

This brings the Imam's person fully into view at the “supreme horizon” to which Shiite thought and spirituality raise him. It seems to us, then, that this work can end in no other way than by turning to the person of the Twelfth Imam, the Hidden Imam. Century after century, his presence endures in Shiite consciousness, entering the lives of believers, the mighty and the humble alike, in moments of doubt, distress, and abandonment. Whether in dreams or in waking life, a fleeting vision shines with trust in the Unseen and the certainty that his presence is always near.

Book VII

The Twelfth Imam and Spiritual Chivalry

Chapter I The Hagiography of the Twelfth Imam

1. The Completion of the Fullness of the Twelve

We have spoken of the Twelfth Imam so often that any attempt to collect all those passages here would risk repetition.
