“Show me, lost as I am in the valley of bewilderment and ignorance, the way to the Truth.” The king answers: “I am al-Tâher—the Pure—son of Mohammad al-Mahdî [the Hidden Imam], son of Hasan al-‘Askarî ...” And he continues, tracing his lineage back through the Imams, one after another, to the First Imam, ‘Alî ibn Abî Tâlib, of whom a Quranic verse says: “We have gathered all things into an illuminating Imam [Guide] (Imâm mobîn)” (36:11).

Once again, then, we find ourselves in the presence of someone belonging to the most extraordinary category imaginable: a son of the Hidden Imam. (On the Green Island, Sayyed Shamsoddîn was a descendant of his in the fifth generation.) Such a person does not enter what we call “history,” but neither is he therefore a “mythical” figure. What follows is perfectly understandable: what human soul could resist such a revelation from a being of this supernatural order? The Shafiite faints.

When he regains consciousness, he murmurs: “Glory be to God, who has at last clothed me in the robe of true Islam and faith, brought me out of the darkness of unquestioning obedience to human authority (taqlîd), and led me into the life-giving expanse of the world of light and certainty known through personal experience.” He and all his companions then profess their allegiance to Shiism.

King al-Tâher invites them all to be his guests for a week. When the week is over, the delightful inhabitants of al-Zâhera each wish to entertain them in turn. And so their stay on the island stretches into an entire year—a year in which they are showered with kindness and consideration, and in which their initiation is brought to completion.

From the Story of the Green Island we learned that it was only one of the islands belonging to the sons of the Hidden Imam. Now we are to learn of the others and their geography.

First, the island where our travelers are staying is so large that it takes two full months to cross, whether by land or by sea. Beyond it lies another island, with a city called al-Râ’yeqa (the Clear City). Its king is al-Qâsem, a son of the Imam (ibn Sâhib al-Amr). This island, too, takes two months to cross from end to end. Beyond it is a third, al-Sâfiya (the Serene City), ruled by Ébrâhîm, another son of the Hidden Imam. It likewise takes two months to cross. Beyond that lies a fourth island, Mazlûm360, ruled by ‘Abdorrahmân, another of the Hidden Imam’s sons; crossing it also takes two months.

Finally, farther still, lies a fifth, ‘Anâtis, ruled by al-Hâshem, a son of the Imam. This is the largest of all, requiring four months to cross. Anyone who enters it knows joy forever. All these islands share the same climate and the same enchanting landscape. All their inhabitants are Shiites; all have the same beauty of face and gentleness of manner.

If we set aside the first city, al-Mobâraka, where our travelers were received by a representative of al-Tâher, we have a group of five islands and five cities, each governed by one of the Hidden Imam’s five sons. Crossing all five from end to end requires a total of twelve months. Groups of five and twelve occur frequently in Shiism—the Five Persons of the Cloak, the Twelve Imams, and so on.

But when five are the sons of a being such as the Hidden Imam, one cannot help thinking of the “Five Sons of the Living Spirit” in Manichaeism. Similarly, the twelve months needed to traverse the five kingdoms recall all the symbolic representations associated with the twelve signs of the zodiac, the “twelve sovereigns of light,” and so forth.

Unfortunately, our travelers do not visit all these islands. They remain for a full year at al-Zâhera because its kindly inhabitants believed the Imam would appear on their island that year. So they too waited, but God did not grant them the grace of seeing him. In the end, only two travelers—the converted Shafiite and one other—decide to stay on the island. The rest begin their return journey. Unfortunately again, we are given no details about the way back, doubtless because it is just as impossible to point out that route as it is to point out the route by which they came.

Let us not forget, however, that all this was related by one of those who made the voyage, on a certain Ramadan evening in Medina, in the house of a vizier who had no sympathy for Shiism or the followers of the Imams. By the time the storyteller finished, the night was almost over.

The vizier withdrew to another room and summoned his guests to him one by one, making each solemnly promise never, for as long as he lived, to repeat a word of the story they had just heard. And, it is said, whenever the guests of that evening subsequently met, they developed the habit of asking one another, “Do you remember that remarkable Ramadan night?” To which the other would reply, “Of course, but we were sworn to secrecy.” Fortunately, one of them—we even know his name—did pass on what he had heard.

4. An Encounter in the Desert, or the Ubiquity of Nâ-kojâ-Âbâd

Yet by no means do all the stories of visions of, or approaches to, the Hidden Imam’s country require such a long journey beforehand. It is as though Nâ-kojâ-Âbâd—the place that is not contained within any place on the map of the world perceived by our senses—suddenly, fleetingly breaks into our world. Or, if we prefer, it makes itself present within the visionary’s inner world. We might equally say, looking at it the other way around, that the visionary suddenly enters it. The two descriptions come to the same thing. For its “where”—its ubi—in relation to our “where,” our place and position (situs) in this world, is an ubique: an “everywhere.”

Another kind of story shows us this, and we shall recount one particularly revealing example. The event was brief and astonishing; so is the account of it. It certainly predates the two preceding narratives, since it is recorded in a book by the great Shiite theologian Ibn Bâbûyeh of Qom (died 381/992, no more than about forty years after the beginning of the Greater Occultation). These dates, of course, refer to the stories themselves.

Events occurring in the “eighth clime” have a time of their own, which cannot be measured in the units of our chronology. What enters our chronological time is the chrysalis—in this case, the stories themselves. From this standpoint, we may say that the account which follows must be roughly contemporary with the account of the apparition at Jam-Karân.

The hero of this fourth story belonged to a Persianized branch of the Arab tribe of the Banî Râshid, which had been settled in Hamadan since the coming of Islam. The entire group was Shiite. This was precisely what had caught the narrator’s attention, prompting him to ask one of their shaykhs, a learned man of sound judgment, how it had come about361. The explanation was as follows. Their devotion to Shiism went back to their ancestor. This man had made the pilgrimage to Mecca.

On his return journey, when the caravan was only two stages from Mecca—and thus still a considerable distance from Hamadan—it was preparing to camp for the night. He decided to walk for a while in the surrounding countryside. He wandered so far that, overcome with weariness, he sat down and fell asleep. He did not wake until the next morning, when the heat of the sun roused him. He tried to catch up with the caravan, but it had already broken camp. He was utterly alone, lost in the desert.

“I was seized with great fear,” he relates, “for I could make out neither a path nor a track. So I entrusted myself to God and said to myself, ‘Let us walk wherever He leads me.’ I had not gone far when, suddenly, I found myself before a land of enchanting greenery. It looked as if rain had just fallen, and a breeze from paradise was blowing there. Amid all this green I saw a castle. ‘I should very much like to know,’ I thought, ‘what castle this is, for I have never seen it before, nor have I ever heard anyone speak of it!’

“So I went closer. When I reached the entrance, I saw two boys dressed in white. I greeted them. They returned my greeting graciously and said, ‘Sit down! God watches over you and wishes you well.’ Then one of them stood up and went inside the house. A little later he came back and said to me, ‘Get up! Come inside.’ I entered a dwelling of such beauty and splendor that I had never seen anything to compare with it.

“We reached a pavilion before which a curtain was hanging. The young attendant lifted the curtain and said, ‘Enter.’ I went into the pavilion. In the center stood a throne on which sat a young man, handsome of face, with beautiful hair and garments, and a delightful fragrance about him. The light of his face filled the dwelling as the rising full moon lights up the night. A sword hung above him. I greeted him, and he returned my greeting with the greatest grace and warmth.

“‘Do you know who I am?’ he asked.

“‘No, God is my witness! I do not know.’

“‘I am the Riser (Qâ’im) from the Family of the Prophet. I am the one who, at the end of this age, will come forth with this sword’—and he pointed to it with his hand—‘to fill the earth with peace and justice, just as it will have been filled until then with violence and tyranny.’” (Here we recognize the theme of the mystical Sword, forged of no earthly metal.)

“When I heard these words spoken by such lips, I fell prostrate on the ground. But he said to me, ‘No, rise.’ Then he asked, ‘Are you so-and-so, from the mountain city called Hamadan?’” (Ancient Ecbatana, the city of Tobias and the Angel.)

“‘You speak the truth, my lord.’

“‘Would you like to return home and see your family again?’

“‘Yes, my lord.’

“Then he signaled to one of the young attendants, who handed me a purse. Taking me by the hand, the attendant walked beside me. We left the castle, and he continued to accompany me. Suddenly I caught sight of a mosque’s minaret, shady trees, groves, and houses. Smiling, the attendant asked, ‘Do you know this place?’

“‘Near my home in Hamadan,’ I said, ‘there is a place called Asadâbâd, and it looks exactly like this.’

“The attendant replied, ‘But that is precisely where you are: Asadâbâd. Go straight ahead now.’

“Astonished, I turned around. The attendant had disappeared. I was alone, and yet I still held the purse he had given me. I entered Asadâbâd. Soon I was in Hamadan, where I gathered my whole family together to tell them of the grace God had bestowed upon me.”

Through these stories—and we could multiply the examples—we enter a world, or see a world manifest itself, that lies beyond the empirical reach of our senses and rational sciences. Were this not so, anyone could find the way into it and establish its existence by ordinary means.

But we cannot even retrace the roads taken by the witnesses—and with good reason. Here the philosopher’s inquiry gathers around themes already brought to light: Nâ-kojâ-Âbâd; the imaginative faculty fully exercising the power of knowledge that properly belongs to it; and “the soul as the spiritual place of the body.”

The testimony of eyewitnesses brings us face to face with a spiritual world—but a spiritual world that is concrete, richer in forms than our own, and whose forms are not subject to decay. (The marvelous cities of the five islands belong to the world of Jâbarsâ, the mundus imaginalis.) The question is ubi: where? Our philosophers’ understanding of how the spiritual world at the level of the Soul—that is, the Malakût, the realm of the soul—relates to the physical world accessible to our senses has already led us to a double answer: everywhere (ubique) and nowhere at once.

This means that the Malakût can break into our sensory world at any point, and that we can enter it from any point, without the Malakût being located anywhere within that sensory world. Such a breakthrough, such an entry, requires the activity of a faculty that is neither sense perception nor abstract reasoning. What this subtle faculty perceives is neither fantasy nor the merely imaginary. The real events it allows us to experience belong neither to myth nor to history.

We referred explicitly earlier to the Persian expression Nâ-kojâ-âbâd, coined by Suhrawardi, because when the Shaykh al-Ishrâq—the master of Illuminationist philosophy—uses this expression, he presupposes the entire understanding of being that gives it meaning362. We have had several occasions to point this out in the course of this book. To come from Nâ-kojâ-âbâd is to come from beyond the cosmic mountain of Qâf. It is from there that the mysterious initiator, the angel who acts as a personal guide, declares himself to have come at the beginning of the initiatory tales of Avicenna and Suhrawardi. We know that in two of Suhrawardi’s tales the angel explicitly answers the person questioning him: “I come from Nâ-kojâ-âbâd363.”

And the reader will have encountered here, in Book II, in the Tale of the Crimson Archangel, what the Archangel suggests to his disciple about the meaning of “crossing the mountain of Qâf” and the path one must take to emerge beyond it. That tale also suggested that anyone who, like the mysterious prophet Khezr, had bathed in the Source of Life could make the crossing without difficulty. And now, in fact, we have met the prophet Khezr twice more: beside the Twelfth Imam in the story of the shaykh of Jam-Karân, and near the small temple on the Green Island where one can communicate with the Imam.

Suhrawardi formed the strange expression Nâ-kojâ-âbâd—which is not found in Persian dictionaries—out of the resources of Persian alone, without borrowing from Arabic. Literally it means the city or country (âbâd) of “no-where” (nâ-kojâ). At first sight, as we have already observed, it seems an exact equivalent of the Greek ou-topia, a word likewise absent from Greek dictionaries, coined by Thomas More as an abstract name for the absence of any location, any situs, within a space our senses can explore and verify. Etymologically, literally, it might therefore be correct to translate Nâ-kojâ-âbâd as outopia.

But in terms of the idea, the intention, and the meaning of the experience itself, that would be a serious misunderstanding. It would repeat the confusion we have already exposed between what is commonly called the imaginary, the unreal, and what our authors have obliged us to distinguish by the technical term imaginal364. Such confusion assumes that the imaginative faculty itself has been diminished, along with its object and its power to know. If imagination is identified with mere “fantasy,” then the world it gives form to must inevitably be a utopia, and anyone who trusts this faculty must be a utopian dreamer.

Once the imaginative faculty is no longer governed by a cognitive power precisely situated between two others, that person becomes, potentially, someone who has lost his bearings: paranoid, hallucinating, schizophrenic, and so on. To understand the meaning and reality of Nâ-kojâ-âbâd as something other than a utopia (outopia), we must also recognize that the imaginative faculty—or imaginative consciousness—is something other than a means of producing the imaginary and the unreal.

But this recognition in turn requires a metaphysics of being that makes room for an intermediate level of existence between the world of pure intellect and the world of the senses. By that very fact (eo ipso), such a metaphysics defines the orientation and function of the faculty of knowledge whose proper object is this intermediate world. That level of existence is the Malakût, a world at once spiritual and concrete. We have already seen throughout the investigations presented here how important it is.

It follows that Nâ-kojâ-âbâd cannot mean something without spatial extent, reduced to a point. The word âbâd means a city, a cultivated and inhabited country—something that occupies an expanse.

We must therefore begin by overcoming the old division between what is spiritual and what has extension. What concerns us here is the realm that Islamic theosophical tradition describes as lying “beyond the mountain of Qâf”: the mystical cities of Jâbalqâ, Jâbarsâ, and Hûrqalyâ, which in turn include many others (among them the Green Island and the islands of the five cities). When our authors tell us that the region of these cities begins “at the convex surface of the Sphere of Spheres,” they are offering the clearest possible image of what this means.

Nâ-kojâ-âbâd begins at the point where one “leaves” the Sphere that defines every possible direction in our world, the Sphere upon which the celestial points of the compass are, in principle, inscribed. Once we have crossed that boundary, the question where? (ubi? kojâ?) plainly loses its meaning—or at least the meaning it has within the space of ordinary experience. This is Nâ-kojâ-âbâd: a “place that is not contained within a place,” a place not enclosed by any geographical setting in which the question “where?” could be answered.

But what, precisely, does it mean to leave this “where” behind?

It cannot mean moving bodily from one location to another, as a physical body moves between places within the same continuous space. Suhrawardi suggests something quite different with his image of a drop of balm passing through to the back of a hand held up toward the sun.

What is involved is a movement inward: entering within, passing through the interior, and in doing so finding oneself outside. The essential relation is between what is outer, visible, and exoteric (ta exô, zâhir) and what is inner, invisible, and esoteric (ta éxô, bâtin). To leave the “where,” the category of ubi, is to pass beyond the outward appearances that enclose hidden inner realities like a shell around a kernel. For the Stranger, the gnostic, it is to come home.

Yet there is something strange about this passage. Once it has taken place, the hidden reality is now what surrounds, embraces, and contains what had previously appeared outer and visible. By turning inward, one has emerged beyond that external reality. It is now immaterial reality that surrounds and contains what we call material reality. Spiritual reality, then, is not located in a “where”; rather, the “where” is within it.

Indeed, spiritual reality is itself the where of everything else. It is therefore not itself situated in a place, and the question where?—the category of ubi—does not apply to it. Its place, its âbâd, is nâ-kojâ, “nowhere,” because its ubi is an ubique: a “where” that is everywhere. Once we grasp this, we have surely grasped what is essential for following the geography of visionary experience and understanding its sense—both its meaning and its direction.

We can also begin to distinguish something crucial: the visionary perceptions of spiritual figures such as Suhrawardi and the traveler to the Green Island from what our modern vocabulary dismisses as inventions, imaginings, or even utopian delusions.

The very idea of an imagination that has “lost its bearings” presupposes a view of the human being that can no longer identify or safeguard the imagination’s proper axis. It is our understanding of the human being that has first lost its mind.

We would do well to reflect on the convergence between the teachings of the masters who shaped the intellectual life of the Islamic East—Avicenna, Suhrawardi, Ibn 'Arabi, Nasir al-Din Tusi, Mulla Sadra Shirazi, and others—and those Western masters whose testimony remains priceless, both for the present and for the future, because it bears witness to precisely what is absent from so-called modern Western thought, at least in its official forms.

In short, can there be a phenomenology of visionary experience—of ek-stasis, a standing outside the space of this world—that does not also account for the experience of coming into this world? Must we not understand departure from this world and arrival in it as two opposite aspects of one and the same phenomenon?

We find a remarkable beginning of such an account in the work of Nasir al-Din Tusi, the great Shiite thinker profoundly marked by Ismaili esotericism. To come into this world is to “leave paradise.”

But that departure is not a movement from one place to another; it is a change of state. As Tusi explains it, we pass from True Reality (haqîqat) and true meaning (bâtin: the inward, esoteric meaning) into what ordinary consciousness undoubtedly takes to be the only reality, but which, in relation to True Reality, is merely metaphor (majâz). In this way, realities in the truest sense have come to seem doubtful and improbable, suspect and ambiguous.

Conversely, leaving this world and reaching its true meaning does not refer to the biological event of death (which even today specialists cannot agree how to define). The true meaning of life and death is the spiritual meaning of each. The question of survival after death is not an extension of a problem in physics. It arises on the level of a spiritual world whose concrete reality Western philosophy may have lost sight of centuries ago, preferring instead the world of logical concepts. This is why the usual expression that the dead “have departed” is misleading.

Many of those so described were already spiritually dead and have never left this world, because dead souls cannot leave it. To leave this world, then, is to have been reborn with Khidr in the Spring of Life; it is to have become a stranger to the world of ghorbat, of exile—that metaphorical world with which ordinary consciousness is satisfied.

In short, one must first be alive, raised to spiritual life, before one can experience death as an exitus, a departure. For death as exitus means precisely this: the soul leaves this world alive. Ecstasy and visionary experiences are anticipations of that departure. To pass beyond the limits of the cosmos, beyond the highest Sphere, is not to accomplish some feat of space travel, like the cosmonauts of our time. It is above all to pass from spiritual infancy into maturity, to pierce the darkness and attain a true consciousness of True Reality.365

A whole body of related testimony could be assembled from the masters of spiritual Protestantism: Valentin Weigel, Jacob Böhme, Gottfried Arnold, and others. In a remarkable passage from 1588, Weigel explains what sacred history—or hierohistory—means when it says that Lucifer left heaven or Adam left paradise. Such an event does not mean being transferred from one location to another.

“Adam, driven out of paradise, remained in the very place where he had been before; for this great universe was his paradise, speaking in the outward sense, just as his inward and heavenly paradise was the Imago Dei, the image of God within him.”366 We should therefore say: “Hell and paradise are not places. Each person carries paradise and hell within himself. Whoever does not know himself does not know his homeland, which is paradise, the kingdom of God [...]. Our material body is not our true dwelling, since death has the power to drive us out of it.”

But “God in us and we in God: whoever lives in this way truly lives at home, in his homeland, and no one can drive him from it.”367

Not even death can drive the gnostic from home, because “in that world” (in jener Welt; Plotinus would have said “there”), there is no natural body made of the elements, occupying a place and looking around itself with bodily eyes. Instead there is “a supernatural heavenly body, a spiritual body,”368 formed by the Holy Spirit and needing no external place. These declarations are in complete harmony with what our philosophers and spiritual masters have taught us about self-knowledge, the resurrection body, and what it means to “see the Imam in Hûrqalyâ.”

Nâ-kojâ-âbâd is the kingdom of subtle bodies, of “spiritual bodies,” the threshold of the Malakût, the world of the Soul. It begins “at the convex surface of the Sphere of Spheres” because that is the boundary at which the relation expressed by the words in or within is reversed. Spiritual bodies are not in a world—not even their own world—as a material body occupies its place or is contained in another body.

The text of Plotinus that all our thinkers, from Avicenna to Qazi Sa'id Qummi, read and annotated under the title The Theology of Aristotle explains that every spiritual entity is “within the whole Sphere of its heaven.” Each certainly exists independently of the others, yet all exist together, and each is within every other. It would be quite wrong to picture this other world as a featureless, undifferentiated heaven. There is multiplicity, but the relations of spiritual space differ from those of the space beneath the starry heavens as profoundly as being inside a body differs from being “within the whole of one's heaven.”

Thus we can say, with the Theology, that “behind this world there is a Heaven, an Earth, a sea, animals, plants, and heavenly human beings; but every being there is heavenly. The spiritual entities there correspond to the human beings there, yet nothing there is earthly.”369 All this seems applicable to the marvels and strange phenomena of the Green Island, the islands of the five cities, and the rest.

What is opening here to every visionary experience is, in effect, a quarta dimensio, a fourth dimension. Following our pilgrims, we find ourselves in a world familiar to any reader of the great Swedish visionary and theosopher Emanuel Swedenborg. Like our Shiite theosophers, Swedenborg had probably read the Plotinian work called The Theology of Aristotle; but he speaks above all from his own experience, from things “seen and heard by himself.”

Several of his pages on the nature of spiritual space deserve to be recalled here, so perfectly do they express the essential point. He explains that “although everything in Heaven appears exactly as it does in the world, in a place and in a space, nevertheless the Angels have no notion or idea of place and space.”

For “all movements in the spiritual world are brought about by changes of inward state, so that movements are nothing other than changes of state ... Those who are in a similar state are near one another, and those who are in a dissimilar state are far apart ... Spaces in Heaven are only outward states corresponding to inward states. It is for this reason alone that the Heavens are distinct from one another ... When someone moves from one place to another ... he arrives sooner when he wishes to, and later when he does not; the road itself lengthens or shortens according to his desire ... I have often seen this and have been amazed by it.

“From this it is again clear that distance, and consequently space, depend entirely on the Angels' inward states. And because this is so, the notion or idea of space cannot enter their thought, although spaces exist among them just as they do in the world.”370

We could hardly ask for a more exact description of Nâ-kojâ-âbâd, the “eighth clime” and its mysterious cities. We are all the more justified in seeing it this way because we find a precise counterpart in Mulla Sadra Shirazi.371 The testimony of these two masters leads, in brief, to this conclusion: there is a spiritual place and there is a bodily place, but unlike the latter, the former cannot be identified by answering the question ubi?, “where?”

For anyone who reaches Nâ-kojâ-âbâd, everything is reversed in relation to ordinary perception and consciousness. It is the where, the place, that dwells within the soul; extended bodily substance dwells within spiritual substance, just as the body dwells within the soul and the soul surrounds and sustains the body. A whole metaphysical tradition could be called upon in support of this.

Let us quote these lines from Solomon ibn Gabirol, which sum up the matter particularly well: “The way universal bodily substance resides within universal spiritual substance should be compared to the way the body resides within the soul. Just as the soul surrounds and sustains the body, so universal spiritual substance surrounds and sustains the universal body of the world. And just as the soul is in itself separate from the body of the world, yet attached to it without touching it, so spiritual substance is in itself separate from the body of the world, yet attached to it without touching it.

“We can form an idea of how spiritual substance is joined to bodily substance, and in general of how spiritual substances are joined to one another and exist within one another, by considering how light or fire is joined to air, color and figure to quantity, quantity to substance, and spiritual accidents to spiritual substances. For since visible things must be images of invisible things, the way the different elements of bodily substance [such as color, figure, quantity, and substance] are joined and exist within one another must be an image of how spiritual substances are joined and exist within one another.”372

This is why we cannot say where spiritual place is: it is not something situated somewhere but something that gives things their situation. The soul itself is the place. The apparent location, the landscape in which the soul moves, is then the image of an inward place. The ubi of this inward place is also an ubique: its “where” is everywhere.

We cannot enter the soul's place, with its own geography, without a break—sudden or gradual—from geographical coordinates. We saw this, for example, in the account of the journey to the Green Island. The traveler sets out; at a certain point the familiar map of the world ceases to apply.

Yet he is unaware of the precise moment when the break occurs. Only afterward does he realize what has happened, with wonder or unease. If he recognized it as it happened, perhaps he could retrace his route or show it to someone else. As things stand, he can describe where he was, but he cannot tell anyone else where the road runs.

Here we come to something essential: the connection, which we noted again above, between Nâ-kojâ-âbâd as a “place” of the soul and the special role of the imaginative faculty. The organ by which the soul makes its migration, returns ab extra ad intra—from outside to inside—and undergoes this reversal of its sense of place is neither the senses nor pure intellect. It is an intermediate power: active, image-forming Imagination. We have already seen how important it is that Mulla Sadra Shirazi regards Imagination as a purely spiritual faculty, independent of the physical organism and therefore independent of that organism's death: something like the soul's “subtle body.”

We can now better appreciate the consequences of this position. Mulla Sadra's theory of knowledge affirms a union between the perceiving subject and the form perceived, which means that the perceived form becomes inwardly present to the perceiver. This principle holds at all three levels of perception: sensory, imaginative, and intellectual.

Imaginative perception and imaginative consciousness therefore possess their own genuine power of knowledge, directed toward the world that belongs to them: the 'âlam al-mithâl, the mundus imaginalis, or imaginal world. This is the world of mystical cities such as Hûrqalyâ, where time can be reversed and space takes its shape from desire, because space is nothing but the outward aspect of an inward state. It is not yet the world of the pure cherubic Intelligences (Jabarût), nor the world of Platonic Ideas. It is the Malakût, the world of the Soul.

Imagination is thus firmly aligned between two other powers of knowing. Its own world stands in symbolic relation to the worlds belonging to those other powers. This relation provides a kind of safeguard against Imagination running wild, allowing it to perform its rightful function: bringing about the events narrated in visionary accounts such as Suhrawardi's.

Every approach to Nâ-kojâ-âbâd takes place through the imaginative faculty, through a concrete “realism” peculiar to imaginative consciousness. This helps explain the extraordinary seriousness of the Persian mystical epic, from Attar to Jami and Nur Ali Shah, which continually unfolds the same archetypes in new symbols. For Imagination to lose its axis, to run unchecked and cease performing its task of producing symbols that lead toward inward meaning, its proper world—the mundus imaginalis, the domain of the Malakût—must first have disappeared.

In the West, should we date that disappearance to the moment when Averroism rejected Avicenna's cosmology, with its intermediate angelic hierarchy of Animae caelestes, the heavenly Souls? These Souls, or Angeli caelestes, distinct from the Angels of pure intellect, had the faculty of Imagination in its pure state. When their universe disappeared, Imagination itself lost its bearings.

Hence the later warning of Paracelsus against confusing the Imaginatio vera, true Imagination, with fantasy, that “cornerstone of fools.”373

Why do Western languages in general, and French in particular, lack an ordinary, satisfactory word for translating 'âlam al-mithâl? We have explained why we use the Latin equivalent mundus imaginalis, and the word imaginal formed from Latin. We need to avoid confusing what people ordinarily call the imaginary with what our philosophers recognize as the fully real object of imaginative perception and consciousness.

To oppose the real to the imaginary, treating the latter as unreal or utopian, reveals the same poverty of understanding as confusing symbol with allegory, or interpreting the spiritual meaning of a text as though it were merely an allegorical interpretation. Suhrawardi's narratives and the journeys to the “country of the Hidden Imam” are not imaginary, unreal, or allegorical. The reason is precisely that Nâ-kojâ-âbâd, the “land of no-where,” is not what we commonly mean by utopia.

We must then ask what we mean by reality if, as soon as we leave it, we can do no more than invent utopias. And what do the traditional thinkers of the East mean by reality, if they can reach Nâ-kojâ-âbâd, leaving the world of sensory places without leaving the real—and indeed entering into reality more fully? Their view presupposes a scale of being with many more levels than our own. One thing is striking today.

We admit that our predecessors understood Imagination in too rationalistic and intellectualistic a way, yet we are also, and rightly, alarmed by certain recent unions of imagination and desire. We speak of the need for a new discipline of imagination, but we struggle to find one, because we still regard imagining merely as a way of stepping back from what we call reality in order to act upon it. We fail to see that if we can speak of imagination only as the “madwoman in the house,” it is because we have forgotten the norms, rules, discipline, and orientation that once secured the image-making faculty's power of knowledge.

And so the word daydream always comes forward as an excuse: literary daydreaming, or, preferably nowadays, social daydreaming. A mapping of the themes of imagination by cultural region—a “topography of imagination,” to borrow Massignon's expression—would help us avoid confusing themes that merely happen to share a name, while allowing us to connect themes that genuinely spring from the same root across different cultures.

But we cannot escape the question of whether the mundus imaginalis had to be lost, leaving only the Imaginary behind, before the fantastic, the horrific, the obscene, the monstrous, the macabre, and the absurd could come to dominate.

By contrast, the art and imaginative creations of traditional Islamic culture are marked by solemn sacred forms, seriousness, stylization, and meaning. Why?

Without pursuing this troubling inquiry further, we can say that neither our utopias nor our science fiction nor the sinister “Omega Point” succeeds in leaving this world or reaching Nâ-kojâ-âbâd. Those who have known Nâ-kojâ-âbâd—the pilgrim of the Green Island, the visionary who built Jamkaran—did not manufacture utopias.

Nor is the final hope of Shiism a social or political daydream: it is an eschatology, an expectation of the ultimate fulfillment, precisely because the act of waiting is already a real Presence in another world, and bears witness to that other world. Conversely, perhaps it is only when the meaning of Nâ-kojâ-âbâd has been lost that utopias, in the ordinary sense, can begin to proliferate. This is why, despite the apparent similarity of the words, we cannot simply translate Nâ-kojâ-âbâd as outopia.

Certain appearances of the Hidden Imam during the “Great Occultation” have thus led us to outline the beginnings of a phenomenology of visionary consciousness. We have done so deliberately, to guard against judgments made too hastily under the influence of an agnostic psychoanalysis or psychopathology.

The world entered by those to whom the Hidden Imam appeared is a perfectly real world—more evident, indeed, more coherent and stable in its own order than the empirical world perceived by the senses. These witnesses afterward knew perfectly well that they had been “elsewhere”; they were not schizophrenics. It is a world hidden within the very act of sensory perception, a world we must recover beneath the apparent objective certainty of that perception.

We cannot therefore call it “imaginary” in the ordinary sense of unreal or nonexistent. To confuse the imaginary with the imaginal is to make ourselves incapable of understanding figures and events that belong neither to myth nor to history. And that failure of understanding is perhaps the gravest sign that a whole continent has been lost.

This “lost continent” really is a place, a topos—an âbâd in Persian—but a place “outside place,” whose geography no longer obeys the laws of the empirical world's geography: the Green Island, the archipelago of five cities, the castle standing in the desert. One finds one's bearings there as though moving through absolute space, and beings invisible to our world can be seen. For one enters it through an ek-stasis, a “displacement” that is a change of state.

Here I think of a magnificent passage by Villiers de l'Isle-Adam, who sometimes saw so far. He writes that Angels “manifest themselves outwardly only within the ecstasy they bring about, an ecstasy that forms part of their own being.” These are words of extraordinary clarity, capable of cutting into the very granite of doubt: “That forms part of their own being.” They also express the secret of the Hidden Imam's being and of his Appearances: the Imam is this ek-stasis itself.

Villiers goes on: “Just as the deep solitudes of the night and its starry worlds appear, in their illusion, reflected in a bronze mirror lying on the ground, so the Angels, through the translucent veils of vision, can leave their impression upon the eyes of the destined, the saints, the magi.” He is thinking of one who, like Solomon at the summit of his being, “is no longer in the universe except as daylight is in a building.”374 We read earlier in Solomon ibn Gabirol: “As light or fire is joined to air.”

Perhaps there is no better image for grasping in a flash what Nâ-kojâ-âbâd is: “As daylight is in a building.” For the daylight filling a building, illuminating it and thereby making it appear as a building, is also the daylight surrounding and containing it. Who, then, could say where Day is, or draw the limits of its presence? When day breaks, it fills both the space and the time of that day. So it is with the “Day of the Imam.” This is why, every time, the Day of the Imam is the Last Day.

Chapter III Spiritual Chivalry

1. From the Knights of St. John's “Green Island” to an Unfinished Poem by Goethe

The theme of “spiritual chivalry” in some measure gathers together the themes developed throughout this inquiry. At the same time, the texts that give expression to it on either side may point the way toward future research: research seeking to bring to light the idea of a spiritual fellowship shared by the three branches of the Abrahamic tradition, whose ethics spring from the same sources and aspire to the same spiritual horizon.

Iran's spiritual vocation is to forge a link between the Abrahamic tradition it made its own through Islam and the Zoroastrian tradition inherited from its origins. We have seen the idea of spiritual chivalry arise within Zoroastrian ethics, inspired by the struggle of the Fravartis. These heavenly beings chose to descend into this world to defend Ohrmazd's creation, just as they had guarded the high ramparts of the world of Light against the forces of Ahriman. This is the primordial struggle told in the Bundahishn, the Mazdean book of Genesis.

With Suhrawardi, who revived the theosophy of ancient Persia within Iranian Islam, we watched the heroic epic of Iran's ancient chivalry become the mystical epic of the pilgrims of God in Iranian Sufism. The continuity can be traced through the very terminology, even in the expression “Espahbod Light”: an ancient Iranian term belonging to the language of command and knighthood, which Suhrawardi uses for those Lights entrusted with governing a body.

We have seen how Suhrawardi's work, bringing the Hellenized Magi home to an Iran that had become Islamic, thereby incorporated the Iranian epic into the Abrahamic tradition. Its echo can still be heard in the works of the Zoroastrian ishrâqî thinkers, the philosophers of illumination, whom we have studied here.

Eugenio d'Ors showed a remarkably sound intuition when, commenting on the Avestan idea of the Angel and the Fravarti—the heavenly archetype of every creature of light—he wrote: “The religion of Zoroaster takes the form of a kind of order of chivalry.”375 In Suhrawardi's epic of the gnostic hero—the exile seeking the Grail of Jamshid and Kay Khosrow, the knight of faith fighting for beings to return to their true being, which is itself the Grail—we have heard deep echoes of the Western mystical epic, the Holy Grail and its knights.

And just as the idea of a mystical hierarchy within the “Order” of the Ishrâqîyûn, the philosophers of illumination, brought us back to the esoteric hierarchy recognized by Shiism, that Shiite hierarchy has repeatedly disclosed echoes of both the chivalric ethic of ancient Iran and the chivalry of the West. A covenant of fidelity is concluded before earthly existence between the Imam and his followers. It forms part of the threefold testimony given in answer to the question A-lasto?—the testimony to divine Oneness, to the Prophet's mission, and to the walâyat, the spiritual authority and bond of devotion, of the Twelve Imams.

What the Fravartis are to Ohrmazd, the Shiites are to the Imam. A common spiritual ethos, a common situation, unites those who await the Zoroastrian Saoshyant, those who await the Imam's return in glory, and those who await the reign of the Paraclete. One of the most revealing findings of our inquiry has been that Shiite theosophers identified the Twelfth Imam with both the Zoroastrian Saoshyant and the Paraclete promised in the Gospel of John.

There is, first, the theme of the Imam as the world's mystical pole. His sacred, cosmic, and metaphysical function remains what it is even if human beings fail to recognize him and do not know that, without this pole and those gathered around him—the “eyes through which God still looks upon the world”—earthly humanity could not continue to exist.

From this follow the cycle of the Imamate, the Imam's companions, their hidden spiritual hierarchy and the anonymity imposed by the Imam's occultation, the expectation of the last things experienced as the nearness of the supersensible world, and the figure of the inner Guide. All these themes form a constellation around the Twelfth Imam.

We can trace their reappearance in the spiritual chivalry of both Islam and Christendom without having to claim a direct historical line of descent. To investigate historical transmission, we could certainly turn to the documented friendship between a Syrian emir such as Usama ibn Munqidh and the Knights Templar, to possible contacts between Druze and Templars, or to the knighthood reportedly conferred upon Saladin and several others.

But this would only revisit familiar ground. A different task awaits us: to extend the phenomenological approach we have attempted here around the Twelfth Imam. For the history of a spiritual tradition is nothing other than that tradition itself; its life continues in every effort to uncover affinities capable of flowering.

Thus, when we say “from the Knights of St. John's Green Island to an unfinished poem by Goethe,” we are not implying an outward, material continuity of motif or institution from the fourteenth to the early nineteenth century. We are speaking of a correspondence across time within a field of consciousness, whose lines of force reveal the same metaphysical realities at work.

The name “Green Island,” belonging to the Knights of St. John in Strasbourg, immediately recalls the Green Island described above as the dwelling of the Hidden Imam and his companions. Geographically the shared name is certainly a coincidence.

Yet a similar secret connects the two islands. We might also recall the theme that develops around the Holy Grail and Joseph of Arimathea: a sovereign from beyond the seas, surrounded on his island by companions over whom time has no power, a “theme in which memories of the Celtic Otherworld mingle with the evocation of the earthly Paradise.”376 There are many other “Green Islands.”

Nevertheless, unexpected resonances can be felt between the Green Island of Strasbourg's Hospitallers and the Green Island of Shiite tradition. The Strasbourg island was a spiritual center of the Knights of St. John. There, in the fourteenth century, a form of spirituality developed around figures whose very name expressed its character: the “Friends of God” (Gottesfreunde). This is the exact equivalent of the Shiite designation Awliyâ' Allah, the Friends of God.

We have learned that walâyat entails a devotion of spiritual love that initiates the believer into self-knowledge. How, then, can we avoid the question raised by the name the two traditions share? Might there not be something in common between the “Friends of God” in Shiite Islam and the “Friends of God” in Western Christendom? Might they not be undertaking a quest that demands the overcoming of similar difficulties and fidelity to similar commitments?

In both traditions these figures remain unknown to the general run of humanity, yet of both we may say that they are the “eyes through which God still looks upon the world.” In both, life is governed by the invisible presence of a personal inner Guide.

The mysterious figure who was the spiritual pole of the Friends of God at the Hospitallers' Green Island, known only as the “Friend of God from the Upper Country” (der Gottesfreund vom Oberland), passes into concealment just like the Twelfth Imam. His companions search for him in this world in vain, just as the knights of Kay Khosrow had searched in vain for their king.

Some years ago in Tehran, during a celebration of the birthday of the First Imam, I was invited to tell the story of the Friend of God from the Oberland before a fairly large audience, all of whose members belonged to Sufi circles. Afterward, I had the impression that some of my listeners understood the story as an appearance of the Hidden Imam in the West, in the fourteenth century!377

The correspondence across time that concerns us—a correspondence that only a phenomenology of spiritual forms can examine—is this: the veil falls upon the final assembly of the Friend of God from the Upper Country and his twelve companions, only to rise again upon another assembly in which the pleroma—the complete circle—of the Twelve once more comes together and is revealed. This second assembly is the gathering of twelve knights described in Goethe's unfinished poem Die Geheimnisse (The Secrets, or The Mysteries). Goethe's understanding of this pleroma of twelve knights corresponds strikingly to the place held by the pleroma of the Twelve Imams in the religious history of humanity.

Between these two assemblies—the twelve gathered around the Friend of God in the Oberland, and the twelve knights gathered by Goethe on the summit of an idealized Montserrat—we can observe the spiritual forces that give rise, within Shiism, to the idea of a chivalry shared by the whole Abrahamic tradition. The same forces give rise, in Wolfram von Eschenbach's work, to the idea of a fellowship uniting the knights of Christendom with those of the East—that is, of Islam.

These broad outlines call for a few details to make clearer how the themes connect.

First come the relations between the Friend of God from the Oberland and the Knights of St. John on the Green Island. They mark a crucial moment in a still little-known current that we may call the esoteric spirituality of the Hospitaller knights, the Sovereign Order of St. John of Jerusalem. It is also crucial because a whole tradition—whose historical reliability we need not assess here—attributes Johann Tauler's transformation into one of the greatest masters of mystical preaching to a secret intervention by the Friend of God.

The change led Tauler toward the inner meaning of Scripture, just as the Friend of God would awaken his correspondents on the Green Island to the meaning of their own inner Guide. The word esoteric is especially fitting because its essential meaning is inwardness. It also reminds us of the testimony of the alchemist Bernard of Treviso. Working on Rhodes in the fifteenth century, he attested that he had rediscovered among the Hospitaller knights of St. John what is customarily called the secret tradition of the Knights Templar. In this connection we may also recall the expression “Lodges of St. John.”378

Tauler's initiation into Gottesfreundschaft, friendship with God, through the Friend of God; the Templar inheritance among the Hospitallers and among the “Templars” of Wolfram von Eschenbach: together these images help define the “spiritual chivalry” in which the Friend of God from the Upper Country and the Hospitallers of the Green Island take part.

The Friend of God and his companions bear enough resemblance to the Hidden Imam and the members of the hidden spiritual hierarchy as they appear in Shiite theosophy that we need not resort to explanatory hypotheses whose first failing is to rule out from the outset what is actually at stake: the reality of the spiritual event as such, a reality belonging neither to myth nor to history in the ordinary sense.

The figure of the Friend of God from the Oberland has remained so mysterious, so impossible to verify historically, that commentators have tried to explain him as a literary hoax or a split personality, thus explaining him away. It is enough to recall the mode of “presence” that the Hidden Imam possesses for Shiite theosophers—and, more specifically, the real presence of the invisible personal Guide (ostâd ghaybî, shaykh al-ghayb) for so many Shiites and Sufis—to understand, whatever the historical questions, Rulman Merswin's conduct and his relationship with the Friend of God.

The Friend of God from the Oberland was a Western contemporary of Haydar Amoli. His sacred biography belongs to the events of our fourteenth century, which began with the violent destruction of the Order of the Temple, went on to witness the terrible ravages of the Black Death, and also saw many spiritual renewals.

Everything we know about the Friend of God comes from the letters and short works he sent to his spiritual companion Rulman Merswin, who lived on the Green Island in Strasbourg, and to a few other people through Merswin's mediation. After Rulman's death, these documents were carefully preserved by the Hospitallers of the Green Island. Taken together, they indicate that the Friend of God's first intervention was the one mentioned above, with the great preacher Johann Tauler in 1346.379 We should note first that the Friend of God was a layman, neither a cleric nor a monk.

Moreover, whenever he appeared to someone in need of spiritual help, it was either in answer to that person's inward call or because his own spiritual sight had revealed to him that a suffering brother needed his aid. These traits recall the hidden guide and master, the ostâd ghaybî, of whom the Sufis of Najm al-Din Kubra's school speak.

The Friend of God spends several months with Tauler, the famous “master of Scripture,” and reveals to him that his sermons still speak only of the outer side of things, failing to express what matters most. They do not kindle the soul's burning fire. They do little more than impose a yoke from outside. The mere letter of Scripture still leaves Tauler spiritually dead. The layman tells the master that whenever his own Guide comes to him, he teaches him more in a single hour than all the learned doctors together could teach him before Judgment Day. “That same letter of Scripture could make you a living man.”

But how is he to attain this? The layman tells him the story of his life and inward trials. Everything he suggests to Tauler can be expressed immediately and precisely in the traditional language of our 'orafâ, our spiritual knowers: it is the spiritual interpretation (ta'wîl) of the inward meaning of Scripture or religious Law (bâtin al-sharî'at).

Indeed, it was this convergence of spiritual interpretation in the face of the phenomenon of the Holy Book that guided our inquiry from its very beginning. Tauler himself then endures severe inward trials in the course of a long retreat. He emerges from it as one of the greatest mystical preachers of all time, living the genuine Gottesfreundschaft, friendship with God.

Here again, a comparative study of spirituality would need to draw upon what we have learned about walâyat (Book I, Chapter VII). Tauler's collected Sermons, unfolding the inward meaning of Scripture through the readings appointed for the liturgical year, can be a Bible for anyone on the spiritual path.

But who, exactly, was this Friend of God? The only answer comes from the long letter he later addressed to the Hospitallers of the Green Island, whose house bore the name Domus Ordinis Sancti Johannis Hierosolymitani ad Viridem Insulam—House of the Order of St. John of Jerusalem at the Green Island.380 This letter is his entire spiritual autobiography. It tells of his family origins—he was the son of a wealthy merchant—and his youthful friendship with a knight's son.

The two traveled the world together, concerned with nothing but being “knights in quest of knighthood.” Then came the painful breaking-off of his engagement after an initial vision showed him that he could not pursue the quest for divine love and the quest for human love at the same time. As we saw in Book III, the mysticism of a lover faithful to love, such as Ruzbihan Baqli of Shiraz, overcomes precisely this dilemma.

The Friend of God goes on to describe his inward life and its trials, including a series of five remarkable visions. Their wealth of symbolic images calls for a spiritual interpretation that cannot even be sketched here.381 Such an interpretation would draw upon all the themes we have encountered: the mundus imaginalis, the nature and spiritual function of the imaginative faculty, the inner master—in short, the whole mystical understanding of the human being implied by these visions. The autobiography then brings us to the decisive event: his meeting with Rulman Merswin and the founding of the Green Island.

And who, in turn, was Rulman Merswin? Once again, the answer lies in an autobiography, part of the papers arranged and devoutly preserved by the Hospitallers after Rulman's death.382 Merswin was a merchant from a patrician family in Strasbourg. He tells us how, in 1347, he gave up all commercial business and withdrew from the social world in which he had lived. One autumn evening, meditating in his garden, he wondered what his true task could be amid all the troubles weighing upon the world. With all the strength of his soul, he called upon the invisible.

Suddenly a vision of clear light appeared, surrounding him and lifting him beyond himself, while certain words resounded within the light. There followed four years of severe inward trials. He spoke of none of this to anyone, nor of his ability to perceive the aura surrounding every human being, until the day when “God inspired a man from the Upper Country to come down to me.

“When he arrived, God made me understand that I could speak to him about everything. This man was wholly unknown to the world; he became my secret friend, my familiar companion.” Rulman confided in him as he would have confided in God himself. What happened was like Tauler's experience: the Friend of God came to Rulman Merswin only in answer to an inward call, and Rulman found in him someone to whom he could entrust the most intimate part of his experience.

Rulman Merswin remained in Strasbourg, while the Friend of God returned to the Upper Country. Some scholars identify this country with the Bernese Oberland; but we may fear that such a geographical identification diminishes the significance, and lowers the very “altitude,” of the “country” at issue.

The two friends began exchanging letters that offer one of the most beautiful testimonies to the spiritual bond between two people—or, more precisely, between a person and his ostâd ghaybî, his hidden master. Their inward bond was so deep that they could experience the same vision at the same time, or the same anguish and pain. Similar instances are found between Najm al-Din Kubra and his shaykh al-ghayb, his “witness in heaven.” It was this bond that gave rise to the founding of the Green Island.

The two friends then received the same vision in a dream. On the following Christmas night, overwhelmed by the misery and spiritual distress of their age, each experienced, in ecstasy, such suffering that he thought he would die.383 They met in Strasbourg. Their vision had revealed that they must establish something like a monastery, and thus the Green Island came into being.

But both men knew very well, and had already said to one another, that “the time for building new monasteries was past.” What would be the point? “If only we could find men who were truly men of the cloister, we would find monasteries enough.”

Yet that was no longer the question. What the two friends wished to establish was a “refuge,” not merely for clerics but for anyone seeking the spiritual way, free from the rules that Church custom and canon law had previously imposed. It would be a place of the Spirit, opening the way to the highest knowledge for people who wished—or needed—to remain active in the world, at a time when the accepted path had been to shut oneself inside a monastery. The idea comes close to that of a Sufi lodge, a khânqâh.

At the same time, it moves toward defining a kind of knighthood that is neither clerical nor lay, while sharing something of both, but in an entirely spiritual sense. This is the distinctive feature of the friends' project, and it best expresses what spiritual chivalry might mean once “the time of monasteries and convents has passed.” Without doubt, this is the very idea behind the orders of chivalry and the driving idea of Wolfram von Eschenbach's epic, transformed into a spiritual knighthood acting within the world while remaining unknown, as the companions of the Twelfth Imam remain unknown.

There is therefore a profound significance in the fact that, four years after its founding, the Hospitaller knights took responsibility for the house on the Green Island at the request of Rulman, who had himself been made a knight. Rulman Merswin had devoted his entire fortune to purchasing a ruined monastery built in the twelfth century by a knight, Werner von Hùneburg, outside the walls of Strasbourg, on the banks of the Ill, at the place called the “Green Island.”

In 1369 the entirely rebuilt and restored building was consecrated. Four years later, when the Hospitallers took charge of it, an agreement with the grand master of the Sovereign Order of St. John, then residing on Rhodes, stipulated that the freedoms established by the founders would be faithfully preserved. In this way, the small community of spiritual seekers gathered around Rulman Merswin joined the community of the Hospitallers, and together they formed the fellowship of spiritual knights of the Green Island.

The Order's prior “in the German lands,” Conrad von Brunsberg, even made his home there.384 Rulman continued his literary work and correspondence. One of his short writings, The Book of the Nine Rocks, is among those masterpieces of mysticism in which the mundus imaginalis becomes manifest, and which call for the kind of spiritual interpretation whose principles we discussed in connection with Suhrawardi's initiatory narratives.

The correspondence continued between the Friend of God, the “pole” of his community in the Upper Country, and Rulman Merswin, the “pole” and founder of the Hospitaller community on the Green Island. Along with the other documents, it constitutes a considerable body of material. This was the collection carefully gathered by the Hospitallers after Rulman Merswin's death in 1382, when they had lost all hope of finding the Friend of God again.385

Throughout his life, Rulman Merswin was the link between the Brothers of the Green Island and the Friend of God. Through him, they heard about this mysterious figure and corresponded with him. None of the Brothers ever saw the Friend of God. What, then, of the little community in the Oberland, the High Country? Four companions gathered around their spiritual centre, the Friend of God.

In his letters to the Johannite knights of the Green Island, he described at length the course of each companion's life, his ordeals and his inward joys. There were also Ruprecht, the messenger who carried the mysterious correspondence, and Conrad, the cook. They lived in a hermitage high in the mountains, beside a spring of running water. This sacred place of the fourteenth century remained unknown to the world. It was like the realm of the Grail, or the Green Island of the Imam.

“No one knew of it who had not approached it by the inward way. Several men are said to have visited the brothers, but unless they had attained inward maturity, none suspected the nature or meaning of their spiritual life.” This is precisely the law of esotericism, and the reason for the spiritual knight's anonymity.

The “call” does not come from outside, nor is it addressed to the crowd. It is heard by individuals alone, when it begins to resonate in the depths of their souls. Then the Friend of God becomes their guide and companion—their ostâd ghaybî, their “inward master.”386 Keeping this in mind, we can understand the accounts of two mysterious gatherings in the High Country. Those accounts fill the Friend of God's final letters, before he himself enters “occultation,” or hiddenness.

One of these letters was sent in the spring of 1379 to the commander of the Johannite knights of the Green Island. It told him that the previous winter, between 15 and 21 November 1378,387 seven Friends of God had assembled in a small chapel deep in the heart of a high, wild mountain, with the Friend of God of the High Country presiding as their eighth.

Every day, in the early afternoon, they went into the forest to a beautiful place beside a spring, well suited to conversation. On the last day, a violent wind swept through the trees, and the Friends found themselves surrounded by a terrifying, absolute Darkness. Then the darkness dissolved as a magnificent, translucent light appeared, so brilliant that bodily eyes could not bear to look upon it. Within that Light a voice was heard, sweeter than all sweetness.

The Friends were told that the dreadful storm threatening the world would be held back for another year. Then the ordinary sunlight shone again. (Darkness surrounding the Spring of Life, and precisely there the revelation of a supernatural Light from the Malakût, the spiritual world: these are themes just as familiar from the experience of the Muslim mystics known as the 'orafâ.)

The final letter, addressed to Rulman Merswin, recounts a second gathering. A year had passed since the first. On Christmas night in 1379, a voice warned the Friend of God that on the following Maundy Thursday, in 1380, twelve Friends would gather at the place in the forest where he had previously met the seven. This time he would be the thirteenth. What happened was this.

Without making any arrangements among themselves, guided solely by a summons from the spiritual world that sounded within each one's soul, the twelve initiates arrived at the appointed place and time, high on the mountain beside the little chapel. Some came from Milan, others from Genoa, others from Hungary. On Good Friday they celebrated the liturgy, then went into the forest beside the spring. Once again the powers of Darkness made themselves felt; then a pure light shone forth, and an invisible messenger dropped a letter that each man could read in his own language.

Would the Friends accept its conditions? For three years they must renounce all outward concerns, sever every attachment to the affairs of this world, and become nothing but the “captives of God.” If they did, the outbreak of the storm threatening the world would again be delayed. The Friends were ready to accept—even for the rest of their lives. On Easter Sunday they witnessed the appearance of the same Light and heard the same voice. As instructed, they lit a fire and cast the heavenly letter into it.

But the bright flame separated itself from the burning wood and vanished into space, taking the letter with it: “The fire from above seized our fire and consumed it.”388 The next day, Easter Monday, the twelve and the thirteenth went their separate ways.

We should notice the identical spiritual role played, unknown to humankind, by the twelve initiates gathered around the Friend of God of the Oberland and by the Friends of God (Awliyâ' Allâh, or in Persian Awliyâ-e Khodâ) gathered around their own spiritual centre, or “pole.”

Shiite traditions, like those of Suhrawardi's Ishrâq, repeatedly tell us that without the mystical pole who is the Imam, and without the companions who surround him—the “eyes through which God still looks upon the world”—humanity, the human world itself, could not continue to exist. This is exactly the role of the Friends of God around their pole in the High Country, as we learn from the letters sent to the commander of the Johannites of the Green Island and to Rulman Merswin.

The same spiritual chivalry is at work in both places, hidden from the world, its members “captives of God,” devoted to the sole sovereignty of the Spirit. This comparison may have consequences we cannot yet foresee.

The letter describing the gathering of the twelve was the last the Friend of God sent to his “other self,” his beloved Rulman Merswin. It was a farewell. He would write no more, and Rulman was not to write to him. They would not meet again unless the Holy Spirit brought them together. The wording recalls the last letter sent by the Twelfth Imam to 'Alî al-Samarrî. Like the Twelfth Imam, the Friend of God of the High Country now enters ghaybat: occultation, the state of hidden presence.

Two years later, in 1382, Rulman Merswin himself died. Discovering the documents he had left behind, the Johannite knights of the Green Island set off in search of the Friend of God they had heard so much about, and whose letters they had read so often. They found nothing. In their grief, all they could do was have the documents beautifully copied and arranged in the house of the Green Island.

We need not recount its later outward history here.389 Every Shiite spiritual seeker knows that “seeing the Imam in Hûrqalyâ,” or joining his companions on the Green Island, is not a matter of travelling across physical distance. In the same way, every Johannite of the Insula Viridis who understood Rulman Merswin's message must have understood how to find in the Friend of God of the High Country a guide and companion.

In the language of symbolic forms, both journeys are an ascent of Mount Qâf. On this point, Suhrawardi and Qâzî Sa'îd Qommî have already told us all that needs to be said. Those who have spoken of a literary hoax or a split personality have therefore missed the meaning of Rulman Merswin's experience altogether.

But is our own age still capable of understanding what it means for a “captive of God” to correspond with his Angel?

We should now return to the gathering of the twelve Friends of God in the High Country as an example of the fullness symbolized by the number twelve: its inherent power to signify a completed reality, to express in number a complete assembly, a pleroma.

Later we shall recall some of these symbolic properties, and the necessary role of the thirteenth, who represents the unity of the twelve as something distinct from their mere sum. (This, too, is a very ancient Iranian mode of reckoning.) As for the twelve Friends gathered in the High Country, we observe that they embody the whole of spiritual humanity. They form an invisible defence, protecting the human multitude from disaster without its knowledge. Their spiritual centre withdraws into hiddenness. These signs are so distinctive that, if this pleroma appears elsewhere, we can recognize it with certainty.

We have just seen what this assembly shares with the “Friends of God” of Shiism.

We shall return to that parallel, but first we need to identify another appearance of the same pattern in the West: Goethe's celebrated unfinished poem, Die Geheimnisse (The Mysteries, or The Secrets). For the purposes of a study of spiritual experience, we believe W. Rath is entirely right to say that “before Goethe's spiritual gaze stood an assembly parallel to the one described in the letter from the Friend of God of the Oberland to Rulman Merswin.”390 We would add that this assembly, too, may be said to meet in the heart—or at the summit—of Mount Qâf.

In the substantial surviving fragment of the poem (352 lines),391 Goethe introduces a young traveller called Brother Marcus. At the end of a long day's journey, he is walking through a high mountain valley, looking for shelter for the night. Climbing from rock to rock, he soon reaches a height overlooking the valley. “Is there anything human in these parts?” he wonders. Then, at the edge of the forest, he catches sight of a noble building glowing in the rays of the setting sun.

The door is closed. Above its arch is a mysterious emblem: a cross entwined with roses. What can it mean? There is not a word or inscription to help him decipher it. “Who has joined roses to the Cross here?” (Wer hat dem Kreuze Rosen zugesellt?) The first stars have already appeared when Brother Marcus knocks. The door is opened. He tells his hosts that he has come from distant lands at the command of higher beings, and they welcome him with open arms.

Who has sent him? We begin to sense the answer when we realize that the enclosure Brother Marcus has entered might be another Montsalvat, the realm of the Grail. Almost immediately an old knight—who might be Gurnemanz instructing Parsifal—tells him of a distressing situation. Having welcomed the traveller, the old man asks whether he brings a message of hope.

We learn, almost in the same breath, what spiritual work this brotherhood has pursued since its founding and what grief and dread now hang over it. The man who held them all together, who founded their brotherhood and was both their guide and friend, has decided to leave them soon and disappear. The name of this Chosen One, this Holy Man and Sage, reveals the tragedy's meaning. He is not Amfortas. He is HUMANUS—the Human One.

In a few striking strokes, the poet sketches the life of this exemplary hero. We might call the tale When Man Was Human. Does the threatened departure mean that humanity faces the inhuman? Or should we see in Brother Marcus's arrival, as he crosses the threshold marked with the mysterious Rose Cross, the promise of rebirth? The youth encounters the emblem again after the evening meal, when the brother-knights lead him into the lofty hall where they pursue their spiritual work.

Beneath its high ribbed vault there is nothing meant to dazzle the eye. Twelve choir stalls surround a thirteenth, arranged against the walls like the stalls of a church choir, each exquisitely carved by skilled hands. Above each hangs a shield bearing symbolic figures, and in front of each stands a reading desk. Everything speaks of meditation, inward recollection, and the studious peace of life among brothers.

Above the thirteenth stall, that of HUMANUS, standing at the highest point of the arc formed by the other twelve, the youth sees the same emblem once more: the Cross entwined with roses. The unfinished poem gives us only a fleeting glimpse of its secret. After a brief sleep, Brother Marcus has a vision in the grounds of the mysterious castle, while the morning mist still hangs about it.

A procession of youthful figures appears, crowned with flowers; in the half-light before dawn, their torches bring out the whiteness of the garments that drape them. From what festivities, from what celebrations in the night, are they returning? The torches go out like the stars, and the figures vanish into the distance.

Thirty years later, some young people asked Goethe what the poem would have become had he finished it, and what it would have revealed about the mysterious brotherhood's work. His reply explains the intention embodied in HUMANUS: the fully HUMAN Man, the centre of a constellation of distinct, representative personalities. Drawn to him by a deep affinity and by their aspirations, they can reach their fullest development only by gathering around him.

Following Brother Marcus on his journey, the reader or listener would have come to understand that each particular religion reaches its richest flowering and fulfilment by drawing nearer to this supreme Guide and mediator—even, ultimately, by becoming perfectly identified with him. The different ages would have been represented by twelve figures so distinctive that they would have made one thing clear: wherever the recognition of God and virtue appears, however surprising its form, it always deserves the fullest reverence and love.

What Goethe's spiritual vision embraced in this mystical gathering, then, was the complete course of humanity's true direction. Humanity may follow that direction unknowingly, even against its own wishes, and misunderstand it. It may also reject it, just as it may reject its invisible Guides, knowing nothing of them and perhaps no longer even suspecting the order of reality to which they belong. That is why Goethe, who had very probably conceived the poem under the influence of the Grail tradition, said in his reply that readers should orient themselves toward a kind of “ideal Montserrat.” The poem was intended to lead the human being—its hero, Humanus—to discover happiness and repose “on the summit of his own Montserrat.”392

Instead of “Mont-Serrat,” another tradition allows us to say “Mont-Salvat.” The essential meaning remains the same. The very idea of this “inner Montserrat” brings us back to the mountain of Qâf, which belongs at once to the soul and the cosmos. Brother Marcus's ascent is the same as that of Suhrawardi's mystical heroes. And there is more. According to Goethe, the twelve knights who meet in chapter beneath the emblem of the Rose Cross, and among whom Brother Marcus finds himself, each represent one of humanity's religions.

Each comes closer to perfection as it draws nearer to the figure who is their common centre, the thirteenth. Now consider what we read in Ibn Abî Jomhûr, one of the greatest Shiite theosophers, who here follows very closely the esoteric teaching of Ibn 'Arabî: “The Twelfth Imam is the pole and the Imam of this age. In him every Imam and every pole converge, from East to West, from Earth to Heaven [...].

“For the world continues to be preserved as long as this Perfect Man remains within it [...]. This shows us that in the twelve Imams, from first to last, all religions are made manifest in both their outward and their inward meaning, and with them all the perfections of the visible and invisible orders. If they were to be lacking, if they were absent, the universe would cease to exist and return to its origin. For through them everything began, and to them everything returns.”393

There is a striking correspondence, in what can be grasped of their spiritual meaning, between Goethe's vision of the twelve knights and the vision of the complete assembly, or pleroma, of the twelve Imams. In each case the central figure is also the thirteenth, because he expresses the unity and completion of the Twelve. This is true of the Friend of God of the Oberland at the final gathering of the twelve Friends, and of Humanus surrounded by the twelve knights of the Rose Cross.

The Twelfth Imam, too, is in a sense the thirteenth, because he comes after the eleven preceding Imams and the Seal of the Prophets. There is, moreover, a perfect correspondence between him and the Seal of the Prophets: he is, as it were, Muhammad returned to life. He gathers the entire pleroma into himself. He is the Seal of Muhammadan walâyat—the bond of divine friendship, Gottesfreundschaft—and the Perfect Man in whom the cycle of appearances of the Muhammadan Light (Nûr mohammadî) in this world reaches its final fulfilment. Shiite ontology certainly places the pleroma of the Imams on a higher level than the twelve at the Oberland gathering or the twelve at Montserrat.

Yet this does not weaken the correspondence between these symbolic forms. Both Western assemblies are manifestations, at the level of the mundus imaginalis, the imaginal world, of that same pleroma of the Twelve.

Let us draw together the essential features shared by these mystical assemblies.

First comes the idea of spiritual Guides who belong to a higher world, or who have been chosen and brought together through the commands or arrangements of beings from such a world. Their assembly of twelve is then an image—and indeed a complete image—of the spiritual cosmos, whose energies decisively affect humanity.

Each time, the number of those assembled suggests a correspondence with particular dimensions of the cosmos. The first gathering of seven Friends in the High Country corresponds, like the groups of seven Imams in Ismailism, to the seven planetary spheres: the seven metals, the seven colours of light, and the seven notes of the scale.

The gatherings of twelve correspond to the twelve zodiacal constellations in the heaven of the fixed stars. Shiite teachings concerning the Imams see those constellations as visible symbols of the twelve Imams' “dwelling places,” themselves represented as twelve “Veils of Light” (and twelve millennia) within which the “Muhammadan Light” resides. In a similar way, each of Goethe's twelve knights is an alchemical, or “philosophers',” dwelling place for the hero Humanus.

The twelve gather around a mysterious figure: the Friend of God, Rulman Merswin's secret companion; Humanus, in Goethe's poem; or the Twelfth Imam, in Shiite teachings about the Imams. In every case, the mysterious figure at the centre of the pleroma of Twelve has resolved to enter occultation (ghaybat). His companions must not search for him in some location within the physical world. Their search would be in vain. (We may recall the knights of Kay Khosraw here.)
