In each case, occultation—the passage into a state of “invisible presence”—is announced as the secret of a new cycle. And the idea of this new cycle is inseparable from the idea of spiritual chivalry.

Whether the new cycle can unfold depends on the fidelity of the Twelve in the High Country and the Twelve on Montserrat. This is the final message sent to the Johannites of the Green Island, and the message Brother Marcus receives on the summit of Montserrat.

The future and fate of humanity depend on their knightly service, although humanity knows nothing of it; for through them it still maintains contact with the spiritual worlds. They hold back the horror of the storm that threatens to destroy the human in humanity, until the Human Being has attained full spiritual stature. Together with their leader, they form the keystone of mystical hierarchies that never cease working upon human existence, yet are known to only a few. Ordinary people know nothing of them; most do not even suspect that they exist.

And yet if these Guides ceased to be, humanity would be engulfed by catastrophe. Conversely, it is through them that humanity fulfils its destiny from one cycle to the next. They alone know the hidden pattern—the “cipher”—of its secret history. Nothing of this can be traced in the outward, material facts studied by sociology or by philosophies concerned only with outward appearances, though those disciplines still claim to deduce, using only the categories available to them, what they call the “meaning of history.”

We find the same signs in the famous conversation in which the First Imam initiated his disciple Komayl ibn Ziyâd into the secret of gnosis and its unbroken line of transmission (silsilat al-'irfân). Ghaybat—occultation, with its consequences and the ethical demands it imposes—is a fundamental theme of Imamite theosophy. Just as the Chosen One and Guide in Goethe's poem bears the name Humanus, meaning the human in the fullest, most complete sense, so the Twelfth Imam, the “Awaited Imam,” is the Perfect and complete Human Being (Insân kâmil, Anthropos teleios).

A dramatic aura surrounds each of the twelve Imams. Each is perceived as the brief appearance in this world of a figure belonging to another, and each appearance has inevitably encountered the rejection of the multitude and the opposition of established political and religious powers. The Twelfth Imam's particular aura is that of his ghaybat: his invisible presence in this world, the anonymity into which human incomprehension has driven him.

Here lies the central paradox of Shiite religious feeling: beauty and perfection are offered to humanity, only to be rejected or reviled. From that paradox arises the feeling at the heart of walâyat, the feeling that shapes the life of the person called, in classical Persian texts, a javânmard—best translated as a “spiritual knight,” a knight of faith. What Brother Marcus is to Humanus, every Shiite believer must be to the Twelfth Imam, the Hidden Imam.

Through faith and fidelity, the believer's own person and life can become the beginning of the Imam's “unconcealment.” The sincerity of the wish spoken whenever the Imam is mentioned—“May God hasten the joy of his coming!”—must be shown in the believer's ethos, in the way that person lives. Each must become the Imam's fellow worker, helping to prepare his return and manifestation (a feeling powerfully expressed in the pilgrim's prayer we shall quote at the end; there are many others). This idea and this way of life have remained deep within Iranian spirituality since the distant age of Zoroaster's preaching.

In Shiite theology, the manifestation that will announce the Resurrection has its exact counterpart in the Zoroastrian idea of Frashkart: the transfiguration or renewal of the world.394 The Zoroastrian ethic of the Fravartis and the ethic of the javânmard together express the whole message of spiritual chivalry handed down by Iran. We have suggested its profound, hidden harmony with the message of the Johannite knights of the Green Island and that of Goethe's knights of the Rose Cross.

But there is more to be said.

2. The Abrahamic Tradition and Spiritual Chivalry (javânmardî)

The Persian word javânmardî, which we have just used, is one of the key terms of Persian mystical vocabulary. It corresponds to the Arabic fotowwat, a word for a way of life found across wide regions of Islamic civilization. Wherever it appears, it bears a distinctly Shiite imprint, and for good reason. We might call fotowwat the ethical category par excellence. It gives spiritual meaning to human fellowship, to the bond between companions, and it was therefore the inspiration behind the many guilds of crafts and other occupations that spread throughout the Islamic world.

Those in Turkish lands have received particular attention from scholars.395 Those in Iran have so far been studied much less (editions of several texts are now being prepared there). This is paradoxical, since the Iranian world was very probably where the idea first took shape. Every scholar of the subject has sensed that the origins of fotowwat must be sought as far back as ancient, pre-Islamic Persia.

Within the Islamic world, fotowwat presented itself as arising from Sufism, and as it gave shape and structure to the fellowship of occupational associations, it brought a sense of “chivalrous service” into every activity of life, complete with ritual, initiations, grades, bonds of brotherhood, secrecy, and the like.396 We ought to compare this with a similar phenomenon in the West: the “Order of the Companions of the Holy Duty of God,” the Devoirants, who knew—and still know—“the Orient and the Line” (l'Orient et le Trait).

Would establishing contact with them be something new, or would it restore a bond lost for centuries? There is much to say, and much to do, on this subject. Naturally we cannot explore here the vast spread of this tradition, still less its inevitable distortions. Our concern is first to clarify what the word means, and then to identify the essential nature of the practice: how Shiite thinkers understand the origin of fotowwat and the relationship between its manifestations, the cycle of prophecy, and the cycle of walâyat.

Our principal source will be the Fotowwat-Nâmeh, written in Persian by Hoseyn Kâshefî, the great Iranian preacher and spiritual teacher of the fifteenth century (d. 910 AH / 1504–05 CE). His book treats the knowledge of fotowwat chiefly as “a branch of the knowledge of Sufism and tawhîd,” the affirmation of divine unity.397

The word itself cannot really be explained without bringing in the very essence of what it names. Our author makes this clear in detail, supporting his account with many quotations. The Arabic fatâ corresponds to the Persian javân (Latin juvenis); mard-e javân means a young man, roughly between sixteen and thirty years of age. The Arabic fotowwat corresponds to the Persian javânî (Latin juvenitas), meaning youth. That is the literal sense, referring to bodily age.

In its technical, spiritual sense, however, the word describes a youth over which time has no power, because it has been won back from time and from the hardening that time brings. It is the youthfulness proper to spiritual beings, the qualities awakened in us by the idea of youth. When the mystic—the pilgrim or wayfarer (sâlik, a word that exactly conveys our idea of homo viator, the human being on a journey)—has gradually freed himself, on his “inward” path, from the passions of the bodily soul, he reaches the station of the heart: the inward, true human being.

In that very place he has entered the dwelling of youth (manzala-ye javânî), of youth that has come to stay. The Persian compound javânmard (Arabic fatâ) therefore means someone in whom human perfections, spiritual energies, and the soul's inward powers (qowwatha-ye ma'nawî) have become fully active. It also describes a person whose shining qualities and exemplary conduct set that person apart from the ordinary run of humankind.

Hence the abstract noun javânmardî (Arabic fotowwat) means—and here we hear again the contrast so characteristic of the Iranian vision of the world—“the manifestation of the light of humanity's original nature (nûr-e fitrat-e insânî), and the victorious mastery of that light over the darkness of the bodily soul, so that a human being, cured of every vice, possesses every moral excellence.” This is the soul's essential youthfulness.

To explain the essence of fotowwat, then, is to return to the fundamental idea of fitrat, humanity's original nature: what the human being was when, at the beginning, the act of existence—its dimension of light—sprang from the creative Act. At the same time, what that being would be, its own distinctive essence, was determined by the “tone” of its response to the question A-lasto? (“Am I not [your Lord]?”; Quran 7:171). That response governs the whole understanding of the human being.

In its complete purity, as we have seen, it includes a threefold testimony: to divine Unity, to the mission of the prophets, and to the walâyat of the Imams. This already points to the bond between fotowwat and walâyat. It also explains why fotowwat is often used as another name for îmân, complete faith in the Shiite sense. Purity of soul is the sign of a return to that original nature.

Thus when Moses asked—our author refers to the Torah here, without specifying a passage—“Lord, what is fotowwat?” the answer came: “To return to God the soul pure and unstained, just as humanity received it in trust.” This alludes to the Quranic theme of the “trust entrusted,” on which we encountered Haydar Âmolî's masterful commentary. It is in this sense that one can say: “Fotowwat is a light emanating from the spiritual world.

“When this light shines into a being and flows through that being, angelic qualities (sifât-e malakî) and the characteristics of the Malakût become manifest within. Every satanic disposition, every habit of the animal nature that stifles the soul imprisoned in the flesh, is banished.”

Of the many definitions of fotowwat, Hoseyn Kâshefî pays particular attention to those given in turn by the Imams, except the Twelfth. As the Seal of fotowwat, the Twelfth Imam has the task of bringing to fulfilment and completion everything his predecessors have taught about it.

Having established its essential link with fitrat, we shall retain here only the words of the Third Imam, Hosayn ibn 'Alî, the martyr of Karbala: “Spiritual chivalry (fotowwat, javânmardî) means remaining faithful to the pre-eternal covenant”—the covenant made in response to A-lasto?—“and walking with firm steps on the great road of the eternal religion (dîn qayyim), the road called the straight path (sirât mostaqîm).” Such is the javânmard, the knight of faith.

We are also told that the knowledge of fotowwat is “a branch of the knowledge of Sufism and tawhîd.” This necessarily brings fotowwat into close relation with the threefold distinction we have encountered throughout this work: sharî'at (the Law, religion in its outward or literal form), tarîqat (the mystical path), and haqîqat (the spiritual truth personally realized).

The inward meaning of “poverty” (faqr) in Sufism is an ontological poverty: the utter dependence of a created being for its existence. One bears witness to this poverty by affirming, as Haydar Âmolî does, the realized spiritual truth—the haqîqat—of tawhîd understood at the level of being itself.

If fotowwat points, in its essence, to fitrat, humanity's original, pre-existent nature, the forms in which it appears cannot be separated from the cycles of prophecy and walâyat as Shiite teaching understands them. There is, in fact, a cycle of fotowwat.

How does it relate to the two cycles of prophecy and walâyat that we have already described at length (above, Book I)? Hoseyn Kâshefî, summing up the teachings of earlier writers, identifies three decisive moments: fotowwat originates with Abraham, who brings it into manifestation as something distinct from the tarîqat, the Sufi path; its pole (qotb), or spiritual centre, is the First Imam; and its Seal (khâtim), the figure who brings it to completion, is the Twelfth Imam.

Everyone agrees that the prophetic mission, nobowwat, began in this world with Adam, after he had left Paradise. In that role, Adam could only be the man of the sharî'at, the revealed Law. The inward meaning of prophecy, later to be called walâyat, was entrusted to his son Seth, the first Imam of Adam's period. “Adam had to spread the carpet of the sharî'at”—that is, of the Law and the religion of legal obligations—“in the arena of human existence subject to the Law ('obûdîyat), while Seth spread the carpet of the mystical path (tarîqat).”

The original distinction was thus established. While Adam's other sons took up various occupations, Seth devoted himself entirely to divine service, “a mystical weaver who wove no garment other than that of Sufism.” (We may recall here the place of Seth among the Sethian Gnostics, and his identification with Zoroaster, while Ismaili gnosis gives the name Melchizedek to the Imam of the first three periods of the prophetic cycle.) In short, Seth was the first Sufi, and there are beautiful legends to explain how this came to be.398

In his person fotowwat was part of the tarîqat. Neither for Seth nor for his followers was there any distinction between the mystical path, or Sufism, and fotowwat: the tarîqat itself set the measure of fotowwat, and both shared the same garment, the khirqa, the cloak symbolizing a Sufi's initiation and consecration.

We learn next that in Abraham's time, people no longer had the strength to wear the khirqa. A whole group admitted this to Abraham and asked him to show them a path by which they could still follow their longing and calling to become people of God. (Here we may remember the concern shared by the Friend of God and Rulman Merswin: the age of cloisters was over, and another kind of spiritual foundation had to be imagined.) Our authors pass down the same story, rich in imagery.

Abraham took this group aboard the ship of the tarîqat. He launched the ship upon the open sea of haqîqat, realized spiritual truth, and brought it to the island of fotowwat, where they made their home. (Here we naturally think of the voyage toward the Imam's Green Island.) The meaning is very subtle. Once aboard the ship of Sufism, the only way to disembark in the midst of the ocean of haqîqat is to reach the island of fotowwat.

Spiritual chivalry is inseparable from Sufism in its origin. Sufism is the path toward realizing haqîqat, the spiritual truth; by that very fact it is the way—the ship, in this image—that makes it possible to land upon an island in the ocean of haqîqat. That island is none other than fotowwat.

Abraham was thus the initiator, the “father,” of all the mystical knights of faith (hence his titles: Arabic abû'l-fityân, Persian padar-e javânmardân). He became their father through a decision that anticipated the famous saying of the Sixth Imam, Ja'far al-Sâdiq: “Islam began in exile, and it will become an exile again, as it was at the beginning. Blessed are those who go into exile for their faith.” Abraham's decision and Imam Ja'far's saying help us understand what it means for the pilgrims to sail toward the island of fotowwat.

Hoseyn Kâshefî writes: “Abraham was the first to choose to separate himself from this world and all its trappings, its vanities and sensual pleasures; to separate himself from the crowd and the tribe, to turn his back on his native land, and to bear the hardships and weariness of the pilgrim's journey and exile for God's sake”—for the javânmard is the pilgrim above all, our homo viator. “He had the courage to fight the idols, so much so that even his enemies paid tribute to his fotowwat: ‘We heard a young man (fatâ, a “knight”) speaking against our gods; they call him Abraham’ (Quran 21:61).

“Thus the original manifestation of fotowwat—both distinct from the path of Sufism and derived from it—was Abraham.” Our author adds: “This knowledge of fotowwat is a fragrance arising from the knowledge of the tarîqat.

“But many people, travellers out of the desert of heedlessness and unawareness, can hold on to nothing except words emptied of meaning. They put on the appearance of Ahl-e fotowwat”—people of spiritual chivalry, claiming to be knights of faith—“and pretend to know the inward truth (haqîqat) of this knowledge. That is why the sages placed a veil over it, to conceal it from the gaze of the uninitiated.”

The cycle of fotowwat inaugurated by Abraham takes the form of a transmission that crosses and intertwines with the transmission of the prophetic light (Nûr mohammadî), passing from prophet to prophet until it reaches the Seal of the Prophets and the complete assembly, or pleroma, of the twelve Imams. Abraham passes fotowwat to Ishmael and Isaac. From Isaac it passes to Jacob, and then through eminent figures whose names appear in both the Bible and the Quran—Joshua son of Nun, Joseph, and others. It passes through Christianity as well, particularly in the persons of the Seven Sleepers mentioned in the Quran (18:8–24).

The line of fotowwat follows the same rule as the line of gnosis (silsilat al-'irfân): it is never without someone to embody it in this world. It can dwell in a prophet or in a “Friend of God” (a walî, above all the Imam). When manifested in a prophet, it is handed on to that prophet's Imam.

Thus the Seal of the Prophets passed it on to Imam 'Alî.

The cycles of prophecy, walâyat or the Imamate, and fotowwat therefore overlap in the following way. The cycle of prophecy first appeared with Adam. Its pole was Abraham. Its Seal was the Prophet Muhammad, the “Seal of the Prophets.” Abraham, the pole of prophecy, inaugurated the cycle of fotowwat. The pole of fotowwat was the First Imam, 'Alî ibn Abî Tâlib. Its Seal is, and will be, the Twelfth Imam, Muhammad al-Qâ'im, the Awaited One (montazar), the longed-for Imam, who is both present and, for now, invisible to human eyes.

The pole and the Seal of fotowwat are thus the very two figures of the Muhammadan Imamate who form the double Seal of the cycle of walâyat, the inward meaning of prophecy (bâtin al-nobowwat), whose cycle began with Seth. The pole of fotowwat is the First Imam, Seal of universal walâyat. The Seal of fotowwat is the Twelfth Imam, who is at the same time the Seal of Muhammadan walâyat. The three great moments of prophecy—Adam, Abraham, Muhammad—are matched by the three great moments of fotowwat: Abraham, the First Imam, the Twelfth Imam.

We learned earlier that all the prophets before Muhammad stood in relation to him, the Seal of Prophecy, as the Awliyâ, the “Friends of God” who come after the Seal of Prophecy, stand in relation to the Twelfth Imam.

It follows that this same relationship defines the place of all the spiritual knights, all the javânmardân, in relation to the Twelfth Imam, the Seal and final perfection of their fotowwat, their spiritual chivalry. This also reveals the bond between walâyat and fotowwat. The latter is the supreme manifestation of walâyat: it expresses walâyat as a way of life.

Each person, wherever he or she stands, is a companion of the Twelfth Imam; and this ethic makes each responsible for helping bring about his future appearance, the manifestation of the Imam as the Perfect Human Being. Spiritual chivalry (javânmardî, fotowwat) is therefore the ethic of the Friends of God (Awliyâ Allâh) in the cycle of walâyat, during this present period of “occultation.”

At this point it is hard not to hear an echo of the final message of Gottesfreundschaft, the friendship of God, entrusted to the Johannite knights of the Green Island. The bond of each javânmard with the Twelfth Imam likewise resembles the bond of each of Goethe's Rose Cross knights with Humanus, the Perfect Human Being who embodies the human condition in its full realization.

The Shiite idea of fotowwat, then, is of a community of javânmardân, or knights, embracing the entire Abrahamic tradition. Their archetype, the knight above all knights, is the Imam. One of the best-known hadiths repeats: “There is no knight but 'Alî, and no sword but Dhû'l-fiqâr”—the sword here symbolizing the power of interpretation that cuts through the obscurities of the Law taken only in its literal sense.399

Since Abraham was the father of fotowwat, this tradition embraces the heroes of the Bible and the “Christian knights” represented by the Seven Sleepers mentioned in the Quran. In the West there is a corresponding ideal of an equally “ecumenical” chivalry, bringing together the knights of Christendom and of Islam. It finds its supreme expression in Wolfram von Eschenbach, for whom the heroic epic of the Knights Templar becomes the mystical epic of the Templars of the Grail. This transformation follows a path converging with the one taken by Suhrawardi, who also transformed the heroic epic into a mystical one.

Let us examine the horizon now opening before us, for it is ultimately this that can make the spiritual aspects of Iranian Islam mean something far more to us than a matter of archaeological or exotic interest.

We have already seen the first signs of this horizon in a conviction Shiism shares with the rest of Islam: the cycle of prophecy is closed. No prophet will come after the “Seal of Prophecy” has been sent into the world.

But Shiite feeling gives rise to an urgent, deeply troubled question: what becomes of humanity if, by its very nature and by the condition that makes it human, it cannot do without a prophet? The answer to this passionate question is the affirmation of the cycle of walâyat, inaugurated with the very closing of the cycle of prophecy. Our examination of fotowwat shows us what kind of human being the idea of walâyat calls upon us to become: a “Friend of God,” whose personal way of life, by that very fact, prepares the appearance of the Imam, the Perfect Human Being, as a divine manifestation.

As the cycle of initiation into the inward meaning of the prophetic message (bâtin al-nobowwat), the cycle of walâyat is also the cycle of fotowwat. Spiritual chivalry is that initiation into the secret of walâyat, the inner meaning of the Revelation communicated to the prophets. These knights, these javânmardân, form around the Imam, their spiritual centre, the silsilat al-'irfân, the unbroken line of gnosis, generation after generation. That line is “tradition” itself.

Yet everyone who joins it must undergo a new birth, so no one can use the authority of predecessors as an excuse for failing to be spiritually alive. This tradition is the very opposite of a funeral procession: it is perpetual rebirth. To join it is to enter the Malakût, the spiritual world. As a saying drawn directly from the Gospel of John declares—a saying our Shiite theosophers particularly love to quote—“No one can enter the Malakût unless born a second time.”

Though unknown to humanity, these “Friends of God” are the means by which it continues to exist, because through them the world of earthly human beings still communicates with the higher invisible world. This idea, and this ideal, are equally those of the disciples of the Friend of God of the Oberland and of the knights of the mystical Montserrat in Goethe's poem.

This implies a distinctive and exalted calling for the person we call a “philosopher.” This calling demands far more than we ordinarily associate with philosophy, and places upon the philosopher a responsibility more profound than any responsibility described today as “social.” We have seen this kind of philosopher—the theosophos, the sage of God—reveal the full meaning of his existence and his spiritual, cosmic role in Suhrawardi and the Illuminationists (Ishrâqîyûn).

We could already discern his emergence in Farabi and Avicenna, and it is among the Shiite theosophers that this ideal bears its fullest fruit. The whole of their metaphysics, and the understanding of human nature that follows from it, is directed toward one goal: the union of the human intellect—and, through it, of the whole inner person, the whole spiritual being—with what philosophers call the Active Intellect. They identify this Intellect with the Holy Spirit, the Angel Gabriel who brings revelation, the Angel of humanity.

We have explained how and why this identification of the Intellect with the Holy Spirit is entirely different from what some interpreters have understood as rationalism or intellectualism. In the mystery of this union, for which the theosopher prepares through sustained inner and intellectual discipline, the Angel-Intellect reveals itself to the mystic of Suhrawardi's tradition as the “Perfect Nature,” the personal Angel, in all the variations of this theme found in gnosis—and ultimately as the Imam, the personal guide.

However we explain or imagine this mystical union, it is through that very union that communication remains open between our world and the higher world of the Malakut, the spiritual realm. Through it, humanity itself continues to exist. This, in turn, is what defines the knightly service of the philosopher as a sage of God and makes him a javanmard, a spiritual knight, in the fullest sense. Such is the philosopher as conceived by the Illuminationists and the Shiite theosophers.

This philosopher is certainly something other, and something more, than the word “philosopher” usually suggests to us. We recognize that additional dimension when we find ourselves obliged to describe his philosophy as prophetic philosophy, because of the role he assumes in the cycle of walayat—the cycle of spiritual initiation and divine friendship that follows the cycle of prophecy. He is a sage of God, a theosophos. He is guided by the Active Intellect, with which he becomes united at the highest point of knowing.

And at the summit of his own faculties there is what the tradition calls the intellectus sanctus, the holy intellect, upon which the Angel pours its light—the Angel who is at once the Angel of knowledge and the Angel of revelation. It is through this that the philosopher can enter the sanctuary of divine wisdom and pass beyond the ordinary horizon of philosophy. For the philosopher, to explore the world of the Intellects is to explore the world brought into existence by the divine Command and, through that world, to know the Source from which it emanates.

But we have seen that for the Shiite theosopher, beyond the horizon of the first Being—the first to be brought into existence—lies the unfathomable mystery of the Absconditum, the hidden God who can be approached only through negative theology, which recognizes the inadequacy of everything we can say about the divine. We have seen that the secret of the Muhammadan Light, the Haqîqat mohammadîya, is the manifestation of this hidden God as Deus revelatus, God revealed: the mystery of the theophany, or divine self-manifestation. And the mystery of this divine Face revealed to humanity is precisely the mystery of the Imam and the Imamate.

Guided by the secret of its teaching about the Imam, Shiite theosophy has carried the metaphysics of being higher—or further—than what is called “absolute” being, because the absolute itself implies the mystery of its own Absolvens, that which releases or makes it absolute. The mystery within the divine of this “absolution” of being is the passage from the hidden God to God revealed. This is the divine gift bestowed upon theosophy as the fulfillment of prophetic philosophy.

At every level we have briefly recalled, the philosopher-theosopher performs the service of a spiritual knight—a javanmard in the fullest sense—because it is through him that these realities continue to have meaning for human beings and continue to concern them. Just as every prophet is called a fatâ, a knight of faith, and his struggle was the struggle of such a knight, so too, without the prophetic philosophy of these theosophers, humanity would become permanently deaf and blind, deprived of every memory of its own preexistent being.

The loss of this inner vision and this memory is the inverted, satanic “service” performed by a philosophy stripped of its sacred character and secularized. Prophetic philosophy, by contrast, affirms a calling shared by prophet and philosopher. The Angel pours its illumination upon the same intellectus sanctus in both.

Thus the philosopher finds himself at home in the mundus imaginalis, the imaginal world: the realm of individual, concrete spiritual realities where the visions of the prophets unfold and where the secrets of worlds and intermediary worlds, eternally present, are inscribed. This is possible because, for the philosopher of prophetic philosophy, the intellect and the imagination communicate through that same holy intellect.

His experience of divine wisdom is therefore no longer expressed in doctrine alone. Doctrine becomes an actual event in the soul. The theosopher becomes the javanmard, the knight of the mystical epic. This is what Suhrawardi's work has enabled us to understand. His mystical narratives stand between the great spiritual epics of Hakim Sana'i and Attar. These narratives and epics—the events whose stories they tell—must therefore be read as revealing the inner, esoteric meaning of a doctrine that, by comparison, still remained at the level of its literal meaning. All too often, we read them the other way around.

The hidden meaning of the events lies higher than the doctrines. It is their personal fulfillment, the truth attained at the end of the quest: the haqîqat. Such is the mystical epic of the spiritual knight. Suhrawardi showed us its source in the Xvarnah, the Mazdaean Light of Glory. We have seen how an inspired hadith finds an echo of this in Sufism, when it salutes Zoroaster as the prophet of the religion of love.

Suhrawardi performed a spiritual knight's service by bringing the Hellenized Magi back into Islamic Persia and leading the “Greek prophets”—the Neoplatonists—back to the “Niche of Lights” of prophecy (mishkât al-nobowwat). The theosopher is thus the knight of a mystical epic in which humanity is raised toward its origin, the origin that sets it free. To “advance” toward that origin is to leave, as Abraham did, the land of one's birth, which is the world of exile.

It was to this epic that an entire spiritual knighthood was called: a knighthood of faith, participating in the Abrahamic tradition.

This explains the correspondences we can discern, for example, between Shiite and Jewish theosophy: in their conception of the philosopher who takes up the message of the prophets; in their recognition that this philosopher has an indispensable role in preserving humanity; and in the distinction they draw between a theosophy established from the outset upon the spiritual interpretation of the Holy Book and a philosophy initially concerned with developing the Neoplatonic inheritance. I do not claim the competence here to discuss the relations between the Kabbalah and philosophy400.

Nevertheless, certain parallels that suggest themselves cannot be passed over in silence.

For Shiite theosophy, beyond the pleroma, or fullness, of the Intellects lies the pleroma of the Fourteen Immaculate Ones, the fullness of the Muhammadan Reality (Haqîqat mohammadîya). This is the receptive aspect (absolutum) of the active divine Command that brings things into existence. As such, it is the primordial absolute being called into existence by that Command, the Absolvens.

Is the Light of Lights itself the supreme Principle, as the Illuminationist philosophers believe? Or is it, as the Muhammadan Light, the first being summoned into existence by the Command of the hidden God—the KN, the divine “Be!” (Esto)? A similar question arises in Jewish Kabbalah because certain philosophers identify the pleroma of the Intellects with the series of Sephirot, understood as Deus revelatus, God revealed. Is the Infinite (En Sof) identical with the first of the Sephirot, the Crown, or does it remain distinct from it401?

We can do no more than raise the question here. It calls for a comparative study of theosophy that has scarcely begun. We mention it because the thinkers for whom, and through whom, such a question arises—at one time or another—belong to the same kind of philosophical tradition in which the study of prophecy and the meaning of philosophy have appeared inseparable. In such a tradition, every precise boundary between philosophy and theosophy disappears: neither can do without the other.

To profess, for example, as certain Jewish theosophers do, that prophecy includes “speculative perceptions” is already to affirm that the true prophet must necessarily be an authentic philosopher as well402. Once again, this presupposes the illuminating action of the Angel who is simultaneously the Angel of knowledge and the Angel of revelation. The Active Intellect may pour its illumination upon the human intellect alone, as in the case of purely speculative philosophers.

Or it may illuminate both the intellect and the imaginative faculty, as in the case of the prophet who is at once a consummate metaphysician and divinely inspired. This is also the case of the Perfect Sage according to Suhrawardi, the master of both speculative wisdom and ta'alloh, the spiritual experience of the divine. Suhrawardi describes this same Sage, in Zoroastrian terminology, as invested with the royal Xvarnah, the Light of Glory, and as the pole of humanity, whether visible or hidden.

Jewish theosophy likewise affirms that the survival of the human species requires a joining or union of the Active Intellect with the human intellect. The existence of the Perfect Human Being, in whom this union takes place, is therefore indispensable to the very continuance of the world. This is exactly what Shiite theosophy teaches about the Imam as the spiritual pole, “since it is in his person that the higher world and the lower world meet.” Abraham is offered as an example of such a person: one whom his people recognized as a “divine prince.”

This teaching corresponds not only to what Suhrawardi says about the Perfect Sage, but also to the central theme of the First Imam's conversation with his disciple Komayl ibn Ziyad. In that conversation, the unbroken lineage—the “tradition”—of spiritual knowledge (silsilat al-'irfân) is solemnly affirmed. Because this lineage is precisely what secures the continued existence of humanity, it constitutes the highest form of fotowwat, spiritual knighthood, throughout the cycle of walayat.

On both sides, the same spiritual journey leads the theosophers to recognize in prophetic inspiration and philosophical illumination the work of one and the same Angel: the Angel of intellectual understanding for the philosopher and the Angel of inspiration for the prophet. The divine prophetic influence flows to the prophets through the same Angel-Intellect that pours intelligible truths into the philosopher's intellect. And just as Shiite theosophy draws its nourishment from the Holy Book and the hadiths that disclose the Book's hidden meanings, so for these metaphysicians of prophetic philosophy the masters are Isaiah, Ezekiel, and Zechariah.

In the words of the prophet Zechariah, “the angel who speaks within me” (VI, 4), the theosopher recognizes that “when prophetic inspiration rests upon the prophet, the prophet and the angel speaking within him become one”403. This is a mystical union, an unio mystica, occurring in the prophet just as it occurs in the philosopher-theosopher who speaks of the union of the soul with the Active Intellect. The Intelligence that brings his potential intellect into full actuality is the very same Angel who “speaks within the prophet.”

This is why, among these prophetic philosophers, the union of the Active Intellect with the soul, contemplated through the visions granted to the prophets, was itself expressed as a vision. Its language possesses a beauty surpassing even that of the finest mystical epics, for the supreme union it announces is also the fulfillment toward which those epics lead. The theosophers of the Bible gave this union its own name: the “kiss of the seraph.” Isaiah's vision becomes a vision of this union and then continues into the musical cadences of the Song of Songs.

Let us listen to one of these theosophers meditating upon Isaiah's vision (VI, 1 ff.)404, in which the seraph flies toward the prophet and touches his mouth with a burning coal. Here the seraph represents the Intellect, the Angel who stands last in the hierarchy of the separate Intellects, and therefore nearest to humanity. In this tradition the Angel is called Michael rather than Gabriel, as he is among the philosophers of Islam. “One of the seraphim flew toward me ... Here is Michael, one of the seraphim, coming to my aid.

“In his hand is a burning coal.” Such, indeed, is the condition of the human intellect in relation to the Active Intellect at the moment when the human intellect becomes an intellect in act, capable of understanding the Angel and joining itself to him. “He touched his mouth and said: See, this has touched your lips; your sin has departed.” “When Isaiah understood the form of the Union, he joined himself to the angel in a union that might more properly be called a transformation into a single being.”

And so the voice that is heard asks not, “Whom shall I send for myself?” but “Whom shall I send for us?” (Isaiah VI, 8). “Understand, O reader, all that is implied here ... Solomon intended to express the same idea in the verse, ‘Draw me after you, and we shall run.’” This shows that the one who sends and the one who is sent stand at the same degree at the moment of the prophetic mission405.

Other thinkers had already developed this theme. Moses ibn Tibbon, for example, in his commentary on the Song of Songs, interpreted the kiss as communion with the Intellect. And Joseph ibn Kaspi writes406: “When a human being knows the greatness [of the divine acts], his intellect unites with what it understands and becomes one with it.

“Solomon, inspired by the Holy Spirit, said, ‘Let him kiss me with the kisses of his mouth’ (Song of Songs 1:2). In the same sense it is written, ‘They dwell at the mouth of God’ (Numbers IX, 18). This is the kiss of the intellect, the only true kiss: not the kiss of the lips, but the kiss of the mouth, the ultimate desire of lovers.” The divine visions of Ezekiel would likewise be interpreted as a communion of Intellects equivalent to prophecy407.

Such texts bring into sharper relief something we have already had occasion to say about the identification of the Active Intellect with the Holy Spirit among the philosophers and theosophers of Islam. This identification does not mean that the Spirit has been reduced to reason, as certain Western interpreters have been too quick to claim. Here the philosopher is raised to the rank of prophet, and their union in the act of complete understanding makes the Angel and the soul a single being composed of two.

In its highest form, the act of knowing is not expressed through the abstract language of general concepts, as it is in our theories of knowledge. This act of knowing, which is communion with spiritual universes, is the “kiss of the seraph,” accompanied softly by the Song of Songs. Other spiritual seekers, the Fedeli d'amore, spoke not of the seraph but of Madonna Intelligenza, Lady Intelligence.

In neither case are we dealing with metaphor, allegory, an abstraction given human form, or a general concept. We are dealing with the vision of an essence in its own individual form. For the spiritual world, above the abstract concepts of logic, possesses its own concrete nature and its own individuality, with forms that cannot be perceived unless we possess the faculty of metaphysical imagination. Prophetic philosophy grants this faculty its rightful place by describing how the Angel's light flows simultaneously into the philosopher's intellect and the visionary's power of imagination.

This is why it fell to a theosopher like Suhrawardi, in his visionary writings, to lead the heroes of the heroic epic toward the spiritual knighthood of the mystical epic (see above, Book II). When “doctrine becomes an event of the soul,” the theosopher perceives that event in Isaiah's vision, as did the Jewish theosopher just quoted; in the Grail narrative of Kay Khosrow, as Suhrawardi did in the account we examined earlier; or in a vision of the Imam, as so many Shiite theosophers have done.

Prophetic philosophy and the mystical epic advance together; each is bound to and connected with the other. From their convergence arises a spiritual knighthood reaching across the entire world shaped by the phenomenon of the Holy Book. Its divine service, through which humanity continues to exist, can be expressed only through visionary narratives and epics of the soul—not through general theories or abstract ideologies. This is why the prophets' visions and the mystical epics call for the same kind of interpretation as the spiritual interpretation of the Holy Book.

And this is how we must read our own medieval Western mystical epic: the cycle of the Holy Grail. Only when we understand it in this way does the Grail epic disclose the secret of its spiritual knighthood. To bring this knighthood together with the companions of the Hidden Imam would be to realize the ideal assembly foreshadowed in Goethe's unfinished poem.

We have seen precisely such a meeting anticipated in the mystical narratives of Suhrawardi, the Shaykh al-Ishraq, which initiate the reader into the secret of his “Oriental theosophy”—that is, into the way of living it inwardly. This meeting draws together all the “guardians of the Logos,” those of the East and those of the West, on paths converging toward one another.

There is something significant here—have we paid sufficient attention to it?—in the fact that at the very time of Suhrawardi, the idea of a single knighthood embracing East and West was taking definite form in the work of Wolfram von Eschenbach. Of course, that would be merely a chronological coincidence, an entirely external one.

But Qazi Sa'id Qommi has taught us that true simultaneity must be sought in the Malakut, the spiritual world. And it seems that there, indeed, we may find it.

Recent studies have rightly emphasized that the Arthurian Round Table seems to be an emanation of the Table of the Grail, from which it receives all its light408. It is for this reason alone that Galahad's journey to the “Spiritual Palace of Sarras” passes through the Arthurian Round Table. What matters most about that table is its symbolic meaning: its correspondence with the structure of the cosmos as a whole. It represents the roundness of the cosmos.

Here we may think of the spirit of the School of Chartres, the influence of commentaries on Plato's Timaeus, and the Hermetic writings (see above, Book II): the World Soul extending from the center to every part of the body of the cosmos and embracing it entirely; a single, solitary, circular heaven, “capable, by its own power, of remaining within itself without needing anything else.” We might already say that the Table of the Grail is the soul of the Arthurian Round Table.

In any case, the cosmic correspondence expressed by the latter is perfectly in keeping with the manifestations of the pleroma of the Twelve that we have encountered here: the fullness of the Twelve Imams, whose invisible dwelling places are symbolized by the twelve signs of the zodiac; the esoteric hierarchy whose totality corresponds to the 360 degrees of the sphere; the fullness of the Twelve gathered around the Friend of God of the High Country; and the twelve Rosicrucian knights in Goethe's poem.

It seems to us, then, that we must begin with this cosmic correspondence if we are to understand how, in Wolfram's work, the castle of the Grail is transformed into an entire world: the “world of the Grail” itself409. This world and its knights must necessarily be situated in a kind of space that we recognize as a quarta dimensio, a fourth dimension—or, better still, as the Malakut.

For reasons that have compelled us throughout this study to speak of the imaginal, we refuse to call this space “imaginary.” The fact that this world is “everywhere and nowhere” is precisely what the Persian expression Nâ-kojâ-âbâd, coined by Suhrawardi, means. This is the defining character of the “eighth clime,” the mundus imaginalis, or the world of Hurqalya: it has its own real location, but that location cannot be defined by our geographical coordinates.

The appearances of the Hidden Imam and his companions have likewise led us back to this ubi, this “where” which, in relation to our earthly space, is an ubique, an “everywhere.” It is right to say that the world of the Grail, while impossible to locate geographically, is a sovereign world with frontiers to defend. Its chosen members may enter it “from the Arthurian world of forests and rivers,” and they may leave it to undertake missions.

I believe that the world of the Hidden Imam and his companions, and indeed the world of the mystical epic generally, correspond to this description. The quest for the Imam as the “Soul of the soul” is a journey like that of Parsifal “toward this world situated outside ordinary space.” One enters this world because one belongs to it by birthright.

But we must remember that everything here takes place in the “eighth clime,” to which all the landscapes, persons, and actions belong.

Thus, when we speak of a “birthright,” we mean birth into this world of the eighth clime—the world of the Grail. This is the birth of the gnostic, the person awakened to spiritual knowledge. It gives him not only the right but also the duty to return to the world to which that birth has made him belong. Such is the meaning of the entire gnostic epic, of the “Hymn of the Pearl,” and of the Iranian mystical epic: the story of the exile (ghorbat) whose conclusion is a return to his own people. The return to the world of the Grail, the return to the mystical Sinai, and the return to the Green Island of the Imam all have this same meaning.

This is why the knighthood whose world is symbolized by the Round Table forms a universal spiritual elite, drawing its members from “pagan lands”—by which our old authors meant the world of Islam—as well as from Christendom. The world it represents is a “perfect world,” a pleroma, a complete spiritual order. One enters it by casting off every attachment and ambition belonging to the ordinary, secular world. This is the very meaning of tajrîd, the stripping away of worldly attachments, in Sufi spirituality.

The bonds of brotherhood joining its companions make them a fellowship comprising the spiritual elite of humanity. In its hierarchy, and in deciding who its heroes are, it recognizes only spiritual qualifications. This is also the distinctive rule of the world of Hurqalya. It therefore appears that the emergence of the world of the Grail, with its entirely distinctive place and order of existence, is what makes possible the meeting and coherence of the two other worlds present in Wolfram's work: the world of the Arthurian cycle and that of Eastern knighthood.

In saying this, we are not concerned with techniques of literary creation410, but with the order of being that determines a world's structure and the way that world is perceived. When Wolfram's epic welcomes the knighthood of Islam, its inner movement mirrors that of the mystical epic through which Suhrawardi brings the Hellenized Magi of ancient Iran back into Islamic Persia.

Throughout Wolfram's writings, the theme recurs of a “pagan” knighthood equal in brilliance and worth to Christian knighthood, “except for baptism.” The finest representatives of this Eastern knighthood—that is, the knighthood of Islam—are considered equally worthy of a place at the Round Table.

In Wolfram, however, it is precisely through the joining of these two forms of knighthood that a spirituality emerges which belongs to the very idea of knighthood and is therefore shared by the knights of Christendom and Islam. It is true that, in the service of the Grail understood as a personal service to God, the knight's relationship with God is much more that of a vassal to his lord than that of a sinner to his redeemer.

We have already encountered an outstanding example of this relationship, and of the ideal governing it, in the struggle of the Fravartis on behalf of Ohrmazd. We also recalled earlier the judgment of Eugenio d'Ors, who rightly perceived that the conception of the spiritual world underlying Zoroastrian ethics leads of itself to the idea of an order of knighthood.

And we have shown that this is precisely the conception inspiring the ethics and mysticism of fotowwat: the preeternal covenant it implies, recalled in the definition given by the Third Imam, and the designation of Ali as the “supreme knight”—lâ fatâ illâ 'Alî, “there is no knight but Ali.” As for Wolfram, it has been said that he was a layman speaking to laypeople. Certainly.

But the world of the Grail already knows nothing of the ecclesiastical hierarchy or the apostolic succession of the Roman See. And what Wolfram presents to laypeople is precisely the ideal of knighthood, because he himself is a knight.

Yet to be a knight, though it is not to be a cleric, is no more simply to be an ordinary layperson. The meeting between the Friend of God of the Oberland and Rulman Merswin belongs to this same spiritual line of development: the age of the cloisters has passed, and the new message leads to the founding of the Knights of Saint John of the Green Island.

The ethics of spiritual knighthood, of which we have just recalled several examples, is expressed among the Shiite theosophers as the covenant and bond between rabb and marbûb: between the sovereign lord and his faithful servant.

What is involved is an essential relationship between the two, an essential coexistence. The first term therefore cannot refer to the Deus absconditus, the hidden God who transcends every attribute and every relation. Rather, it refers to the theophanic Figure of that hidden God, the Face shown to the faithful servant—and that Figure is the Imam.

The bond between rabb and marbûb is fundamentally a covenant of faithfulness. To betray this covenant is not to destroy what the rabb is in himself—the Imam remains the Imam even when he is ignored and rejected. It is to destroy the relationship outside which rabb and marbûb cannot exist for one another. And for the faithful servant, this means destroying himself by allowing the world they constitute together to be destroyed. The Imam dies for him only if he himself dies to the Imam. This is why the Fravartis did not betray Ohrmazd.

The same ethics is shared by every form of spiritual knighthood: the Templars of Wolfram's epic, the knights of Goethe's poem, and the knights of the Imam. Once again, we may borrow from a Kabbalistic writer words that express exactly what governs the ethical relationship we have in mind: “God needs his presence to dwell in the Temple.” “In all their afflictions, he himself was afflicted” (Isaiah LXIII, 9)411.

This is also why anyone who refuses to see the presence of God as making Wolfram's Parsifal a theological and mystical poem thereby admits an inability to read it as every narrative of initiation and every mystical epic must be read: in the way one reads the Holy Book. Here we may follow the same instruction Suhrawardi gave for reading the Quran: each person should read it as though it had been revealed for that person's own particular case.

The events related in Wolfram's epic take place in the mundus imaginalis. The battles fought there, the weapons used, the celebrations held—all these events are so many affirmations or sudden irruptions of the imaginal world into the poet's imaginative consciousness. We have learned that such appearances announce, by their very nature, the elevation into the imaginal world of a doctrine that has become an event of the soul and within the soul. It is therefore the task of spiritual interpretation to disclose their esoteric meaning.

But this must not be done by descending again to the level of the logical clarity of doctrinal concepts. It must be done by following the path along which doctrine is transformed into event, without ever denying the reality of that event.

This is why, despite what has sometimes been said, there is no opposition between the eschatological meaning of the world of the Grail—as the heavenly Jerusalem, the City of God—and the mystical meaning of the Quest. It would be absurd to set against one another, on the one hand, an eschatological meaning concerning the final union of the community with God, or even the “assumption” of history into a higher reality, and, on the other, a mystical meaning of the Quest grounded in a doctrine of personal union with God within “human time”412. Such an artificial opposition seems inspired by an underlying assumption that gives priority to the collective from the outset.

There can be no final union of the community without the successful completion of the personal Quest undertaken by each of its members. Nor is that personal Quest pursued within “human time.” It unfolds precisely within “knightly time,” which is why the Quest is itself eschatological and brings about its own eschatological fulfillment.

The time of each Quest is one portion, one quantum, of “knightly time.” Yet knightly time unfolds “between times.”

We can speak of an “assumption of history” only in the sense of a passage into the time of the Malakut, the spiritual world.

But this time breaks through the chronological time of irreversible history because it is, in its very essence, a mysterium liturgicum, a liturgical mystery. Galahad was real and truly completed his Quest in the ecstatic death he experienced at Sarras. And yet Galahad's adventure remains forever about to happen. It does not end when the reader reaches the last page of the book. Knightly time is brought to a close neither by a date in chronology nor by the final page of a book.

In this sense, it is the time of the ghaybat, the occultation. This is why we have already drawn a parallel between the occultation of the Imam and the concealment of the Holy Grail. The Imam's occultation does not end with the founding of the sanctuary of Jam Karan or with the last page of his sacred biography. We have seen that his hidden history continues throughout the period of his occultation. Similarly, the history of the Grail did not end with its concealment following its “return to the East.”

But the Grail's secret history can continue only by breaking, each time, into the course of collective, outward history. Each of its manifestations, like each appearance of the Imam, breaks the fabric of “dark and dense time,” because it raises the visionary into another order of time, one whose repetitions and reversibilities belong to a liturgical mystery. Here lies the very secret of a knighthood that persists incognito in this world, with members in East and West alike.

A liturgical mystery: many indications suggest precisely this. It is on the day of Pentecost that the young Galahad, the “awaited” knight, the “Desired One,” appears at King Arthur's court and sets out from there upon the Quest of the Grail. We have also already noted how confidently several Shiite theosophers identify the “awaited” Imam with the Paraclete—the divine Comforter or Spirit promised in the Gospel (see also below).

The liturgical mystery in which the knights of West and East meet invisibly thus appears as the very mystery of Pentecost. It is also a mystery whose ceremonial unfolding was contemplated by the princess Narkes (Narcissus), mother of the Twelfth Imam, in the dream visions we related earlier. Within the precincts of an ideal temple of Holy Wisdom, Hagia Sophia, she saw Christ with his twelve apostles, and the Prophet with his eleven Imams, ascend together the steps of a single pulpit of light.

But before Narkes could finally see the Twelfth Imam, her mystical bridegroom, she had first to be initiated in a dream by Fatima and to accomplish the tawhîd, the acknowledgment of the One beyond all oneness. And now we read in Wolfram that Feirefiz, Parsifal's brother, could not see the Grail until he had received baptism. Only then, too, did his marriage to the Grail queen, Repanse de Joie, become possible. These are not “scientific” findings, but subtle and suggestive resonances.

Everything happens as though one voice were sounding the theme of a fugue on a great organ, and another voice were answering it by reversing that theme. Whoever can hear these resonances may perhaps discern in the first voice the counterpoint called forth by the second. Episode by episode, the entire fugue would then unfold to completion.

But that completion is precisely the “mystery of Pentecost,” and only the Paraclete has the mission of unveiling it.

3. The Twelfth Imam and the Reign of the Paraclete

Our study of Shiite prophetology has led us to recognize two convictions that sustain the faith of the Shiite spiritual seeker. The first is that the cycle of walayat, the cycle of initiation through the “Friends of God,” corresponds perfectly to the cycle of prophecy. Just as each prophet (nabi) manifests an aspect of the eternal prophetic Reality, so each Friend of God manifests, in his own particular way, the perfection of the Perfect Human Being whose final Seal is the presently Hidden Imam—the Seal of walayat.

It follows that each Friend of God stands in relation to the final Seal of walayat, the Twelfth Imam, just as each prophet stands in relation to the Seal of prophecy. This first conviction implies a second, which gives the followers of Shiite spirituality a distinctive inner strength. They are called to realize mystically, in their most intimate depths, a relationship with the Imam as the Seal of spiritual initiates, analogous to the relationship of the prophets with the Seal of prophecy.

This personal manifestation is, in a sense, the fruit of the celebrated hadith upon which the very concept of the Friends of God is founded: “The sages of my community correspond to the prophets of Israel.” The masters warn us that by these sages we must understand the “Sages of God” ('âlimân-e rabbânî), the “theosophers”—those whose knowledge of the divine mysteries comes to them as a divine gift, through inward unveiling (kashf) and direct inspiration, rather than through the dialectical instruction of a human teacher413.

By establishing this correspondence, the hadith declares that every mystical theosopher has a prophetic calling. Certainly, it applies in the first instance to those who are the Friends of God in the highest sense and who, precisely for that reason, are the Guides who initiate others into spiritual meaning: the Twelve Imams.

But we also know that the Imams communicated their own walayat to their followers by initiating them into their spiritual knowledge. And because that teaching came from the Imams, it was divine initiation rather than a tradition passed down merely by human beings.

The essential distinction has already been explained to us: in the person of the Imam, who is the source of walayat for the entire mystical hierarchy, even at levels invisible to ordinary humanity, walayat has the nature of the sun. In the persons of his followers, who become Friends of God through him, walayat has the nature of the moon.

Yet the illumination bestowed upon them by the Imam's light is no less complete414. For this light is wholly present in each Perfect Being whom it invests, in the sense that it illuminates the entirety of that person's being.

This explains why a number of these spiritual figures have felt themselves to be, in truth, unique beings. Several of them, in both the recent and distant past, have experienced themselves as the “Seal of Initiation” (khâtim al-walâyat). Such was the certainty Ibn Arabi experienced, as we have noted, following a symbolic dream vision.

A master of Shiite Sufism such as Shamsoddin Lahiji invites us to understand how all of them could have been sincere, and in what sense all of them spoke the truth. In other words, he explains how every initiate may be the Seal of Initiation, and every Friend of God the Seal of the Friends of God415.

“Through the perfection of their vision,” he says, “the gaze of each of them came to rest upon the pure and eternal Reality of walayat, beyond their personal individuality. If we understand their claims without the rigidity of religious bigotry, those claims show that each of them, at his own particular moment, was the most perfect being of that moment, and that each then possessed the eminence of the supreme spiritual pole—the polar function (qotbîyat) proper to the eternal Muhammadan Reality416.”

Yet this event takes place, and has its validity, only within the secret world of souls, within the Malakut. It is not an event that becomes publicly known and establishes itself as a fact of outward history. To manifest within oneself, in anticipation, the Seal of the Initiates is to bring about within oneself, and for oneself, the parousia—the appearing or manifestation—of the Imam. This does not in any way suspend the time of occultation (ghaybat) or proclaim that it has ended. Rather, it hastens its ripening.

For it is in this way that the Night of esotericism progresses—the cycle of walayat, the Night of Destiny, “in which the Angels and the Spirit descend”—toward the dawn that will be the Imam's manifestation for all. Here we recognize the profound meaning of the cycle of walayat and the very force that animates Imami spirituality in Iran. After the Seal of the Messengers, humanity has no further prophet to await. The majority have consequently devoted themselves with fanatic zeal to guarding the closed letter of revelation.

But without the complementary idea of the Seal of walayat, embodied in the Imam who is still to come, the idea of the Seal of prophecy becomes the sign of a human tragedy: humanity shuts itself, without hope, inside a past that has no future.

The Shiite understanding of the cycle of Initiation, by contrast, transforms the meaning of this closure by bringing forth from it the necessity of Renewal.

What is therefore required of every follower of Shiite spirituality is the quest for the Hidden Imam. For the follower, this means allowing the Imam to reveal himself within the secrecy of one's own consciousness—to “bring the Hidden Imam to birth” within oneself.

And this, precisely, is the “history” of the Hidden Imam throughout the period of the Great Occultation: a history of souls and a history unfolding within souls. It allows us to sense what is shared by Brother Marcus's quest at Montserrat, the final message of the Friend of God of the High Country, and the dream vision of the princess Narkes. This anticipation of the final Seal within each follower is what gives rise to the eschatological philosophy and spirituality characteristic of Shiism. For this sense of the ultimate fulfillment expresses the living relationship between the faithful follower and the Hidden Imam, the Twelfth Imam.

As we have already emphasized, this relationship must be understood in such a way that the manifestation of the Hidden and Awaited Imam is not simply an event that will happen one fine day. To await the Imam means that the Imam's manifestation depends, in a corresponding measure, upon each follower.

For ultimately—and this is how a distinguished shaykh once explained to me the meaning of one of his own books417—the deepest significance of the ghaybat, the occultation, is that human beings have themselves hidden the Imam from their own sight. They have made themselves incapable or unworthy of seeing him. We might express this by turning a familiar account around: sacred history tells us that God banished Adam from paradise, but the mystic discovers that it was Adam—humanity—who banished God from paradise. And that is the reality of the Infernum, of Hell.

Hell is this night of human consciousness, and it is this night that makes the hidden, inner meaning of revelation necessary. Only when the Resurrector appears is the night dispersed, because then every secret meaning of every Revelation becomes manifest: the triumph of ta'wîl, spiritual interpretation.

At that point, there will be no more esotericism, because nothing will remain hidden. This is the thought inspiring a great many traditional texts, of which we can recall only a few here. The Shaykhi school has admirably clarified, even in our own time, the profound meaning of the Imam's occultation: human beings themselves have become incapable of seeing him.

But we must emphasize that, from a very early period, the Imamis were already quoting and meditating upon a statement of the First Imam as a confirmation of their faith. For that statement had foretold the ordeal they would undergo among skeptics declaring: “God's Proof (Hojjat) has departed; the Imamate has disappeared; it is all over.” The Imam had announced: “Certainly, the Earth will never be deprived of a Proof of God.

“But human beings will be blind, unable to see him, because of their darkness, their excesses, and the crimes they commit against themselves”—that is, against their own souls. The Imam offered his disciples the story of Joseph as an example. Joseph stood there before his brothers, yet none of them recognized him. The great mystical poet Attar would say that every one of us, at every moment, commits the crime of selling a Joseph418. So it is today: the Imam sees each of us, but no one sees him419.

And this night is so deep, so desperate, that escaping from it requires the radical act of going into exile. The same shaykh mentioned above recalled to me a hadith declaring that a day will come when it will no longer be possible even to pronounce God's name in this world.

On occasion, disciples of the Fifth and Sixth Imams asked them about the meaning of a tradition whose words carry a deeply moving resonance, and which we recalled a few pages earlier: “Islam began as a stranger in exile, and it will become a stranger in exile again, as it was at the beginning. Blessed are those who go into exile.”

The two Imams gave essentially the same answer: “When the one among us [the Twelve] who is the Resurrector (Qâ'im) arises, he will proclaim to humanity an entirely new Call (da'wat, the Greek kerygma) to something entirely new, just as the Messenger of God proclaimed his Call”420.

Those exiles who are declared blessed are the ones who leave behind a religion defined by law and social order in order to join the spiritual worship to which the Imam calls them. To the extent that these exiles hear that Call here and now, the night of esotericism advances toward the dawn of the Resurrector, and the Imam's manifestation is already being accomplished through each of his followers. This is what is meant by the mystical growth of the Perfect Human Being.

The relationship between the event still to come—the Final Manifestation—and the event that is already taking place within the secret depths of human hearts is therefore essentially a process of inward realization. It gives the idea of the Imam's manifestation its present and practical meaning by showing us that the outward event is conditioned by the inward event. Such is the teaching of the masters of Shiite spirituality.

We have already quoted here the famous hadith in which the Prophet announces the manifestation of the last Imam, a declaration repeated afterward from Imam to Imam: “If the world had only one day left to exist, God would lengthen that day until a man of my descendants appeared. His name will be my name, his kunya [honorific name] will be my kunya. He will fill the Earth with harmony and justice, just as it will until then have been filled with violence and oppression.”

Sayyed Haydar Amoli interprets this hadith through ta'wîl, returning it to its inner meaning. The Prophet announces that the Imam “will fill the Earths of all hearts—those Earths which are as numerous as human hearts—with tawhîd and gnosis, after they have been devastated by shirk, the unconscious fragmentation of the divine and of being421.” For this is indeed what the manifestation of the last Imam means.

The texts describe the tumultuous struggle that he and his companions wage against the Adversaries, but that tumult is the very struggle being fought now within human hearts. And the struggle will continue until every heart has recognized the meaning of the theophanies, until all recognize that wherever they turn, “there is the Face of God” (3:109), because God alone truly is, because divine Oneness is precisely what makes the multitude of divine manifestations possible, and because the multiplicity of beings is the very essence and universe of the One.

Another very great master of Sufism, Sa'doddin Hamuyah (thirteenth century), whom we have quoted more than once already, declared: “The Hidden Imam [the Mahdi] will not appear until people are capable of understanding the secrets of tawhîd even in the straps of his sandals422.”

By this he meant the esoteric significance of bearing witness to the One and to divine Oneness: that beneath all the different divine forms, one and the same divinity is manifested. It is this same secret that Haydar Amoli perceived in the beautiful poem by Ibn Arabi with which he opened and closed one of his major works: “My heart has become capable of every form ... I profess the religion of love, and whichever direction its mount may take, love is my religion and my faith” (see above, Book IV, p. 189).

Ultimately, this secret is gathered together in the person of the Awaited Imam, just as it was in the person of the hero Humanus in Goethe's poem. For the Imam is the Perfect Human Being, the Human Being in the fullness of his spiritual reality.

Sa'doddin Hamuyah's saying, then, means that the Imam will appear only when, one follower after another, human beings have become capable of understanding what his very person announces. For the hidden reason why he remains concealed is none other than humanity itself. This saying is complemented by another: “When the Hidden Imam appears, through him stones, plants, and animals will begin to speak.”423

We shall return below to an Ismaili saying that echoes it: when a thing comes alive, it becomes a threshold to the spiritual world. Here, too, lies the secret of the “Night of Destiny.” We have seen how Imam Hasan al-Askari asked the venerable Hakima to recite over the newborn Imam the Qur'anic verses that announce this Night.

All of this, together with Lahiji's commentary, allows us to grasp the full meaning of the Imam's appearance and reign. The justice with which, according to every tradition concerning him, he will fill the world is not the prize in a struggle over social arrangements: it is the salvation of the cosmos. That is what gives meaning, generation after generation, to the efforts of those who are the “companions of the Imam.”

The Perfect Human is a theophany (mazhar), a visible manifestation of the supreme divine Name that gathers all the Names into itself. In his person he gathers together all the manifestations of the divine Names. This alone makes the human being “God's representative on earth,” and it is this humanity in its fullness that is identified with the Hidden Imam. The task of this divine representative is to uncover and bring to light the divine Name entrusted to each being, hidden in the sleep of seemingly lifeless nature or in human unawareness. As the perfect theophany, the Perfect Human enters into the secret of the divine manifestation within beings.

Through him, each being's hidden potential for perfection becomes actual: its secret, its inner meaning, is disclosed. Stones, plants, and animals will reveal their hidden meaning; so will every doctrine and every human religion. Divine Unity will thus reveal its very essence through the multitude of its manifestations. This is what the Coming—the Parousia—means. When the Imam's justice “levels” all opposition, it does so through the multiplicity of theophanies that disclose the secret of their unity. A spiritual teaching concerned with hidden meanings will naturally understand the renewal of all things as the unveiling of what lies concealed within them.

But Lahiji reminds us that we can know something perfectly only by becoming that thing. A mystic's verse says: “Become resurrection, and then behold resurrection.” The same truth is hinted at when it is said that God can be known only through God.424 This is why the resurrecting Imam, as Perfect Human and perfect theophany, is called the Initiator without equal, the “Seal of Initiation,” the Seal of walayat—the spiritual bond of guardianship and initiation. He places that Seal upon each of the Friends of God.

Against this background, the declaration of faith made by Shi'i spiritual philosophers who identify the Twelfth Imam with the Paraclete promised in John's Gospel takes on its full weight and meaning. There is nothing surprising about this identification once we recall how readily both Twelver Shi'i and Ismaili authors turn to the Gospel of John.425 We have already examined texts that make this identification.

Let us bring them together one last time, beginning with the scriptural passages on which they rely.

First comes the verse in John: “The Paraclete, whom the Father will send in my name, will teach you all things” (John 14:26; compare 14:16 and 15:26–27). Then comes this Qur'anic verse (61:6): “Jesus son of Mary said: Children of Israel, I am God's messenger to you, confirming the Torah that is in your hands and announcing a messenger who will come after me, whose name will be Ahmad”—a name understood as “most praised,” equivalent here to the Greek periklytos. A common Muslim interpretation holds that Parakletos, meaning comforter or consoler, is a distortion of periklytos, “most praised,” the Greek equivalent, on this account, of the Arabic Ahmad or Muhammad.

According to that interpretation, Christians made this alteration to prevent John's verses from being read as foretelling the Seal of the Prophets.426 In this reading, the promised Paraclete is the Prophet Muhammad himself. Shi'i interpretation, however, applies the title to the Twelfth Imam. The shift presents little difficulty. In announcing the Imam of Resurrection as his own descendant, the Prophet speaks of him almost as another self: “His name will be my name, and his byname will be my byname.”

More importantly, the promised Paraclete will not proclaim a new sacred Law. He will reveal the inward, hidden meaning of all the earlier Laws. Muhammad brought a new Law; the Twelfth Imam's mission is to reveal the meaning concealed within revelation. Historians of religion will notice that this is precisely the role the Manichaeans attributed to the prophet Mani, whom they too regarded as the Paraclete. Mani came above all to “resolve” what had remained unresolved: he was “the Solution.”427

Let us return, then, to the passage in which Haydar Amoli comments on the Prophet's words announcing the Imam of Resurrection: “Even if only one day remained…” Having quoted them, he adds: “This is what Jesus alluded to when he said: ‘We bring you the outward wording of Revelation (tanzil). As for its spiritual interpretation (ta'wil), the Paraclete (al-Faraqlit) will bring that to you at the end of this age.’ Now, in Christian terminology, the Paraclete is the awaited Imam, the Mahdi. The underlying meaning of the Prophet's words is therefore this: the Paraclete will bring you the spiritual meaning and true understanding of the Qur'an, just as I have brought you its revealed wording (tanzil) and its literal explanation.

“For the Qur'an has an outward and an inward aspect, a literal explanation and a spiritual interpretation. [...] As the Prophet also said: ‘The Qur'an has an outside and an inside; that inside has an inside of its own, and so on, through seven hidden depths—seven inward meanings.’”428 This text makes the identification unmistakable: for Haydar Amoli, the Paraclete promised by Jesus is the Twelfth Imam, now invisible, whose coming was foretold by Muhammad. It is for the Imam-Paraclete, as both Jesus and Muhammad are said to have declared, to reveal the hidden meaning of Revelation. The very principle of Shi'i spiritual interpretation is therefore inseparable from the idea of the Paraclete.

Another great Shi'i spiritual philosopher whom we have already encountered, Ibn Abi Jumhur (fifteenth century), comments on the same saying of the Prophet—“Even if only one day remained…”—in words taken here from a longer discussion: “When Jesus said, ‘We bring you the outward wording of Revelation; as for its spiritual interpretation, the Paraclete will bring that to you,’ his words refer to Muhammad, son of Imam Hasan al-Askari. He is the Imam of this age, recognized as the Mahdi, for the Paraclete, in Christian terminology, is Muhammad the Awaited One”—that is, the Twelfth Imam. “This is also what Kamal al-Din Abd al-Razzaq Kashani means in his spiritual interpretation of the three letters alif, lam, mim.429

“The letter alif refers to the divine Self (dhat Allah), the first principle of being (awwal al-wujud). The letter lam refers to the Active Intelligence, also called Gabriel, which stands at the centre—the middle point—of being (awsat al-wujud), as being flows from its Principle and pours forth to its furthest limit. The letter mim refers to Muhammad, the awaited Imam, who is the end of being (akhar al-wujud), the one through whom the cycle of being reaches completion. The end rejoins the beginning: the Seal is set in place.”430 Here again, the Seal of the cycle of being and the cycle of walayat is the Paraclete promised by Jesus. He is the Seal destined to bring our aeon, our present world-age, to its close.

As I said earlier, these statements by Twelver Shi'i thinkers have their counterpart in the work of an Iranian Ismaili spiritual philosopher, Abu Yaqub Sijistani (fourth/tenth century). In a chapter especially characteristic of the openness these thinkers showed toward the hidden meanings of other religions, Sijistani seeks to demonstrate that the inward meaning of the Christian Cross's four arms is the same as that of the four words making up the profession of God's oneness, the shahada.

He writes: “Jesus announced to his people that when the Imam of Resurrection—of whom Jesus himself was a symbol—laid bare, without any veil, the inner truths hidden beneath the structures of the revealed religions, whose very framework rests upon these truths, human beings would recognize them and could no longer deny them. [...] Jesus announced to his people that it would be easy for the Imam of Resurrection and his companions to draw out the spiritual meaning of every thing. [...] For it is reported that on the Night of Destiny light pours forth. At that moment walls, trees, and every lifeless body worship this light. This symbolizes the power of the Imam of Resurrection, the Qa'im, and his companions.”431

We already know what the “Night of Destiny” is: “In that Night the angels and the Spirit descend … and there is peace until the break of dawn” (Qur'an 97:1–5). These are the verses recited over “the Imam of this age” at his birth, precisely because he is that Night.
