When the Ismaili interpreter discovers the same secret in the inner meaning of the Cross as in the Night of Destiny, his interpretation approaches the mystery of the Cross of Light in the Acts of John, which replaces the outward Cross of Calvary. The secret of the Night of Destiny is that it is our present cycle of concealment, lasting until the dawn of the Imam's appearance.

The mystery of this Night is one with the mystery of the Cross of Light. That is why Jesus foretold and prefigured the Paraclete, the Imam of Resurrection. The Night of Destiny transforms the night of concealment (ghaybat), just as the Cross of Light, made up of all souls of light, transforms the Cross of Calvary. In both cases, this transfiguration comes about through those who hear the same Call. Because the Night itself is the Imam, the dawn it announces is already present, for and through each faithful follower, in the “entirely new Call” to which we heard the Fifth and Sixth Imams allude a few pages ago.

The imaginative consciousness—the faculty by which spiritual realities are perceived in images—makes such visionary anticipations possible because it perceives events in the Malakut, the spiritual world. Since the soul itself is the place where these events unfold, chronological distances fall away. Shi'i consciousness can already hear the words that the Imam will one day address to humanity, because he is already speaking them in the world of the soul. And the words in which he announces himself ring out triumphantly: in the essence of his being, he gathers together the entire meaning of prophecy and walayat.

Standing against the sacred sanctuary of the Kaaba, the Imam declares that whoever wishes to dispute with him about Adam should know that he, the Imam, is closer to Adam than any other human being. He makes the same claim concerning every prophet: I am closest to Noah, Abraham, Moses, Jesus, Muhammad. “I am closest to the Qur'an, closest to the tradition of the Prophet.” More forcefully still, he names each pair formed by a prophet and his first Imam: whoever has set his heart on Adam and Seth, Adam's son and Imam, should know that I am Adam and Seth.

And so on: I am Noah and Shem; I am Abraham and Ishmael; I am Moses and Joshua; I am Jesus and Simon; I am Muhammad and the Commander of the Faithful; I am Hasan and Husayn; I am all the Imams. Anyone who has read God's ancient books—the books of Adam, Noah, and Abraham, the Torah, the Psalms, and the Gospel—must recognize me, for they all speak of me.

Then comes the solemn appeal: “I adjure, in God's name, everyone who hears my words, now that the Witness has appeared among you—the one who until now was Hidden.”432 With the appearance of the one called the Resurrector (Qa'im), the era of all the sacred Laws (shari'at) reaches its completion. His coming brings back into this world the companions, the “knights,” who will fight beside him in the final struggle that must bring our aeon to its end before the Great Resurrection (Qiyamat kubra).

The pilgrims of whom it is said, “Blessed are those who leave their homeland…,” will surely answer the Imam's call.

But not everyone will do so. Here Shi'i eschatology reveals its deepest foreboding. It is as though the Resurrection cannot be announced without alarming those who have seized possession of the “divine cause” and used it to subject others to their ambitions, holding each person's destiny captive. A tradition attributed to the Fifth Imam, Muhammad al-Baqir, shows the last Imam, the Resurrector, approaching the city of Kufa. A procession of several thousand men comes out to meet him. They are all thoroughly respectable people: professional reciters of the Qur'an, doctors of religious Law, and so forth—in short, the whole company of authoritarian devotees that official piety has built into a social force. Every one of them rejects the Imam: “Son of Fatima! Go back where you came from. We have no need of you. We have no need of a son of Fatima.”433

When I first read this text, I had the sense that I had encountered something like these words before, sounding from far away. They led me back to the refusal spoken by the Grand Inquisitor in Dostoevsky's famous novel, addressing Christ, returned to Seville, on the night the Inquisitor holds him prisoner: “Why have You come back to disturb us? … Have You the right to reveal to us a single one of the mysteries of the world from which You come? … Had You forgotten that tranquillity, and even death, are preferable to man than the freedom to distinguish good from evil? … Go away and do not come back, ever again.”434

The resemblance between the reception awaiting the returning Imam and that awaiting the returning Christ was striking. I mentioned it to a shaykh whom I knew to be both profound and discreet. In reply, he first reminded me of texts saying that the Twelfth Imam passes through a concealment comparable to Joseph's after his brothers sold him, and that of all human beings he most closely resembles Christ, for he must return just as Christ will return. The Qur'an (4:156) teaches that Christ did not die upon the Cross but was “taken up by God,” as Enoch and Elijah had been. When the Imam returns, the doctors of religious Law, in Kufa and elsewhere, will tell him in vain: “Go away and never come back.”

For the Imam will wield a sword not forged from earthly metal, a sword that penetrates souls. With him will come not only the mighty, proud Companions sleeping their mysterious sleep until his arrival, but legions of angels: those who were with Noah in the ark; with Abraham when he was cast into the fire; with Moses when he divided the sea; with Jesus when God took him up; with Muhammad at the Battle of Badr; and with Imam Husayn on the day of his martyrdom at Karbala, although Husayn refused even their help.435 Then Christ, the Messiah (Masih), will return. A magnificent visionary ceremony shows him descending at dawn from the white minaret east of Damascus, supported by two angels, and performing the Prayer behind the Imam. “Yes,” the shaykh told me, “Christ son of Mary will return.

“But you see, he will not return until our Imam has destroyed the power of all those who might still say to him: ‘Go away and never come back.’” Any commentary would only weaken the force of that remark. The shaykh had meditated on the relationship between Christianity and Shi'ism, between Christ and the Imam, in a way that was his own secret. Yet this secret shines through the many references to Christ found in Shi'i teaching about the Imams.

Consider the extraordinary sermons in which, speaking through the lips of one Imam or another, an eternal Imam declares: “I am the one called Elijah in the Gospel”—making Shi'ism a witness to the Transfiguration on Mount Tabor. Or again: “I am the Christ who heals the blind and the lepers, who gives life to birds made of clay and disperses the clouds”—“that is, the second Christ,” a commentary specifies. “I am he and he is I (ana huwa wa huwa ana).”436 There is also a direct retelling of an episode in the Infancy Gospels, the teaching of the secrets of the philosophical alphabet, in which the young Imam Muhammad al-Baqir, the Fifth Imam, simply takes Jesus' place.437

And there is the wonderful visionary dream of Princess Nargis, mother of the Twelfth Imam, in which she sees Christ and his apostles, the Prophet and his Imams, ascending the same pulpit of light together—a story we translated earlier. We may add that four of the Gospel Beatitudes appear in the spiritual testament of the Seventh Imam of Twelver Shi'ism, Imam Musa Kazim (d. 183/799).438 For a long time these texts, these events, and the considerable writings they inspired remained unknown in the West. Once brought to light, however, they confront scholars of sacred learning, and everyone concerned with comparative theology among the “religions of the Book,” with questions too new to be settled by ready-made answers.

Perhaps we can avoid such ready-made answers, while taking inspiration from what I earlier called the “mystery of Pentecost,” by making one final comparison. Its implications remain to be explored, but by now the reader may already have thought of it. I have in mind Joachim of Fiore and his followers in the twelfth and thirteenth centuries. Shi'i spiritual philosophers speak of the “eternal religion” and the “Paraclete.” Drawing upon a tradition of prophetic Christianity, Joachim's followers speak of the “Eternal Gospel” and the “reign of the Paraclete.”

For Shi'is, the coming of the Imam-Paraclete will inaugurate the reign of the pure spiritual meaning of divine revelations. This is what they mean by the “Eternal Religion,” and it is what the reformed Ismailism of Alamut sought, perhaps prematurely, to bring about through the proclamation of the Great Resurrection on 8 August 1164. For Joachim's followers, the reign of the Holy Spirit, the Paraclete, will be the age in which spiritual understanding (intelligentia spiritualis) of the Scriptures prevails. This is what they mean by the “Eternal Gospel.” The resonance between the two is striking.

We can speak of a shared “hermeneutic situation”—a common way of understanding—despite the differences arising from the Qur'anic Revelation. Those very differences make the comparison all the more instructive.

The driving idea behind the Eternal Gospel in the teaching of Joachim of Fiore (1145–1202), the celebrated founder of the Ordo Florensis (Saint John in Flower), is that humanity develops through the unceasing work of the Holy Spirit. This development will culminate in the reign of the Paraclete promised in John's Gospel. At its culmination, human beings will attain the Spirit's perfect freedom, born of the love that the Holy Spirit awakens in the human heart.439 Adam will no longer be under the satanic power that prompts him to choose “against God.” It is true that Joachim's teaching influenced thinkers century after century, reaching even the philosophy of freedom in German idealism.

Yet we must avoid a fundamental confusion. The unfolding of the “history of salvation” is not the unfolding of a principle inherent in history, advancing in a straight line according to what is now called “historical causation.” Quite the contrary: salvation unfolds only through the Holy Spirit's continuous and active intervention. This creative intervention repeatedly breaks the course imposed on things by bodily desire and worldly ambition. It is not a natural transition in which the old disappears to make room for the new.

Each time, it is an act of spiritual creation. Such creations are continually threatened by the world. Their gravest danger is that the very idea of creation by the Spirit may be degraded into the idea of an ordinary historical power at work within the world. That is precisely how sacred history—the history that takes place, as we would say, in the Malakut—is turned into secular history, how an inward history is replaced by an outward, supposedly objective one. This is the process of secularization in its specifically metaphysical sense: the elimination of metaphysics itself.

Yet such a process cannot accommodate the idea of the Holy Spirit working in human hearts, any more than it can accommodate the Imam-Paraclete working in the hearts of his followers.

For Joachim, this work of the Spirit unfolds within the famous scheme dividing the history of salvation into three ages, each bearing the Seal of one Person of the divine Trinity.440

First, there is the age of the Father, the revelation of the Law. Here human sinfulness comes to the fore, although the ideal of the coming spiritual life (vita spiritualis) is already foreshadowed in figures such as the prophet Elijah and John the Baptist.

Second comes the age of the Son, the revelation of Redemption. Humanity becomes the “Son of God” and discovers deliverance from sin. Its representative spiritual figure is the cleric, or better still the monk, as conceived in the ideal of the Byzantine Greek Church.

Third comes the age of the Spirit, marked by the arrival of the order of the viri spirituales, the spiritual human beings in whom the divine character of humanity's creative nature is revealed.

Each age has its own kind of human being and its own spiritual way of life. The viri spirituales of the age of the Spirit are neither “fathers,” as defined by the Old Testament, nor “sons,” as defined by the New. They are angelic spirits, formed in the image and likeness of the Holy Spirit (Angelici spiritus, qui neque patres sunt, neque filii, ad similitudinem Spiritus Sancti).441 To the world around them they can appear only as something beyond the ordinary human. Their knowledge is essentially spiritual, with nothing in common with the doctrina litteralis, the learning tied to the literal text, of the clerical Church. That Church now occupies the position of the merchants driven from the Temple.

If the Father's age can be represented by manual labour, and the Son's by the efforts of doctrinal theology, the Spirit's age is an outpouring of hymns, an intoxication of the spirit (ebrietas), best expressed by jubilatio and gaudium: exultation and joy. This is the very “joy” which, in Shi'i language, names the appearance of the Imam-Paraclete, when, as we have been told, trees and stones will speak. One might say that the difference between the viri spirituales and the clerics is the same as that between the urafa, the mystics and spiritual philosophers, and the fuqaha, the doctors of religious Law who reject the Imam when he appears.

The viri spirituales, in whom the contemplative life (vita contemplativa) reaches its highest form, are the people of Joachim's Ecclesia spiritualis, the Spiritual Church. It is “virginal” because it “knows no man”: it has no part in the interests and ambitions of those who are not spiritual human beings. (Here we may recall the Shi'i injunction to befriend everything that draws one nearer to the Imam, and to keep apart from whatever is not the Imam, is not directed toward him, or is directed against him. We have seen this as the “fourth pillar” of the Shaykhi school, supporting both the idea of a hidden spiritual hierarchy and the idea of the final transformation.)

This Ecclesia spiritualis, this reign of the Paraclete, is the “Church of John” succeeding the “Church of Peter.” As Berdyaev writes, the Church of John is not a guardian of the poor adjusted to the weakness of sinners, to the mediocrity of humanity at large, or even indulgent toward every form of human wretchedness. It is the eternal, mysterious Church, “discovering within itself the true face of man and of his ecstasy upon the heights.”442 The idea of the Paraclete's reign as the final form of spiritual life could only strike at and shake the central pillar of Peter's Church, the institutional Roman Church.

In this vision that institution becomes merely a transitional stage in the history of salvation. The papacy belongs to the second age, that of the Son; it disappears with the Paraclete's reign, when the viri spirituales, the people of the Spirit, succeed the bishops. It would be illuminating to compare the way Joachim's spiritual interpretation of the four Gospels works toward the coming of the Paraclete with the way Shi'i interpretation of the Qur'an works toward the coming of the Imam.

The passage from one age to another is not the result of a historical cause operating within the world. Each transition is a resurrection. Only a creative act of the Holy Spirit can set an age condemned to die upon the path toward resurrection from the dead. This is also the technical sense of qiyamat, resurrection, in Ismaili spiritual philosophy. Without that ever-renewed act of creation, every tradition merely lengthens its funeral procession along the road of historical causation. No Tradition remains alive without continual rebirth: an ever-new birth.

The ages of the Father and the Son lead toward the age of the Spirit, the reign of the Paraclete, just as the cycle of prophecy and the cycle of walayat lead toward the final Seal of walayat: the Twelfth Imam, in whom our thinkers have recognized the Paraclete. The Church of John, the Paraclete's reign, is the Nova Hierosolyma, the New Jerusalem, built of different stones after a migration that transforms the meaning of the departure from Egypt, the land of exile. We have heard the call to this migration in Shi'ism too, in the Imam's words: “Tuba li'l-ghuraba!

“Blessed are those who leave their homeland for the sake of the Spirit.” And we have been told that humanity continues to exist thanks to these travellers, who, unknown to the multitude, perform the divine service of the highest “heavenly” chivalry. Through that service—through their union with the Intelligence that is the Holy Spirit—the higher worlds remain in communication with ours. We might therefore compare the viri spirituales with the “Friends of God,” since both belong to the same “spiritual chivalry.”

The reign of the Paraclete is the manifestation of these spiritual human beings, these Friends of God, into whom the Holy Spirit pours intelligentia spiritualis in the new Temple. Their knowledge is no longer a literal understanding shut up within itself, something that can be fixed in the written letter, whether of theology or of the most modern science. It is an inexhaustible treasure of wisdom, a spring of living water welling up into eternal life (fons aquae salientis in vitam aeternam). And here, once again, as so often in our texts, we return to the threshold of the “Spring of Life” (ayn al-hayat).

Yet does this “vision of ecstasy upon the heights” contain its own danger—a temptation to rush ahead? We can glimpse the danger in the very success of Joachim's idea: not only in its later development among the Hussites of fifteenth-century Bohemia, but also in its powerful influence upon so many philosophers and theologians of history—philosophers such as Fichte, Schelling, and Hegel, and spiritual thinkers such as Franz von Baader, Solovyov, Berdyaev, and Merezhkovsky. Philosophers, admittedly, bear a responsibility here from which those who are “theosophers,” in the original sense of the word, are exempt.

A few pages ago, I warned against the danger that the Paraclete idea in Joachim's teaching might be secularized. That danger became reality. Philosophy treated it as a triumph to separate the idea of the Paraclete from the spiritual world that both grounds it and guarantees its truth. Agnosticism turned the Church of John into a social messianism, a caricature of the original. Despair methodically closed off every way by which human beings might escape the absurdity of death. A phenomenology of the historical Spirit was no longer a spiritual interpretation guided by the Holy Spirit. And perhaps the primary cause of this change was a confusion of places and times.

The realm in which sacred history, the history of salvation, takes place is not the realm addressed by the philosophy of history. The Holy Spirit's creative action breaks through both history and the philosophy of history, for it sets human beings free from them. It takes place in the invisible spiritual world, the Malakut. Nor does it take place in the chronological time of outward history. Joachim of Fiore's three ages are not three successive periods of historical time.443 In fact, we know no exact dates separating them. If we tried to identify such boundaries, it would be difficult to find in the events of outward history the evidence needed to draw them.

Rather, the three ages are units of existential time, of inward time. Think here of Semnani's psycho-spiritual time (zaman anfusi), of subtle time (zaman latif), and of the measure of time allotted to each being in the thought of Qazi Sa'id Qummi. The succession of these ages is played out within souls, in the mystery of each individual soul: in its consent and refusal, its generosity and its withholding, or, in Qazi Sa'id's terms, in the states through which its own eternally allotted measure of time passes. In historical time, the ages actually coexist.

It is not within humanity's collective historical time that the Church of John succeeds the Church of Peter. Such a succession can occur only by bringing historical time itself to an end, together with its chains of events and determining precedents. How could we place it within history, when history is no longer there—just as concealment (ghaybat) “is no longer there” when the Imam appears? Existential time breaks the fabric of historical time for every soul that enters the world of the Spirit and anticipates the mystery of death.

But outward history continues after each soul's breakthrough. Each soul must break through it in turn. Thus the two Churches are divided among souls: invisibly, within each soul, the Church of John succeeds the Church of Peter, in the measure of time belonging to that soul alone, a measure that is also the measure of its being.

Yet because souls coexist in this world's mode of existence, the two Churches also coexist in historical time. This is already the arresting meaning that Joachim drew from a single Gospel passage, where Jesus says to Peter, “Feed my sheep,” only to say immediately afterward, speaking of John, “If I want him to remain until I come, what is that to you?” (John 21:16 ff., 22).

Does the fate of Joachim's idea in the West not give us two reasons for reflection? On the one hand, it supports the comparison we have just made between the Ecclesia spiritualis of the Paraclete's reign and the coming of the Imam, whom his followers recognize as the Paraclete promised in John's Gospel. On the other, it reveals a difference that, if properly understood, may open an unexplored perspective for philosophical thought. We have already noticed that familiar words in our languages, such as secularization and laicization, have no exact equivalents in Arabic or Persian. These terms presuppose the existence of clerics, and thus a clergy, clerical status, and finally the phenomenon of the Church.

But that phenomenon is absent in Islam. And in Joachim's view, the Church of the clergy is precisely what characterizes the age of the Son. Islam and Islamic spirituality, however, have no age of the Son.444 In Shi'i theology, the teaching about the Imams corresponds to Christology in Christian theology.

But everything we have seen shows that it corresponds no less to a theology of the Holy Spirit as Paraclete. This double correspondence is also found in certain early Christologies, where the distinction between the Son and the Spirit had not yet been clearly established. Its implications reach very far, and we cannot pursue all of them here.

For Islamic spiritual philosophy, sacred history moves not through three stages but through two: descent (nuzul) and ascent (su'ud); origin (mabda') and return (ma'ad); the revelation of the sacred text (tanzil) and its spiritual interpretation (ta'wil); and so on. It cannot have a reign of the “Son,” precisely because the Qur'anic Revelation comes after Christianity, after the reign and history of the “Son.” It passes directly from the cycle of prophecy, the reign of the Law (shari'at) revealed through the prophets, to the cycle of walayat, of intelligentia spiritualis: the cycle of the Imamate, whose Seal is the Twelfth Imam. Here there is no reason to say that the reign of the creative Spirit presupposes “redemption”: it is that redemption.

There is thus no need for an intervening age like the one in which the specifically Christian process of secularization arises. That process follows from the Church of the clergy, and it in turn explains why the political and social ideologies of the West are secularized theologies. Philosophy may no longer be the “handmaid of theology” (ancilla theologiae), but it has become the handmaid of sociology. The importation into Islam of a secularization and an ideology alien to its theological history could therefore be all the more disastrous.

By contrast, our Shi'i thinkers' identification of the Imam with the Paraclete promises a particularly liberating meaning. It agrees perfectly with their identification of the Active Intelligence with the Holy Spirit: an identification that puts each philosopher in direct contact with the spiritual world, without the intervention of any teaching authority, clerical or secular. Where no clerical authority of this kind has existed, it cannot turn into its opposite—something like a post-Church.

But wherever secularization and the reshaping of religion as a social institution presuppose the Church, and hence the age of the “Son,” they show by that very fact that the passage from the Church of the clerics to the Church of John, the Church of the viri spirituales, has been missed. There may still be a “philosophy of Spirit,” but the Spirit itself will soon have vanished from it. Islamic spiritual philosophy, like Christian spiritual philosophy, will instead continue to pursue a metaphysics of the Holy Spirit. In inward sacred history, the cycle of walayat has succeeded the prophets' cycle of shari'at.

Yet the two coexist in historical time, just as the Churches of Peter and John coexist, because the reign of the shari'at continues until the Imam-Paraclete appears. The arif, the mystic possessed of inward knowledge, is a pilgrim on the road, a salik, a homo viator. He already belongs to the reign of the Paraclete; in this sense he, too, is a follower of John.

Shall we ask how the pilgrimage to which he sacrifices everything can be reconciled with the demands of the surrounding world, the demands supposedly made by “his times”? It will always be too soon to ask that question as long as the world cannot see the Imam where he is. Because it has failed to see him where he is, the hope and preparation for the resurrection of the dead have collapsed under their own weight. Instead of the resurrection of the dead, people now expect nothing more than social revolution. But Islam is not responsible for that transformation.

It is all too easy to put Christianity on trial from the outside. Very few Christian thinkers have had the clarity and courage to confront Christianity's tragedy. Berdyaev was one of them. It is no accident that we cited him at the beginning of our inquiry and return to him now at its close. The themes he brings to light are precisely those that Shi'i spiritual philosophy and its teaching about the Imams can suggest to a student of sacred learning.

We are not trying to argue a case before the court of history; that would be as pointless as it would be absurd. We are trying to find a way toward the world—or worlds—without whose presence human beings cannot endure. Berdyaev wrote that Christianity's tragedy lay in its failure to discover the whole of the “Christology of man”: the mystery of humanity's divine nature, although discovering that mystery is the very mission of religious consciousness.445 “The Church of Golgotha, in which the Christological truth is only imperfectly disclosed, stands opposed to the integral Church of Christ.”446

Only the discipline demanded by a free act of creation brings humanity face to face with this new aspect of Christology. In a passage inspired throughout by the spirit of John and Joachim, Berdyaev writes: “If redemption demands great obedience, creation—the creative act—demands great daring. We glimpse Christ advancing only when we make a bold attempt. The spirit of obedience has always seen in Christ only the Crucified, only the aspect of the redeemer. The sacrifice of courage, the heroic decision, is needed to launch ourselves beyond these safe shores.

“We must stand without fear over the abyss. The third revelation in Spirit will have no sacred text; it will not be a voice from above. It will take place within man and humanity. It will be the anthropological revelation, the discovery of the Christology of man.”447

Our Shi'i spiritual philosophers know, too, that the awaited Imam, the Paraclete, will bring no new shari'at, no new sacred Book, but will reveal the meaning hidden in all the sacred texts. And he himself is that meaning, as the Perfect Human (Insan kamil, anthropos teleios). When the Russian philosopher meditates on the significance of the future Christ's appearance, and when our Iranian Shi'i thinkers meditate on the coming of the “Awaited Imam,” both are awaiting the same full “anthropological revelation”—the disclosure of what humanity truly is. This revelation cannot come from outside. It must take place within human beings living in the Spirit. For this is not a revelation humanity is still waiting to receive from God. It is one that God is waiting to receive from humanity.

But only a metaphysics of the last things—an eschatological metaphysics—can give us a horizon wide enough for such a thought. That is why our texts have led us to consider Joachim's understanding of the final age. A tradition offered us the image of the “Hidden Treasure,” longing, in its solitude before the worlds, to be known. Ismaili spiritual philosophers derive the name of God, Allah, from the root w-l-h, with its suggestion of grief and longing. Berdyaev, for his part, wrote that the image of “God's sorrow over man and love for man brings us close to the ultimate secrets.” The mystics have spoken of the birth of God within the human being, he says.

But there is another mystery: the birth of the human being within God. Humanity cries out for God to be born within it; God cries out for humanity to be born within him.448 We earlier encountered a verse from Isaiah translated by a Kabbalist: “And in all their anguish, it was He who was anguished.” The Russian philosopher called this birth of humanity within God the “Christological consciousness of man,” the “new aeon,” the “reign of the Paraclete.”

What, then, of everything that has appeared, and continues to appear, in Shi'i consciousness under the figure of the Twelfth Imam? What of the events of his sacred story—his birth, concealment, appearances, and coming as Paraclete? Even, and especially, if these are visionary events rather than historical events in the ordinary sense—even, and especially, if the story teaches us less about what happened outwardly than about what appeared and was genuinely experienced within Shi'i consciousness—all of it must now acquire meaning for a Western reader. From now on, no attempt we make at an eschatological metaphysics ought to ignore the Shi'i theme of the Hidden Imam.

The Shi'i spiritual philosopher Haydar Amoli showed us Adam—humanity—bowed beneath the “burden that the heavens, the earth, and the mountains had refused,” but that Adam had agreed to bear. This burden was what Haydar Amoli technically calls ontological tawhid: the inwardly lived recognition that the One alone truly is, the hidden meaning of the monotheistic profession of faith. If humanity is too weak to bear that meaning, then in losing God it loses itself. All that remains is to cry, “God is dead,” without realizing that this is the cry of someone already dead: humanity itself died first. Unfortunately, our fashionable theologies and philosophies of the death of God and the death of humanity are still the scholastic exercises of more or less secularized clerics.

The inward meaning of tawhid, culminating in the highest of all the divine manifestations that mark humanity's spiritual growth, is the mystery of the supreme theophany: the appearance of the last Imam, finally bathing in peace and light those ravaged and devastated Earths “of which there are as many as there are human hearts,” as Haydar Amoli said. With the coming of the Seal of walayat, the teaching about the Imams reaches its fulfilment and brings forth the dawn of humanity's resurrection—the day of humanity's birth within God. Here, too, we may say that “the ultimate secret lies in this: the divine mystery and the human mystery are one and the same mystery; within God is kept the mystery of humanity, and within humanity the secret of God.”449

4. The Personal Guide

This brings us, at last, to the innermost life of the Shi'i spiritual seeker: to what the theme of the Twelfth Imam means in lived experience. His invisible Presence safeguards the spiritual life against being reduced to a social phenomenon. It is a Presence at once infinitely distant and intimately near: withdrawn to the outermost limit of our aeon, yet immediately present in the depths of the heart. It is tied to no fixed geographical place, yet it can break into any place and carry the person to whom the Imam appears into the Imam's own world: to the Green Island, for example, or to some uncharted place in the heart of the desert, beyond the reach of any map. We have seen examples of this. The Twelfth Imam, the Hidden Imam, is above all the form in which the invisible Personal Guide makes himself known to Shi'i consciousness.

The theme is inexhaustibly rich, and it defines a kind of spiritual life as intensely personal as Shi'i spirituality itself. We have encountered many variations on it. There are the Uwaysis, those who are set upon the spiritual Path by an invisible Guide, without needing any human master.

There is the “Perfect Nature,” the philosopher's personal angel among the Ishraqiyun, the philosophers of illumination who inherited the Hermetic tradition; the “heavenly companion” of the Gnostics; Mani's “heavenly Twin”; the “invisible master” (ostad ghaybi), the “witness in heaven,” spoken of by Najm al-Din Kubra and his school. (Who is the seeker, and who is the one sought? Kubra answers: “The one sought is the divine Light; the seeker is a particle of that Light.” He perceives the presence of the “invisible Personal Guide” in the meeting blaze of two flames, one reaching from heaven and the other from earth.) There are the “prophets of your being” in Semnani; “the angel who speaks within you” among certain Kabbalists; the “Friend of God” for Rulman Merswin, and others.

All are recurring forms of a single archetypal Figure. In Shi'i spirituality, this figure reaches its highest and most commanding manifestation in the Imam, the “Friend of God,” as invisible Personal Guide. Between him and the faithful person he guides there is formed a bond of knightly loyalty, expressed most movingly in the “pilgrim's prayer” that we shall translate on the final page. This bond springs from the feeling of the traveller, the salik, the homo viator. He is not a sinner or an invalid but an exile, someone far from home, searching for the road that will take him “home” again. The Imam shows him that road. And the person to whom the Imam reveals it through his intimate presence has no need of a human master or guide.

One of the best-known Uwaysis was the Iranian Sufi Abu'l-Hasan Kharraqani (d. 425/1034), to whom the following saying is attributed: “I am astonished at disciples who declare that they must have this or that master. You know perfectly well that I have never been taught by any human being. God himself was my guide, although I have the greatest respect for all masters.”450 Kharraqani was guided by the spiritual presence, the “Angel” (ruhaniyya), of Abu Yazid Bastami; Attar of Nishapur (d. around 617/1220) had for his guide the Angel, or “being of light,” of Hallaj. We could assemble many testimonies of this kind.

I shall recall only one already discussed here, showing that such teaching is still given today. An eminent shaykh, a professor at the theological university of Qom, advised his students to study mystical spiritual philosophy and practise Sufi spirituality, but to avoid entering a tariqa, a Sufi order. To join an order is to bind oneself in subjection to a shaykh, and thereby to confine oneself within that shaykh's personality and spiritual horizon. The Shi'i mystic, the irfani, must choose the Imam himself directly as his qutb, his spiritual pole, and follow this Personal Guide without an intermediary. His only shaykh is the Imam.451

All spiritual teaching thus centres on the quest for and encounter with the Personal Guide. Its purpose is to awaken, in the depths of a person, the capacity to meet the “invisible personal master” who is the Imam.

Indeed, the word imam itself means guide. This personal encounter gives Shi'i spirituality its most distinctive form. We saw an exemplary instance in the life of Shaykh Ahmad Ahsai. That is why, in Book I, chapter VII, we dwelt at length on the mutual relationship between knowing—or becoming conscious of—the Imam and knowing—or becoming conscious of—oneself. Through the particular calling that Shi'i teaching about the Imams addresses to every spiritual seeker, prophetic religion reaches its fulfilment. The Imam, the Guide, brings no new Law. He uncovers and resolves the hidden meaning of all prophetic revelations, enabling his followers to be born into the reign of the Paraclete.

Any reader familiar with the changes sweeping through the modern East will inevitably ask: what will these things mean to the generations to come? What, for example, does the mysterious figure of the Twelfth Imam mean to the Iranian young people of our day? I think the reflections that have emerged throughout this long inquiry show that I am not inclined to minimize the immensely serious problems raised by the transformations now under way.

But I have considered these problems according to measures that do not necessarily coincide with those of today's prevailing anthropology. For that very reason, I am all the more struck by certain enduring features of spiritual life that escape, and always will escape, every survey, sociological or otherwise. Each Shi'i has always maintained absolute discretion on these matters—the practice of taqiyya. This is why I attach such importance to a testimony I related elsewhere and now think it fitting to reproduce.

It came from a young Iranian friend of mine, not yet thirty, highly representative of students educated in the West, among whom practically all the conditions for spiritual uprooting are present. (We might say: all the conditions that lead the young Parthian prince in the “Hymn of the Pearl,” in the Acts of Thomas, to forget his origins.) He was completing his studies at a Swiss university. That country might have offered him everything he could wish for; yet he spent most of his evenings with another young Iranian student, nostalgically recalling the wide deserts of Iran and the pilgrimage to the holy city of Qom, about 140 kilometres south of Tehran.

Then one night he made, in a dream, the pilgrimage he had longed to undertake in waking life. His account bore so clearly the marks of an initiatory dream, and the power of the archetype was so strongly felt in it, that I asked him to write it down. With his permission, and referring to him discreetly by his initials, H. B., I reproduce his account here.

“One night I dreamed that my friend and I had set out on foot from Tehran for Qom. We were not wearing our everyday clothes but the garments worn by dervishes, the Sufis, in our country. We followed paths through the fields leading south toward Qom. We were about to enter the desert south of Tehran when immense creatures suddenly appeared before us, something like dragons. All at once I could no longer see my friend. I had the impression that he had turned back and gone north. I felt that I was alone.

“But now I found something like a spear in my hands, so long that I had never seen anything like it in real life. I fought the dragons for a long, long time. At last I must have succeeded in cutting them to pieces, for I saw that a torrent flowing nearby was carrying away their dismembered bodies, and I myself was immersed in the torrent. I came out of that bath and felt that I was naked. Then someone threw a long piece of cloth across my shoulders.

“At that moment the ground beneath me seemed to be giving off steam or mist, so that nothing could be seen. Suddenly the holy city appeared in the distance, with the glittering golden dome and minarets of its sacred precinct. I made my way toward the city and reached a crossroads covered by a vaulted roof. There someone pointed out to me the house of the Awaited Imam. Its door stood wide open. Only a short distance, a few hundred paces, separated me from the Imam's house. … At that moment I awoke from my dream.

“But it has left a deep impression on me. What matters most to me is the distance that separated me from the open door of the Imam's house. Ever since that night, I have felt that my life, whether I am dreaming or awake, consists of crossing that distance. It is the exact measure of my life. It governs the time and harmony of my whole existence. It is the real time and space that I experience upon this Earth.”

Once again, many other testimonies of this kind could be cited. All bear witness to the presence of the Hidden Imam, “invisible to the senses, but present in the hearts of his faithful,” and therefore visible in dreams or visionary encounters. The “history” of the Twelfth Imam thus continues through events kept secret within the consciousness of those devoted to him. The testimony I have been allowed to reproduce seems to gather them all into itself. Here, in modern Iran, a young Iranian of our own time teaches every student of religion what the religion of the Personal Guide means.

A religion reveals its secret most fully in its prayers and liturgies, far better than in any systematic account of its doctrines. It therefore seems fitting to close our inquiry with a prayer addressed by pilgrims to the mysterious person of the Twelfth Imam. In him, through the dream of his mother, Princess Nargis, the spiritual descendants of Christ and of Muhammad meet. Whatever a Shi'i's personal position, whether Sufi or not, the same hope stirs in all of them. As soon as they try to state it in words and explain it in one way or another, their interpretations may differ.

Yet some forms of expression stand above the rest, capable of uniting them all; these are found in the prayers addressed to the Twelfth Imam. We should recall that the Imam's very “absence”—the fact that he is not physically present to lead the communal Prayer in the mosque—has especially encouraged Shi'ism to develop forms of private devotion and liturgy. The oldest of these were taught by the Imams themselves.

Enriched over the centuries, they constitute an extensive body of literature arranged according to an exceptionally rich liturgical calendar. It deserves systematic and comparative study. (We have quoted some examples earlier.) Among these personal devotions are the “prayers of Visitation,” recited either during pilgrimage to the shrines of the holy Imams or, more simply and more often, during a “visitation in the mind,” undertaken in the quiet concentration of a private place of prayer.

We have already sketched the story of the founding of the sanctuary at Jamkaran. In Samarra, where the sacred biography of the Twelfth Imam led us earlier, two shrines still stand. One houses four tombs: that of the Tenth Imam, Ali Naqi; that of his son, Imam Hasan al-Askari; that of Hasan's wife, the Byzantine princess Nargis; and that of his aunt, the venerable Hakima Khatun, sister of Imam Ali Naqi. A second shrine shelters the underground place through which the young Imam, Princess Nargis's child, Muhammad al-Qa'im or al-Mahdi, disappeared, becoming the Hidden Imam. Pious and learned Shi'is have composed many prayers for these pilgrimages, whether they are undertaken bodily or spiritually. Such texts disclose more clearly than almost anything else the deepest spirit of Shi'ism.

We have come to know that spirit as, above all, a spiritual chivalry. The pact of loyalty uniting the javanmard, the spiritual knight, to his Imam inspires ardent words and commitments.

We must understand that the passage into the reign of the Paraclete, whether in the inward time of each human being or at the close of the entire span of historical humanity, does not take place without a struggle against all the powers of denial, hardening, and death. The Shi'i mystic, too, is attentive to the impermanence of things, the passing nature of every substance, and the threat that personal existence may dissolve.

But it is one thing to accept all this as the normal law of existence, and to make the emptying away of being the aim of meditation and spiritual discipline, so as to recover the primordial Void. It is quite another to experience it as a wound in being, the result of a satanic and destructive hold that must be fought so that existence may be restored to its wholeness.

In the latter view, the governing idea is apokatastasis: the “restoration” or “return” of all things to their original purity and fullness. It was this idea that set Zoroastrian consciousness against the powers of Ahriman, and it is this idea that we find again in the Shi'i spiritual ethos. Haydar Amoli identified the Twelfth Imam with the Paraclete of the Gospel; Qutb al-Din Ashkevari identified him with the last of Zoroastrianism's three Saoshyants, the future saviours. The millennium of the last Saoshyant and the millennium of the last Imam are the setting for this struggle. Every javanmard, every knight of faith, longs to take part in it at his Imam's side.

Here, then, is the pilgrim's prayer. Like all prayers of this kind, it has the virtue of allowing both the believer of simple heart and the most deeply initiated interpreter to make its words their own, while understanding them each in their own way. I translate it here, with only some slight abridgment.

“Peace be upon you, O representative of God and successor to your rightly guided fathers, the Mahdis. Peace be upon you, heir of the spiritual heirs (awsiya) of ages past […], Scion of the Immaculate Family, Treasury of prophetic knowledge, Threshold of God that none can reach without crossing it, Path of God that none can leave without going astray. You who behold the Tree of Tuba and the Lotus Tree at the furthest boundary […], God's Guarantor to those in heaven and those on earth: peace be upon you from those who recognize you as God has made you known to them, and who give you some of the titles you deserve, although you are beyond them.

“I bear witness that you are God's Guarantor to those who lived before and those yet to come; that those who triumph are your followers, and those who are deprived are those who reject you. You preserve all knowledge and open all that was sealed […]. O my lord! I have chosen you as my Imam and Guide, my protector and teacher, and I desire no one in your place.

“I bear witness that you are the unchanging truth, in which there is no alteration; that God's promise concerning you is certain.

“However long your concealment (ghaybat) may last, however far off the appointed hour, I have no doubt. I will not join those who, knowing nothing of you, wander astray and speak foolishly of you. I remain in expectation of your Day, for you are the Intercessor whose right none may dispute, the Friend whom none may disown […].

“I call God to witness! I call his angels to witness! I call upon you yourself to witness my vow: inwardly it is what it is outwardly; in the secret of my consciousness it is exactly what my tongue declares. Be witness, then, to my promise to you, to the covenant of loyalty between you and me […] as the Lord of the worlds commands me.

“Though time stretch on, though the years of my life follow one upon another, my certainty concerning you will only grow, my love for you only deepen, and my trust in you only increase. I shall await your coming all the more eagerly, and make myself ever readier for the struggle to be fought beside you. For my own self, my possessions, my family, all that my God has granted me in this world, I give to you to dispose of as you will, O my Imam!

“If my life lasts long enough for me to see your radiant Day arise and your banners shine, here I am, your faithful follower. May I be granted the supreme Witnessing at your side!

“But if death overtakes me before you have appeared, then I ask for your intercession, yours and that of your fathers, the Immaculate Imams, so that God may count me among those whom he will allow to return (raj'at) at the hour of your coming, when your Day dawns. May my devotion to you thus bring me to the fulfilment of my longing.”452

Whatever region of the Malakut may be the scene of the final struggle, whatever immaterial weapons may determine its outcome, this prayer expresses the spirit of all Iranian chivalry, from the heroes of the Zoroastrian epic to those of Shi'i Persia's mystical epic. Shi'i and Zoroastrian ideas alike become living realities in a fellowship of knights of faith. The Iranian spirit preserves and joins the ancient tradition of the pahlavan, the heroic champion, with the Abrahamic tradition of futuwwat, spiritual chivalry. The companions of the Saoshyant and the companions of the Hidden Imam alike are drawn toward the same final goal.

“May we be among those who bring about the Transfiguration of the world,” repeated a liturgical refrain of the Zoroastrian faithful. “May God hasten the joy of his coming,” says every faithful Shi'i whenever the Twelfth Imam's name is mentioned. The two brief invocations sound in unison. They bear witness to the ethic of the knight of faith, inseparable from a metaphysics of the last things: a fundamental note sounding again and again through all the complex themes of spiritual philosophy we have studied in this inquiry.

The mystic concerned with inward realities can read the pilgrim's prayer in the light of all that has been said here about the reciprocal relationship between knowledge of the Imam and knowledge of oneself. It becomes the prayer and vow of the “knight of the soul,” making a pilgrimage in quest of his own We. Not a word need be changed; the tone remains the same.

And perhaps this best gathers together what the philosopher has learned from the hospitality offered him in Iranian Islam. But there can be no spiritual hospitality without reciprocity: the guest who is welcomed must inwardly be a host who welcomes in turn. Without that reciprocity, there is no hope of understanding.

Eventually the man asks: “Of this or that molla and Mîr Dâmâd, who is the greater?” Mollâ Sadrâ answers without hesitation: Mîr, his teacher. Just then Mîr Dâmâd arrives at the madrasa, sees the two speaking, and approaches quietly, having thought he heard his name. He hears what follows. The merchant asks: “And between Abû 'Alî Sînâ (Avicenna) and Mîr Dâmâd, who, in your opinion, is the greater?” Once again Mollâ Sadrâ does not hesitate: Mîr. The visitor presses him: “And between the Magister secundus (Mo'allim thâni, that is, al-Fârâbî) and Mîr, who, in your opinion, is the greater?” This time Mollâ Sadrâ hesitates, when a voice suddenly comes from behind him: “Don't be afraid, Sadrâ! Go on, say it: Mîr is the greater!” (Qisas al-'Olamâ, p. 253). ↩

This monumental autograph has a “sister” manuscript (Majlis catalogue IV, 1471), which, despite its 795 folio leaves (1,590 pages), lacks its beginning. Mollâ Sadrâ's great Summa, the “Four Spiritual Journeys” (al-Hikmat al-mota'âliya fîl-asfâr al-'aqlîya al-arba'a), was lithographically printed in Tehran in 1282/1865, with glosses by Mollâ Hâdî Sabzavârî. Hosayn Tabâtabâ'î has recently begun a typeset edition; six volumes have appeared so far (Parts One, Two, and Three of the First Journey; Part One of the Third Journey; and Parts One and Two of the Fourth Journey, Qomm, 1378 lunar Hijri onward), though it is not yet a critical edition. Among works published for the four-hundredth anniversary of Mollâ Sadrâ's birth, we should particularly mention his Persian treatise Seh Asl (The Three Sources), together with his mathnawî and rubâ'îyât, edited with introduction and notes by Seyyed Hosseïn Nasr (Faculty of Theology, Tehran University), 1380 lunar Hijri/1961. By Sayyed Jalâloddîn Ashtiyânî: Sharh-e hâl o ârâ-ye falsafa-ye Mollâ Sadrâ (biography and philosophical doctrines of Mollâ Sadrâ), Mashhad, 1341 solar Hijri; Hastî, az nazar-e falsafa o 'irfân (Being, from the Perspectives of Philosophy and Mysticism), Mashhad, 1380 lunar Hijri; his editions of Mazâhir al-ilâhîya, Mashhad, 1380 lunar Hijri, and Shawâhid al-robûbîya, Mashhad, 1968; and the Anthologie announced above, p. 12, n. 6. By M.-T. Dânesh-Pajûh: the edition of Kasr asnâm al-jâhilîya (The Shattering of the Idols of Ignorance, directed against a certain kind of Sufism), Tehran, 1340 solar Hijri/1961. Ja'far Langarûdî's commentary on this work by Mollâ Sadrâ, Mashhad, 1964. We should recall our two studies: La Place de Mollâ Sadrâ Shîrâzî dans la philosophie iranienne, in Studia Islamica, fasc. XVIII, Paris, 1962, pp. 81–113; and Le Thème de la résurrection chez Mollâ Sadrâ Shîrâzî, commentateur de Sohrawardî, in Studies in Mysticism and Religion Presented to Gershom G. Scholem on His Seventieth Birthday, Jerusalem, 1967, pp. 71–116. The main substance of these two studies is incorporated here. In addition, at the École des Hautes-Études we devoted three years of lectures to the major work that most fully expresses Mollâ Sadrâ as a Shiite philosopher: his commentary on Kolaynî's Osûl mina'l-Kâfi. Finally, see the passages from Mollâ Sadrâ translated in our Terre céleste et corps de résurrection..., pp. 257–265. Mollâ Sadrâ's struggle continues the work of Haydar Âmolî. “Tradition” involves handing down the spiritual trust to its rightful heir, who alone can receive it—but only by undergoing a new birth. Ma'qul and manqûl (rational philosophy and theology grounded in transmitted authority) still belong to the outward domain, dependent upon a chain of purely human intermediaries. Only the esoteric sciences ('olûm al-bâtin) are passed on through spiritual inheritance ('olûm irthîya), and this transmission does not happen simply “in the course of history.” It depends on an unveiling or direct insight (kashf) whose source lies in another dimension: the Malakût, the spiritual world. That is what Mollâ Sadrâ's opponents cannot understand. ↩

Momkin al-wojûd does not mean possibility in general—something merely conceivable, feasible, or capable of coming about—but a possible being that has actually come into existence without owing that realization to itself. But it owes that necessity to its principle. To avoid confusion, therefore, we prefer the translation “a being not necessary through itself.” ↩

  196. Commentary on § 5. We should recall here what Suhrawardi means by 'ilm hozûrî (hodûrî): knowledge that arises not through a form representing its object, but as direct insight, effective presence—“knowledge by presence.” The human being is not in time, still less a person “of his time.” Time is the measure or quantity of his very being. In the subtle state of the Malakût, that measure stretches out across pasts and futures, arranged together in the simultaneity of a spatial order that dense, material time (kathîf) can perceive only as succession. When time folds inward, an absolute presence arises—that is, a presence free from the conditions of dense time. Events of this world are no longer seen in their material, sensory condition, as successive happenings in dense time, but in their malakûtî condition, established in their proper places within the space of the Malakût. ↩

  218. As for the traditional precursors of the Shaykhi school, future research should note the Shiite figures whom Khwânsârî lists (ibid.) as “links in the chain of transmission,” stretching back to the holy Imams, of akhbâr (traditions) with a particularly “gnostic” character. First are three close companions of the Fifth and Sixth Imams (Mohammad Bâqir, d. 115/733, and Ja'far Sâdiq, d. 148/765): Mofazzal b. 'Omar al-Jo'fî, Jâbir al-Ansârî, and Jâbir al-Jo'fî (the importance of their riwâyât, or transmitted accounts, in Ismaili theosophy is well known). Next is Shadhân ibn al-Khalîl Neyshâpûrî, an associate of the Ninth Imam, Mohammad Jawâd (d. 220/835; Mâmâqânî, Tanqîh al-Maqâl, 5470); Abû Ja'far Moh. Saffâr Qommî (d. 290/903), who knew the Eleventh Imam, Hasan 'Askarî (d. 260/874), and his son, who became the Hidden Imam; Saffâr wrote the Basâ'ir al-darajât (Rayhânat al-adab, II, p. 483, no. 873). Then Farât b. Ibrâhîm al-Kûfî (Mâmâqânî, 9412), one of Ibn Bâbûyeh's sources and author of one of the earliest Shiite tafsîrs (alongside which we may place the tafsîr attributed to the Eleventh Imam); 'Alî b. Ibrâhîm ibn Mâhûyeh Qazwînî (ibid., 8202); Shaykh Sâdûq Ibn Bâbûyeh of Qomm (d. 381/991), one of the foremost Shiite theologians of his generation and author of some three hundred works, particularly the Kitâb al-Majâlis (Rayhânat, II, p. 470, no. 855); Sayyed Razî (d. 406/1015), particularly his Kitâb al-A'imma (ibid., II, p. 259, no. 539); Qotboddîn Sa'îd Râwendî (d. 573/1177–1178), buried in Qomm at the shrine of Hazrat Fâtima, younger sister of the Eighth Imam (ibid., p. 305, no. 477); Yahyâ ibn Batrîq (d. 600/1284, as given in the source), especially his Khasâ'is (a comprehensive work on the First Imam) and 'Omdat (ibid., V, p. 270, no. 532); Sayyed Razîoddîn 'Alî b. Tâ'ûs (d. 664/1265–1266; ibid., VI, p. 60, no. 67); 'Alî ibn 'Isâ Arbelî (d. 696/1296–1297), author of Kashf al-Ghamma (ibid., I, p. 56, no. 121); and finally Mollâ Rajab Borsî (d. ca. 800/1397), best known for Mashâriq al-Anwâr, written around 774/1372. Under Shâh Solaymân, that work received a monumental Persian commentary, Matâli' al-asrâr, by Hasan Khatîb Qârî Mashhadî, comprising 503 folio leaves (see Annuaire de la Section des Sciences religieuses, 1968–1969, pp. 148 ff.). Rajab Borsî is often quoted by Shaykh Ahmad Ahsâ'î (ibid., II, p. 259, no. 539). This list is far from complete. It needs to be developed both to write a full history of Shiite theology and to locate the Shaykhi school within it. ↩

  220. We mention A. L. M. Nicolas's Essai sur le cheïkhisme, Paris, 1910, only for the record. It is no longer genuinely usable: the entire work rests solely on the polemical account of an opponent of Shaykhism who understood very little of it, and its technical vocabulary is highly unreliable. E. G. Browne gave a short account of Shaykhism in his Traveller's Narrative, II, pp. 243–244. We need not discuss Babism or Bahaism in their own right here, because, as we shall note below, both movements placed themselves ipso facto outside Shiism. When Baha'is express admiration for Shaykh Ahmad Ahsâ'î, one can only agree. But when they claim him as their spiritual ancestor, that unwarranted claim must be rejected. There are, we might say, two ways of “leaving” a school. One may flow from it as a stream flows from a spring. Or one may leave it as someone leaves a room, slamming the door—that is, in a way that makes it difficult to claim descent from those who remained inside. ↩

  226. Consider the episode reported by the author of Tanbîh al-ghâfilîn, from a manuscript in Mîrzâ Ismâ'îl Tabrîzî's own hand. In Basra the shaykh met a man renowned both for his moral character and his learning. He asked him for lessons in hikmat (philosophical wisdom), but the man excused himself because of pressing administrative duties. The shaykh then asked him to name what he regarded as the foundation of a philosophical teaching. He replied: “Do not stop at movements; seek what sets movements in motion. Do not stop at causes; seek what gives causes their causality. Living beings move toward God along the longitudinal (or vertical) dimension; minerals (inert things) move toward God along the latitudinal (or horizontal) dimension.” (Silsilat al-tûl and silsilat al-'arz are characteristic terms of Suhrawardi's “Eastern theosophy.”) “You will then see the mountains you thought immovable begin to move as clouds move” (Quran 27:90). “On hearing these words from this perfected man,” the shaykh added, “many difficulties that had remained in my mind concerning philosophical questions were resolved. I asked him for guidance on the Itinerarium ad Deum, the journey toward God. ‘How, in your view,’ I asked, ‘is it possible to reach God?’ ‘Cast this world far from you,’ he replied. I left his majlis (gathering), and in my heart there remained no trace of love for this world” (p. 183). ↩

  227. For six of these ijâzât, see the list of shaykhs on pp. 188–189 of the same work. They include ijâzât-e rawâyat (licenses certifying the right to transmit texts or traditions) and ijâzât-e dirâyat (licenses attesting the ability to teach and interpret on one's own authority). An ijâzat is a “license” a shaykh gives to a disciple who has studied with him for several years, covering books they have studied together. It is therefore an essentially personal certificate. This gives it its special significance: such licenses authenticate spiritual lines of descent. For this reason we shall take account of the ijâzât of each of the Mashâyekh (Shaykhi masters). ↩

  235. Over the centuries, Shiites had filled the Baqî' cemetery with rich and pious monuments—domes, chapels, and shrines. When the Wahhabis established their rule in Arabia after entering Mecca (1924), the entire complex was demolished in the name of religious puritanism and reduced to ruins. During a pilgrimage to Mecca in 1956, the Iranian sovereign, accompanied by his entire entourage, made a lengthy visit to the Baqî' and paused before the sites of the tombs revered by Shiites. Restoration was then promised wherever possible. The event caused a particular stir because an Iranian sovereign had not visited these places for a considerable time; Iranian periodicals published many illustrations of the occasion. ↩

Where Khwânsârî says of these misguided disciples that “all they did was practice ta'wîl”—that is, give esoteric interpretations of the lessons they heard from Shaykh Ahmad and Sayyed Kâzem—this was translated: “The shaykh's disciples were the organ (instrument, means) of ta'wîl (!).” ↩

  237. Compare this declaration of our author's Imamite faith: “Fully acknowledging Muhammad's prophetic message entails love and devotion to the Imams of his house and to their teaching. If this is Islam and professing Shiism (tashayyo'), so be it. If it is called error or falling short, so be it. If it is called excessive exaltation (gholow), so be it. Let all those who behave as Sunni theologians and refuse to acknowledge the eternal, inalienable preeminence of the holy Imams call us extremists (gholât) if they wish. If extremism means placing the Imams below the rank of divinity but above all creatures, as close to God as possible, we acknowledge that this is, God willing, our only title to glory” (p. 40). These words point directly to the metaphysical level of the doctrine of the Imams. ↩

  347. We give here the translation of this passage (Majlisî, pp. 146–147): “I said: ‘My lord, I find that some of the verses have no connection either with what comes before or with what follows them. My limited understanding cannot penetrate the reason.’ ‘Indeed,’ the Sayyed replied, ‘things are as you observe. The reason is this. When the prince of humankind (the Prophet), Mohammad ibn 'Abdillah, passed from this perishable dwelling to the everlasting Dwelling, and the two men of the Quraysh (the first two Sunni caliphs, Abû Bakr and 'Omar) did what they did, seizing the outward and public caliphate by force, the Commander of the Faithful (the First Imam) gathered the whole Quran into a leather covering and brought it to them while the Quraysh were assembled in the mosque. He said: “This is the Book of God which the Messenger of God commanded me to present to you, so that, on the Day of Resurrection, a witness may rise before God to testify against you.” But the Pharaoh and Nimrod of this community (that is, Caliph 'Omar ibn al-Khattâb) answered: “We have no need of your Quran.” The Imam replied: “The Messenger of God, my dearest friend, foretold that you would give me this answer. Yet I wished, by doing this, to bring forth testimony against you.” And the Commander of the Faithful returned to his home, saying: “There is no God but You, You alone. You have no partner. No one can overturn what has always been within Your knowledge, or oppose what Your wisdom requires. So be Yourself the Witness who will testify on my behalf against them on the Day of Resurrection.” Then Ibn Abî Qahâfa summoned the Muslims and said to them: “Whoever has in his possession a verse or a sura of the Quran, let him bring it here.” Then came Abû 'Obaydallah, 'Othmân, Mo'awiya, and others [...]. Each brought a verse or a sura, and from these they assembled the Quran we now have. But they left out everything that would have proved the wrongs they had committed since the Prophet's death. This is why the verses are not connected with one another. As for the Quran which the Commander of the Faithful compiled in his own handwriting, that is preserved with the Sâhib al-Amr (the Hidden Imam). It contains everything, absolutely everything. Nevertheless, concerning the Quran in our hands, there must be no doubt of its validity, nor of its being truly the Word of God. What I have just said I transmit exactly as it came from the Imam.’” ↩

We sent down Iron; in it is formidable strength, but also benefit for humankind.” Shiite gnosis has meditated at length on this verse, seeing in it a reference to the Imam's sword and his place in fotowwat, or spiritual chivalry. It notes that the verse says anzalnâ (“We sent it down”), not kholiqa (“it was created”). The reference, therefore, is not to iron as a metal of this world, but to a source—or symbol—of invincible strength that does not belong to earthly creation and descends from Heaven through the ministry of the angels. As an attribute of the Imamate, this sword illuminates its nature. See the introduction to Haydar Âmolî's commentary on Ibn 'Arabî's Fosûs, Jarullah 1470, fol. 42b (edition in preparation). ↩

  353. Here are the details of the episode. The mysterious horseman says to 'Alî ibn Fâzel: “Spend the night with the people who live there. Tell them what religion you were born into. You need not observe taqîyeh (the ‘discipline of secrecy’) with them, for they are all, like the inhabitants of several villages south of Damascus, believers of utterly sincere heart, serving God according to the religion of 'Alî ibn Abî-Tâleb and the Immaculate Imams of his line. Did not everything happen exactly so, O Ibn Fâzel?” “I said: ‘Indeed it did! I went to the people of that village. I spent the night with them, and they showed me every courtesy. I asked them about their religion. They answered, without the slightest taqîyeh toward me: “We follow the religion of the Commander of the Faithful, heir of the Messenger of the Lord of the worlds, and of the Immaculate Imams descended from him.” I asked them: “How did this religion reach you? Who brought it to you?” They replied: “Abû Dharr al-Ghaffârî (one of the Prophet's companions), when 'Othmân (the third Sunni caliph) exiled him from Medina to Syria, and then Mo'awiya exiled him from Damascus to this country of ours. His spiritual influence extends to us all.” When morning came, I asked them to help me rejoin my caravan, and I in turn told them my religion. They provided two men who guided me back to my caravan.’” ↩

  364. Let us recall the essential point about this word, used frequently throughout the present work. Imaginal (Latin imaginalis) derives from imago, like other words formed in the same way (compare derivatives of origo: originarius, originalis, etc.). Latin distinguishes imaginare, to present an image as a mirror presents it (the function expressed by Arabic mazharîya, and above all the nature of the 'âlam al-Mithâl, mundus imaginalis), from the deponent verb imaginari, to imagine or picture something to oneself. ↩

  365. See our Avicenne et le Récit visionnaire, vol. I, pp. 18, 27, 31. We must distinguish the fact of exitus (departure) from spiritual death. If exitus is to be a real “departure” from this world, spiritual resurrection must have preceded it. Otherwise, those who are spiritually dead—that is, dead in the true sense—will never “leave” this world. Their exitus is only entry into the “second death,” for only those who are truly “alive” depart from this world. This teaching appears both in the Gospel of Philip and in an Ismaili treatise by Nasîroddîn Tûsî. Indeed, the entire spiritual education of Ismaili gnosis is founded on the “resurrection of the dead” (see Kitâb al-'âlim wa'l-gholâm, Annuaire, 1970–1971, pp. 226 ff.). Shaykh Ahmad Ahsâ'î also teaches extensively on the subject in his commentary on the Ziyârat al-Jâmi'a. ↩

  383. See the letter sent by the Friend of God to the commander of the house on the Green Island. In it he reminds the commander of the extraordinary bond between himself and Rulman: they had the same inward visions at the same time and experienced the same bodily pains at the same hour. He explains that this house, placed under the care of the Knights of St John four years after its foundation, was genuinely the work of the Spirit, not an arbitrary human initiative. “Now you must know, dear friend, that Rulman and I both had, on the same night of St Denis, the same vision in a dream. We dreamt that we should help one another and should plan to build a cloister (Kloster) in Strasbourg. After this dream, I came down to Rulman within ten days and immediately asked him whether he had recently dreamt anything strange. He answered yes, and told me that down here in Strasbourg he had had the very same dream that I had had up above (in the Highlands).” The Friend of God then explains how both men came to conclude that “the time for building new cloisters had passed,” before continuing: “Then, the following Christmas night, at midnight on that holy night of Christ, we both—he below and I above—felt at the same time, in our nature (that is, in our bodies), such pain and suffering that we each imagined ourselves at the point of death. And in this suffering we received a revelation, so clear that it could only be believed, that we must found a cloister in Strasbourg. Thus the Green Island came into being” (ibid., p. 53). ↩

  384. Ibid., pp. 53–55. Hélyot's Dictionnaire des Ordres religieux ou Histoire des Ordres monastiques, religieux et militaires, vol. II (Migne, Encyclopédie théologique, vol. XXI), Paris, 1848, cols. 855 ff., gives an entirely outward, historical account of the Green Island. He knows Rulman Merswin's role well but does not mention the Friend of God. After completely restoring the Green Island, Rulman Merswin “gave it to the Order of St John of Jerusalem on condition that the chaplain brothers of that Order would celebrate the divine office there in perpetuity. This donation was accepted by Conrad de Brunsberg, Grand Prior of Germany, and later confirmed by Grand Master Raymond Bérenger and the general chapter.” Raymond Bérenger, from the Dauphiné, was the Order's thirty-second Grand Master (d. 1373). ↩

  385. Ibid., p. 55. Letters and short works written respectively by the Friend of God and Rulman Merswin were carefully collected and copied by the brothers of St John into magnificent manuscripts. Treasured within the Order as sacred relics, these are the source of what we know about the Friend of God. In brief, the collection comprises (1) the “Great German Memorial” (Das grosse deutsche Memorial), of which a Latin translation was made but has not survived; (2) the “Master's Book” (Das Meisterbuch), a collection of illustrated documents owned by Grand Prior Conrad von Brunsberg but now lost; and (3) the “Book of Letters” (Das Briefbuch). See W. Rath's description of the surviving Strasbourg manuscripts, op. cit., pp. 119–127. Nearly all this material has been published and, to some extent, translated, but unfortunately it is scattered through unrelated books that are now unobtainable. There is an urgent need to bring it together in one corpus, with the original texts and full translations. Several scholars have attempted to pierce the Friend of God's “anonymity,” identifying him, for example, with Nicholas of Basel. We believe these attempts to identify the historical individual have taken the wrong path; in any case, they fall outside our present concern. ↩

Nor do we need to consider here the later history of the Sovereign Order of St John of Jerusalem: the failure, if not betrayal, of Grand Master Ferdinand von Hompesch, who handed Malta over to Bonaparte; the knights' election of Tsar Paul I as Grand Master, by which the Order became ipso facto an “ecumenical religion”; or the papal order known as the “Order of Malta,” which was in fact newly created by a motu proprio of Pope Pius VII in 1803. ↩

  392. See Ernst Benz, “Der Montserrat in der europäischen Geschichte,” in Zeitschrift für Religions- und Geistesgeschichte, XVIII, 1966, no. 1, pp. 15 ff. (Montserrat with its twelve hermitages!). The connection between Montserrat and classical Weimar began when Wilhelm von Humboldt described his ascent of that mountain as a completion of the Stimmung, the mood or emotional atmosphere to which Goethe had given form in his poem Die Geheimnisse. Goethe later forgot that he had learned of Montserrat only some twenty years after composing the unfinished poem, and then through Humboldt's description. Hence his reply to the Göttingen students who questioned him about the poem in 1816: Goethe retrospectively felt that he had already seen the description of Montserrat at the time. That impression was doubtless mistaken chronologically, but it had a deeper truth—the same truth that allows us to recognize the same mystical mountain in Montserrat, Montsalvat, and Montségur. For the ubi (the “where”) of Mount Qâf is an ubique (“everywhere”), and that “everywhere” is the place where the Hidden Imam manifests himself. (We intentionally retain the etymological two-word spelling in our text.) ↩

The angels visit him, then return to heaven and announce to the others: there is someone “clothed in wool” (sâfî) who devotes himself to divine service on earth! Thus, from the time of the prophet Seth, the name “those clothed in wool” is given to the group called “Sufis.” This tale illustrates the most common explanation of the word Sufi. Arguments

Argument des livres I et II

Le monde islamique n'est pas un monolithe; son concept religieux ne s'identifie pas avec le concept politique du monde arabe. Il y a un Islam iranien, comme il y a un Islam turc, indien, indonésien, malais, etc.

Malheureusement, si une littérature abondante est à la disposition du lecteur curieux de connaître l'archéologie et les arts de l'Iran, avant et depuis l'Islam, peu de livres, en revanche, répondent à la question du chercheur qui s'interroge sur les « motivations » de la conscience iranienne ayant configuré ces formes.

A l'intérieur de la communauté islamique, le monde iranien a formé dès l'origine un ensemble dont les traits caractéristiques et la vocation ne s'élucident que si l'on considère l'univers spirituel iranien comme formant un tout, avant et depuis l'Islam. L'Iran islamique a été par excellence la patrie des plus grands philosophes et mystiques de l'Islam; pour eux, la pensée spéculative ne s'isole jamais de sa fructification et de ses conséquences pratiques, non point simplement quant à ce que nous appelons aujourd'hui le milieu social, mais quant à la totalité concrète que l'homme nourrit de sa propre substance, par-delà les limites de cette vie, et qui est son monde spirituel.

C'est en restant fidèle à cette prise de position que l'auteur a édifié le monument qu'il présente ici en sept livres, et qui est le résultat de plus de vingt ans de recherches, menées en Iran même, dans les bibliothèques comme dans l'intimité de ses amis iraniens, conjuguées avec l'expérience d'un enseignement donné à Paris et à Téhéran. Sa méthode se veut essentiellement phénoménologique, sans se rattacher à une école phénoménologique déterminée. Il s'agit pour lui de rencontrer le fait religieux en laissant se montrer l'objet religieux tel qu'il se montre à ceux à qui il se montre. D'où le sous-titre essentiel donné à l'ouvrage : aspects spirituels et philosophiques. Qui dit aspect suppose spectateur, mais ici le spectateur, qui est le phénoménologue, doit devenir l'hôte spirituel de ceux à qui se montre cet objet et en assumer avec eux la charge. Toute considération historique restera donc immanente à cet objet, sans lui imposer du dehors quelque catégorie étrangère, considération dialectique ou autre. C'est à cette condition que sont possibles, synchroniquement, les recroisements suggérés par l'auteur en maints passages, parce qu'il s'agit des variations d'un même objet.

Les deux premiers tomes contiennent les livres I et II de l'ouvrage.

Le livre Ier s'applique à montrer quelques aspects essentiels du shî'isme duodécimain ou imâmisme, fortement implanté dès les origines en Iran, et devenu depuis le XVIe siècle religion officielle. Ces aspects sont dégagés et analysés à partir de ce que l'auteur a déjà proposé d'appeler le « phénomène du Livre révélé », tel qu'il se montre à ceux que le Qorân désigne comme Ahl al-Kitâb, cette « communauté du Livre » qui englobe judaïsme, christianisme et Islam. Dans chacun des rameaux de la tradition abrahamique, interprètes de la Bible et du Qorân se sont trouvés placés devant les mêmes problèmes et les mêmes tâches : pour tous il s'est agi de savoir quel est le sens vrai du Livre. De part et d'autre, la recherche du sens vrai, qui est le sens spirituel caché sous l'apparence littérale, a développé des méthodes semblables pour faire apparaître le sens ésotérique, c'est-à-dire intérieur, de la Révélation divine. Le « phénomène du Livre » est à l'origine de l'herméneutique, c'est-à-dire du « Comprendre ». Il est probable que les herméneutes ésotéristes de la Bible et du Qorân ont encore beaucoup à apprendre aux philosophes qui de nos jours se montrent si préoccupés, précisément, d'herméneutique.

Le terme technique désignant l'herméneutique ésotérique du Qorân est le mot ta'wîl, lequel signifie « reconduire » une chose à son origine, à son archétype. La métaphysique shî'ite est dominée par l'idée du Dieu inconnaissable, inaccessible, innommable en son Essence, et par l'idée de son épiphanie dans le plérôme des Quatorze entités de lumière, manifestées sur terre en la personne des « Quatorze Immaculés » (le Prophète, sa fille Fâtima, les Douze Imâms). Le sens ésotérique que le ta'wîl shî'ite dégage des données qorâniques littérales, concerne principalement ce plérôme des Quatorze. Il illustre, par le fait même, le concept proprement shî'ite de la prophétologie, duquel il résulte que le shî'isme refuse d'avoir son avenir derrière soi.

A la différence de l'Islam sunnite majoritaire, pour lequel, après la mission du dernier Prophète, l'humanité n'a plus rien de nouveau à attendre, le shî'isme maintient ouvert l'avenir en professant que, même après la venue du « Sceau des prophètes », quelque chose est encore à attendre, à savoir la révélation du sens spirituel des révélations apportées par les grands prophètes. Telle fut la tâche herméneutique dont ont été investis les saints Imâms, et leur enseignement remplit des volumes. Mais cette intelligence spirituelle ne sera complète qu'à la fin de notre Aïôn, lors de la parousie du Douzième Imâm, l'Imâm présentement caché et pôle mystique de ce monde.

L'herméneutique comporte ainsi une perception propre de la temporalité, laquelle s'exprime dans une périodisation de l'histoire : au temps de la mission des prophètes, succède le temps de l'initiation spirituelle.
